units.la: ECcas tibi denuò, Amice Lector, animadversiones, ut jam antea monui, absq; omni studio partium, ruri exaratas, ut exipsostylo vel primo senties intuitu, in Libros Novi Testamenti, quâ potui curâ à mendis repurgatas, & in gratiam tuam quàm licuit breviter contractas. Multa
units.tr: Here, friendly reader, I present to you once more my remarks, written in the country, as I said before, free of all partisan zeal; as you will perceive at first sight, I have cleared them of errors in the New Testament books with all the care I could, and have condensed them as briefly as possible for your benefit. Quod si quis arguat à sensu recentiorum vel veterum Interpretum recessisse (ut jam priùs dictum) non est quod reponam, imò si id non fecissem,
units.tr: For I have deliberately omitted from this edition the lesser points, or those which were not so necessary for the Sacred Book (which was chiefly my wish), that is, the solecisms which interpreters commonly charge against the sacred writers, both in exposition and in translation, so that I might spare you useless weariness. If anyone objects that I have departed from the sense of the more recent or the older interpreters (as I said before), I have no reply to make; indeed, if I had not done so,

units.la: cissem, omnino uon scripsissem. Rursus vero dico, me vehementer utrisque suam debere reverentiam, sed nec meam nec alterius fidem velim mancipari. Si quid profecerim in voto, mercedem habeo, sin minus, operam non totus perdidi, in magno conatu voluisse sat est. Tu interim qui has chartulas perlegeris, pro candore tuo, si quid erratum sit, ignosces. Vale.
units.tr: I would certainly not have written it otherwise. Again I say that I owe each of them (the Vulgate and the older interpreters) their due respect, but I would not wish my own trustworthiness or anyone else's to be made a slave of. If I have achieved anything in my purpose, I have my reward; if not, I have not wholly wasted my labour, since it is enough to have wished for it in a great undertaking. Meanwhile you who read through these little pages will, in your kindness, pardon whatever error there may be. Farewell.

units.la: In Matthæum.
units.tr: On Matthew

units.la: MATTH. c. 1. v. 19. δίκαιος ὢν, i. e. ‎צדיק חסר‎, vir misericordiæ, ut apud LXX, Is. 57. 1. Et sic vocem ‎חסד‎, quæ affectum pietatis & misericordiam χυρίου significat, LXX sæpius vertunt δικαιοσύνη. Ut Gen. 19. 19. ἐμεγάλυνας τὸ ἔλεός σου (ꝓ, Es magnificasti) ‎חסד‎ misericordiam tuam 20. 13. Ταύτην τὴν δικαιοσύνην ποιήσεις εἰς ἐμέ, ‎זה חסדך‎ Hanc misericordiam tuam facies mecum. Exod. 15. 13. ᾿Οδήγησας τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ σου: Dux fuisti in misericordia tua populo tuo quem redemisti, & alibi. Quod si Evangelista voluisset Josephum esse justum vulgati sensu, eo ipso nomine oportuisset eum Mariam ἀγαθὴν ἐπὶ ... Exemplum statuere. Clam vero dimisit illam, quod plane arguit eo facto misericordem magis quam familiari sensu justum. Hinc Chrysostomus, δίκαιος ὢν ὁ τῆς ἐπιεικείας ... i. e. mitis & benignus: & Theophylactus, ἐκ ἐβούλετο ἀπλῶς εἶναι, ἀλλ' ἐπιλαρβανόμενος ἀπὸ πολλῆς χρηστότητος: Nolebat crudelis esse, sed ex multa benignitate misericordia eam prosequi atur, ut Interpres.
units.tr: MATT. ch. 1, v. 19. "Being just" [δίκαιος ὢν], that is, [צדיק חסר], a man of mercy, as in the Septuagint at Isa. 57. 1. In the same way the Seventy often translate the word [חסד], which denotes the affection of piety and the mercy of the LORD, as "righteousness" [δικαιοσύνη]. For example, Gen. 19. 19: "you have magnified your mercy" [ἐμεγάλυνας τὸ ἔλεός σου] (the Vulgate: "you have magnified" [magnificasti]), where the Hebrew is [חסד], "your mercy." Gen. 20. 13: "This kindness you shall show to me" [Ταύτην τὴν δικαιοσύνην ποιήσεις εἰς ἐμέ], where the Hebrew is [זה חסדך], "this your mercy, you shall show to me." Exod. 15. 13: "You led in your righteousness" [Ὠδήγησας τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ σου]: "You in your mercy have been a guide to your people whom you have redeemed," and elsewhere. If the Evangelist had meant that Joseph was just in the ordinary sense, he would by that very name have been obliged to set Mary forth as an example of the opposite. Yet he secretly dismissed her, which plainly shows that by the act he is described as merciful rather than just in the ordinary sense. Hence Chrysostom: "being just, that is, of gentleness" [δίκαιος ὢν ὁ τῆς ἐπιεικείας], that is, mild and kind; and Theophylact: "he did not wish to be merely [harsh], but, taking hold of her out of great kindness," that is, he did not wish to be cruel, but out of much kindness he chose to deal with her mercifully, as the Interpreter renders it.

units.la: C. 2. v. 6. Οὐδαμῶς ἐλαχίστη. Locus iste pugnat ex diametro cum Mich. 5. 2. Et tu Bethlehem non es minima, & tu Bethleem es parvula ut sis inter Principes Judæ. Quoad vero sensum consentiunt universi utrumque idem velle. Magis vero explicitus locus iste ut aiunt in Matthæo, quem ipsum sum restituisse à quibusdam creditur: At verò verba ista Matthæi non sunt, ab illo tantùm historicè recitantur; verba sunt Sacerdotum & Scribarum, qui percontanti responderunt Herodi, In Bethleem Judæ, sic enim scriptum est per Prophetam, Et tu Bethleem non es minima &c. Atque eos ita respondisse vel secundum lectionem tunc temporis vulgatam Græcorum codicum, vel secundum vulgò receptum sensum, non est cur quis dubitet. At quid si forte neutra lectio sit ipsa vera? Est enim certè possibile, aliquod vitium irrepsisse in codice Hebræo, legendo forte [Hebrew] pro [Hebrew], vel incuriâ vel errore aliquo apographi à primis etiam temporibus, quem bonâ fide sequebantur posteri, cùm fit adeò pronum errare in literis Hebraïs ob similitudinem characterum, sicut in aliis locis erratum esse, sine controversiâ palam est. Atque error iste in hoc loco proclivis admodum ob similitudinem literarum ד & ר, ו & ז. Neque verò hoc omnino novum, in eâdem enim ipsâ voce erraverunt LXX, Gen. 49. 22. legentes [Hebrew], & vertendo veά- τες, adolescentior, pro [Hebrew], progrediebatur super murum, ob literarum ד & ר similitudinem, & æquè facilis est error inter ד & ו, qui etiam occurrit in singulis. Ezek. 34. 16. Ubi Græci pro [Hebrew], perdam, habent [Greek] φυλάξω, custodiam, vel servabo, legendo ר pro ד, & ו pro ז.
units.tr: Ch. 2, v. 6. "By no means least" [Οὐδαμῶς ἐλαχίστη]. This passage flatly contradicts Mic. 5. 2: "And you, Bethlehem, are not least, and you, Bethlehem, are little, so that you may be among the princes of Judah." As to the sense, however, all agree that both say the same thing. The passage in Matthew, as they say, is more explicit, and it is thought by some to have been restored from Matthew himself. But these words are not Matthew's; he only recounts them historically. They are the words of the priests and scribes, who answered Herod when he asked, "In Bethlehem of Judah, for so it is written by the Prophet: And you, Bethlehem, are not least," and so on. That they answered in this way, either according to the reading of the Greek manuscripts commonly used at that time or according to the generally received sense, there is no reason for anyone to doubt. But what if perhaps neither reading is the true one? It is certainly possible that some fault crept into the Hebrew codex, by reading perhaps [Hebrew] for [Hebrew], through carelessness or some error in a copy from the earliest times, which later generations followed in good faith. It is so easy to err in Hebrew letters because of the similarity of the characters, as it is plainly beyond dispute that error has occurred in other places. And this error is very likely in this passage because of the similarity of the letters ד and ר, and ו and ז. Nor is this at all new, for the Seventy erred in this very word at Gen. 49. 22, reading [Hebrew] and translating it "younger" [νεάτες] instead of [Hebrew], "progressed over the wall," because of the similarity of ד and ר. An error between ד and ו is equally easy, and it occurs in individual cases at Ezek. 34. 16, where the Greeks, for [Hebrew], "I will destroy," have [φυλάξω], "I will keep" or "I will preserve," reading ר for ד and ו for ז.

units.la: Atque hoc errore concesso in hoc ipso Michææ loco, legendo è contrario ו pro ז, & ר pro ד i.e. [Hebrew], pro [Hebrew], optimo sensu vertitur [Hebrew], Et tu Bethleem Ephrata progredere, sive cum pompa progredere, secundum vim Hebraam, ut sis inter Chiliadas Judæ, ex te enim egredietur, qui erit dominator in Israel.
units.tr: Granting this error, and in this very passage of Micah, reading conversely ו for ז and ר for ד, that is, [Hebrew] for [Hebrew], it is rendered in the best sense: [Hebrew], "And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, go forth," or "go forth with pomp," according to the force of the Hebrew, so that you may be among the thousands of Judah, "for out of you shall come forth one who will be ruler in Israel."

units.la: V. 10. Ἰδόντες δὲ τὸν ἀστέρα, subaudi ἐχάρησαν vel ἐθεώρησαν. Dicitur enim versu præeunte, & ecce stella stella quam viderant in oriente praibat eis, usque dum veniit & stetit supra ubi erat puer. Cum igitur viderent stellam subsistentem, vel ubi stetit (non poterant enim non videre stellam antea, quam sequebantur ducem) gavisi sunt gaudio magno.
units.tr: v. 10. "But when they saw the star" [Ἰδόντες δὲ τὸν ἀστέρα]; supply "they rejoiced" [ἐχάρησαν] or "they beheld" [ἐθεώρησαν]. For it is said in the preceding verse: "And behold, the star which they had seen in the east went before them, until it came and stood over where the child was. When therefore they saw the star standing still, or where it stood (for they could not but have seen the star before, since they followed it as their guide), they rejoiced with exceeding great joy."

units.la: V. 16. Ἀπὸ διετοῦς καὶ κατωτέρω, A bimatu & infra, ut vetus; à bimulo & infra, ut alii; utrum vero vis legatur, haud multum refert, vel substantivè vel adjectivè, dummodo idem omnes intelligant, ἀπὸ διετίας καὶ πλέον διετίας, à biennio expleto, ut dicitur Act. 24. 17. Quod ego nullo modo huic loco convenire sentio; verba vero reddenda & intelligenda secundum morem loquendi & apud Græcos & Latinos, atque ipsam rationem & mentem loci, in hunc modum. Tum Herodes videns quod illusus esset à Magis, iratus esset valdè, & mittens occidit omnes pueros qui erant in Bethleem & in finibus ejus, à bimulo & infra, nempe incipiendo à bimulis exclusivè, & descendendo ad eos qui infra bimatum erant, (& non ut est in Anglico, (From two years old and under.)) interpretando διετεῖς, ἀπὸ διετίας ἀρχομένης, & non πλεονδιετίους, à bimatu incipiente & non expleto. Quasi diceret, omnes unius anni pueros & infrà, secundùm tempus quod exquisierat à Magis. Ab anno enim integro & supra puer incipit vocari ab Hebræis בן שנתים, filius duorum annorum, i.e. secundi anni, apud Græcos διετῆς, apud Latinos bimus; sic בן שנתים LXX rectè, opinor, vertunt διετῆς ἔτος, secundo anno post diluvium, Gen. 11. 10. Sic Noah dicitur Gen. 7. 6, & 11, בן שש מאות שנה, sexcentorum annorum filius בשנת שש מאות, in sexcentesimo anno vitæ suæ. Sic sensit Hesychius, διετῆς, ὁ ἓνα τῶν ἐτῶν, post annum integrum, quasi tum. tnm demum inciperet puer esse vel vocari διετής, διὰ posito pro ὡς, quod fieri solet cùm de interjecto tempore dicitur, ut δι' ἡμερῶν, post dies aliquot. Mar. 2.1. Δι' ἐτῶν τ πλειόνων, post plures annos. Act. 24.17. Et δι' ἐτῶν ᾱδον τετραχοσίων, post annos fere quadraginta, Plut. Sic etiam Aristoteles lib. 9. c. 5. de Hist. Animal. cujus verba de cervo sunt hujusmodi: φύσει ἡ διετὴς τὰ μὲν τὰ κέρατα, bimi primùm generant cornua. At verò nihil certius quàm quòd cervi incipiant generare cornua simul ac primum excesserint ætatis annum, & secundum intraverint. Et ut hoc demonstretur planius, qui apud nos vocatur, The Calf of a red Leer, toto primi ætatis anni spatio apud eum vocatur ἐνιαύσιος, ut etiam in Scriptura vocatur agnus Hebraicè שנה apud Græcos ἐνιαύσιος, apud Latinos, anniculus, in bibliis Anglicis, a Lamb of the first year. Et qui apud nos secundo ætatis anno vocatur, a Brocket, apud eum dicitur παταλία, sive διετής, apud Latinos, Jubulo vel bimus, in initio cujus anni cornua generat, in fine abjicit. Τῷ τρίτῳ ἔτει, ut idem dicit, i.e. ac primùm ingrediuntur tertium ætatis annum, διχαν φύσει, bifida generant, & vocantur tertio ætatis anno apud Latinos, trimi, Anglicè Spayds. Ubi liceat obiter observare, διετὴς & τῷ τρίτῳ ἔτει, unam eandemque esse phrasim apud Aristotelem, adeò ut æque dixisse poterit, τῷ δευτέρῳ ἔτει ac διετὴς, & τριετὴς æquè ac τῷ τρίτῳ ἔτει. Unde liquet, ἀπὸ διετὴς accipi posse vel à bimatu incipiente vel definente, à tempore quo puer incipit esse duorum annorum filius, vel a tempore quo esse definit, est enim ἀπὸ alterutri exclusiva vel initio vel fini. Quia verò τὸ καταντικρύ infra additur, videtur hoc loco debere accipi à bimatu incipiente, à tempore quo puer ingredi-turtur secundum ætatis annum, & infrà, ut contrà 2 Paral. 31. 16. ἀπὸ τεσσαρῶν χ᾽ ἱ πάνω, à triennio & supra, vel à filio trium annorum & supra, ut elt in Hebræo, non potest intelligi nisi de masculis qui tertium ætatis annum jam excesserant, quasi diceretur, ἀπὸ τετάρτης πληρωθέντος. Sic etiam Aristoteles lib. 2. c. 1 de hist. Animal. ἀπὸ δλλει ἢ τὰ κέρατα μόνον ἐλαφὸς ἔχει τ᾽ ἔτῳ, ἀρξάμενο ἀπὸ διετοῦς χ᾽ πάλιν φύει. Cervus solus singulis annis abjicit cornua, incipiens [abjicere] à bimatu & rursus generat. In quo etiam loco necessarium est intelligere ἀπὸ διετίας πληρωθέντος à bimatu expleto, usque enim ad illud tempus, cornua non abjiciunt, at immediate incipiente trimatu πάλιν φύει rursus nova generat, ut antea dictum, τῷ ἢ τείτῳ ἔτει ἀξιῶν φύσει. Quod si ergo Evangelista intellexisset pueros duos jam totos annos natos, dixisset certius ἀπὸ τετάρτης χ᾽ καταντέρω, à trimatu & infrà. Est enim discrimen certe inter à bimatu vel trimatu & infrà, & à bimatu vel à trimatu & supra. Nec apud Latinos omnino differt mos loquendi. Idem enim significant bimus ac διετής, bimatus ac διετία, trimus ac τριετής, &c. Bimus vulgariter, qui in bimatu est. Bima dies, tempus biennii. Vall. Habemus etiam in vulgari Latino, Isai. 15. 5. vitulam contemnantem, i.e. ut exponunt Grammatici, quæ est in complexione anni tertii, & apud LXX vocatur δάμαλις τετράτης, apud Interp. Arab. vitula trima. Ita ut ab utroque dicendi genere vel Græco vel Latino necessariò exponendum, nè unum quidem bimulum ab Herode interfectum, eos verò solùm occisos, qui erant infrà, i.e. unius anni expleti, pueros, quorum omnes perierunt, usque ad infantem recens natum. Et jam restat demonstrare, quomodo interpretatio ista fit magis commoda scopo loci, & rationi magis consentanea. Idque reor ob hanc præcipuè causam, eò quòd Herodes ceciderit infantes, xT' ὁ χρόνον ὃν ἠκρίβωσεν τ μάγων, secundum tempus quod exquisierat à Magis. Atque hoc fuit tempus quo apparuit eis stella in Oriente, quam Herodes qui accuratè perquisiverat ab eis momentum temporis quo apparuit, non vanè poterat supponere designâsse conceptum istius quem quærebant regis. Cometæ enim signa sunt rerum imminentium non præsentium, ut Josephus Scaliger, unde verissimum esse argumentum: natalem filii Dei illo ostento denunciatum magis longo tempore antequam incideret. Neque est omnino nobis à ratione alienum conjicere, stellam illam apparuisse magis primo in ipso temporis articulo, quo Virginem salutavit Angelus. Circa quod tempus in quo filius Dei descendit è cœlo, ut fieret filius hominis in utero Virginis, rursus aio, non est à ratione alienum conjicere magos primò vidisse stellam, atque ea visa protinus, divinitus prius admonitos eam portendere regem Judæis nasciturum, incœpisse se parare itineri ad Hierusalem: divinitus aio prius admonitos, non enim credo eos ita calluisse prophetiam Balaami, vel aspectum astrorum, ut ex iis scire poterint stellam illam portendere regem Judæis nasciturum; si non fuissent è supra divinitus admoniti, non magis quàm sciebant habuisse Herodem in animo infantem interimere, si non per somnum fuissent prius χρηματισθέντες. In cujus itineris expeditione cum fecissent circà quadraginta septimanas, cum impleti essent dies quibus ipsa pareret, Luc.2.6. (quod spatium temporis fas est dare absolvendo itineri, præcipuè si sit verum quod Josephus ait, eos qui habitabant supra Euphratem fecisse ad Hierosolymam quinque mensium iter, sive venerint ex Persia, ut volunt aliqui, sive venerint ex Arabia, quæ etiam secundùm Ptolemaum Iudæam ab oriente terminat, ut alii, quorum argumenta licet eis ipse potiùs adstipulor non est opus nostrum hic repetere) civitatem illam duce stella tandem advenerunt. Quibus quadraginta septimanis fi duodecim addamus dies post nativitatem Iesu, includentes diem in quo venerint ad eum adorandum magi, quod tempus æquum est conjicere eos expendisse in inquirendo ubinam esset recens natus Iudæorum rex, usque dùm apparuit eis rursùs stella, & prævii eis usque dum venit & stetit supra ubi erat puer, & deinceps circà viginti & octo dies usque dùm dies purificationis Mariæ & præsentationis filii in templo secundùm legem Moysis jam præterierant, circa quod tempus magi forte reverterunt in regionem suam, dando etiam ulteriùs pro reditu à Ierusalem in urbem suam Nazaret; cum perfecissent omnia secundùm legem Domini, Luc. 2, 39. atque indè rursùs retrò in Ægyptum, Matt. 2. 14. & 16, secundùm ordinem historiæ, antequam Herodes videns se illusum esse à magis, iratus est valdè & mittens occidit pueros, sex septimanas amplius, erunt in toto quinquaginta duo, spatium anni integrum à tempore quo primùm dicimus apparuisse stellam magis usque ad tempus quo Herodes intercmit pueros. Adeò ut non omninò præter rem sit dicere, Herodem occidisse pueros omnes ἀπὸ διετοῦς καὶ κατωτέρω à secundo ætatis anno & infrà, i. e. omnes qui primum expleverant ætatis annum & infrà secundùm tempus quod exquisierat à magis, posito eum supposuisse τὼν φάσιν τῆς ἀστέρος eo tempore portendisse conceptionem istius quem timebat regis.
units.tr: V. 16. From a bimatu and below, as the old version has it; from a bimulo and below, as others have it. Whichever reading you prefer hardly matters, whether substantive or adjective, provided everyone understands the same thing: ἀπὸ διετίας καὶ πλέον διετίας [from two years and more than two years], from a completed biennium, as is said at Acts 24. 17. This I do not think fits this place at all. The words must instead be rendered and understood according to the idiom of speaking both among the Greeks and Latins, and according to the very reason and purpose of the passage, in this manner. Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the Magi, was very angry, and sending he killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in its borders, from a bimulo and below, namely beginning from those of two years exclusive, and descending to those who were under two years (and not as it is in the English, "From two years old and under"), translating διετεῖς as ἀπὸ διετίας ἀρχομένης [from a biennium beginning], and not πλεονδιετίους [more than two years], from a bimatu beginning and not completed. As if he said: all boys of one year and under, according to the time he had ascertained from the Magi. For a boy begins to be called by the Hebrews (בן שנתים), son of two years, that is, of the second year. Among the Greeks he is διετῆς, among the Latins bimus. So the Seventy rightly, I think, render בן שנתים as διετῆς ἔτος, in the second year after the flood, Gen. 11. 10. So Noah is said in Gen. 7. 6 and 11 to be (בן שש מאות שנה) son of six hundred years, (בשנת שש מאות) in the six hundredth year of his life. Hesychius understood it thus: διετῆς, ὁ ἓνα τῶν ἐτῶν [the one of the years], after a full year, as if the boy then first began to be, or to be called, διετής, with διὰ put for ὡς, which is usually done when a time elapsed is meant, as δι' ἡμερῶν [after some days], Mark 2. 1; δι' ἐτῶν πλειόνων [after several years], Acts 24. 17; and δι' ἐτῶν ᾱδον τετραχοσίων [after nearly four hundred years], Plutarch. So also Aristotle, book 9, chapter 5 of the History of Animals, whose words about the stag are these: φύσει ἡ διετὴς τὰ μὲν τὰ κέρατα [in two-year-olds the horns first grow], the bimi first generate horns. But nothing is more certain than that stags begin to generate horns as soon as they have passed the first year of age and entered the second. And to make this clearer: the animal which among us is called the calf of a red deer, for the whole span of its first year, is called by him ἐνιαύσιος, as also in Scripture a lamb is called in Hebrew (שנה), among the Greeks ἐνιαύσιος, among the Latins anniculus, in the English Bibles a Lamb of the first year. And what among us in the second year of age is called a Brocket, by him is called παταλία, or διετής, among the Latins jubulo or bimus, at the beginning of which year it generates horns and at its end casts them off. Τῷ τρίτῳ ἔτει [in the third year], as the same author says, that is, as soon as they enter the third year of age, they generate forked horns, and in the third year of age are called among the Latins trimi, in English Spayds. Here it is worth observing in passing that διετὴς and τῷ τρίτῳ ἔτει are one and the same phrase in Aristotle, so that he could equally have said τῷ δευτέρῳ ἔτει for διετής, and τριετής for τῷ τρίτῳ ἔτει. Whence it is clear that ἀπὸ διετοῦς can be taken either from a bimatu beginning or from a bimatu ending: from the time when the boy begins to be a son of two years, or from the time when he ceases to be so, for ἀπὸ excludes one of the two limits, either the beginning or the end. But since τὸ καταντικρύ [the opposite] is added below, it seems that in this place it must be taken as from a bimatu beginning, from the time when the boy enters the second year of age, and downwards. Conversely, 2 Chronicles 31. 16 reads ἀπὸ τεσσαρῶν χ᾽ ἱ πάνω [from four years and upward], from a triennium and above, or from a son of three years and above, as it is in the Hebrew; this can only be understood of males who had already passed the third year of age, as if it said ἀπὸ τετάρτης πληρωθέντος [from a completed fourth]. So also Aristotle, book 2, chapter 1 of the History of Animals: ἀπὸ δλλει ἢ τὰ κέρατα μόνον ἐλαφὸς ἔχει τ᾽ ἔτῳ, ἀρξάμενο ἀπὸ διετοῦς χ᾽ πάλιν φύει [the deer alone casts its horns every year, beginning from the bimatu, and again generates them]: the stag alone casts its horns each year, beginning to cast them from the bimatu, and again generates them. In this passage too it is necessary to understand ἀπὸ διετίας πληρωθέντος, from a completed bimatu, for until that time they do not cast their horns, but immediately as the trimatu begins they again generate new ones, as was said before: τῷ ἢ τείτῳ ἔτει ἀξιῶν φύσει [in the third year]. If therefore the Evangelist had meant boys who were already two full years old, he would more certainly have said ἀπὸ τετάρτης χ᾽ καταντέρω, from a trimatu and below. For there is certainly a difference between from a bimatu or trimatu and below and from a bimatu or from a trimatu and above. Nor does Latin usage differ at all: bimus means the same as διετής, bimatus the same as διετία, trimus the same as τριετής, and so on. Bimus, commonly, is one who is in his second year; bima dies is a period of two years. Vall. We have also in ordinary Latin, Isaiah 15. 5, vitulam contemnantem, that is, as the grammarians explain, one who is in the course of the third year; and among the Seventy it is called δάμαλις τετράτης, and in the Arabic interpreter a three-year-old heifer. Thus from either mode of speaking, Greek or Latin, it must necessarily be explained that Herod did not kill even a single two-year-old, but only those under it, that is, boys of one completed year, all of whom perished, down to the newborn infant. And now it remains to show how this interpretation is more suited to the purpose of the passage and more consistent with its reason. I think this is chiefly for this reason: that Herod slew the infants κατὰ τὸν χρόνον ὃν ἠκρίβωσεν τῶν μάγων [according to the time which he had ascertained from the Magi]. This was the time at which the star appeared to them in the East, which Herod, having carefully asked them the moment when it appeared, could not idly be supposed to have taken as the indication of the conception of that king whom they sought. For comets are signs of things imminent, not present, as Joseph Scaliger says, whence this most true argument follows: that the birth of the Son of God was announced by that portent long before it took place. Nor is it altogether foreign to reason for us to conjecture that that star first appeared to the magi at the very moment when the angel saluted the Virgin. Around the time when the Son of God came down from heaven to become the son of man in the womb of the Virgin, again I say, it is not foreign to reason to conjecture that the magi first saw the star, and, as soon as they saw it, were divinely admonit- I say divinely admonitted beforehand, for I do not believe they had so mastered the prophecy of Balaam, or the aspect of the stars, that from these they could know that star portended a king to be born for the Jews; if they had not been divinely admonished from above, they would no more have known that Herod had in mind to destroy the infant, unless they had first been warned in a dream - they began to prepare for the journey to Jerusalem. In the course of that journey, when they had spent about forty weeks, when the days were fulfilled that she should be delivered, Luke 2. 6 (a span of time which may rightly be given for completing the journey, especially if what Josephus says is true, that those who lived beyond the Euphrates made a journey of five months to Jerusalem, whether they came from Persia, as some hold, or from Arabia, which according to Ptolemy also bounds Judaea on the east, as others hold; their arguments I need not repeat here, to which I would rather agree) they at last arrived at that city, the star leading them. If to these forty weeks we add twelve days after the birth of Jesus, counting the day on which the magi came to adore him, it is fair to conjecture that they spent that time in inquiring where the newborn king of the Jews was, until the star appeared to them again and went before them until it came and stood over where the child was; and then about twenty-eight days more, until the days of Mary's purification and the presentation of the son in the temple according to the law of Moses had already passed, about which time the magi perhaps returned to their own region, allowing further for the return from Jerusalem to their city Nazareth, when they had fulfilled all things according to the law of the Lord, Luke 2. 39, and from there back again into Egypt, Matthew 2. 14 and 16, in the order of the history, before Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the magi, was very angry and, sending, killed the boys: six weeks more, there will be in all fifty-two, a full year from the time when we say the star first appeared to the magi until the time when Herod destroyed the boys. So that it is not altogether beside the point to say that Herod killed all the boys ἀπὸ διετοῦς καὶ κατωτέρω [from a bimatu and below], from the second year of age and below, that is, all who had first completed the first year of age and below, according to the time he had ascertained from the magi, supposing that he took τὴν φάσιν τῆς ἀστέρος [the appearance of the star] at that time to portend the conception of that king whom he feared.

units.la: Quod si quis criminetur distributionem temporum rum, velim eum scire non fuisse nobis in animo ea ita exacte aptare, ut nullus relinqueretur exceptioni vel correctioni locus: satis vero esse mihi, si quod hic propositui habeat in se (quoad summam) speciem veri. En vero quam absurdum errorem peperit Dionis χεὸν@· ille perperam intellectus? Verba sunt Scaligeri supra nominati, Lib. 6. de emend. temp. Errorem vero ille intelligit eorum, qui voluerunt Iesum fuisse Dionì i. e. eorum sensu duos totos annos natum, cum Herodes pueros occidi jusserit à bimatu & infrà. Apud quem videre licet plura, quæ non parum faciunt pro sententia nostra. Positive enim non veretur dicere, Cometes ille quo duce magi in Judæam profecti sunt, non est dubium, quin longo intervallo Christi natalem præcesserit. Atque ego istud intervallum aio, præter vel contra (detur venia verbo) ipsius opinionem, à Christi conceptione incœpisse, quam ille cometam præcessisse ait.
units.tr: If anyone should accuse me of a faulty arrangement of the times, I would have him know that I never meant to fit them so exactly that no room was left for exception or correction. It is enough for me if what I propose has, in its main outline, the appearance of truth. Indeed, what an absurd error has the misreading of Dio's word [χρόνου] produced! These are the words of the Scaliger named above, book 6 of De emendatione temporum. He means the error of those who wanted Jesus to have been two years old, in the sense of Dio's word, since Herod ordered the boys to be killed from two years old and under. In that work one may find much more that does not a little support our view. For he does not hesitate to say positively: That comet under whose guidance the magi set out for Judea, there is no doubt, preceded the birth of Christ by a long interval. I say that this interval, beyond or against (let the word be pardoned) his own opinion, began at the conception of Christ, which he says the comet preceded.

units.la: C. 3. V. 4. ἉH ὃ τεγγὴ αὐτῶν λῶ ἀκείδες χὴ μέλι ἄγριον. Quid ἀκείδες hoc loco significet, non parum discrepat inter Interpretes: in hoc vero consentiunt universi, Baptistam vesci solitum in deserto cibo tenuissimo & parabili, i. e. quem Natura sponte ministraverat, qualis erat quo vescebatur, τὸ μέλι ἄγριον, mel sylvestre. Quo concesso, summitates foliorum arborum vel plantarum, quas τὸ ἀκείδες hoc loco significare putarunt aliqui, quales erant τὰ κεράτια, Siliquæ, quibus implere cupiebat ventrem suum prodigus, Luc. 15. 16. erant certe cibus & tenuissimus, multoque magis parabilis quam Locustæ. Non enim usquam legi Locustas omnino crudas escam fuisse alicujus populi, paratas autem fuisse semper, priusquam ederentur, arte aliquâ coquinariâ; vel ad ignem coquebantur vel assabantur, vel ad Solem arefactæ; vel fumo & sale duratæ, vel conditæ edebantur, quarum artium ullâ vix credere est usum fuisse Baptistam in deserto, & utrum laboris tædium in arefaciendo coram sole, vel in venando vel in aucupando sumpserit, cordatis egomet submitto. Cùm è contra, τὰ ἀκρίδια, siliquæ sive summitates frondium sine ullo laboris tædio paratæ erant ad manum. Atque has ἀκρίδας non fuisse locustas, sed ἀκρίδος μελιτῶν [?], ἢ φυλλῶν, summitates herbarum, plantarum sive frondium, constanter asseruit Isid. Pelus, lib. 1. ep. 5. & 132. Cujus sententiæ fuit & Paulinus & Nicephorus, & alii quorum meminerunt Eu-thymius & Theophylactus, quæ etiam non displicere videtur Optimo & Doctissimo Hammondo nostro, nec Baronio, cujus verba sunt ejusmodi. Hæc cùm scribat Isidorus, & non nisi majorum auctoritate, quid de his sentiendum, definiendum nobis non est, sed totum relinquimus Lectoris arbitrio; nam constat Græcam dictionem, ἀκρίδες, & Locustarum insecti genus infirmas habens alas ad volandum, & summitates herbarum significare. Præterquam etiam quod me multùm movet, quòd hæc κεράτια, quæ ita vocantur Græcè, quoniam sint reflexo sicut cornu, & Latinè redduntur siliquæ, vel à ξυλίνη, eò quod sint ejus lignea, vel à Silo, propter formæ similitudinem, eò quòd Silus appellatur, naso sursum versus repando ut sunt illæ, apud Germanos ad huc vocantur St Johans Brot, i. e. Sancti Johannis panis, quasi constans foret opinio inter ipsos, Baptistam vesci solitum his frondium summitatibus in deserto. Adde etiam περὶ πάντων, quòd oculatus testis Sandys noster fidus & nobilis historicus, in relatione peregrinationis suæ cum iter faceret per Judæam circa annum 1611. lib. 3. pag. 183. 183. edit. 2. hanc ipsissimam montanam regionem, in qua Baptista vesci solitus, depinxir in tabula sparsim arboribus refertam, inscripto nomine: The desert of St John Baptist, Desertum Iohannis Baptistæ, paulo inferius addens, beholding onely to the Locust tree, foli locustæ devinctum arbori. Quæ arbor utiúm sit Acacia, vel Siligna, vel Ceratium, statuant in botanicis eruditi. Nobis vero aptum est statuere, ex hoc itinerario & suprà nominatis testimoniis eam esse ipsissimam, ex qua Baptista vesci solitus, quam etiam hodiè locustam vocant. Adeò ut mihi, dum hæc simul reputo, quicquid nihilominus ita strenuè contradicitur, æquè si non magis apposita videatur versio: Esca autem ejus erat summitates foliorum arborum, & mel sylvestre. Neque Erasmus, cùm pro viribus vindicâsset eos qui hic locustas volunt, id tamen confidenter asserit, sed modestè concludit, Neq; hæc commemoramus, quòd omnino negem hic ἀχείδας accipi posse pro frutice aut herbæ genere. Ceratia autem illa sive siliquas in regionibus in quibus nascuntur, frequenter escam esse pauperum testantur abundè Autores. Inter alios Lobelius, in Adversf. Multum hæc, nempe siliquæ, cognita Nicææ & maris Ligustici accolis, ubi eam esitant pueri etiam & porci. Et Galenus 2. de Alimentt. περὶ κεράτιον, ἐστι ὁ ἐδώδιμα χαμόχυλόν τε, &c. Est autem (i e. Keratium,) pravi succi edulium & lignosum; proinde satius est à regionibus Orientalibus in quibus nascitur, ad nos non importari. Fuit verò ille ex Pergamo minoris Asia, à cujus latere haud longè distat versùs Orientem Judæa, è qua regione fieri potest hæc Ceratia importata fuisse usque ad Pergamum tempore Galeni saltem à Syria, quæ utrisque fuit contermina. Sic etiam apud Ælian, Diogenes dicitur manducâsse φύλλων ἄκρα, summas foliorum extremitates.
units.tr: Chapter 3, verse 4: "His food was locusts and wild honey [ἡ δὲ τροφὴ αὐτοῦ ἦν ἀκρίδες καὶ μέλι ἄγριον]." What ἀκρίδες means here is not a little disputed among the interpreters. All agree, however, that the Baptist was accustomed to eat in the desert the most slight and easily found food, that is, what nature had supplied of its own accord, such as was the wild honey, mel sylvestre. Granting this, the tops of the leaves of trees or plants, which some have thought ἀκρίδες means here, such as the κεράτια, siliquae, on which the prodigal longed to fill his belly (Luke 15:16), were certainly food, and very slight, and far more easily found than locusts. For I have never read that locusts were eaten raw as the food of any people; they were always prepared by some culinary art before being eaten. They were either cooked over a fire, or roasted, or dried in the sun, or hardened with smoke and salt, or preserved and then eaten. I hardly think the Baptist used any of these arts in the desert, and I leave it to the discerning to judge whether he would have taken on the tedium of drying them in the sun, or of hunting or catching them. On the other hand, ἀκρίδια, siliquae, or the tops of the fronds, were ready to hand without any tedium of labour. And that these ἀκρίδες were not locusts but the tops of herbs, plants or fronds, Isidore of Pelusium consistently asserted in book 1, letters 5 and 132. Paulinus and Nicephorus held the same view, and others whom Euthymius and Theophylact mention. This opinion does not seem to displease our most excellent and learned Hammond, nor Baronius, whose words are these: Since Isidore writes this, and on no authority but that of greater men, what should be thought of these things we are not required to decide, but we leave it entirely to the judgement of the reader; for it is established that the Greek word ἀκρίδες signifies both a kind of locust insect with weak wings for flying, and the tops of herbs. Besides, what moves me much is this: these κεράτια, so called in Greek because they are curved like a horn, and rendered in Latin siliquae, whether from ξυλίνη, because they are woody, or from Silo, from the likeness of shape, because the Silus is so called, with a nose turned up and curved as they are, are still called St Johans Brot among the Germans, that is, Saint John's bread, as if there were a settled opinion among them that the Baptist was accustomed to eat these tops of fronds in the desert. Add also, above all, that our faithful and noble historian, the eyewitness Sandys, in his account of a journey through Judea about the year 1611, book 3, page 183, edition 2, painted this very mountainous region, in which the Baptist was accustomed to eat, on a map scattered with trees, with the name inscribed: The desert of St John Baptist, Desertum Iohannis Baptistae. A little lower he adds: beholding onely to the Locust tree, fixed to the tree of the locust alone. Learned botanists may determine whether this tree is an Acacia, a Siliqua, or a Ceratium. For us it is fitting to determine, from this travel account and the testimonies named above, that it is the very tree from which the Baptist was accustomed to eat, which they still call the locust tree today. So that for me, when I weigh these things together, whatever is nonetheless so vigorously contended against, the translation seems equally, if not more, suitable: His food was the tops of the leaves of trees, and wild honey. Nor does Erasmus, although he defended as best he could those who want locusts here, assert this confidently. He modestly concludes: We do not mention these things because I entirely deny that here ἀκρίδες can be taken to mean a shrub or a kind of herb. But ceratia, or siliquae, in the regions where they grow, are frequently attested by the authors to be abundant food for the poor. Among others, Lobelius, in his Adversaria, says: this plant, namely the siliqua, is known to the people of Nice and of the Ligurian sea, where boys and even pigs eat it. And Galen, in book 2 de alimentorum, speaks of the keratia: they are food of bad juice and woody; therefore it is better that they not be imported to us from the eastern regions in which they grow. He came from Pergamum in Asia Minor, from whose side Judea lies not far to the east, and from that region these keratia could have been imported as far as Pergamum in the time of Galen, at least from Syria, which bordered both. So too in Aelian, Diogenes is said to have eaten the tips of leaves, the extremities of the fronds.

units.la: C. 5. v. 19. "Ος ἐαν' ἓν λύζῃ μίαν τῶν ἐντο- λῶν τύτων τῶν ἐλαχίστων. Quisquis ergo solveri unum ex mandatis bisce minimis. Sic plerique, ac si esset quædam insignior emphasis in versione ista Mandatis bisce minimis: verùm ego nullo modo sentio, Christum in his verbis aliquam sermonis magis Emphaticam affectâsse elegantiam, sed locutum fuisse receptâ phrasi & obvio sensu, trajectione in N. T. familiari, Quisquis ergo solveris unum ex minimis horum mandatorum, quale est illud c. 25. 40. ἐνὶ τύτων τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου τῶν ἐλαχίστων, uni ex minimis horum meorum fratrum.
units.tr: Chapter 5, verse 19: "Whoever therefore breaks one of these least commandments [ὃς ἐὰν οὖν λύσῃ μίαν τῶν ἐντολῶν τούτων τῶν ἐλαχίστων]." So most read it, as if there were some more pronounced emphasis in the phrase "these least commandments." But I by no means think Christ aimed at any more emphatic elegance in these words. He spoke in the accepted phrase and the obvious sense, a transposition familiar in the New Testament: "Whoever therefore breaks one of the least of these commandments," as in chapter 25, verse 40: "one of the least of these my brothers [ἑνὶ τούτων τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου τῶν ἐλαχίστων]," that is, one of the least of these my brethren.

units.la: V, 42. Καὶ τὸν θέλοντα ἀπὸ σοῦ δανίσασθαι μὴ ἀποστραφῇς. Rectius, opinor, vertitur, quam vulgò solet, Ne avertas volentem mutuari à te. Habet enim ἀποστρέφομαι Activum etiam significationem, ut & alia Passiva plurima in N. T. Et sic Symmachus legit, Psal. 132.0. μὴ ἀποστραφῇς τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ Χριστοῦ σου, Ne avertas faciem Christi tui.
units.tr: Verse 42: "And from him who wants to borrow from you do not turn away [καὶ τὸν θέλοντα ἀπὸ σοῦ δανίσασθαι μὴ ἀποστραφῇς]." I think this is rendered more rightly than is usual: "Do not turn away one who wishes to borrow from you," rather than "Do not turn away from one who wishes to borrow." For ἀποστρέφομαι also has an active sense, as do many other passive forms in the New Testament. So Symmachus read in Psalm 132: "μὴ ἀποστραφῇς τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ Χριστοῦ σου," that is, "Do not turn away the face of your Christ."

units.la: C. 6. v. 2. Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ἀπέχουσι τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν, Amen dico vobis, receperunt mercedem suam. Sic plerumque Interpretes, vel in eundem sensum. Verùm verò priore planè dicitur, Si eleemosynam faciatis coram hominibus ut ipse dicitur ab iis, μισθὸν οὐκ ἔχετε, præsenti pro futuro, mercedem non habebitis apud Patrem vestrum qui est in cœlis, adeò ut sit mera contradictio; ideòque sensus qui sequitur magis foret accommodus, si qui eleemosynam faciunt in plateis vel Synagogis, ut gloriam consequantur ab hominibus, potiùs dicantur non habituri, quàm habere mercedem suam. In cujus remedium hæc verba velim reddi omnino aliter, Amen dico vobis, prohibent mercedem suam. Captando gloriam apud hanc ipsissimam montanam regionem, in qua Baptista vesci solitus, depinxit in tabula sparsim arboribus refertam, inscripto nomine, The desert of St John Baptist, Desertum Johannis Baptistæ, paulo inferius addens, beholding onely to the Locust tree, soli locustæ devinctum arbori. Quæ arbor utrum sit Acacia, vel Siliqua, vel Ceratium, statuant in botanicis eruditi. Nobis vero aptum est statuere, ex hoc itinerario & suprà nominatis testimoniis eam esse ipsissimam, ex qua Baptista vesci solitus, quam etiam hodie locustam vocant. Adeo ut mihi, dum hæc simul reputo, quicquid nihilominus ita strenuè contradicitur, æquè si non magis apposita videatur versio: Esca autem ejus erat summitates foliorum arborum, & mel sylvestre. Neque Erasmus, cùm pro viribus vindicâssct eos qui hîc locustas volunt, id tamen confidenter asserit, sed modestè concludit, Neque hæc commemoramus, quod omnino negem hic ἀκρί-δας accipi posse pro frutice aut herba genere. Keratia autem illa sive siliquas in regionibus in quibus nascuntur, frequenter escam esse pauperum testantur abundè Authores. Inter alios Lobelius, in Adversf. Multum hæc, nempe siliquæ, cognitæ Nicææ & maris Ligustici accolis, ubi eam esitant pueri etiam & porci. Et Galenus 2. de Alimentt. περὶ κερατίων, ἐστι δ' ἐδώδιμα χαλκόχυμά τε, &c. Est autem (i e. Keratium,) pravi succi edulium & lignosum; proinde satius est à regionibus Orientalibus in quibus nascitur, ad nos non importari. Fuit vero ille ex Pergamo minoris Asiæ, à cujus latere haud longè distat versùs Orientem Judææ, è qua regione heri potest hæc Keratia importata fuisse usque ad Pergamum tempore Galeni saltem à Syria, quæ utrisque fuit confermina. Sic etiam apud Ælian, Diogenes dicitur manducâsse φύλλων ἄκρα, summas foliorum extremitates.
units.tr: Chapter 6, verse 2: "Amen I say to you, they have received their reward [ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ἀπέχουσι τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν]." So most interpreters read it, or in the same sense. But the earlier passage clearly says: "If you give alms before men, as they are spoken of by them, you have no reward [μισθὸν οὐκ ἔχετε]," the present for the future: you will not have a reward with your Father who is in heaven. So it is a plain contradiction. Hence the sense that follows would be better suited if those who give alms in the streets or synagogues, seeking glory from men, were said rather not to have their reward than to have it. As a remedy for this, I would have these words rendered quite differently: "Amen I say to you, they withhold their reward." Seeking glory from men in this very mountainous region, in which the Baptist was accustomed to eat, painted on a map scattered with trees, with the name inscribed, The desert of St John Baptist, Desertum Johannis Baptistae, and a little lower adding, beholding onely to the Locust tree, fixed to the tree of the locust alone. Learned botanists may determine whether this tree is an Acacia, a Siliqua, or a Ceratium. For us it is fitting to determine, from this travel account and the testimonies named above, that it is the very tree from which the Baptist was accustomed to eat, which they still call the locust tree today. So that for me, when I weigh these things together, whatever is nonetheless so vigorously contended against, the translation seems equally, if not more, suitable: His food was the tops of the leaves of trees, and wild honey. Nor does Erasmus, although he defended as best he could those who want locusts here, assert this confidently. He modestly concludes: We do not mention these things because I entirely deny that here ἀκρίδας can be taken to mean a shrub or a kind of herb. But keratia, or siliquae, in the regions where they grow, are frequently attested by the authors to be abundant food for the poor. Among others, Lobelius, in his Adversaria, says: this plant, namely the siliqua, is known to the people of Nice and of the Ligurian sea, where boys and even pigs eat it. And Galen, in book 2 de alimentorum, speaks of the keratia [περὶ κερατίων]: they are food of bad juice and woody; therefore it is better that they not be imported to us from the eastern regions in which they grow. He came from Pergamum in Asia Minor, from whose side Judea lies not far to the east, and from that region these keratia could have been imported as far as Pergamum in the time of Galen, at least from Syria, which bordered both. So too in Aelian, Diogenes is said to have eaten the tips of leaves, the extremities of the fronds.

units.la: C. 5. v. 19. "Os ἐὰν ἓν λύσῃ μίαν τῶν ἐντολῶν τύτων τῶν ἐλαχίστων. Quisquis ergo solveris unum ex mandatis hisce minimis. Sic plerique, ac si effet quædam insignior emphasis in versione ista Mandatis hisce minimis: verùm ego nullo modo sentio, Christum in his verbis aliquam sermonis magis Emphaticam affectâsse elegantiam, sed locutum fuisse receptâ phrasi & obvio sensu, trajectione in N. T. familiari, Quisquis ergo solveris unum ex minimis horum mandatorum, quale est illud c. 25. 40. ἑνὶ τῶν τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου τῶν ἐλαχίστων, uni ex minimis horum meorum fratrum.
units.tr: Matt. 5:19, "Whoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments" [ὃς ἐὰν λύσῃ μίαν τῶν ἐντολῶν τούτων τῶν ἐλαχίστων]. Most commentators take this as a special emphasis on "these least commandments," but I do not think Christ aimed at any elaborate emphasis in these words. He spoke in the ordinary phrase with its obvious sense, using the inversion common in the New Testament, so that it means "whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments." Compare Matt. 25:40, "one of the least of these my brethren" [ἑνὶ τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου τῶν ἐλαχίστων].

units.la: V, 42. Καὶ τῷ θέλοντι ἀπὸ σοῦ δανίσασθαι μὴ ἀποστραφῆς. Rectius, opinor, vertitur, quam vulgò solet, Ne avertas volentem mutuari a te. Habet enim ἀποστρέφομαι Activam etiam significationem, ut & alia Passiva plurima in N. T. Et sic Symmachus legit, Psal. 132.10. μὴ ἀποστραφῇς τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ Χριστοῦ σου, Ne avertas faciem Christi tui.
units.tr: John 5:42 (as printed, Matt. 5:42), "And from him who wishes to borrow from you do not turn away" [Καὶ τῷ θέλοντι ἀπὸ σοῦ δανίσασθαι μὴ ἀποστραφῆς]. I think this is rendered more correctly than is usual: not "do not turn away one who wishes to borrow from you," but "do not turn away from him who wishes to borrow from you." For ἀποστρέφομαι has an active sense as well, as do many other passive forms in the New Testament. So Symmachus also reads Ps. 132:10, "do not turn away the face of your Christ" [μὴ ἀποστραφῇς τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ Χριστοῦ σου].

units.la: C. 6. v. 2. Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ἀπέχουσι τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν, Amen dico vobis, receperunt mercedem suam. Sic plerumque Interpretes, vel in eundem sensum. Versu verò priore plane dicitur, Si eleemosynam faciatis coram hominibus ut ab hominibus videamini ab iis, μισθὸν οὐκ ἕξετε, præsenti pro futuro, mercedem non habebitis apud Patrem vestrum qui est in cœlis, adeò ut sit mera contradictio; ideòque sensus qui sequitur magis foret accommodus, si qui eleemosynam faciunt in plateis vel Synagogis, ut gloriam consequantur ab hominibus, potius dicantur non habituri, quàm habere mercedem suam. In cujus remedium hæc verba velim reddi omnino aliter, Amen dico vobis, prohibent mercedem suam. Captando gloriam apud homines, prohibent mercedem suam apud Deum: apud quem non sunt habituri mercedem, si eleemosynam faciunt coram hominibus, ut spectentur ab iis. Sat scio priorem sensum salvari commodè, ut aliqui putant, distinctione; Habere quidem eos mundanam & fragilem mercedem, non verò habere solidam & coelestem. At quid opus est sensu extraneo & allegorico, quid, inquam, distinctione opus est quæ plane est coacta, si sensus sit sine distinctione planus, idque ferat verborum usus? At verò apud omnes Lexicographos, κωλύω, ἀπέχω, & ἐμπορίζω, ταυτὸ σημαίνουσιν, idem significant. Atque in hoc sensu pace doctissimorum Bezæ & Grotii accipi voluit eandem vocem Plutarchus in Solone, ubi narrans aliquid lege sancitum durius, videlicet, e meretricibus procreatos non astrictos esse lege ad alendum parentes, rationem insuper addit, verbis sequentibus. Ὁ γὰρ ἐν γάμῳ παρὰ ἀξίων τὸ καλὸν ἐκ τέκνων ἔνεκα ἡδονῆς ἀλλ᾽ ἡδονῆς ἀμελὴς γυναῖκα, τὸν τε μισθὸν ἀπέχει, ἢ παρρησίαν αὐτῷ πρὸς τὰς γενομένας ἐκ ἀπολείποντος, οἷς αὐτὸ τὸ γενέσθαι πεπίστευκεν ὀνειδή. Quæ verba ut sibi mutuò constent, omninò debent verti in hunc modum: Qui nuptiarum decus vilipendit, palam ostendit se non liberorum gratia, sed voluptatis, mulierem ascisecre, prohibetque mercedem suam, & non reliquit sibi libertatem loquendi ad natos suos, quibus ipsum nasci fecit probrum. In eo quod non reliquerit sibi libertatem loquendi ad natos suos, ἀπέχει ἢ μισθὸν, prohibet mercedem suam alimoniæ, quam ab honeste natis liberum fuit parentibus lege postulâsse. Neque credo de distinctione illa mundanæ & coelestis mercedis Plutarchum unquam somniâsse. Atque in hanc sententiam pronius etiam feror, eò quòd apud eundem occurrit eadem vox in eodem sensu in libro de defectu Oraculorum versus finem, (forte & alibi) ὡς ἓν ἀπέχει τὴν μαντικὴν ἀναδυμίασιν, nihil prohibet vaticinandi spiritum &c. Quam etiam phrasin dissertissimè reperire est apud Dion. Halic. in ipsissimo sensu: Οὐδείς με ἀφέξει φόβος μὴ οὐχ ἃ φρονῶ λέγειν: Nullus me prohibebit terror, quo minus dicam quod sentio. In summa, in vanum recurritur ad sensum mysticum, ubi habemus literalem, atque ita statuendum in locis parallelis arbitror.
units.tr: Matt. 6:2, "Amen I say to you, they have received their reward" [Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ἀπέχουσι τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν]. Most interpreters render it this way, or to the same effect. But the verse before plainly says, "If you give alms before men so that you may be seen by them, you will not have a reward with your Father who is in heaven," so that the translation would be a flat contradiction. The sense that follows would fit better if those who give alms in the streets or synagogues to win glory from men were said not to have their reward, rather than to have it. To remedy this, I would have these words rendered quite differently: "Amen I say to you, they forbid their reward." Seeking glory among men, they forbid their reward with God, with whom they will have no reward if they give alms before men so as to be seen by them. I know that the former sense can be saved neatly by a distinction, as some think: they do indeed have a worldly and fleeting reward, but not a solid and heavenly one. But why is there any need for a strained and allegorical sense, and why for a distinction which is plainly forced, when the sense is plain without any distinction and the usage of the words allows it? In fact, all the lexicographers agree that κωλύω, ἀπέχω and ἐμπορίζω mean the same thing. In this sense, with all respect to the most learned Beza and Grotius, Plutarch in his Solon used the same word, where, describing a harsh law, namely that sons born of prostitutes were not bound by law to support their parents, he adds a reason in the following words: "For the man who in marriage disregards the honour of his wives and children, and takes a wife for pleasure rather than for pleasure's sake... (as printed) ὁ γὰρ ἐν γάμῳ παρὰ ἀξίαν τὸ καλὸν ἐκ τέκνων ἔνεκα ἡδονῆς ἀλλ᾽ ἡδονῆς ἀμελὴς γυναῖκα, τὸν τε μισθὸν ἀπέχει, ἢ παρρησίαν αὐτῷ πρὸς τὰς γενομένας ἐκ ἀπολείποντος, οἷς αὐτὸ τὸ γενέσθαι πεπίστευκεν ὀνειδή." So that these words agree with one another, they must be rendered in this way: "He who makes light of the honour of marriage plainly shows that he takes a wife for the sake of pleasure and not for the sake of children, and he forbids his own reward, and he has left himself no freedom of speech before the children born to him, for whom being born itself is a reproach." The phrase "ἀπέχει ἢ μισθὸν," "forbids his reward," refers to the maintenance which children born in wedlock were free to demand from their parents by law. I do not believe Plutarch ever dreamed of the distinction between worldly and heavenly reward. I am the more inclined to this view because the same word occurs in the same sense in Plutarch's On the Obsolescence of Oracles near the end, (perhaps elsewhere too): "nothing forbids the prophetic spirit" (ὡς ἓν ἀπέχει τὴν μαντικὴν ἀναδυμίασιν) and so on. The same phrase may be found most clearly in Dionysius of Halicarnassus in exactly this sense: "No fear shall prevent me from saying what I think" (Οὐδείς με ἀφέξει φόβος μὴ οὐχ ἃ φρονῶ λέγειν). In short, it is pointless to take refuge in a mystical sense when we have a literal one, and I think this is how the parallel passages should be understood.

units.la: C. 9 v. 5. & 6. Vulgaris punctatio & importuna versuum divisio & parenthesis ita involvunt sensum, ut non fine causa dixerit Erasmus, Orationem esse duriusculam. Ut vero facilis & plana fiat, distinguantur tantum verba, & punctentur prout sequitur v. 5. Τί γάρ ἐστιν εὐκοπώτερον, εἰπεῖν, ἀφίενταί σοι αἱ ἁμαρτίαι, ἢ εἰπεῖν, Ἔγειρε καὶ περιπάτει, ἵνα δὲ εἰδῆτε ὅτι ἐξουσίαν ἔχει ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἀφιέναι ἁμαρτίας; v. 6. τότε λέγει τῷ παραλυτικῷ· Ἔγειρε ἆρόν σου τὸν κράβαττον, καὶ ὕπαγε εἰς τὸν οἶκόν σου. (Cu. v. 5. Virum enim est facilius dicere, remittuntur tibi peccata, an dicere, surge & ambula, sed ut sciatis quod filius hominis habet potestatem in terra remittendi peccata? 6. Tunc ait Paralytico, surge & tolle lectum tuum, & abi domum. Vulgarissima loquendi formula posthabita tantum interrogatione, Quasi diceret, Jesu sentiens cogitationes eorum, quod dicebant intra se, eum blasphemare, quia dixit Paralytico, remittuntur tibi peccata, dixit eis, unum idemque est mihi dicere, remittuntur tibi peccata, & surge & ambula, sed ut vos sciatis me habere potestatem in terra remittendi peccata, ideo dixi Paralytico, remittuntur tibi peccata. Sæpissimè siletur quod intelligitur, & tum demum, ut viderent utrumque sibi esse ex æquo facile, jubet Paralyticum surgere & tollere lectum, & abire domum, prout immediatè fecit.
units.tr: Matt. 9:5-6. The usual punctuation and the awkward division of the verses and the parenthesis so muddle the sense that Erasmus was not wrong to say the expression is somewhat harsh. To make it easy and plain, let the words alone be divided and pointed as follows in verse 5: "For which is easier, to say, Your sins are forgiven you, or to say, Arise and walk? But that you may know that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins?" Verse 6: "Then he says to the paralytic, Arise, take up your bed and go home." (Latin version as printed: "For is it easier to say, your sins are forgiven you, or to say, arise and walk? But that you may know that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins; then he says to the paralytic..."). The most common way of speaking is simply to drop the question mark. As if he said: Jesus, perceiving their thoughts, since they were saying to themselves that he blasphemed because he had said to the paralytic, "Your sins are forgiven," said to them: it is all one to me to say, "Your sins are forgiven," and to say, "Arise and walk." But so that you may know that I have power on earth to forgive sins, I said to the paralytic, "Your sins are forgiven." What is understood is very often left unsaid. Then at last, so that they might see that both are equally easy for him, he bids the paralytic arise, take up his bed and go home, which he did at once.

units.la: V. 18. Ἀρτι ἐτελεύτησεν, Filia mea propè defuncta est. Neque enim omnino fuisse mortuam, patet ex historia in locis parallelis, Mar. 5. 23. & Luc. 8. 42. ἄρτι enim significat etiam τὸ ὑπάρχον, vicinum, & τὸ μέλλον γίνεσθαι, quod brevi vel illico futurum est. Phav.
units.tr: Matt. 9:18, "My daughter has just now died" [Ἄρτι ἐτελεύτησεν]. That she was not altogether dead is clear from the parallel accounts, Mark 5:23 and Luke 8:42. For ἄρτι means also "what is present, near at hand," and "what is about to happen, which will be soon or immediately." Phavorinus.

units.la: V. 23. Τὸς αὐλητὰς, Tibicines. Maxime ad rem hujus loci facit quod servus in Virgilium; Majoris ætatis funera ad tubam proferebantur, minoris ad tibiam. Quod etiam tetigit Statius. Tibia cui teneros suetum producere manes Pelopen monstrâsse ferebant Exequiale sacrum carmenq; minoribus umbris Utile.
units.tr: Matt. 9:23, "the pipers" [τοὺς αὐλητάς]. What Servius says on Virgil is very much to the point here: "The funerals of persons of greater age were conducted with the trumpet, those of younger persons with the pipe." Statius also touched on this: "The pipe, which they said Pelops first showed how to produce for tender shades, a sacred funeral song, and useful for lesser ghosts."

units.la: Vocatur enim hoc loco hæc præfectî filia κοράσιον, puellula, Mar. 5. 23. θυγάτριον, filiola, & Luc. 8. 42. ὡς ἐτῶν δώδεκα, filia circiter duodecim annorum.
units.tr: For this daughter of the ruler is called here κοράσιον, "little girl," in Mark 5:23; θυγάτριον, "little daughter," in Luke 8:42; and "about twelve years old" [ὡς ἐτῶν δώδεκα].

units.la: Cap. 10. v. 11. Ἐξετάσατε τίς ἐν αὐτῇ ἄξιός ἐστι, exquirite quis in ea dignus sit, & manete illic. Dignus, i. e. dignus apud quem maneatis. Siletur τὸ κοσμούμενον & suppletur ex verbis præcedentibus vel subsequentibus: ut Matth. 22. 8. οἱ κεκλημένοι οὐκ ἦσαν ἄξιοι. Invitati non erant digni, i.e. digni paratis nuptiis; Noluerunt enim venire, sed abierunt alius ad villam, alius ad negotiationem suam, &c. Et Apocal. 3. 4. Ambulabunt mecum in stolis albis, ὅτι ἄξιοί εἰσιν, quoniam digni sunt, nempe ut ambulent, quia non inquinaverunt vestimenta sua. Et 16. 6. Sanguinem eis dedisti bibere, ἄξιοί γάρ εἰσιν, Digni enim
units.tr: Matt. 10:11, "Inquire who in it is worthy, and stay there" [Ἐξετάσατε τίς ἐν αὐτῇ ἄξιός ἐστιν]. "Worthy," that is, worthy to have you as guests. The word which is to be supplied (τὸ κοσμούμενον) is left unsaid and must be understood from the words before or after, as in Matt. 22:8, "those who were invited were not worthy" [οἱ κεκλημένοι οὐκ ἦσαν ἄξιοι], that is, not worthy of the wedding feast; for they would not come, but went away, one to his farm, another to his business, and so on. And Rev. 3:4, "They shall walk with me in white robes, for they are worthy" [ὅτι ἄξιοί εἰσιν], that is, worthy to walk so, because they have not defiled their garments. And Rev. 16:6, "You have given them blood to drink, for they are worthy" [ἄξιοί γάρ εἰσιν].

units.la: Digni enim sunt, i. e. digni ut bibant sanguinem, quoniam sanguinem Sanctorum & Prophetarum effuderunt. In utramque partem vox accipitur, prout variatur sensus.
units.tr: "For they are worthy," that is, worthy to drink blood, since they have shed the blood of saints and prophets. The word is taken in each sense according to how the meaning changes.

units.la: V. 17. Πεφυλάχετε ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, cave ab his hominibus, i. e. à lupis, inter quos sum vos missurus. v. 16. ὡς pro ὡσεί, quod adeo familiare. vide animad. in c. 11. v. 19. & alibi.
units.tr: V. 17. Πεφυλάχετε ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων [Beware of men]: beware of these men, that is, of wolves, among whom I am about to send you. v. 16. ὡς [as] for ὡσεί [as if], which is so common. See the animad. on chapter 11, v. 19, and elsewhere.

units.la: V. 23. Οὐ τελέσητε, non obieritis, i. e. Praedicando non peregrabitis omnes civitates Israel, donec veniat filius hominis, nempe ad excidium Hierosolymæ.
units.tr: V. 23. Οὐ τελέσητε [you will not finish]: you will not have gone over, that is, by preaching, all the cities of Israel, until the Son of Man comes, namely to the destruction of Jerusalem.

units.la: C. 11. v. 19. Ἡ σοφία, ἡ frequenter intelligitur pro ζωή, ut Luc. 21. 23, & alibi. Sic apud Hesychium, τῶ ἡ πάντων. Sic etiam Mar. 6. 2. καὶ τίς ἡ σοφία ἡ δοθεῖσα αὐτῷ; recte vertit opinor Beza, & quae est haec sapientia quae data est ei? Ut non minus etiam recte & apte hoc loco vertitur: Et justificata est haec sapientia à filiis suis, additur à Luca, omnibus nempe à Scribis & Pharisæis, qui se solos putarunt sapientiæ filios, qui sederunt in cathedra Mosis, & amabant vocari Rabbi, justificârunt illi sapientiam, quæ noluit attendere ad vocem vel Christi vel Baptistæ hortantium ad resipiscentiam.
units.tr: C. 11. v. 19. Ἡ σοφία [wisdom] is often understood for ζωή [life], as in Luke 21. 23 and elsewhere. So in Hesychius: τῶ ἡ πάντων. So also Mark 6. 2: καὶ τίς ἡ σοφία ἡ δοθεῖσα αὐτῷ [and what wisdom is this that is given to him?]. I think Beza translates it rightly, quae est haec sapientia quae data est ei? [what is this wisdom that is given to him?]. But the same word is rendered no less rightly and aptly here: Et justificata est haec sapientia à filiis suis [and wisdom is justified by her children]. Luke adds omnibus [all], namely the Scribis [scribes] and Pharisæis [Pharisees], who thought themselves alone the sons of wisdom, who sat in the chair of Mosis [Moses] and loved to be called Rabbi [Rabbi]. They justified that wisdom which refused to heed the voice of either Christi [Christ] or Baptistæ [the Baptist] urging repentance.

units.la: C. 12. V. 18. Καὶ κείων τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἀπαγγελεῖ, ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλῃ εἰς νῖκος τῶν κείων. Et judicium annuntiabit gentibus usque dum proferat judicium in æternum, vel in victoria. Quæ intervenient Parenthesi includenda. κείων ἔοικε τῷ νόμον ἀγαλεῖν, Judicium vocat legem suam; τῶν ἀπ' ἐκκλησίας διδάσκων, Ecclesiæ administrationem, Procop. in Isai. i. e. Evangelium: εἰς νῖκος, recte satis, in æternum, ut in veteri intelligunt, & vertunt LXX ... 2 Sam. 2. 26. Job. 36. 7. Jerem. 3. 5. & alibi: vel in victoria ita ut Evangelium gelium gelium triumphabit in Gentilismum, conversis ad ejus nomen universis gentibus. 'Ουκ εείσει &c. non contendet &c. quae in Parenthesi includuntur, monstrant in promulgando Evangelium lenitatem.
units.tr: C. 12. V. 18. Καὶ κείων τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἀπαγγελεῖ, ἕως ἂν ἐκβάλῃ εἰς νῖκος τῶν κείων [And he will declare judgement to the Gentiles, until he brings forth judgement unto victory]: And he will announce judgement to the Gentiles until he brings forth judgement to eternity, or to victory. What comes between is to be enclosed in a parenthesis. κείων [judgement] seems to be what he calls his law, Judicium vocat legem suam; and the teaching from the Church, Ecclesiae administrationem, the administration of the Church, according to Procopius on Isaiah, that is, the Gospel. εἰς νῖκος [unto victory] is fairly rendered in æternum [for ever], as they understand it in the Old Testament, and the LXX translate it so: 2 Sam. 2. 26; Job 36. 7; Jer. 3. 5, and elsewhere. Or in victoria [in victory], so that the Gospel will triumph over the Gentile world, with all the nations converted to his name. The words 'Ουκ ἐρίσει [he will not strive] etc., non contendet etc., which are enclosed in the parenthesis, show the gentleness in proclaiming the Gospel.

units.la: V. 20. Λίνον τυφόμενον ὁ σβέσει, Lucernam moribundam non extinguet. Linum per Metonymiam est Ellychnium, τυφόμενον, μαρανόμενον, marcescens, Hesych. in ɩ eb. ɩ ɩ ɔ fumigans, ferè extinctum. Kirch. Moribundum legit Persicus, Caligans aliqui. Vide Job. 13. 25.
units.tr: V. 20. Λίνον τυφόμενον οὐ σβέσει [a smoking wick he will not quench], a dying lamp he will not extinguish. Linum [wick] by metonymy means the wick of a lamp. τυφόμενον [smoking] means μαρανόμενον [withering], marcescens [wilting], according to Hesychius, and fumigans [smoking], almost extinguished. Kircher. The Persian reads moribundum [dying]; some read caligans [dim]. See Job 13. 25.

units.la: V. 43. Δι ἀνύδρων τόπων, per desertum. Æthiop. Sic Hebræum מדבר, quod proprie significat solitudinem, vel desertum, LXX saepius reddunt ἀνύδρῳ, ut Psal. 106. 14. ἐν ἐπιέσσαν ἀ Θεὸν ἐν ἀνύδρῳ, & tentarunt Deum in deserto; & Isai 43. 19. ἐν ἐν τῇ ἀνύδρῳ ποταμούς, & in deserto fluvios. Parabolam aptavit Dominus ad opinionem vulgi, quae forte fuit eadem quam meminit Psellus de Daemoniis, πῶς γὰρ μυχαιτέρας τόπους συνδυάζουσι ψυχὰς ἑαυτῶν ἐν ἀνίκ- μοις ἔσται, quod versentur in locis penitissimis, quae extremè frigida sunt & sicca. Neque fuit haec vana opinio: dicitur enim Matth. 4. 1. Jesum subductum fuisse à Diabolo, ut tentaretur, in deser- tum, in loca ubi ipse maximè versabatur. Daemones enim apud Syros vocantur שדין, vel שאדיין, à שדד, vastavit, eò quòd habitent in locis vastis & desertis. Schindl.
units.tr: V. 43. Δι᾽ ἀνύδρων τόπων [through waterless places], per desertum [through the desert]. Ethiopic. So the Hebrew midbar [מדבר], which properly means solitude or desert. The LXX often render it ἀνύδρῳ [waterless], as in Ps. 106. 14: ἐπείρασαν τὸν Θεὸν ἐν ἀνύδρῳ [they tempted God in the waterless place], and Isa. 43. 19: ἐν τῇ ἀνύδρῳ ποταμούς [rivers in the waterless place]. The Lord fitted the parable to the opinion of the common people, which was perhaps the same as the one Psellus mentions about demons: πῶς γὰρ ... ἐν ἀνύδροις ἔσται [for how ... will they be in waterless places], because they dwell in the most remote places, which are extremely cold and dry. Nor was this an empty opinion, for at Matt. 4. 1 it is said that Jesus was led by the Devil into the desert to be tempted, into the places where he himself most often dwelt. Among the Syrians demons are called shedin [שדין] or shedayin [שאדיין], from shadad [שדד], to lay waste, because they dwell in waste and desert places. Schindler.

units.la: C. 13 v. 44. ἐκρυψε, celavit. Fuit Thesaurus jam occultus & abconditus, quem inventum celavit ne aliis innotesceret. Frustrà vero fuisset rursus abscondere, quod jam erat abscondidum.
units.tr: C. 13 v. 44. ἔκρυψε [he hid], he concealed. It was a treasure already hidden and buried, which the finder concealed so that it would not become known to others. It would have been pointless to hide again what was already hidden.

units.la: C. 15. v. 5. Ὅμεῖς δὲ λέγετε, ὃς ἂν εἴπῃ τῷ πατρὶ ἢ τῇ μητρὶ, Δῶρον, ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς, τό πονηρόν &c. Frustrà est repetere varias in hunc locum expositiones Interpretum, liceat mihi tantùm meam addere. Sensus ergò supplendus, ut opinor ego cum aliis in Vatablo nominatis, in Mar.7. 11. ex præcedentibus, quæ vel subaudiuntur, vel mutatis mutandis sunt από τῶ κοινῶ repetenda, ut sæpè alibi fieri solet; & vertendum in hunc modum. Nam Deus mandavit, honora patrem tuum, & matrem tuam, &c. Vos autem dicitis, [honorabo patrem suum, & matrem suam] quisquis dixerit patri vel matri, Donum [est] quicquid juvatus fueris ex meo, & non honorabit (nempe in posterum) patrem suum vel matrem suam, & irritum fecistis mandatum Dei per traditionem vestram. Atque ita debere exponi, ut licitè fieri potest; τό ἱκ ἔστι quod sequitur in Marco, strenuè sinnuit si non plane indicat: in eo enim quòd dicit, ἱκ ἔστι ἀφιετε &c. non finitis eum amplius aliquid facere patri vel matri suæ, clarè monstrat filium antea quàm dicaverat Deo, ut (τό διακονικόν hoc loco significat) quicquid habuit quo parentem aleret, fecisse aliquid patri vel matri suæ, i.e. persolvisse eis debitum alimoniæ. Dictum videtur de filio, qui piè solitus est parentem alere secundùm legem Mosaicam, usque dum edoctus est à Pharisæo, quomodo eluderet præceptum Dei, & cum specie etiam sanctitatis fraudaret eos alimoniâ. Ac si diceret filius, cùm parentes, ut fecissent antea, jam rursus peterent alimoniam; Non possum ego nunc vos juvare amplius, quicquid enim habeo est jam devotum Deo: à quo voto, semel obstrictâ, non poteramus absolvi, adeò ut si filius, qui jam suâ voto devovisset Deo, beneficentiâ suâ parentem adjuvaret, violati voti reus fieret, secundùm illud Num 30. 2. Atque hæc fuit egregia Pharisæorum sanctitas quam docebant populum
units.tr: Mark 15:5. "But you say, whoever says to father or mother, 'Whatever you might have gained from me is a gift,' [Ὅμεῖς δὲ λέγετε, ὃς ἂν εἴπῃ τῷ πατρὶ ἢ τῇ μητρὶ, Δῶρον, ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς] ... and so on. It is pointless to repeat the various interpretations of the Interpreters on this passage; let me add only my own. The sense must be supplied, as I think, with others named in Vatablus, from what precedes, which either is understood or, with the necessary changes, must be repeated [ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ] from the common material, as often happens elsewhere. It should be rendered in this way: "For God commanded, Honour your father and your mother, etc. But you say, [I will honour his father and his mother] whoever says to father or mother, 'It is a gift whatever you might have been helped with from me,' and he will not honour (namely from now on) his father or his mother, and you have made void the commandment of God through your tradition." And it must be explained this way, as can be done legitimately. The words [τὸ ἐὰν ἔστι] that follow in Mark strongly suggest this, if they do not plainly show it: for in what he says, [οὐκ ἔστι ἀφιέναι] etc., "you no longer allow him to do anything for his father or mother," he clearly shows that the son, before he had dedicated it to God, had done something for his father or mother, that is (the word [διακονικόν] here means this), whatever he had with which to support his parent, i.e. had paid them the debt of maintenance. It seems to be said of a son who had been accustomed to support his parent devoutly according to the Mosaic law, until he was taught by a Pharisee how he might evade the command of God and, under a show of holiness, defraud them of maintenance. It is as if the son were saying, when the parents, as they had done before, now again asked for maintenance: "I can no longer help you, for whatever I have is now devoted to God." From such a vow, once bound, we could not be released, so that if a son, who had already vowed his goods to God, aided his parent by his kindness, he would become guilty of a broken vow, according to that passage in Num. 30:2. And this was the remarkable holiness of the Pharisees, which they taught the people.

units.la: {c} C populum. Dum filius fictum persolvit votum Deo, honorat patrem, nec prævaricatur legem Mosis, etsi perire sinat: χ᾽ ὕπως ἐμέε̈ζον αὐτὰ μὴ τὴν παιδῶν τὰ χρήματα, & sic ipsi cum filiis partiebantur opes. Theophyl. ἐξ ἐμοῦ, recte vertitur ex meo, sive ex re mea, sic τὸ ἐμὸν, res mea, apud Sophoclem. Rogabit vero forte aliquis quid sibi vult honorat & non honorabit? Expeditur in hunc modum; honorat parentem voto suo (secundùm Pharisæum) faciendo Deum eis propitium propter votum quod ei voverat, non tamen de futuro honorabit eum alimoniâ, quia quicquid habet est jam dicatum Deo, depositum in ærario in usum templi, i. e. revera in commodum Sacerdotum.
units.tr: {c} C populum. When the son pays a feigned vow to God, he honours his father and does not transgress the law of Moses, even if he lets him perish; χ᾽ ὕπως ἐμέε̈ζον αὐτὰ μὴ τὴν παιδῶν τὰ χρήματα [garbled in the source], and so they themselves shared the wealth with the sons. Theophylact. ἐξ ἐμοῦ is rightly rendered ex meo, from what is mine, or from my property; thus τὸ ἐμὸν, my property, in Sophocles. But someone may perhaps ask, what does honorat & non honorabit [he honours and will not honour] mean? It is explained in this way: he honours his parent by his vow (according to the Pharisee), by making God propitious to them because of the vow he had made to him; but he will not honour him in future with maintenance, because whatever he has is now dedicated to God, deposited in the treasury for the use of the temple, that is, in fact, for the advantage of the priests.

units.la: Cap. 16. v. 28. Amen dico vobis, sunt quidam ex his qui adstant, qui non gustabunt mortem, donec videant filium hominis venientem in regno suo. Locus iste vix mysticè, literaliter verò non potest intelligi, nisi de adventu Christi ad excidium Hierosolymæ, qui tum verè venit in regno suo, ut triumphum ageret in Judæos, justam & severissimam capiendo in eos ultionem. Quosdam verò adstantium in vivis remansisse usque ad eum diem, & verum est & notum. Atque in hoc sensu verum est, Amen dico vobis, non præteribit generatio ista, donec hæc omnia fiant, 24, 34. Nec ante hoc tempus adventûs ejus pertransierunt discipuli omnes civitates Israel, 10. 23. Atque in hoc sensu remansit Johannes inter alios in vivis, usque dum venit Christus. Joh. 21. 22.
units.tr: Cap. 16. v. 28. Amen dico vobis, sunt quidam ex his qui adstant, qui non gustabunt mortem, donec videant filium hominis venientem in regno suo. [Truly I say to you, there are some of those standing here who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.] This passage can hardly be understood mystically, and literally it can only be understood of Christ's coming to the destruction of Jerusalem, when he truly came in his kingdom, to triumph over the Jews, taking just and most severe vengeance upon them. That some of those standing there remained alive until that day is both true and well known. And in this sense it is true: Amen dico vobis, non praeteribit generatio ista, donec haec omnia fiant [Truly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things happen], 24. 34. Nor before this time of his coming had all the disciples gone through the cities of Israel, 10. 23. And in this sense John remained alive among the others until Christ came, John 21. 22.

units.la: Cap. 17. v. 11. Καὶ ἀποκαταστήσει πάντα, & consummabit omnia. Sic 11. 13. Omnes enim Prophetæ prophetârunt, & lex fuit usque ad Johannem, dictum per Hyperbaton, ut explanat Lucas 16. 16. Lex & prophetæ usque ad Johannem, in eo habuere consummationem sive finem. Apud Hesychium & Pharorinum, ἀποκαταστάσεως, τελέωσις, & apud utrosque, ut opinor, perperam ἀποκαταπῆνυσαι, τελεῶ-σαι, pro ἀποκατασῆσαι, τελειῶσαι.
units.tr: Cap. 17. v. 11. Καὶ ἀποκαταστήσει πάντα [and he will restore all things], and he will consummate all things. So in 11. 13: For all the Prophets prophesied, and the law was until John, a statement made by hyperbaton, as Luke 16. 16 explains: The law and the prophets until John; in him they had their consummation or end. In Hesychius and Photius, ἀποκατάστασις means τελέωσις [completion]; and in both, I think, wrongly, ἀποκατα πῆνυσαι and τελεῶ-σαι stand for ἀποκατασῆσαι and τελειῶσαι.

units.la: V. 21. Τῦτο δὲ τὸ γένος οὐκ ἐκπορεύ-εται εἰ μὴ ἐν προσευχῇ καὶ νηστείᾳ: Hoc vero genus non egreditur nisi per orationem & jejunium. De dæmoniis plerumque interpretantur, quasi esset præ cæteris malignum quoddam genus dæmonum, ad quos ejiciendos opus foret prece & jejunio. Dixit vero eis Jesus versu præcunte, διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν ὑμῶν, propter inopiam vestram fidei non potuistis ejicere, si vero habeatis fidem sicut granum sinapis, i. e. ut Beza, quantulum est granum sinapis, nihil impossibile erit vobis. Non dixit propter defectum orationis & jejunii. Vocantur γενεὰ ἄπιστος, generatio incredula, quia non poterant ejicere. Mar. 9. 18. 19. Adeo ut præsentia verba respondeant aptius, si de fide exponantur, idque eo magis, quia γενεὰ & γενεῶ sæpius idem significant. Hæc vero generatio [i e. hominum qui habent fidem sicut granum sinapis] non procedit vel progreditur nisi precibus & jejunio. Per fidem solam ejecerunt dæmonia, fides vero illa non erat à Deo impetranda, nisi fervidâ prece & jejunio. Neque est credibile, cum ejicienda essent dæmonia, quæ inexpectato sæpius occurrebant, eos, priusquam ejicerent, postulâsse sibi tempus jejunandi. Parallelum etiam illud Marci, ubi dixit eis Jesus, τοῦτο τὸ γένος ἐν οὐδενὶ δύναται ἐξελθεῖν &c. hoc genus nullo modo potest exire nisi prece & jejunio, fortius arguit de fide esse, ut antea exponendum: Improprium enim foret dicere, dæmoniorum genus non posse exire nisi prece & jejunio, impotentiam dæmoniis imputando, quæ fuit in discipulis propter inopiam fidei. Quod si intellexisset Jesus dæmoniorum genus, respondisset (opinor) plane & apposite, ἐν ᾧ δύναμι ἐκβάλλεσθαι, nullo modo potest ejici nisi prece & jejunio. Notandum vero, τὸ ἐξελθεῖν, hoc etiam loco melius exponi, si vertatur, nullo modo potest progredi vel procedere. Ἐξελθεῖν enim apud Authores quandoque significat progredi vel procedere, i. e. in altiorem statum evehi; ut ἐξέρχονται εἰς τὰς ἐφήβους, progrediuntur vel procedunt in ephebos. Xenoph.
units.tr: V. 21. "But this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting" [Τοῦτο δὲ τὸ γένος οὐκ ἐκπορεύεται εἰ μὴ ἐν προσευχῇ καὶ νηστείᾳ]: This kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting. Commentators mostly explain this of demons, as if there were a certain kind of demon more malignant than the rest, which needed prayer and fasting to be cast out. But Jesus, in the preceding verse, had said to them: "Because of your unbelief; for lack of faith you could not cast it out. If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed," that is, as Beza puts it, "however small a grain of mustard seed is, nothing will be impossible for you." He did not say "because of lack of prayer and fasting." They are called "an unbelieving generation" [γενεὰ ἄπιστος], an incredulous generation, because they could not cast the demon out (Mark 9:18, 19). So the words before us fit better if they are explained of faith, and all the more so because γενεά and γενεῶ often mean the same thing. This generation [that is, of men who have faith like a grain of mustard seed] does not come forth or proceed except by prayer and fasting. They cast out demons by faith alone; but that faith was not to be obtained from God except by fervent prayer and fasting. Nor is it credible that, when demons had to be cast out, which often appeared unexpectedly, the disciples asked for time to fast before they cast them out. The parallel passage in Mark, where Jesus said to them, "This kind can by no means come out except by prayer and fasting" [τοῦτο τὸ γένος ἐν οὐδενὶ δύναται ἐξελθεῖν], argues more strongly that it concerns faith, as explained above. For it would be an improper way of speaking to say that the kind of demons could not come out except by prayer and fasting, imputing an inability to the demons, when the inability lay in the disciples through lack of faith. If Jesus had meant a kind of demons, he would (I think) have answered plainly and to the point: "which kind [ἐν ᾧ δύναμι ἐκβάλλεσθαι] can by no means be cast out except by prayer and fasting." It should also be noted that τὸ ἐξελθεῖν would be better rendered here, if translated, can by no means proceed or advance. For in the authors ἐξελθεῖν sometimes means to proceed or advance, that is, to be raised to a higher state; as in Xenophon, ἐξέρχονται εἰς τὰς ἐφήβους, they advance into the ephebi.

units.la: Cap. 22. v. 13. Tunc dixit Rex famulis, ligatis pedibus & manibus ejus, tollite eum & ejicite eis τὸ σκότος καὶ τὸ ἐξώτερον, in tenebras exteriores, i.e. a cælo remotissimas, ut Grotius; ἐξώτερος & ἐξώτατος. Phavor. Vulgatissimum enim est comparativa poni pro superlativis. Quis vero non ex his verbis mutuatum esse credat Senecam illud in Agamemnone.
units.tr: Chap. 22. v. 13. "Then the king said to the servants, bind his feet and hands, take him away and cast him out" [εἰς τὸ σκότος καὶ τὸ ἐξώτερον], into the outer darkness, that is, the most remote from heaven, as Grotius puts it.
