(Compare ἐξώτερος and ἐξώτατος in Phavorinus.) For it is very common for comparatives to be used in place of superlatives. Who would not believe that Seneca took that line in his Agamemnon from these words?

units.la: Abripite famuli monstrum & avectum proculVincite scelum noste tenebrosi specus.
units.tr: Servants, drag the monster away and carry him far off; bind the criminal in the gloom of our dark cave.

units.la: Idem enim valent procul, & τὸ ἐξώτερον; quale est illud etiam in Virgilio, Pallentes umbras Erebi, noctemque profundam, i e. cujus fundus quàm longissimè procul est. In quo sensu licitè & aptè exponi reor Sap. Sol. 17. 2. μακρὰς πεδύτας ζυγῶν, longinquis; i.e. profundæ captivi noctis, μακρὰς pro μακρὰν ἀπόστασιν, procul distantis noctis. De loco enim dicitur μακρὸς, etiam ut de tempore. Sic legimus apud Plutarchum in Alcibiade, διαπόντιον καὶ μακρὰν στρατείαν transmarinam & procul distantem expeditionem; & apud Lucam. 15. 13. ἀπεδήμησεν εἰς χώραν μακρὰν, peregrè profectus est in regionem longinquam.
units.tr: For procul and τὸ ἐξώτερον have the same force, as in the line of Virgil, the pale shadows of Erebus and the deep night, that is, a night whose depth lies very far off. In this sense, I think, Wisdom 17:2 can be fairly and aptly explained: "long [μακρὰς] chains of darkness", that is, of the deep night of captivity, with μακρὰς standing for μακρὰν ἀπόστασιν, a night distant far away. For μακρός is said of place as well as of time. So we read in Plutarch's Alcibiades, διαπόντιον καὶ μακρὰν στρατείαν, an expedition across the sea and far away; and in Luke 15:13, ἀπεδήμησεν εἰς χώραν μακρὰν, he went abroad into a far country.

units.la: C. 24. v. 22. Et nisi breviatis forent dies illi, non non servaretur ulla caro, sed propter electos breviabuntur dies illi. Maxime recepta hujus loci interpretatio est hujusmodi. Tot & tam atroces fuisse in Jerusalem mutuas cædes (quod jam prædixit Christus,) ut nisi valde accelerata fuisset urbis obsidio, non fuisset ullus relictus in vivis, sed ipsi se mutuo trucidàssent universi, & funditus extirpàssent. At quoniam habuit Deus electos suos in civitate, quos servari voluit, & ex publicâ calamitate liberari, accelerare fecit Titum & Vespasianum obsidionem modis omnibus quibuscunque, atque ita dies illos breviari. Verum potest & alter dari hujus loci sensus non minus accommodus, capiendo vocem ἐκολοβώθησαν secundum phrasin sacræ Scripturæ. Et nisi dies illi, i. e. excidii Hierosolymæ, breviati forent, Judæorum nullus salvaretur: nam quamdiu Templum stetit, & sacrificia, cæremoniæ & ritus Judaici manebant, talis erat petra scandali universæ genti, ut fere omnes in eam impingerent, nec pauci indies devenerunt Apostatæ à Christianâ fide quam antea fuerant amplexati, eo forte nomine & scrupulo, quod ipsorum vetus religio esset verior, quia sivit Deus manere eorum Templum & sacrificia, de quorum certâ & brevi futurâ abolitione edocti fuerant in Christianâ fide. Ob quam etiam causam videtur eos exhortari Author Ep. ad Heb. 10.25. ut non deserarent congregationem credentium, ut quibusdam mos erat, sed ut hortarentur seipsos invicem ut manerent in fide, idque tanto magis, quod viderent diem illum appropinquantem, i.e. diem decurtationis, diem excidii Hierosolymæ, & desolationis Templi. Namque ita dies ille hic & alibi, ut & adventus Domini, & finis omnium, referuntur ad excidium Hierosolymæ.
units.tr: Chap. 24. v. 22. "And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would have been saved, but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened." The most accepted interpretation of this passage is the following. There were so many and so savage mutual slaughters in Jerusalem (as Christ had already foretold) that, unless the siege of the city had been greatly hastened, no one would have been left alive, but all would have slaughtered one another and been utterly destroyed. But since God had his elect in the city, whom he wished to save and free from the public calamity, he caused Titus and Vespasian to hasten the siege by every means available, and so those days were shortened. But another sense of this passage, no less suitable, may also be given by taking the word ἐκολοβώθησαν [were shortened] according to the idiom of Holy Scripture: "And unless those days, that is, the days of the destruction of Jerusalem, had been shortened, no one of the Jews would have been saved." For as long as the Temple stood, and the sacrifices, ceremonies and rites of Judaism remained, the stone of stumbling was such for the whole nation that almost all stumbled over it, and not a few daily fell away from the Christian faith they had earlier embraced, perhaps on this pretext and scruple, that their old religion was truer, because God had allowed their Temple and sacrifices to remain, although they had been taught in the Christian faith of their certain and near abolition. For this reason also the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews seems to exhort them (10:25) "not to forsake the assembly of believers, as some were in the habit of doing, but to encourage one another to remain in the faith, and all the more because they saw that day drawing near", that is, the day of the shortening, the day of the destruction of Jerusalem and the desolation of the Temple. For that day is referred here and elsewhere to the destruction of Jerusalem, as are both the coming of the Lord and the end of all things.

units.la: V. 28. Ὅπου γάρ ἐὰν ᾖ τὸ πτῶμα, Ubicunque enim cadaver fuerit, ibi congregabuntur aquilæ. Cadaver notat statum Iudaicum jam expirantem, aquilæ, vexilla Romanorum, in quibus pingebantur aquilarum imagines. Sensus est ejusmodi; Quemadmodum aquilæ sagacitate excellentes frequenter comitantur exercitus expectatione prædæ post cladem, pari etiam modo Romanos milites praefiguratos in aquilis, quorum effigies portabant in vexillis, coactos fore in unum, ubi Iudaicus starus jacebat jam expiraturus, si non plane emortuus, sub spe etiam & expectatione prædæ. Quærebant discipuli, Luc. 17. 37. Ubi sierent, quæ prædixerat futura Dominus, ipse vero dixit eis, ὅπου τὸ σῶμα, &c. ubi corpus, ibi congregabuntur aquilæ, quasi expresse denotans desolationem & subitum exitium Iudæorum, de quibus jam antea verba fecerat, non posse alio loco evenire quàm in ipsis, ut factum est, Hierosolymis; idque in signum fore, desolationem ibi futuram, ubi Romani milites in unum cogerentur, ut factum est, ad obsidionem illius urbis. "Ὅταν δὲ ἴδητε κυκλουμένην &c. quum autem videritis Hierosolymam circundari ab exercitibus, tunc scitote quod immineat desolatio ejus. Luc. 21, 20.
units.tr: V. 28. "For wherever the carcass is, there the eagles will be gathered together" [Ὅπου γάρ ἐὰν ᾖ τὸ πτῶμα]. Carcass denotes the Jewish state, now breathing its last; eagles denote the standards of the Romans, on which images of eagles were painted. The sense is this: just as eagles, excelling in keenness of sight, often accompany armies in expectation of prey after a slaughter, so in the same way the Roman soldiers, prefigured by the eagles whose images they carried on their standards, would be gathered together where the Jewish nation lay, about to expire if not already quite dead, and in the hope and expectation of plunder. The disciples asked (Luke 17:37) where the things the Lord had foretold would happen. He himself said to them, "Where the body is [ὅπου τὸ σῶμα], there the eagles will be gathered together," as if plainly indicating that the desolation and sudden destruction of the Jews, of whom he had already spoken, could not happen in any place other than where they were, that is, in Jerusalem, as it did happen. And this would be the sign that the desolation would come upon the place where the Roman soldiers were gathered together, as happened at the siege of that city. "But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies [Ὅταν δὲ ἴδητε κυκλουμένην], then know that its desolation is at hand" (Luke 21:20).

units.la: Cap. 27. v. 9. 10. Τότε ἐπληρώθη τὸ ῥηθὲν διὰ Ἰερεμίου τοῦ προφήτου, λέγοντος, καὶ ἔλαβον τὰ τριάκοντα ἀργύρια (τὴν τιμὴν τοῦ τετιμημένου ὃν ἐτιμήσαντο) ἀπὸ τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ, καὶ ἔδωκαν αὐτὰ εἰς τὸν ἀγρὸν τοῦ κεραμέως, καθὰ συνέταξέ μοι ὁ Κύριος. Et accepi triginta argenteos (pretium æstimati quem æstimaverunt) à filiis Israel, quia vel illi dederunt eos pro agro figuli, sicut præcepit mihi Dominus. Atque ista distinctione & versione tollitur ἡ ἀκολουθία, & incoherentia loci; & verba illa, Quemadmodum præcepit mihi Dominus, referendent recte voci ἔλαβον, in persona prima, quo modo etiam legit Zacharias, καὶ ἔλαβον &c. primâ persona singulari, & accepi triginta argenteos, & projeci illos (sicut & hic etiam jam antea dictum retulisse eos Judam in Templum) εἰς τὸ οἶκον κυρίου εἰς τὸ χωνευτήριον, in domo Domini pro conflatorio, (ut vertunt Interpretes εἰς τ' ἀγροῦ κεραμέως, pro agro figuli,) ut filii Israel, nempe Sacerdotes, darent illos pro agro figuli, quod disertè dicitur v. 7. Nomen Jeremiæ errore aliquo insertum credo. Vocem καὶ in hoc sensu frequenter usurpari, abundè tritum est. Occurrit Ruth, 1. 11. μὴ ἔτι υἱοί γοι ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ μου, καὶ ἔσονταί υμῖν εἰς ἄνδρας; Nunquid ultra filii mihi in ventre meo, qui [vel & illi] erunt vobis in viros? In quo loco videtur esse Hebraismus; est enim in Hebræo יהיו. Sic etiam occurrit 2 Reg. 23. 29. וילך המלך יאשיהו לקראתו וימיתהו במכרו Et abiit Rex Josiah in occursum ejus, qui [vel & ille i. e. Pharaoh Necho] occidit eum in Megiddo. Reperiri est etiam apud Scriptores Ethnicos. Plutarchus habet in Timoleonte, ἐπίκινον τῆς στρατιωτικῆς, καὶ εἰς πεφυχῶς τὴν θεῶν ἐρέφοντο, monstrarunt eos militibus, qui [sive & illi] ad precandum Deos conversi sunt. Videre est etiam in recentiore, Ζεὺς γὰρ ἐν προμηθείᾳ λέγεις, ὦ ἄνδρες Λατῖνοι, ἡ ἔστιν ἀνοίκειον, statim enim in proœmio dicis, o viri Latini, quod [sive & illud] est insuetum Sigurop. Hist. Conc. Flor. vide Matth. 14.11. Mar. 1.9. & 10. Joh 15.6. 20. 18. Act. 6.6. & alibi.
units.tr: Chap. 27. vv. 9, 10. "Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: And they took the thirty pieces of silver (the price of him who was valued, whom they valued) from the children of Israel, and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord commanded me." I received thirty pieces of silver (the price of the one they valued), from the sons of Israel, because they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord directed me. By this punctuation and translation the sequence and the coherence of the passage are restored; and the words, as the Lord directed me, rightly refer to the word ἔλαβον, in the first person, as Zechariah also reads: καὶ ἔλαβον, etc., in the first person singular, "and I took thirty pieces of silver, and cast them" (as the text earlier says that Judas had also brought them back into the Temple) "into the house of the Lord, into the treasury" [εἰς τὸ οἶκον κυρίου εἰς τὸ χωνευτήριον], into the house of the Lord, for the smelting-house. (The translators render εἰς τ' ἀγροῦ κεραμέως as for the potter's field.) That the sons of Israel, namely the priests, gave them for the potter's field is stated plainly in verse 7. I believe the name of Jeremiah was inserted by some error. That καὶ is frequently used in this sense is well enough known. It occurs in Ruth 1:11: "Are there any more sons in my womb, who [or also they] will be your husbands?" Here there seems to be a Hebraism, for in the Hebrew it is יהיו [yihyu]. So also in 2 Kings 23:29: "And King Josiah went out to meet him, and he [or also he, that is, Pharaoh Necho] slew him at Megiddo" [וימיתהו]. It may also be found among the Gentile writers. Plutarch has in Timoleon that they showed them to the soldiers, who [or also they] turned to pray to the gods. It is found also in a later writer: "For you say at once in your preface, O Latin men, what [or also that] is unusual", as in Syropulus, Hist. Conc. Flor. See Matt. 14:11; Mark 1:9 and 10; John 15:6; 20:18; Acts 6:6, and elsewhere.

units.la: In Marcum.
units.tr: On Mark.

units.la: M A R.c.3.v.19,20,21. Καὶ ἔρχονται εἰς οἶκον, καὶ συνέρχεται πάλιν ὁ ὄχλος, ὥστε μὴ δύνασθαι αὐτοὺς μήτε ἄρτον φαγεῖν, καὶ ἀκούσαντες οἱ παρ' αὐτοῦ ἐξῆλθον κρατῆσαι αὐτόν· ἔλεγον γὰρ ὅτι ἐξέστη. Versione plerumque receptâ Jesus dicitur apud se non esse, vel extra se esse, interpretatione (si fas sit dicere) Filio Dei indigna nimis, præcipuè cùm modestior poterit dari sensus & constructio, idque magis etiam accommodus. Et veniunt in domum, & convenit iterum turba, adeo ut nè panem quidem possent edere, & audientes, sive quidam ab eo audientes exiverunt ut eam sisterent, vel comprimerent, dicebant enim quòd fureret. Scilicet, turba, quæ præ stupore vel vehementi desiderio ad Jesum appropinquandi, ita violenter irrueret, ut cibum non possent edere. Non est τὸ αὐτὸν relativum τῷ αὐτῷ, sed voci ὄχλῳ : κρατῆσαι apud Hesychium est μένειν, i. e. sistere, manere facere: καὶ ἀκούσαντες οἱ, dicitur frequenti trajectione pro οἱ ἀκούσαντες παρ' αὐτοῦ ἐξῆλθον, Et qui audiverunt, sive audientes quòd turba ita fureret, ab eo exiverunt ut eam cohiberent. Vel οἱ παρ' αὐτοῦ, secundum Grammaticos sunt, aliqui ab eo missi. Præterquam etiam quòd ipse Jesus erat intrà in domo, ita ut non posset commodè affirmari, eos qui audiverant exivisse extra domum, ut tenerent ipsum, qui erat in domo. Dicere etiam cognatos ejus è domiciliis exivisse ut tenerent ipsum, nec est congruum, nec omnino verisimile. Unde enim ad eos tam cita pervasit fama, ut undequaque derepente in unum cogerentur? quod si etiam forte id ita foret, τὸ προσηλυτον magis fuisset accommodum quàm ἐξῆλθον, advenerunt potius quàm exiverunt. Atque hanc interpretationem non possum mirari satis, cur exploserint eruditi, quæ cum sensu, & syntaxi, & more loquendi, & quod instar omnium, cum locis parallelis persectè convenit. Dicitur enim apud Matthæum, 12. 23. eodem loco & tempore, ipsissimo etiam verbo, ἐξίσταντο πάντες οἱ ὄχλοι &c. Obstupuit tota turba, i.e. ut interpretatur Beza, præ admiratione apud se non erat. Hoc tantùm discrepat, Matthæus habet ἐξίσταντο, in Passivo plurali, Marcus ἐξέστη in Actīvo singulari, quos verbo Synonymo (est enim apud Phavorinum, ἐξέστλω, ἐδαύμασαν, ἐξεπλάγησαν) interpretatur Lucas, 11. 14. καὶ ἐθαύμασαν οἱ ὄχλοι, Et mirata est turba. Loca esse parallela, ideóque pari modo exponenda, dubitabit nullus qui seriò inspexerit.
units.tr: Mark 3:19-21. "And they come into a house, and the crowd gathers again, so that they could not even eat bread; and when those from his side heard it, they went out to seize him, for they said he was beside himself." [Καὶ ἔρχονται εἰς οἶκον, καὶ συνέρχεται πάλιν ὁ ὄχλος, ὥστε μὴ δύνασθαι αὐτοὺς μήτε ἄρτον φαγεῖν, καὶ ἀκούσαντες οἱ παρ' αὐτοῦ ἐξῆλθον κρατῆσαι αὐτόν· ἔλεγον γὰρ ὅτι ἐξέστη.] In the version commonly received, Jesus is said not to be with himself, or to be outside himself. That rendering, if it may be called so, is far too unworthy of the Son of God, especially since a more modest sense and construction can be given, and one that fits the context better. And they come into the house, and the crowd comes together again, so that they could not even eat bread; and hearing this, those who were with him, or some of those who had heard him, went out to restrain him or hold him back, for they said that he was raving mad. That is, the crowd, in its amazement or its intense desire to approach Jesus, pressed in so violently that they could not eat. The αὐτὸν is not relative to τῷ αὐτῷ but refers to ὄχλῳ. In Hesychius, κρατῆσαι means μένειν, that is, to stop or keep in place. The clause καὶ ἀκούσαντες οἱ is, by a common transposition, equivalent to οἱ ἀκούσαντες παρ' αὐτοῦ ἐξῆλθον: And those who heard, or hearing that the crowd was raging in this way, went out from him to check it. Or οἱ παρ' αὐτοῦ, according to the grammarians, means some sent by him. Besides, Jesus himself was inside the house, so it cannot conveniently be said that those who had heard him went out of the house to seize him, who was in the house. Nor is it fitting or at all likely to say that his relatives came out of their homes to seize him. For from where did the report reach them so quickly that they were suddenly gathered together from every side? And even if it were so, τὸ προσηλυτον would have suited better than ἐξῆλθον: they came rather than went out. I cannot sufficiently wonder why learned men have rejected this interpretation, which agrees perfectly with the sense, the syntax, the manner of speaking, and, above all, with the parallel passages. For in Matthew 12:23, in the same place and at the same time, and even with the very same verb, we read ἐξίσταντο πάντες οἱ ὄχλοι, etc. The whole crowd was astonished, that is, as Beza interprets it, they were not themselves for amazement. The only difference is that Matthew has ἐξίσταντο, in the passive plural, while Mark has ἐξέστη, in the active singular. Luke, using a synonymous verb (in Phavorinus, ἐξέστλω, ἐδαύμασαν, ἐξεπλάγησαν), renders them at 11:14: καὶ ἐθαύμασαν οἱ ὄχλοι, And the crowd marvelled. That these are parallel passages, and so must be explained in the same way, no one who has looked at them seriously will doubt.

units.la: Cap. 9. v. 22, 23, 24, Ἀλλ' εἴ τι δύνασαι, βοήθησον ἡμῖν σπλαγχνισθεὶς ἐφ' ἡμᾶς. ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν αὐτῷ, τὸ εἰ δύνασαι πιστεῦσαι, πάντα δυνατὰ τῷ πιστεύοντι. Interpretes in hoc loco plerumque præterm ittunt articulum, τὸ, in quo videtur esse quædam emphasis nullo modo silenda. Nè pereat ergò emphasis, nec syntaxis violetur, distinguì velim verba ut suprà, & congruenter verti. Sed si quid potes, succurre nobis miserescens nostri, Jesus verò dixit ei, si potes? crede tu, omnia credenti possibilia. Tò accipitur hoc loco τεχνικῶς, & præsupponit materiam de qua agitur, nempè quæstionem de potentiâ Christi. Pater enim pueri, qui jam antea filium adduxerat ad discipulos, qui eum sanare non poterant διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν, propter inopiam fidei. ut dixit eis Iesus, Matth. 17.14. videtur dubitâsse, num etiam Christus cum sanare poterat, ideóque dixit, εἰ τι δύνατai, si tu quid potes, discipuli enim tui non possunt, miserere nostri. Cui Iesus respondet, illico corripiens eum cum indignatione propter incredulitatem, ac si diceret, An dubitas utrum ego possum? si potes, inquis? Crede tu, nec de mea potentia desepera, omnia enim credenti fieri possibilia. Qualia sunt verba ejus ad Centurionem, Matth. 8.13. & ad caecor, 9. 28. Atque hunc esse hujus loci sensum sequentia valde arguunt. Nam continuò pater pueri exclamans cum lachrymis aiebat, Credo, Domine, adjuva incredulitatem meam. Unicum hoc erat tempus, quo unquam quaestio facta est Christo de potentia ejus à quoquam, qui sanari ab eo petiit; vox enim vulgo fuit, Κύριε ἐὰν θέλῃς, δύνασαί με καθαρίσαι, Domine, si vis, potes me mundare. Matth. 8. 2. &, Dic verbum tantum & sanabitur puer meus. ibidem 8. De potentiâ nulla quaestio, voluntatem tantùm implorabant, adeò ut non fit omnino mirum Christum hoc loco exprobrare patri pueri incredulitatem ejus. Πιστεύω pro accentu potest esse vel Aoristus primus vocis mediae, vel Infinitivus Activa, subaudiendo θέλε vel μέλλνοσ, ut frequenter fieri solet.
units.tr: Chapter 9, verses 22-24. "But if you can do anything, help us, having compassion on us. And Jesus said to him, 'If you can believe, all things are possible to the one who believes.'" [Ἀλλ' εἴ τι δύνασαι, βοήθησον ἡμῖν σπλαγχνισθεὶς ἐφ' ἡμᾶς. ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν αὐτῷ, τὸ εἰ δύνασαι πιστεῦσαι, πάντα δυνατὰ τῷ πιστεύοντι.] The translators in this passage mostly pass over the article τό, in which there seems to be a certain emphasis that must in no way be ignored. So that the emphasis may not perish and the syntax may not be violated, I would have these words punctuated as above and translated accordingly: But if you can do anything, come to our help, having pity on us. But Jesus said to him, "If you can?" Believe, and all things are possible to the one who believes. The τό here is used technically and presupposes the matter under discussion, namely the question of Christ's power. For the father of the boy, who had earlier brought his son to the disciples, who could not heal him διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν, because of their lack of faith, as Jesus said to them (Matt. 17:14), seems to have doubted whether Christ too could heal, and so he said, εἰ τι δύνασαι, if you can do anything, for your disciples cannot, have pity on us. To this Jesus replies, rebuking him at once with indignation for his unbelief, as if he were saying: Do you doubt whether I am able? "If you can," you say? Believe, and do not despair of my power, for all things are possible to the one who believes. Words of this kind are those to the centurion (Matt. 8:13) and to the blind men (Matt. 9:28). That this is the sense of the passage is strongly confirmed by what follows. For immediately the father of the boy cried out with tears, I believe, Lord; help my unbelief. This was the only occasion on which anyone who sought healing from him ever raised a question with Christ about his power. The common form of request was: Lord, if you will, you can make me clean (Matt. 8:2), and Only speak the word and my servant will be healed (Matt. 8:8). There was no question about power; people only implored his will. So it is not at all surprising that Christ in this place reproaches the boy's father for his unbelief. The word πιστεύω, as to accent, may be either the first aorist of the middle voice or the infinitive of the active voice, with θέλε or μέλλνοσ understood, as often happens.

units.la: Cap. 11. v. 13. Οὐ γὰρ ἦν καιρὸς σύκων. Nondum enim erat tempus ficuum. For the time of figs was not yet. Quod si unquam dixerit aliquid opportune Vir Clarissimus, certè emendatio ejus in hoc loco est idonea, mutando spiritum lenem in asperum (non enim sunt accentus ab authore) & legendo ἢ γὰρ ἦν, & subintelligendo ἦν, quod frequens est singulis fere paginis. Ubi enim fuit, tempus erat ficuum. For where he was, was the time of figs. Atque ita historia perfecte quadrat, si referatur ad Judaeos, apud quos æquum erat Deo, si terrarum usquam, expectare fructum, fuit enim ibi certe idoneum si non inexcusabile tempus fructuum. At non est idoneum dicere, Christum e via divertisse cum esuriret, ut adiret a longe ficum sperans in ea fructum invenire, ubi jam antea sciret non esse tempus ficuum, praeterquam etiam quod fuisset durum nimis innocenti maledixisse ficui, si in eo loco non fuisset tempus ficuum. In eo loco dico, ut quorundam objectioni satisfiat, qui unum & idem fuisse simul volunt per totam Judaeam tempus ficuum, ideoque vanum fore legisse. Varia enim fuerunt etiam in Judaea climata licet parvula, ideoque etiam varia fructuum tempora, prout erat regio vel montana vel vallosa, vel meridionalis vel Arctica, &c. Nec possum reperire in authore quovis vel sacro vel prophano vocem καιρὸς significare feracem annum, ut putarunt aliqui, ita ut legitime possit verti, Non fuit enim tempus ferax ficuum, phrasi anglica, For it was not a fig peare. Et si detur, non fuisset minus durum maledixisse ficui, cum non esset annus ferax ficuum, quam si non fuisset adhuc tempus ficuum. ut semel dicam, Non fuit vitium vel in solo vel in tempore, sola maledictionis causa erat sterilitas in arbore.
units.tr: Chapter 11, verse 13. "For it was not the time of figs." [Οὐ γὰρ ἦν καιρὸς σύκων.] Nondum enim erat tempus ficuum. For the time of figs was not yet. If that most distinguished man has ever said anything to the purpose, his emendation in this passage is certainly appropriate: changing the soft breathing to the rough (the accents are not by the author), and reading ἢ γὰρ ἦν, and supplying ἦν, which occurs in almost every page. For where he was, was the time of figs. For where he was, was the time of figs. The history then fits perfectly if it is referred to the Jews, among whom it was fitting for God, if anywhere on earth, to expect fruit; for there it was certainly a suitable, if not an inexcusable, season for fruit. But it is not fitting to say that Christ turned aside from the road because he was hungry, hoping from a distance to find fruit on the fig tree, when he already knew there was no season for figs there. Besides, it would have been too harsh to curse an innocent fig tree if it had not been the season for figs in that place. I say "in that place," so as to meet the objection of those who want the season of figs to have been one and the same throughout all Judaea, and so think the reading is pointless. For there were various climates even in little Judaea, and so various seasons for fruit, according as the region was mountainous or in a valley, southern or northern, and so on. Nor can I find in any author, sacred or profane, that the word καιρὸς means a fruitful year, as some have thought, so that it could properly be rendered, For it was not a fruitful season for figs, in the English idiom, For it was not a fig year. And even if this were granted, it would not have been any less harsh to curse the fig tree when it was not a fruitful year for figs than if it had not yet been the season for figs. To say it once more: the fault lay neither in the soil nor in the season; the sole cause of the curse was the barrenness of the tree.

units.la: Cap. 14. v. 3. Καὶ συντρίψασα τὸ ἀλάβα‐στρον, & concutiens ampullam sive vas unguentarium. Quod si fregisset, quomodo potuit effundere? Neque eam fregisse dicitur in Matth. Concussit ergo vel conquassavit, ut unguentum gratiorem odorem redderet, vel ut totum effundieret, deret, nec quiequam in imo vasis resideret. Est enim συντείβω concutio. Gloss.vet. & συντείλει, συνθλᾷ i.e. conquassat. Phav 'Αλάβαστρον dicitur ἄγχ⁠ῳ μὴ ἔχον λαβὰς, vas quod non habet ansas, quod minime prehendi potest, ab a privativa, & λαμβάνομαι. Est etiam λήκυθος μύρου, vas olearium, sive ampulla unguentaria, apud eundem.
units.tr: Chapter 14, verse 3. "And breaking the alabaster (flask)." [Καὶ συντρίψασα τὸ ἀλάβαστρον,] And concutiens ampullam sive vas unguentarium, shaking the flask or unguent vessel. But if she had broken it, how could she have poured it out? Nor is it said in Matthew that she broke it. She therefore shook or crushed it, so that the ointment would give a sweeter fragrance, or so that she would pour out the whole of it, and nothing would remain at the bottom of the vessel. For συντείβω means to shake; the old glossaries have συντείλει and συνθλᾷ, that is, he crushes. Phavorinus says that ἀλάβαστρον is a vessel ἄγχῳ μὴ ἔχον λαβὰς, a vessel that has no handles, which cannot be easily grasped, from the privative a and λαμβάνομαι. In the same author it is also λήκυθος μύρου, an oil vessel, or unguent flask.

units.la: V. 72. Καὶ ἐκβαλὼν ἔκλαιε. subaudi ἑαυτὸν. Et se praecipitans, vel dans praecipitem vel cum impetu projiciens, i e. exiliens sive se proripiens flevit. Sic apud Theogn. posit, ἠ εἰς μεγαλήτερα πόντον Ρηγίων, subaudiendum ἑαυτὸν monet Stephanus, apud quem ἐκβάλλεσθαι est jacere vel mittere, ut etiam apud Hesychium ἐκβαλεῖ, ἐκπέμπει. Adeo ut τὸ ἐκβαλὼν hoc loco nihil aliud denotet quam τὸ ἐξελθὼν ἔξω Matth. 26. 75. & Luc. 22. 62. Et egressus foras flevit amare, nisi quod impetum in exeundo magis innuat.
units.tr: V. 72. And going out he wept bitterly [Καὶ ἐκβαλὼν ἔκλαιε]. Supply himself [ἑαυτὸν]: he threw himself forward, or cast himself headlong, or rushed out violently, that is, he sprang out or hurried away and wept. So in Theognis: or into the sea of Rhegium [ἠ εἰς μεγαλήτερα πόντον Ρηγίων], where Stephanus advises that himself [ἑαυτὸν] is to be supplied, and where ἐκβάλλεσθαι means to throw or to send. Likewise Hesychius gives throws [ἐκβαλεῖ] and sends out [ἐκπέμπει]. So the ἐκβαλὼν here means nothing other than having gone out, ἐξελθὼν ἔξω, as in Matth. 26. 75 and Luc. 22. 62: "and going out he wept bitterly," except that it suggests more of a rush in going out.

units.la: LUC. c. 1. v. 17. Versus iste, si cum venia deleatur punctum post δικαίων, exponitur meliore, ni fallor, sensu & grammatica quàm vulgò solet in hunc modum. Καὶ αὐτὸς προσελεύσεται ἐνώπιον αὐτῆ ἐν πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει Ἡλίου, ἐπιστρέψαι καρδίας πατέρων ἐπὶ τέκνα, καὶ ἀπειθεῖς ἐν φρονήσει δικαίων, ἑτοιμάσαι Κυρίῳ λαὸν κατεσκευασμένον. Et ipse antecedet cum in spiritu & virtute Eliae, ut convertat
units.tr: LUKE ch. 1 v. 17. If the point after δικαίων is removed, this verse can, I think, be explained with better sense and grammar than is usually given: "And he himself shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to prepare for the Lord a people made ready" [Καὶ αὐτὸς προσελεύσεται ἐνώπιον αὐτῆ ἐν πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει Ἡλίου, ἐπιστρέψαι καρδίας πατέρων ἐπὶ τέκνα, καὶ ἀπειθεῖς ἐν φρονήσει δικαίων, ἑτοιμάσαι Κυρίῳ λαὸν κατεσκευασμένον].

units.la: catchword omitted: "zeriam" printed at foot right, read as "xeriam"[?] vertat corda patrum ad filios, & infideles instrue-at in sapientia justorum p pulum paratum Do-mino. Nempe ut sint populus paratus Domino. Est enim τὸ λαὸν κατεσκευασμένον appositivum τῷ, ἀπειθεῖς. Ut convertat corda patrum ad filios, vel ut vertit Pagninus Malach. 4. 5. cor patrum super filios & cor filiorum super patres eorum, intelligendum reor, usque ad filios &c. ut τὸ בער & τὸ ὅτι quandoque significant in veteri, i e. ut plane Vatablus, ut convertat patres unà cum filiis. Occurrit omninò eadem distionis formula Judith. 9. 10. πάταξον δοῦλον ἐν χείλεσιν ἀπάτης μου ἐπ' ἀρχοντα ἡ ἀρχοντα ὅτι διεφθαρται αὐτος. Percute servum ex labiis deceptionis meæ super principem & principem super ministrum ejus, ut est in versione Latina, i. e. ut in Malachia, usque ad principem & principem usque ad ministrum ejus, vel ut vertimus anglicè magis plane, Smite by the reeeit of my lips the servant with the Prince and the Prince with the servant. Ut etiam vertit Junius, Percute servum labiis fraudulentis meis cum Domino & Dominum cum servo ipsius. Officium enim erat præcursoris, qui parabat vias Domini, resipiscentiam prædicare omnibus hominibus à patribus ad filios & a filiis ad patres, ut pareatiores fierent ad recipiendum, quod appropinquabat, regnum Dei. τὸ ἐν φρονήσει δικαίων ἑτοιμάσας, & τὸ δοῦναι γνῶσιν σωτηρίας &c. v. 77. unum idemque significant, est enim tantùm verborum periphrasis, in utrisque verò locis unus idemque sensus.
units.tr: "…to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and to instruct the unbelieving in the wisdom of the just, a people prepared for the Lord." That is, so that they may be a people prepared for the Lord. For the phrase λαὸν κατεσκευασμένον is in apposition to τῷ, "the disobedient." As for "to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children," or as Pagninus translates it at Malachi 4:5, "the heart of the fathers upon the sons and the heart of the sons upon their fathers," I think it should be understood as "even to the children," etc., just as the Hebrew particle [בער] and the Greek ὅτι sometimes mean in the Old Testament; that is, as Vatablus plainly renders it, "to turn the fathers together with the children." The very same construction occurs at Judith 9:10: "Strike the servant with the words of my deceit upon the ruler and the ruler upon his minister" [πάταξον δοῦλον ἐν χείλεσιν ἀπάτης μου ἐπ' ἀρχοντα ἡ ἀρχοντα ὅτι διεφθαρται αὐτος], as it stands in the Latin version: "Smite the servant with the lips of my deceit upon the prince and the prince upon his minister." That is, as in Malachi, "even to the prince and the prince even to his minister." Or, to put it more plainly as we render it in English: "Smite by the reeeit of my lips the servant with the Prince and the Prince with the servant." Junius likewise translates: "Smite the servant with my deceitful lips together with the Lord, and the Lord together with his servant." For the office of the forerunner was to prepare the ways of the Lord, to preach repentance to all men, from fathers to children and from children to fathers, so that they might be more willing to receive the kingdom of God, which was drawing near. The phrase τὸ ἐν φρονήσει δικαίων ἑτοιμάσας and the phrase τὸ δοῦναι γνῶσιν σωτηρίας, etc., at verse 77, mean one and the same thing: the one is merely a periphrasis of the other, and in both places the sense is one and the same.

units.la: V. 54, 55. Ἀντελάβετο Ἰσραὴλ παιδὸς αὐτοῦ μνησθῆναι ἐλέους ( καθὼς ἐλάλησε πρὸς τοὺς πατέρας ἡμῶν ) τῷ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. Et sublevavit filium suum Israel reminiscendo misericordiam (ut locutus est ad patres nostros) Abrahamo & semini ejus in aeternum. Quam facili remedio ingens curatur solœcismus? semen Abrahami sunt fideles. Jam adimpletum est quod prædixit Michaeas iisdem fere verbis, 7. 20. Δώσεις ἀλήθειαν τῷ Ἰακὼβ, &c. dabis veritatem Jacobo, misericordiam Abrahamo, quæ juràsti patribus nostris à diebus antiquis: & quod prædixit David, Psal. 98, 3. ἐμνήσθη ἐλέους τῷ Ἰακὼβ &c. Recordatus est misericordiæ suæ Jacobo, & veritatis suæ domui Israel; viderunt omnes termini terræ salutare Dei nostri. LXX legunt in Michaea, δώσεις ἐλεος pro δώσεις; sed hoc fuisse scriptoris vitium nullus dubito.
units.tr: Luke 1:54–55: "He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy (as he spoke to our fathers), to Abraham and his seed for ever" [Ἀντελάβετο Ἰσραὴλ παιδὸς αὐτοῦ μνησθῆναι ἐλέους (καθὼς ἐλάλησε πρὸς τοὺς πατέρας ἡμῶν) τῷ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα]. With how easy a remedy is this great solecism cured? The seed of Abraham are the faithful. What Micah foretold, in almost the same words, is now fulfilled (Mic. 7:20): "You will give truth to Jacob, mercy to Abraham, which you swore to our fathers from ancient days" [Δώσεις ἀλήθειαν τῷ Ἰακὼβ, &c.]; and what David foretold (Ps. 98:3): "He remembered his mercy to Jacob, etc." [ἐμνήσθη ἐλέους τῷ Ἰακὼβ &c.], "He remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel; all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God." The Seventy read "mercy" [ἐλεος] for "you will give" in Micah; but I have no doubt that this was the fault of the copyist.

units.la: C. 2. V. 34. 35. Ἰδοὺ οὗτος κεῖται εἰς πτῶσιν καὶ ἀνάστασιν πολλῶν ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ, καὶ εἰς σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον (καὶ σοῦ αὐτῆς τὴν ψυχὴν διελεύσεται ῥομφαία) ὅπως ἂν ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν ἐκ πολλῶν καρδιῶν διαλογισμοί. Ecce positus est hic in casum & resurrectionem multorum in Israel, & in signum cui contradicetur (& tuam ipsius animam pertransibit gladius) ut revelentur ex multis cordibus cogitationes. Atque huic lectioni & versioni consentiunt plerumque interpretes, quid vero velit sibi gladius ille, non consentiunt. Alii de mæroris gladio interpretantur, qui cor penetraret matris cum spectaret miserandam passionem filii. Alii de gladio diffidentiæ, quo perculsa est cum videret ipsum mori, quem credebat esse Deum, usque dum per resurrectionem & restituta & confirmata est in fide. Alii de gladio calumniæ vel opprobrii, qui pertransibat animam, cum audiret impios & incredulos Judæos & Romanos contumelias suas in filium conjicientes, quales sunt Matth. 27.42.
units.tr: Luke 2:34–35: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against (yea, a sword shall pierce through your own soul also), that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed" [Ἰδοὺ οὗτος κεῖται εἰς πτῶσιν καὶ ἀνάστασιν πολλῶν ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ, καὶ εἰς σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον (καὶ σοῦ αὐτῆς τὴν ψυχὴν διελεύσεται ῥομφαία) ὅπως ἂν ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν ἐκ πολλῶν καρδιῶν διαλογισμοί]. Most interpreters agree with this reading and this rendering, but they do not agree on what that sword means. Some interpret it as the sword of grief, which would pierce the mother's heart when she saw the pitiable suffering of her son. Others take it as the sword of doubt, by which she was struck when she saw him die, whom she believed to be God, until through the resurrection she was both restored and confirmed in faith. Others take it as the sword of calumny or reproach, which pierced her soul when she heard the impious and unbelieving Jews and Romans heaping their insults upon her son, such as those in Matt. 27:42.

units.la: Alios salvos fecit, seipsum non potest salvare: si rex est Israel descendat nunc de cruce, & similia. Et pro proprietate metaphorae singulus interpres habet exempla suo sensui accommoda, verum quam interpretationem velis capias, non est una, quae sine vi potest applicari scopo loci, ideoque videntur verba abrupte interposita, eoque nomine a textu reliquo parenthesi divisa. Cum ergo vulgaris sensus ita sit incommodus, quid ni tentemus lectionem, constructionem & interpretationem aliam, quae forte magis apta, certe magis plana, nec a grammatica aliena? Qualis haec est. 'Ἀλλὰ ἑαυτὸν &c. sine parenthesi, Ecce positus est hic in casum & resurrectionem multorum in Israel, & in signum cui contradicetur, Imo tuus quoque gladius pertransfibit animam, ut revelentur multorum cordium cogitationes. Quasi familiari trajectione legeretur, καὶ σὺ δὲ αὐτῆς ῥομφαία τὴν ψυχὴν διελεύσεται, ὅπως ἂν ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν &c. τῶν ψυχῶν, i.e. αὐτῶν ψυχῶν. ut frequenter intelligitur. Sensu sequenti in hunc modum. Et ut revelentur multorum cordium cogitationes, tuus & etiam gladius pertransfibit eorum animam i.e. Verbum Dei quod procedet ex ore tuo, quod penetrantius erit quovis gladio, pertransfibit multorum corda, adeo ut revelet ipsorum intima secreta. Ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ, &c. Sermo enim Dei vivus & efficax & acutior gladio, qui binas habet acies, pertingens usque ad divisionem animae ac spiritus, — & discretor cogitationum & intentionum cordis. Heb. 4: 12. Adeo ut metaphora ista non sit huic loco omnino incommoda. Occurrit etiam in eodem sensu, Apocal. 1. 16. ῥομφαία ὀξεῖα, & 19. 15. ῥομφαία ὀξεῖα. Et ex ore ejus procedit cedit gladius acutus. Qui, ut inquit Grotius, est Evangelicus sermo ex ore Christi proficiscens, qui intima penetrat, neque actiones tantum, sed & cogitata bona malaque discernit. Sic Eph. 6. 16. habemus gladium spiritus quod est verbum Dei. Et quid mirum si mater Domini gladio spiritus, i. e. verbo Dei ex ore suo prodeunte ita penetrarit multorum corda, ut occulta eorum manifesta ejs facta sint? ut loquitur Apostolus
units.tr: "He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the king of Israel, let him come down now from the cross," and so on. As to the proper sense of the metaphor, each interpreter brings examples suited to his own meaning; yet whichever interpretation you take, it is not one that can be applied to the purpose of the passage without strain. For this reason the words seem abruptly inserted, and on that account are set apart from the rest of the text as a parenthesis. Since the common sense is therefore so unsuitable, why should we not try another reading, construction and interpretation, one that is perhaps more apt, and certainly plainer, and not foreign to grammar? It is this: "But himself" [Ἀλλὰ ἑαυτὸν] etc., without a parenthesis: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against. Yes, your own sword too shall pierce the soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed." It would be read by a familiar transposition as [καὶ σὺ δὲ αὐτῆς ῥομφαία τὴν ψυχὴν διελεύσεται, ὅπως ἂν ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν] etc. [τῶν ψυχῶν], that is, [αὐτῶν ψυχῶν], as is often understood, in the following sense: "And that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed, your sword too shall pierce their soul." That is, the word of God, which will proceed from your mouth and will be more piercing than any sword, shall pierce the hearts of many, so that it reveals their innermost secrets. "For the word of God is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart" (Heb. 4:12) [Ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ, &c.]. So this metaphor is not at all unsuitable to this place. It also occurs in the same sense in Rev. 1:16, "a sharp sword" [ῥομφαία ὀξεῖα], and 19:15, "a sharp sword" [ῥομφαία ὀξεῖα]: "And out of his mouth goes a sharp sword." Grotius says this is the gospel language proceeding from Christ's mouth, which penetrates the inmost parts and distinguishes not only actions but also good and evil thoughts. So Eph. 6:16: we have "the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God" [μάχαιραν τοῦ πνεύματος, ὅ ἐστι ῥῆμα Θεοῦ]. And what wonder if the Lord's mother, with the sword of the Spirit, that is, the word of God coming forth from her mouth, so pierced the hearts of many that "the secrets of their hearts were made manifest," as the Apostle says?

units.la: 1 Cor. 14. 15. Quis dubitet quin divinum ejus Magnificat penetrarit omnium auditorum corda? Occurrit etiam eadem Metaphora saepius in Psalmis.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 14:15: Who can doubt that her divine Magnificat pierced the hearts of all who heard it? The same metaphor also occurs quite often in the Psalms.

units.la: ὠσεὶ saepius prae, ut ὠσεὶ πάντων εὔχομαι prae omnibus opto te prosperè agere & valere, 3 Joh. 2. & ὠσεὶ πάντων θέλειν prae omnibus cupere. Dion. Halic.
units.tr: ὠσεὶ, which occurs very often for "prae" (above, before), as in ὠσεὶ πάντων εὔχομαι, "I pray above all things that you prosper and are in good health" (3 John 2), and ὠσεὶ πάντων θέλειν, "to desire above all things." Dionysius of Halicarnassus.

units.la: Cap. 3. v. 23: Καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ἀρχόμενος, ὢν &c. Haec verba optime, opinor, exponuntur per metathesim, quasi legeretur, Καὶ ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα, αὐτὸς ἀρχόμενος ὢν &c. Et erat Jesus circa triginta annos natus, ipse incipiens existens (ut putabatur) filius Ioseph &c. i. e. ἀρχόμενος ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα, incipiens genealogiam, scilicet paternam ascendendo, ut maternam recensuit Matthæus descendendo; non enim aptè vel significanter dicitur, Iesus incæpit esse quasi vel circa triginta annos natus, est enim tautologum vel dubium, eò quòd τὸ ὡσεὶ indefinitum tempus significat, videlicet circà, vel post, vel ante.
units.tr: Ch. 3, v. 23: "And Jesus himself was about thirty years old when he began, being" etc. [Καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ἀρχόμενος, ὢν]. I think these words are best explained by a transposition, as if it read: "And Jesus was about thirty years old, himself beginning, being" etc. [Καὶ ἦν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα, αὐτὸς ἀρχόμενος ὢν]. "And Jesus was about thirty years old, beginning, as was supposed, to be the son of Joseph," etc.; that is, "beginning, about thirty years old, the genealogy," namely by ascending the paternal line, just as Matthew recounted the maternal line by descending. For it is not properly or meaningfully said that Jesus began to be about thirty years old, since this is tautologous or uncertain, because ὡσεὶ signifies an indefinite time, namely about, or after, or before.

units.la: Cap. 6. v. 35. καὶ δανείζετε μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες, & mutuum date nihil inde sperantes. Nusquam vero apud Authores τὸ ἀπελπίζειν in eo sensu reperitur. Melius ergò legitur cum Apostrophe, μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες, & vertitur in Hebraeorum Hipbil, neminem desperare facientes, ut intellexerunt Syrus, Arabicus, & Persicus interpres. Quale est illud in Matth. 5. 42. τὸν θέλοντα ἀπὸ σοῦ δανείσασθαι μὴ ἀποστραφῇς, nè averias volentem à te mutuari, i.e. ἀπελπίζειν. In quo sensu habetur verbum Isai. 29. 19. οἱ ἀπελπίζοντες τὴν ἀνθρώπων, desperati homines implebuntur lætitiâ. Et Ecclesiastic. 27. 24. ὁ δὲ ἀποκαλύπτων μυστήρια, qui autem denudavit mysteria, desperavit, i.e. desperare fecit: quale est illud in Plinio, lib. 22. c. 24. Ulcera jam desperantia cicatrice includit, i.e. quæ medicos faciunt desperare sanationem.
units.tr: Ch. 6, v. 35: "And lend, hoping for nothing in return" [καὶ δανείζετε μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες]. Yet the verb ἀπελπίζειν is nowhere found in that sense in the Authors. It is better, therefore, to read it with an apostrophe, μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες, and to render it as the Hebrew hiphil, "causing no one to despair," as the Syriac, Arabic and Persian interpreters understood it. Compare Matthew 5:42: "Do not turn away him who wishes to borrow from you" [τὸν θέλοντα ἀπὸ σοῦ δανείσασθαι μὴ ἀποστραφῇς], that is, do not make him despair. In this sense the word is used in Isaiah 29:19: "the men who make despair [οἱ ἀπελπίζοντες] of men shall be filled with joy." Also Ecclesiasticus 27:24: "but he who discloses secrets has made [others] despair" [ὁ δὲ ἀποκαλύπτων μυστήρια ἀπελπίζει], that is, has caused despair. Similar is the phrase in Pliny, book 22, ch. 24: "He closes up ulcers that were already past hope with a scar," that is, ulcers which make the physicians despair of a cure.

units.la: C. 7. v. 36. Τὴν βουλὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἠθέτησαν εἰς ἑαυτὸς: vulgari trajectione, spreverunt voluntatem Dei erga semetipsos, qui eos voluit ad pœnitentiam vocari per Baptistæ prædicationem & baptismum.
units.tr: Ch. 7, v. 36: "They rejected the counsel of God against themselves" [Τὴν βουλὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἠθέτησαν εἰς ἑαυτούς]: by the common transposition, "they rejected the will of God towards themselves," which willed that they be called to repentance through the preaching and baptism of the Baptist.

units.la: C. 11. v. 41. Πλὴν τὰ ἐνόντα δότε ἐλεημοσύνην, καὶ ἰδοὺ πάντα καθαρὰ ὑμῖν ἔστιν, imò quæ intus sunt date eleemosynam, & omnia vobis erunt mundá munda. ἔνεσιν ἀντὶ τῆς ἐντὸς ὄεων, & ἐνὶς, ἐνδέ- κμῳ. Phav. Allusione habita ad superius dicta, τὰ ἐνδοτερα sunt, τὰ ἔσωθεν τῆς πατιεύς, juxta locum paralielum. Matth. 23. 26. Καθάρισον πρῶτον τὸ ἐντὸς τῆς ποτηρίου, ἵνα γένηται καὶ τὸ ἐκτὸς αὐτοῦ καθαρόν. Purga prius quod intus est poculi, ut id quoque quod extra est fias purum. Quasi diceret, Vos Pharisæi quidem pulchram præ vobis fertis speciem ad extrà, longas facitis precationes, & datis eleemosynas pauperibus in plateis, intùs verò estis rapinâ pleni. At verò si velitis omnia quæ habetis fieri munda, i. e. acceptâ Deo, date pauperibus hæc male parta omnia, τὰ ἔσωθεν, & τὰ ἐνδοτερα, quæ intùs latent occulta ab oculis ho-minum, hoc enim est vere purgare interius poculii. Frigidum foret dicere, Date pro facultatibus, vel ex omnibus quae habetis. Non ita certè voluit Dominus. Omnia verò ex rapinâ malè parta erant priùs penitùs refundenda, quàm quicquid darent acceptum foret Leo.
units.tr: Ch. 11, v. 41: "But give alms of the things that are within, and behold, all things are clean to you" [Πλὴν τὰ ἐνόντα δότε ἐλεημοσύνην, καὶ ἰδοὺ πάντα καθαρὰ ὑμῖν ἔστιν]; indeed, "give alms of what is inside, and all things will be clean to you." ἔνεσιν is used instead of ἐντὸς ὄντων, and ἐνδοτερα [inner things] and ἐνδέκμῳ [...]. Phavorinus. The allusion is to what was said above: τὰ ἐνδοτερα are τὰ ἔσωθεν τῆς πατιεύς [the things within the dish], in accordance with the parallel passage, Matthew 23:26: "Cleanse first what is within the cup, that the outside of it may become clean too" [Καθάρισον πρῶτον τὸ ἐντὸς τοῦ ποτηρίου, ἵνα γένηται καὶ τὸ ἐκτὸς αὐτοῦ καθαρόν]. It is as if he said: "You Pharisees indeed present a fine appearance outwardly, you make long prayers and give alms to the poor in the streets, but within you are full of rapine. But if you wish all that you have to become clean, that is, acceptable to God, give to the poor all these ill-gotten goods, τὰ ἔσωθεν and τὰ ἐνδοτερα, which lie hidden within from the eyes of men; for this is truly to cleanse the inside of the cup." It would be cold to say, "Give according to your means, or from all that you have." The Lord certainly did not mean this. But all things gained by rapine had first to be wholly restored before whatever they gave could be accepted. Leo.

units.la: Cap. 12. v. 49. Πῦρ ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰς τὴν γῆν, καὶ τί θέλω; εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη. &c. Ignem veni mittere in terram, & quid volo? utinam jam accensus esset. Baptisma autem habeo baptizari, & quomodo constringor usque dum perficiatur? Vox est turbati animi, cujus parallelum est videre Job 12. 27. Nunc anima mea turbata est, & quid dicam? Pater libera me ab hac hora, sed propterea veni in hanc horam, glorifica Pater nomen tuum. Optime utriusque loci sensum exprimit Calvinus in suo commentario in Job in verba illa, Et quid dicam? quae idem volunt ac quid volo? Hic tanquam sub oculis cernimus, quanti constiterit salus nostra filio Dei, dum in ultimas angustias redactus neque verba invenit quibus exprimat doloris magnitudinem, nec consilium secundum hominem. Quod autem mentem unum re stat, confugit ad preces, & se libe- rari à morte postulat. Rursum quia simul videt se æterno Dei consilio destinatum esse victimam pro peccatis, votum illud, quod ingens mestitia ex- presserat, mox corrigit, & quasi injecta manu se- ipsum retrahit, ut totus acquiescat Patris arbitrio. Et ponitur pro ἐι ϑε, utinam. Quo sensu legit Ori- genes, Πῦρ ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰς τὴν γῆν, καὶ τἰ θέλω εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη, Ignem veni mittere in terram, atque utinam jam arsisset, ut Interpres. Sic ἐι[?] sæpius accipitur apud Authores Ethnicos, ut videre est apud Ste- phanum, & apud LXX, ut Num. 14. 2. εἴθε ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ταύτῃ ἀπεθάνομεν, vel in deserto hoc utinam fuissemus mortui: & Jos. 7. 7. καὶ εἰ κα- τῳκεύαμεν &c. Et utinam mansissemus & habi- tassemus apud Jordanem, & alibi. Nec multum differt illud Luc. 22. 42. εἰ βούλει παρένεγκε ἀπ' ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο, ἀλλ' ἐμῷ, & positis genibus precatus est dicens, Pater, Utinam (ut interpretatur Grotius) velis transferre hoc poculum à me, veruntamen non mea voluntas, sed tua fiat. Πῦρ hoc loco de- notat, ut videtur 51. Διαιρεσισμὸν, divisionem; quia forte ignis dissipat, alibi persecutionem sive afflictionem, idque sæpius. Matthæus vocat μάχαιραν. 10. 34.
units.tr: Ch. 12, v. 49: "I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will? If only it were already kindled!" [Πῦρ ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰς τὴν γῆν, καὶ τί θέλω; εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη]. "I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled. But I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how am I constrained until it is accomplished?" It is the voice of a troubled mind, whose parallel is seen in John 12:27: "Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour; but for this cause I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name." Calvin, in his commentary on Job, expresses the sense of both passages very well on the words "And what shall I say?", which mean the same as "what do I will?" Here we see, as it were before our eyes, how much our salvation cost the Son of God, when, brought to the utmost straits, he finds neither words to express the greatness of his sorrow, nor a counsel according to man. Since his mind is at a standstill, he flees to prayers and asks to be freed from death. Again, because at the same time he sees that he has been appointed by the eternal counsel of God to be the victim for sins, he soon corrects that wish which great sadness had expressed, and, as if drawing back a hand that had been thrust out, he surrenders himself wholly to the Father's will. And it is used for εἰ θε, "would that." In this sense Origen reads: "I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it had already blazed," as the translator renders it. So εἰ is quite often taken in the Gentile Authors, as may be seen in Stephanus, and in the LXX, as in Numbers 14:2: "Would that we had died in this wilderness" [εἴθε ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ταύτῃ ἀπεθάνομεν], and Joshua 7:7: "and if we had dwelt" [καὶ εἰ κατῳκεύαμεν], etc., "Would that we had remained and dwelt beyond the Jordan," and elsewhere. Nor does Luke 22:42 differ much: "If you are willing, remove this cup from me, but not my will, but yours be done" [εἰ βούλει παρένεγκε ἀπ' ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο, ἀλλ' ἐμὸν θέλημα, ...]; and, kneeling down, he prayed, saying: "Father, would that (as Grotius interprets) you were willing to take this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will, but yours be done." Here πῦρ, as it seems, denotes at verse 51 division [διαιρεσισμός], because perhaps fire scatters; elsewhere it denotes persecution or affliction, and that often. Matthew calls it a sword, 10:34 [μάχαιραν].

units.la: Cap. 13. v. 33. "Οτι οὐκ ἐνδέχεται, quia non fieri potest, ut Propheta pereat extra Jerusalem. Atque in eo sensu vox ἐνδέχεται frequenter occurrit apud Epicurum; ἔστι τε ἐνδέχεται τὸ σεληνοῦ ἐξ ἑαυτῆς ἔχειν τὸ φῶς, ἐνδέχεται ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου: Fieri etiam potest Lunam habere lucem ex se, fieri autem potest a Sole. Et quo minus aliter fieri posset, quin Prophetae perirent omnes in Hierosolymis, optime observavit Drusius, Prophetas non judicari nisi a Judicibus Sanhedrim, qui Hierosolyma residebant in exedra domus [sanctae,] ideoque sequitur, Jerusalem, Jerusalem, quae occidis Prophetas. &c.
units.tr: Ch. 13, v. 33: "Because it is not possible" [Ὅτι οὐκ ἐνδέχεται], "because it cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem." In this sense the word ἐνδέχεται frequently occurs in Epicurus: "It is possible for the Moon to have light from itself, and it is possible that it has it from the Sun." And that it could not otherwise happen than that all the Prophets perished in Jerusalem, Drusius has very well observed: the prophets were not judged except by the judges of the Sanhedrin, who sat at Jerusalem in the hall of the house [sanctae], and therefore it follows: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kill the Prophets" etc.

units.la: Cap. 15. v. 4. Οὐ καταλείπει τὰ ἐννενηκοντα ἐννέα, ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ καὶ πορεύεται &c. Non relinquit nonaginta novem, & vadit in deserto post eam quae perdita est? Sic Matth. 18, 12. οὐχὶ πορευθεὶς, profectus in montes quaerit eam quae erravit? Desertum & montes idem valent. Iesus ubi vixit & docuit Baptista, Matth. 3. 1. vocatur ἐρήμῳ τῆς Ἰουδαίας, Desertum Judaeae, & ubi habitavit Zacharias, Luc. 1. 39. ἡ ὀρεινὴ, montana [Regio.]
units.tr: Chap. 15, v. 4. "Does he not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that is lost?" [Οὐ καταλείπει τὰ ἐννενηκοντα ἐννέα, ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ καὶ πορεύεται] Non relinquit nonaginta novem, & vadit in deserto post eam quae perdita est? So Matth. 18:12, "Having gone off into the mountains, does he not seek the one that went astray?" [οὐχὶ πορευθεὶς]. Desert and mountains mean the same thing. Where Jesus lived and John the Baptist taught is called "the wilderness of Judaea" [τῇ ἐρήμῳ τῆς Ἰουδαίας] in Matth. 3:1, and where Zechariah lived is called "the hill country" [ἡ ὀρεινή] in Luke 1:39 [region].

units.la: Cap. 18. v. 5. "Ἵνα μὴ εἰς τέλος ἐρχόμενη ὑπωπιάζῃ με. Ne veniendo in fine fatiget me. least by her comming in the end the weary me.
units.tr: Chap. 18, v. 5. "Lest by coming at the last she wear me out" [Ἵνα μὴ εἰς τέλος ἐρχομένη ὑπωπιάζῃ με]: Ne veniendo in fine fatiget me.

units.la: V. 7. Καὶ μακροθυμῶν ἐπ' αὐτοῖς; subaudi ἔσται, ut Vet. Lat. ἐπ' αὐτοῖς, bifariam exponitur. Si Electos intelligas, vertendum, Et habebit habebit diu patientiam propter illos? ἔτι enim apud Grammaticos cum Dativo sæpè significat propter. Quod si verò, adversarios, quod nec omnino incongruum, ut etiam videntur fecisse illi qui verterunt, & in longum differet iram in illos? reddendum erit, et patientiam habebit diu erga illos? nempe adversarios electorum, cujus nominis fit mentio v. 3. in parabolâ viduæ, quo modo verterunt aliqui Ecclesiastic. 35. 18. οὐκ μὴ μακρο-θυμήσῃ ἐπ' αὐτοῖς ὁ Κράτιστος, neque patientiam habebit diu erga illos Fortissimus; intelligendo Gentes, superbos, & iniquos qui immediate memorantur. Vide etiam Matth. 18. 26.
units.tr: V. 7. "And will he have patience with them?" [Καὶ μακροθυμῶν ἐπ' αὐτοῖς]; the verb will be [ἔσται] is to be understood, as in the Old Latin. The phrase ἐπ' αὐτοῖς can be explained in two ways. If you understand the elect, it should be rendered, And will he have patience with them for a long time, and will he bear with them on account of them? For among the Grammarians the ἔτι with the Dative often means on account of, propter. But if you understand adversaries, which is not altogether inappropriate, as those who translated seem to have done, the sense is "will he defer his anger against them for a long time?" It should be rendered, and will he have patience with them for a long time? namely the adversaries of the elect, whose mention is made in v. 3, in the parable of the widow. Some have translated in this way in Ecclesiasticus 35:18, οὐκ μὴ μακροθυμήσῃ ἐπ' αὐτοῖς ὁ Κράτιστος, "neither will the Most Mighty have patience with them" [neque patientiam habebit diu erga illos Fortissimus], understanding the Gentiles, the proud, and the wicked, who are named immediately before. See also Matth. 18:26.

units.la: V. 8. Πλὴν ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀνθρώπου ἐλθὼν ἆρα εὑρήσει τὴν πίστιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς; Verùm cùm filius hominis venerit, an invenuet hanc fidem in hac terrâ? scilicet Judæa: τῆς pro ταύτης, & τὴν pro ταύτην, frequentissimum: τῆς δὲ τῆς χώρας, hanc verò regionem. Plat. in Timæo. Eminenter dicitur 21. 23. ἔσται γὰρ ἀνάγκη μεγάλη ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς καὶ ὀργὴ ἐν τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ· Erit enim pressura magna in hac terrâ [Judææ] et ira in populo isto. Vide Matth. 11. 19. Sensus est, cùm filius hominis venerit ad excidium Hierosolymæ, [ita enim adventus ejus frequenter intelligitur] an inveniet hanc fidem? i. e. similem in terrâ Judææ, nempe fidem quæ obtundet Deum precibus, (qualis erat fides importunæ viduæ, quæ tandem exoravit injustum Judicem,) quæ continuò precabitur, & non deficiet, ut præceperat Dominus v. 1.
units.tr: V. 8. "But when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?" [Πλὴν ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀνθρώπου ἐλθὼν ἆρα εὑρήσει τὴν πίστιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς;] Verùm cùm filius hominis venerit, an invenuet hanc fidem in hac terrâ? That is, in Judaea: τῆς stands for ταύτης, and τὴν for ταύτην, a very common usage, as in τῆς δὲ τῆς χώρας, "but this region" [hanc verò regionem, Plato in the Timaeus]. It is said emphatically in 21:23, "For there will be great distress upon the earth [of Judaea] and wrath upon this people" [ἔσται γὰρ ἀνάγκη μεγάλη ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς καὶ ὀργὴ ἐν τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ]. See Matth. 11:19. The sense is: when the Son of Man comes to the destruction of Jerusalem [for his coming is often understood in this way], will he find this faith? That is, a similar faith in the land of Judaea, namely a faith that wearies God with prayers (such as the faith of the importunate widow, who at last prevailed upon the unjust judge), a faith that will pray continually and not faint, as the Lord had commanded in v. 1.

units.la: Cap. 22. v. 32. Καὶ σύ ποτε ἐπιστρέψας στήρισον τοὺς ἀδελφούς σου. Fateor sæpissimè in N.T. Passivum accipi pro Activo, & quandoque, licèt rarius, Activum pro Passivo, ut id verò hoc loco fiat, nulla omninò mihi videtur cogere necessitas, cùm propria interpretatio è contrario magis conveniac scopo loci. Dixit Petro Dominus, Simon, Simon, ecce Satanas expetivit ut te cribraret sicut triticum, ego autem rogavi pro te ne fides tua deficeret, et tu aliquando cum converteris, confirma fratres tuos, i. e. per trajectionem valde familiarem, cùm tu converteris, in futuro Activo Subjunctivo, fratres tuos. Quasi diceret, ut ego rogavi pro te ne fides tua deficeret, cùm te tentaverit Satan, similiter & tu cùm converteris aliquando ad fidem aliquos e fratribus tuis, [Apostolus enim erat ad Circumcisionem] confirma eos etiam tuis precibus, ne deficiat fides, cùm tentaverit eos Satan: Parem charitatem petit. Ac si legeretur, καὶ σὺ ποτὲ ἐπιστρέψας τὰς ἀδελφούς σου, στήριξον [αὐτούς] quod saepe subauditur. Eadem loquendi formula frequenter occurrit, ut versu 54. ἀλλὰ- ξόντες δὲ αὐτὸν ἤγαγον, pro ἤγαγον αὐτόν, Comprehendentes autem eum, duxerunt eum, accusativum ἀπὸ τῆς οἰκίας reperiendo, vel relativum subaudiendo. Vide Animad Act. 13. 27 Quod si vulgari sensu exponitur, legendum foret proprie in Passivo, καὶ σὺ ποτὲ ἐπιστραφεὶς, neque vero videtur valde proprium dicere, Et tu aliquando cum conversus fueris, qui jam antea certè conversus erat, etsi postea cecideris, ut praedixit ei Dominus. Nolunt enim, opinor, stauere momentum conversionis Petri in gallicinio, quod si ita faciant τὸ ποτε, in vanum dicitur, magis enim [τὸ ἀλλὰ- quando] distans tempus innuit, quàm pauc arum horarum spatium.
units.tr: Chap. 22, v. 32. "And you, when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers" [Καὶ σύ ποτε ἐπιστρέψας στήρισον τοὺς ἀδελφούς σου]. I admit that in the New Testament the passive is very often taken for the active, and sometimes, though more rarely, the active for the passive; but I see no compelling necessity for doing so here, since the proper interpretation agrees better with the purpose of the passage. The Lord said to Peter, "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have at some time turned again, strengthen your brothers." That is, by a very familiar transposition, "when you turn" is in the future active subjunctive, "your brothers." As if he said: just as I prayed for you that your faith might not fail when Satan tempted you, so you too, when at some time you have turned again to the faith, strengthen some of your brothers [for the Apostle was sent to the Circumcision] also by your prayers, so that their faith may not fail when Satan tempts them. He asks for a similar love. It is as if one read καὶ σὺ ποτὲ ἐπιστρέψας τὰς ἀδελφούς σου, στήριξον [αὐτούς], which is often understood. The same form of speech occurs frequently, as in v. 54, ἀλλὰξαντες δὲ αὐτὸν ἤγαγον, for ἤγαγον αὐτόν, "seizing him, they led him away," where the accusative from the house is found, or the relative is understood. See my Animadversions on Acts 13:27. But if it is explained in the ordinary sense, it would properly have to be read in the passive, καὶ σὺ ποτὲ ἐπιστραφεὶς, "and you, when you have been converted." Nor does it seem very appropriate to say, "And you, when you have at some time been converted," for he had certainly already been converted, even though he afterwards fell, as the Lord foretold to him. For I suppose they are unwilling to ascribe the moment of Peter's conversion to the cock-crow; but if they do so, the word ποτε is said in vain, since ἀλλὰ [quando] indicates a time that is distant rather than a space of a few hours.

units.la: In Iohannem.
units.tr: In Iohannem.

units.la: IOH. cap. 4. v. 17. Καλῶς εἶπας. Dicitum bonicè. Dixisti bellè. Well spoken, faintly. Non verò dixit bene, vel mentiens, vel loquens æquivocè.
units.tr: John 4:17. "Καλῶς εἶπας" [Well said]. "Dicitum bonicè. Dixisti bellè." Well spoken, faintly. But he did not say well, either as a liar or as one speaking ambiguously.

units.la: V. 29. Μήτι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ Χριστός; Numquid hic est ipse Christus? Vox est affirmantis & non dubitantis, ut manifestè arguit oratio sequens v. 42. Non amplius propter sermonem tuum credimus, ipsi enim audivimus, & scimus quòd hic est verè salvator mundi, ipse Christus. In quo sensu usurpatur μήτι. Matth. 12. 23. & τὸ μὴ, infra 18. 17. & 25.
units.tr: Vers. 29. "Μήτι αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ Χριστός;" [Is this not the Christ himself?] This is the language of one who affirms and does not doubt, as the following verse, 42, plainly shows: "No longer do we believe because of your words; for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is truly the Saviour of the world, the Christ himself." In this sense "μήτι" is used. See Matt. 12:23, and "τὸ μὴ" below, at 18:17 and 25.

units.la: C. 5. v. 4. Ὁ γὰρ ἄγγελος κατέβαινε &c. Et qui prior descendisset in piscinam post motionem aquæ sanabatur. Multa concurrebant (ut ait Gre-gorius) hoc naturalis per aquam medicatio credere-tur. Ego hoc unum opinor esse satis, quod nemo sanabatur nisi qui primus ingrediebatur post motionem aquæ. Uno tantum aquæ motu sanabatur unus. Quod si medicatio fuisset naturalis, cur non omnes, qui festinarunt procul dubio sub idem tempus ingredi, sanabantur? Certè fuit in hoc negotio supernaturale aliquid, nec est opus ultra rationem inquirere, cum habeamus testem authoritatem Evangelicam.
units.tr: Chap. 5, vers. 4. "Ὁ γὰρ ἄγγελος κατέβαινε, &c." [For an angel went down at a certain season]. "And whoever went down first into the pool after the stirring of the water was healed." Many things come together (as Gregory says) to make it credible that the healing was natural, through the water. For my part I think this one fact is enough: no one was healed except the one who went in first after the stirring of the water. Only one person was healed by a single movement of the water. But if the healing had been natural, why were not all who undoubtedly hurried to enter at the same time healed? Certainly something supernatural was at work in this affair, and there is no need to inquire beyond reason, since we have the testimony of the Evangelist's authority.

units.la: C. 7. v. 22. Διὰ τοῦτο Μωσῆς δέδωκεν ὑμῖν, &c. Propterea Moses dedit vobis, &c. At sine dubio, διὰ τοῦτο, melius referuntur ad antecedentia, διὰ τοῦτο. Μωσῆς δέδωκεν. Et omnes circumcidimini propter illud donum, &c. Moses dedit vobis circumcisionem, &c. τὸ θαυμάζειν, cum Praepositione familiare, ut ἐθαύμαζε διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν αὐτῶν, & mirabatur propter incredulitatem eorum. Mar. 6. 6. & alibi. Atque ita cessat omnis disquisitio de insolentia phrasis, vel de verborum inconsequentia.
units.tr: Chap. 7, vers. 22. "Διὰ τοῦτο Μωσῆς δέδωκεν ὑμῖν, &c." [For this reason Moses gave you, etc.]. "Propterea Moses dedit vobis, &c." But undoubtedly "διὰ τοῦτο" is better referred to what precedes: "διὰ τοῦτο, Μωσῆς δέδωκεν" [for this reason, Moses gave]. And you all are circumcised because of that gift, etc. "Moses gave you circumcision," etc. The verb "θαυμάζειν" [to wonder], with a preposition, is a familiar construction, as in "ἐθαύμαζε διὰ τὴν ἀπιστίαν αὐτῶν" [he marvelled because of their unbelief], "and he marvelled because of their unbelief," Mark 6:6, and elsewhere. In this way every difficulty about the strangeness of the phrase, or about the lack of connection between the words, disappears.

units.la: C. 8. v. 4. ἐπαυτοφώρῳ μοιχευομένη. Haec mulier deprehensa est in ipso facinore, ut Beza, modo, ut Vetus, aperte ut Syrus. Verùm ego rectius opinor scribi cum apostrophe, ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ, ut passim scribitur apud authores Ethnicos. Haec mulier deprehensa est in sui ipsius conspectu adulterans. Adeò ut ipsa sui sit ita conscia facta adulterii, ut id nulla facie negare poterit. Ab αὐτὸς & praeterito perfecto verbi ἔλεγχω, πεφώρασμαι. Ideoque recte Phavorinus, ἐπ' αὐτίπῳ, ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ, & αὐτόφωρος· ὁ ὑπ' ἑαυτῆς ἐλεγχόμενος, ἡ πεφωραμένη, ὢν, qui à seipso redarguitur, & conspectus est.
units.tr: Chap. 8, vers. 4. "ἐπαυτοφώρῳ μοιχευομένη" [caught in the very act of adultery]. This woman was caught in the very deed, as Beza has it; "in the act" in the Old Version; "openly" in the Syriac. But I think it is more correctly written with an apostrophe, "ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ" [in the very act], as it is commonly written in the Gentile authors. This woman was caught committing adultery in her own sight; so that she herself was made so conscious of the adultery that she could not deny it in any way. It comes from "αὐτός" [self] and the perfect passive of the verb "ἔλεγχω" [to convict], "πεφώρασμαι" [I have been caught]. And so Phavorinus rightly gives "ἐπ' αὐτίπῳ" and "ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ" and "αὐτόφωρος: ὁ ὑπ' ἑαυτῆς ἐλεγχόμενος, ἡ πεφωραμένη, ὢν" [one convicted by himself, or caught, and seen].

units.la: C. 11. v. 10. Ὅτι τὸ φῶς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτῷ. Quoniam lux non est in eo, i.e. in mundo. Si quis ambulat in die non offendit, ὅτι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου βλέπει, quia videt lucem mundi; at si quis ambulat in nocte, offendit, quia lux non est in eo. Non enim, opinor, convenit interpretari de homine, ut doctissimus Beza, & alii.
units.tr: Chap. 11, vers. 10. "Ὅτι τὸ φῶς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτῷ." [Because the light is not in him]. Because the light is not in him, that is, in the world. "If anyone walks in the day he does not stumble, because he sees the light of the world; but if anyone walks in the night he stumbles, because the light is not in him." For I think it is not fitting to interpret this of man, as the most learned Beza and others do.

units.la: V. 33. Ἐνεβριμήσατο τῷ πνεύματι, καὶ ἐτάραξεν ἑαυτόν: Ingemuit spiritu qui turbavit ipsum. Eadem dicendi formula occurrit saepius in N. T. & etiam apud Evangelistam, ut videre est in animad. 15. 6. 20. 18. Apocal. 1. 6. ex Hebraeorum idiotismo, ut ait Beza, quam dum non observant Interpretes, syntaxin etiam turbant, & sensum, ut hoc ipso loco; ἄλογον enim foret dicere, Jesum turbare semetipsum. Priore verò sensu omnino idem dicitur 13. 21. ἐταράχθη τῷ πνεύματι, turbatus est spiritu.
units.tr: Vers. 33. "Ἐνεβριμήσατο τῷ πνεύματι, καὶ ἐτάραξεν ἑαυτόν" [He groaned in spirit and troubled himself]. "Ingemuit spiritu, qui turbavit ipsum." [He groaned in the spirit, and he who troubled himself]. The same form of expression occurs more often in the New Testament, and also in the Evangelist himself, as can be seen in the Animadversions on Acts 15:6, 20:18, and Revelation 1:6. It is a Hebrew idiom, as Beza says. Because the interpreters do not observe it, they also disturb the syntax and the sense, as in this very passage; for it would be absurd to say that Jesus troubled himself. But in the former sense, the same thing is said at 13:21: "ἐταράχθη τῷ πνεύματι" [he was troubled in spirit].

units.la: V. 39. V. 39. Τεταρταῖος γὰρ ἦν, Est enim quatriduanus. Non possum quin apponere in hunc locum animadversionem Quistorpii, nempè, Rasim scriptum reliquisse, lege constitutum fuisse, ut Apoplecticì non sepelirentur nisi post septuaginta duas horas; idque optimè sancitum esse, eò quia omnes humores perfecerunt tribus diebus motus suos, nempè horis 72. unde transacto termino motus humorum, non est quidquam ultrà expectandum. Atque hinc inferre, Christum à mortuis suscitâsse Lazarum quatriduanum, ut nullus locus naturaliter stemulantibus relinqueretur objiciendi: qui negasient forte miraculum, si ante id tempus eum suscitâsset.
units.tr: Vers. 39. "Τεταρταῖος γὰρ ἦν" [For he was of four days]. "Est enim quatriduanus" [For he has been dead four days]. I cannot refrain from adding to this place the observation of Quistorp: that Rhasis left it written that by law it was ordained that apoplectics should not be buried until seventy-two hours had passed; and that this was very well decreed, because all the humours had completed their motions within three days, that is, within seventy-two hours. So once the period of the motion of the humours was over, nothing more was to be expected. From this he infers that Christ raised Lazarus after four days, so that no place would be left, naturally speaking, for those who opposed him to object; those who perhaps would have denied the miracle if he had raised him before that time.

units.la: Cap. 13. v. 10. Ὁ λελουμένος οὐ χρείαν ἔχει τοῦ νίψασθαι, ἀλλ᾽ ἔστι καθαρὸς ὅλος, Qui ablutus est, non opus habet vel ipsos lavari pedes, sed totus mundus est. Quid enim opus est lavare ejus pedes, qui jamjam lavatus totus est a capite ad calcem. Sequitur, Et vos mundi estis, sed non omnes, sciebat enim quisnam esset qui traderet eum. Sed hoc non erat quod tum voluit Iesus, sed ut ipsos doceret humilitatem suo exemplo, ut patet ex sequentibus. Ad significandum quod tunc voluit, satis erat pedum lotio. Clarius.
units.tr: Chap. 13, vers. 10. "Ὁ λελουμένος οὐ χρείαν ἔχει τοῦ νίψασθαι, ἀλλ' ἔστι καθαρὸς ὅλος" [He who has bathed has no need to wash, except his feet, but is wholly clean]. "Qui ablutus est, non opus habet vel ipsos lavari pedes, sed totus mundus est." [He who has been washed has no need even to have his feet washed, but is wholly clean]. For what need is there to wash the feet of one who has already been entirely washed from head to heel? It follows: "And you are clean, but not all of you; for he knew who would betray him." But this was not what Jesus meant at that time, but to teach them humility by his own example, as is clear from what follows. To signify what he meant then, washing of the feet was enough. More clearly.

units.la: Cap. 15. v. 6. Ἐάν τις μὴ μείνῃ ἐν ἐμοί, ἐβλήθη ἔξω ὡς τὸ κλῆμα, καὶ ἐξηράνθη. Si quis in me non maneat, projicitur foras, ut palmes qui exaruit. Habet eandem phrasim Evangelista, 20. 18. ὅτι ἑώρακα τὸν Κύριον καὶ ταῦτα εἶπεν αὐτῇ, quod vidisset Dominum qui ea sibi dixisset: ut vertit Beza τὸ καὶ, non solum in eo loco, sed etiam Luc. 15. 15. Act. 6. 6. 7. 10. & alibi. Vide animad. in Matth. 27. 10. & Apocal. 1, 5, 6. & Act. 2. 2.
units.tr: Chap. 15, vers. 6. "Ἐάν τις μὴ μείνῃ ἐν ἐμοί, ἐβλήθη ἔξω ὡς τὸ κλῆμα, καὶ ἐξηράνθη" [If anyone does not abide in me, he is cast out like a branch, and withers]. "Si quis in me non maneat, projicitur foras, ut palmes qui exaruit." [If anyone does not abide in me, he is cast out, like the branch that has dried up]. The Evangelist has the same phrase at 20:18: "ὅτι ἑώρακα τὸν Κύριον καὶ ταῦτα εἶπεν αὐτῇ" [that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her], "that she had seen the Lord who had said these things to her." So Beza renders the "καί", and not only in that place, but also at Luke 15:15, Acts 6:6, 7, 10, and elsewhere. See the animadversions on Matthew 27:10, and on Revelation 1:5, 6, and Acts 2:2.

units.la: V. 20, Ἐὰν ἐμὲ ἐδίωξαν, καὶ ὑμᾶς διώξουσιν· εἰ τὸν λόγον μου ἐτήρησαν, καὶ τὸν ὑμέτερον τηρήσουσιν.
units.tr: Vers. 20. "If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my word, they will keep yours. [Ἐὰν ἐμὲ ἐδίωξαν, καὶ ὑμᾶς διώξουσιν· εἰ τὸν λόγον μου ἐτήρησαν, καὶ τὸν ὑμέτερον τηρήσουσιν.]

units.la: Cap. 15. v. 6. Ἐάν, etc.: Greek text printed in the note line above; see main text. τηρῆσαι. Verbum τηρεῖν absque dubio non debet hoc loco sumi pro servare, vel custodire simpliciter, ut vulgò solet, sed in deteriorem partem potius accipi, & videtur poni pro παρατηρεῖν, insidiose observare, Anglicè, to watch, eodem sensu quo dicitur Luc. 14. 1. καὶ αὐτοὶ ἦσαν παρατηρούμενοι αὐτόν, Et ipsi observabant cum, And they watched him; nempè ut caperent quod in eo reprehenderent, ut animadverit Stephanus; & 20, 20. καὶ ἀποστείλαντες ἐγκαθέτους, ἵνα ἐπιλάβωνται αὐτοῦ λόγου, Et observantes eum miserunt insidiatores, ut caperent eum in sermone. Atque istum hoc loco esse sensum verborum ἐνεδρεῦσαι & τηρήσωσι, valdè innuit quod τὸ, ἐν ἐνεδρεύειν ita aptè respondeat & convertiat deteriorem sensu cum τῆς, ἐν ἐδιώξαν. Clarè verò arguit totius sermonis series, repetendo à versu 18. Εἰ ὁ κόσμος ὑμᾶς μισεῖ, &c. Si mundus vos odit, scitote quòd me prius oderit quàm vos. Meministote sermonis quem dixi vobis, Non est servus major Domino, si me persecuti sunt, & vos persequentur, si meum sermonem observaverint, & vestrum etiam observabunt. Sed haec omnia facient vobis propter nomen meum. Omnia certè in malam partem. Nec est omninò insolens vocis τηρεῖν pro observare notio, ut videre est apud Stephanum. Convenit enim τὸ τηρέω cum voce Heb. שָׁמַר servavit, quia in utramque partem sumitur, plerumque in malam. Observavit aliquando ut in eum commodo tempore iram & vindictam effunderet, ut ingenter meritus de republica literaria Castellus noster habet in lexico suo Epanglotto. Ut eandem etiam vocem Mansterus vertit, Jer. 3. 5. Nunquid observabit in saeculum? cui respondet Deus, 12. non observabo in aeternum. Nempè ut iram meam & vindictam in vos effundam; Quo modo & sine observa- verunt Pharisæi sermonem Domini. In quo e- tiam sensu sæpiùs occurrit vox שמר in veteri; ut Psal. 56. 7. שמרו ישמרו, vestigia mea observabunt, τλω πλεγναν μου φυλάξωσι: & 71, 11. נשמרי נפשי, & observatores animæ meæ consulunt pariter, καὶ οἱ φυλάσσοντες τὴν ψυχήν μου ἀπεκάλυψαν, Anglicè, They that lay wait for my soul consult together: In margine Heb. watch, or observe. In quibus utrisque locis æquè legitimè, nec non uno eo- demque sensu verti poterat, τηρῶν & τηροῦντες, pro φυλάξων & φυλάσσοντες. Fateor me debere primam notionem hujus animadversionis Eximio viro Claudio Sarravio, in cujus Epistolis eam repereram.
units.tr: Chap. 15, vers. 6. "Ἐάν, etc.": Greek text printed in the note line above; see main text. "τηρῆσαι" [to keep]. The verb "τηρεῖν" must undoubtedly not be taken in this place to mean simply to keep or to guard, as it commonly is, but rather in a worse sense, and it seems to stand for "παρατηρεῖν" [to watch closely], to observe insidiously, in English to watch, in the same sense as at Luke 14:1: "καὶ αὐτοὶ ἦσαν παρατηρούμενοι αὐτόν" [and they themselves were watching him], "And they watched him"; namely that they might catch something in him to find fault with, as Stephanus observed. And at 20:20: "καὶ ἀποστείλαντες ἐγκαθέτους, ἵνα ἐπιλάβωνται αὐτοῦ λόγου" [and they sent spies, that they might catch him in his words], "watching him, they sent spies, that they might catch him in speech." That this is the sense of the words "ἐνεδρεῦσαι" [to lie in wait] and "τηρήσωσι" [to watch] in this place is strongly suggested by the fact that "τὸ ἐνεδρεύειν" so aptly corresponds to, and turns into a worse sense, the "ἐδίωξαν" [persecuted]. But the course of the whole discourse plainly proves it, going back to verse 18: "If the world hates you," etc. If the world hates you, know that it hated me before it hated you. Remember the saying that I told you: "A servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you; if they have observed my saying, they will also observe yours. But all these things they will do to you for my name's sake." All of them certainly in a bad sense. Nor is the meaning of "τηρεῖν" as to observe altogether unusual, as can be seen in Stephanus. For "τηρέω" agrees with the Hebrew word "שָׁמַר" [he kept], because it is taken in either sense, but for the most part in a bad one. He observed at some convenient time in order to pour out his anger and vengeance upon him, as our Castell, who deserved well of the republic of letters, has in his Heptaglot lexicon. The same word Munster also renders at Jer. 3:5: "Will he observe for ever?" to which God replies (v. 12): "I will not observe for ever." That is, that I may pour out my anger and vengeance upon you. In this same way the Pharisees observed the Lord's word without observing it. In this sense also the word "שמר" [to watch] occurs more often in the Old Testament, as in Psalm 56:7: "שמרו ישמרו" [they watch, they mark my steps], "τὰ ἴχνη μου φυλάξωσι" [they will watch my steps]; and 71:11: "נשמרי נפשי" [those who watch my soul], "καὶ οἱ φυλάσσοντες τὴν ψυχήν μου ἀπεκάλυψαν" [and those who guard my soul have conspired]; in English, "They that lay wait for my soul consult together"; in the Hebrew margin, "watch, or observe." In both these places "τηρῶν" and "τηροῦντες" could equally legitimately, and in one and the same sense, be translated for "φυλάξων" and "φυλάσσοντες". I confess that I owe the first notion of this observation to the distinguished man Claude Sarrau, in whose letters I had found it.

units.la: Cap. 16. v. 26. Ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου αἰτήσεσθε, καὶ οὐ λέγω ὑμῖν, ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐρωτήσω τὸν πατέρα περὶ ὑμῶν. In illo die in nomine meo petetis, & non, dico vobis, quod ego rogabo patrem pro vobis, ipse enim pater amat vos, quia vos me amastis, & credidistis quòd ego à Deo exivi: τὸ, λέγω ὑμῖν, dico vobis, respondet utriq; membro, ἀπὸ τῆς χάριτος; quasi diceret, In illo die, dico vobis, petetis in meo nomine, & non, vel sed non, quod ego rogabo patrem pro vobis, ipse enim pater sine mea intercessione amat vos, dumm- odo in nomine petatis meo, quia amatis vos ideo quia vos amastis me, &c. vel τὸ, λέγω ὑμῖν parenthesi includatur.
units.tr: Chapter 16, verse 26: "In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf" [Ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου αἰτήσεσθε, καὶ οὐ λέγω ὑμῖν, ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐρωτήσω τὸν πατέρα περὶ ὑμῶν]. The Vulgate reads: "In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father for you; for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came out from God."
