The words "I say to you" (λέγω ὑμῖν) answer to both clauses, as though he said: "In that day, I tell you, you will ask in my name, and not (but not) because I will ask the Father for you; for the Father himself, without my intercession, loves you, provided you ask in my name, because you love me, since you have loved me," and so on. Or the words "I say to you" may be enclosed in a parenthesis.

units.la: V. 30. Νῦν οἶδαμεν ὅτι οἶδας πάντα, καὶ οὐ χρείαν ἔχεις ἵνα τίς σε ἐρωτᾷ, ἐν τούτῳ πιστεύομεν ὅτι ἀπὸ Θεοῦ ἐξῆλθες. Nunc scimus quod nosti om- nia, nec opus habes ut quis te interroget, propter hoc credimus te à Deo exivisse. Si quis quærat, quid sibi velit, non opus habes ut quis te interroget, retrospiciat versum 19, ubi dicitur Jesum cognoscere quòd volebant eum interrogare, etsi tamen dixerunt tantùm inter se, quid est hoc quod dicit nobis? Modicum & non videbitis me, &c. Propterea hoc nunc ergo aiunt se credere eum à Deo exiisse, quia novit quid ipsi in animo agitarent, nec opus habuit ut illi eum priùs interrogarent; Δεῖ γὰρ εἰδέναι τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς καρδίας, Dei enim est scire occulta cordis. Theophylact.
units.tr: Verse 30: "Now we know that you know all things, and you have no need that anyone should question you; by this we believe that you came out from God" [Νῦν οἶδαμεν ὅτι οἶδας πάντα, καὶ οὐ χρείαν ἔχεις ἵνα τίς σε ἐρωτᾷ, ἐν τούτῳ πιστεύομεν ὅτι ἀπὸ Θεοῦ ἐξῆλθες]. The Vulgate reads: "Now we know that you know all things, and have no need that anyone should ask you; therefore we believe that you came out from God." If anyone asks what this means, "you have no need that anyone should question you," let him look back to verse 19, where it is said that Jesus knew that they wished to question him, although they had only said to one another, "What is this that he says to us? A little while and you will not see me," and so on. So now they say they believe he came out from God, because he knew what they were thinking in their minds, and he did not need them to question him first. "For it is necessary to know the secrets of the heart" [Δεῖ γὰρ εἰδέναι τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς καρδίας]: "for it belongs to God to know the hidden things of the heart." Theophylact.

units.la: Cap. 20. v. 17. Μή μου ἅπτου (οὔπω γὰρ ἀναβέβηκα πρὸς τὸν πατέρα μου)· πορεύου δὲ &c. Et sic legit Plantini vetus, & interlinearis cum parenthesi; Noli me tangere (nondum enim ascendi ad Patrem meum) vade autem ad fratres meos, & dic eis, Ascendo ad patrem meum, & patrem vestrum. Noluit eam in ejus amplexu immorari, sed ut confestim iret ad discipulos, & eos tam beato nuncio, nempe eum nondum ascendisse, sed brevi ascensurum, reficeret, qui proculdubio manebant omnes perturbati & exanimes.
units.tr: Chapter 20, verse 17: "Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father; but go to..." [Μή μου ἅπτου (οὔπω γὰρ ἀναβέβηκα πρὸς τὸν πατέρα μου)· πορεύου δὲ &c.]. So reads the old Plantin edition, and the interlinear text, with the parenthesis: "Touch me not (for I have not yet ascended to my Father), but go to my brothers, and say to them, I ascend to my Father and your Father." He did not wish her to linger in his embrace, but that she should go at once to the disciples and refresh them with this blessed message, namely that he had not yet ascended but would ascend shortly; for without doubt they all remained troubled and despairing.

units.la: Cap. 21. v. 22. Et si eum volo manere donec veniam, quid ad te? Atque hoc sermone innuere voluit Dominus Johannem revera mansurum in vivis donec ipse veniret, sicut ipso facto vixit, nempe ad excidium Hierosolymæ, & triginta annos postea, si qua fides Chronologis: in quo numero censendi illi, quos tunc adstantes non gustaturos mortem affirmat Jesus, donec viderent filium hominis venientem in regno suo. Matth. 16. 28. De excidio Hierosolymæ passim intelligitur adventus Domini & regnum Christi, quod tamen eo tempore non innotuit, Exiit enim sermo iste inter fratres, discipulum illum non moriturum. Atque hoc errore seductus Tertullianus affirmavit falsam fuisse spem illorum, qui Johannem in adventum Domini remansurum expectabant, obiit enim Iohannes. Non enim intellexit ille de adventu Domini in ultionem Iudaeorum ad excidium Hierosolymæ, sed de ultimo in extremum judicium.
units.tr: Chapter 21, verse 22: "And if I wish him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" By this saying the Lord meant to indicate that John would really remain alive until he himself came, as in fact he did live, namely until the destruction of Jerusalem, and thirty years afterwards, if the chronologers are to be trusted. In this number are to be counted those who, Jesus affirms, were standing by and would not taste death until they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (Matt. 16:28). The coming of the Lord and the kingdom of Christ are often understood of the destruction of Jerusalem, although that was not then known, for "this saying went out among the brothers, that that disciple would not die." Led astray by this error, Tertullian affirmed that the hope of those who expected John to remain until the coming of the Lord was false, for John died. He did not understand this of the coming of the Lord in vengeance on the Jews, at the destruction of Jerusalem, but of the last coming to the final judgment.

units.la: In Acta Apostolorum.
units.tr: On the Acts of the Apostles.

units.la: ACT. c. 1. v. 4. Παραγγείλας αὐτοῖς, ἀπὸ Ἱεροσολύμων μὴ χωρίζεσθαι, ἀλλὰ περιμένειν τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ πατρός, ἣν ἠκούσατέ, φησί. Verba hæc vertuntur rectius quam vulgò solent sine supplemento salvâ syntaxi, & accommodo sensu in hunc modum. Præcepit eis, nolite ab Hierosolymis discedere, sed expectate promissionem patris, quam audistis, mei. Eundem habemus sensum fere ipsissimis verbis in loco parallelo Evangelii Luc. 24. 49. Et ecce ego mittam promissionem patris mei in vos, vos autem residete in civitate, quoad usque induamini virtute ex alto. Vide etiam Joh. 14. 26. 15. 26. Violenta vero est constructio, ἡμᾶς pro ἡμῖν, Elleipsi etiam valdè familiari Infinitivus usurpatur pro Imperativo, subaudiendo vocem θέλετε, vel simile, ante τὸ χωρίζεσθαι, & τὸ περιμένειν. Qualia exempla sunt frequentissima apud Phocilidem, in unoquoque fere carmine.
units.tr: Acts, chapter 1, verse 4: "Commanding them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he says, you have heard" [Παραγγείλας αὐτοῖς, ἀπὸ Ἱεροσολύμων μὴ χωρίζεσθαι, ἀλλὰ περιμένειν τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ πατρός, ἣν ἠκούσατέ, φησί]. These words are rendered more correctly than they usually are, without supplying anything and with the syntax preserved, and with a suitable sense, in this way: "He commanded them, do not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which you have heard from me." We have almost the same sense in the very same words in the parallel passage of the Gospel, Luke 24:49: "Behold, I will send the promise of my Father upon you; but you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high." See also John 14:26 and 15:26. The construction "us" for "to us" is forced; and by a very familiar ellipsis the infinitive is used for the imperative, with the words "you wish" or something similar understood before "to depart" and "to wait." Examples of this are very frequent in Phocylides, in almost every poem.

units.la: Μὴ πλουτεῖν ἀδίκως, ἀλλ' ἐξ ὁσίων βιοτεύειν. Ἀρχῆσθαι παρέσται, καὶ ἀλλοτρίων ἀπέχεσθαι, Πᾶσι δίκαια γέμειν, &c.
units.tr: "Do not grow rich unjustly, but live from honest means. You will be able to rule, and to keep away from what belongs to others, and to be full of justice toward all" [Μὴ πλουτεῖν ἀδίκως, ἀλλ' ἐξ ὁσίων βιοτεύειν. Ἀρχῆσθαι παρέσται, καὶ ἀλλοτρίων ἀπέχεσθαι, Πᾶσι δίκαια γέμειν, &c.].

units.la: Nè ditescas injustè, sed ex justè partis vives. Esto contentus præsentibus, & ab alienis abstine, Omnibus justa tribue.
units.tr: Do not grow rich by injustice, but live by a just share. Be content with what you have, and keep your hands off what belongs to others; render just things to all.

units.la: Necnon etiam in N.T. Rom. 12. 14, 15. Εὐλογεῖτε τὸὺς διώκοντας ὑμᾶς· εὐλογεῖτε καὶ μὴ καταρᾶσθε· χαίρειν μετὰ χαιρόντων, κλαίειν μετὰ κλαιόντων. Benedicite & nolite maledicere, gaudete cum gaudentibus, flete cum flentibus. vide etiam Ruth 1. 6. Matth. 5. 39. Luc. 5. 14. Act. 23. 22. & 24.
units.tr: Likewise in the New Testament, Romans 12:14, 15: "Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep" [Εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς διώκοντας ὑμᾶς· εὐλογεῖτε καὶ μὴ καταρᾶσθε· χαίρειν μετὰ χαιρόντων, κλαίειν μετὰ κλαιόντων]. Bless and do not curse; rejoice with the rejoicing, weep with the weeping. See also Ruth 1:6; Matt. 5:39; Luke 5:14; Acts 23:22 and 24.

units.la: Cap. I. v. 25. Σὺ Κύριε καρδιογνῶστα πάντων, ἀνάδειξον ἐκ τούτων τῶν δύο ἕνα, ὃν ἐξελέξω, λαβεῖν τὸν κλῆρον τῆς διακονίας ταύτης καὶ ἀποστολῆς, ἐξ ἧς παρέβη Ἰούδας, πορευθῆναι εἰς τὸν τόπον τὸν ἴδιον, i.e. εἰς τὸν τόπον τὸν ἴδιον τῆς Ἰούδα, vel εἰς τὸν τόπον αὐτοῦ. Atque ἴδιον hoc loco posse accipi pro αὐτοῦ, clare indicat Oecumenius in expositione sua in haec verba, τόπον τὸ ἴδιον, ἢτοι ἀγχέλου κλῆσις, &c. ἢ ὅτι, τῆς Ἰούδα ἐξαπωσμένης καὶ τὸν ἴδιον χώραν, τὸν ἐκείνου λαμβάνων ἀποσταλεῖ. Locum suum, vel suspendium nominat, &c. vel quoniam Juda lapso vel amoto, illa qui accipit ejus Episcopatum, habeat ejus locum. Nec quid aliud potest hoc loco Oecumenii, τὸ ἴδιον, significare, quàm τὸν ἴδιον τόπον, locum ejus, in quem oportuit Matthiam succedere, ut ex his ipsis verbis recte animadvertit Clarius. In locum suum, si ad Judam referas, videtur intelligere laqueum, quo se dignum judicavit ob proditionem, sin ad Matthiam, intellige Episcopatum cui successit, i.e. Apostolatum, nondum enim constituti erant Episcopi, nisi Episcopatum munus intelligas. Suus pro ejus frequentissimè usurpat Cicero, idque Graecorum imitatione affirmat Budaeus, Suus enim non modò τὸ ἴδιον ἑαυτῆς, sed etiam τὸ ἴδιον αὐτῆς significat, & utroque modo accipitur apud Graecos, ut ὅς saepissimè pro sibi, & pro ei. Bud.Compag. 28. Adeò ut genuina interpretatio sit hujusmodi Tu Domine, qui cordis nosti omnium, ostende ex his duobus unum, quem elegeris, accipere sortem hujus ministerii & Apostolatus, à quo descivit Judas, ut adeat locum suum, nempè ut is quem elegeris, succedat in locum ejus qui descivit, i. e. in locum Apostolatûs Judæ. Πορευθῆναι εἰς τὸν τόπον, est eadem phrasis ac πορευθῆναι εἰς τὰ κτήματα apud Demosthenem, quam Budæus interpretatur, Hereditatem adire; Hereditatem enim adire apud Ciceronem, est Hereditatem subire vel suscipere, & se heredem profiteri, ut rectè exponit noster De sacra Quercu, Anglicè To enter upon, or to take upon one the inheritance. Atque hæc interpretatio mihi videtur rationi magis consona, quàm eorum, qui interpretantur de ipso Judâ, quasi Lucas vellet ipsum abiisse in locum suum, nempè ut volunt in Gehennam. Non enim credo aliquid ejusmodi unquam in animum ascendisse Evangelistæ, suspicio verò cum Chrysostomo, τὸ φιλόσοφον τῆς ἀνδρὸς, πῶς ὑχ' ὑβρίζει, &c. prudentiam viri, quomodo non dicit contumeliam, non insultas, &c. Quod planè arguit eum non sensisse Lucam in inferos adjudicâsse Judam, quid enim magis contumeliosum dixisset Lucas, quàm eum abiisse in locum suum, si intelligas Gehennam? Neque fuit Historici vel Evangelistæ suam sententiam adeòque severam interponere, sed Judam reliquisse judicio Dei; satis erat ei rem de facto enarrâsse, ut promiserat in initio Evangelii, καθὼς παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν οἱ ἀπ' ἀρχῆς αὐτόπται καὶ &c. sicut tradiderunt nobis, qui ab initio fuerunt spectatores, vel oculati testes, &c. Quem verò spectatorem dixeris Judæ in inferis?
units.tr: Chapter 1, verse 25: "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show from these two the one whom you have chosen, to take the lot of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas turned aside, to go to his own place" [Σὺ Κύριε καρδιογνῶστα πάντων, ἀνάδειξον ἐκ τούτων τῶν δύο ἕνα, ὃν ἐξελέξω, λαβεῖν τὸν κλῆρον τῆς διακονίας ταύτης καὶ ἀποστολῆς, ἐξ ἧς παρέβη Ἰούδας, πορευθῆναι εἰς τὸν τόπον τὸν ἴδιον], that is, "into his own place," i.e. into the place of Judas, or "into his place" [εἰς τὸν τόπον τὸν ἴδιον τῆς Ἰούδα, vel εἰς τὸν τόπον αὐτοῦ]. That the word ἴδιον here can be taken for αὐτοῦ is clearly indicated by Oecumenius in his commentary on these words, "the own place" [τόπον τὸ ἴδιον], that is, the calling of the apostle, etc., or because, Judas having been cast out, he who receives his place should take the place of that man. "He names his own place, or the noose, etc., or because, with Judas fallen or removed, she who receives his office should have his place." Nor can anything else be meant by ἴδιον in Oecumenius here than "his own place," the place into which Matthias ought to succeed, as Clarius rightly observes from these very words. "If you refer 'his own place' to Judas, he seems to mean the noose by which he judged himself worthy because of his betrayal; but if to Matthias, understand the bishopric to which he succeeded, that is, the apostleship, for bishops were not yet appointed, unless you understand the office of bishop." Suus for ejus is very frequently used by Cicero, and Budaeus affirms that this is in imitation of the Greeks, for suus signifies not only τὸ ἴδιον ἑαυτῆς but also τὸ ἴδιον αὐτῆς, and among the Greeks it is taken in both ways, as ὅς is most often used for "to himself" and "to him." Budaeus, Compag. 28. So the genuine interpretation is of this kind: "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show from these two the one whom you have chosen to receive the lot of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas fell away, so that he may go to his own place," namely that the one you have chosen may succeed to the place of the one who fell away, i.e. into the place of Judas's apostleship. "To go into the place" [πορευθῆναι εἰς τὸν τόπον] is the same phrase as "to go into the possessions" [πορευθῆναι εἰς τὰ κτήματα] in Demosthenes, which Budaeus translates "to enter upon the inheritance"; for adire hereditatem in Cicero means to take up or assume an inheritance and to declare oneself heir, as our countryman rightly explains it in De sacra Quercu, in English "To enter upon, or to take upon one the inheritance." This interpretation seems to me more consistent with reason than that of those who understand it of Judas himself, as though Luke wished him to have gone into his own place, namely, as they would have it, into Gehenna. For I do not believe that anything of the kind ever came into the mind of the Evangelist; I suspect rather, with Chrysostom, the wisdom of the man, how he does not reproach, does not insult [τὸ φιλόσοφον τῆς ἀνδρὸς, πῶς οὐχ ὑβρίζει], etc. This plainly proves that he did not think Luke had consigned Judas to the lower world; for what more insulting thing would Luke have said than that he went into his own place, if you understand Gehenna? Nor was it the place of the historian or Evangelist to interpose his own opinion, still less so severe, but to leave Judas to the judgment of God; it was enough for him to relate the fact, as he had promised at the beginning of the Gospel: "as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses delivered them to us" [καθὼς παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν οἱ ἀπ' ἀρχῆς αὐτόπται καὶ &c.]. But what eyewitness of Judas in the lower world could you name?

units.la: Cap. 2. v. 2. Καὶ ἐγένετο ἄφνω ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἦχος
units.tr: Chap. 2, v. 2. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound [Καὶ ἐγένετο ἄφνω ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἦχος]

units.la: ἤχος ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ὥσπερ φερομένης πνοῆς βιαίας, καὶ ἐπλήρωσεν ὅλον τὸν οἶκον οὗ ἦσαν καθήμενοι. Et factus est repente de caelo sonus tanquam irruentis vehementis flatus, & replevit totam domum ubi erant sedentes. Τὸ, καὶ, hoc loco primo intuitu, etiam & Grammatice copulat τὸ ἦχος, & ἐπλήρωσεν: Sed certè flatus intelligitur qui replevit domum, & non sonus; ἐπλήρωσεν ὃ ὅλον τὸ οἶκον τὸ ἄνωθεν κολυμβήθρας τάξιν ἀναπληροῦσα, ἐπὶ καὶ ἐπεμίψατο αὐτοῖς, ἐν πνεύματι βαπτισθήσεσθε καὶ πνεῖ: Replevit domum totam flatus sive spiritus, Baptisterii sive lavacri vicem supplens, quoniam promissum erat illis, baptizabimini in Spiritu & igne. Græc. Schol. Ideoque Beza pro more suo, pro & replevit, vertit, qui replevit. Eadem enim est loquendi formula cum ea quam adnotavimus Matth. 27. 10. Joh. 15. 6. Act. 6.6. & alibi. Anglicus subaudit αὐτὴ, And it filled all the house where they were sitting.
units.tr: v. 2. "There came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting" [ἦχος ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ὥσπερ φερομένης πνοῆς βιαίας, καὶ ἐπλήρωσεν ὅλον τὸν οἶκον οὗ ἦσαν καθήμενοι]. The Vulgate reads: "And suddenly there was a sound from heaven, as of a rushing, violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting." Here, at first sight, the "and" grammatically joins "sound" with "filled"; but it is surely the wind, not the sound, that filled the house. The Greek Scholiast says that the wind filled the whole house from above, taking the place of a baptistery, since it had been promised to them, "You shall be baptized in the Spirit and fire." Beza, true to his custom, therefore renders "and it filled" as "which filled." This is the same idiom that we noted at Matt. 27.10, John 15.6, Acts 6.6 and elsewhere. The English version supplies "it" (αὐτὴ): "And it filled all the house where they were sitting."

units.la: V. 22. Ἰησοῦν τὸν Ναζωραῖον ἀνδρα ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀποδεδειγμένον εἰς ὑμᾶς δυνάμεσι καὶ τέρασι &c. Jesum Nazarenum hominem à Deo esse demonstratum ad vel apud vos, sive vobis per virtutes & miracula & signa, quæ edidit per eum Deus in medio vestrum. Subaudiendo verbum εἶναι. Ideoque Chrysostomus legit inverso ordine Ἰησοῦν Ναζωραῖον ἄνδρα ἀποδεδειγμένον ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ εἰς ὑμᾶς δυνάμεσι &c addens, ὃν ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀπεστάλη. Eò quòd à Deo missus erat. Ut etiam animadvertit Scholiastes Græcus ἀποδεδειγμένον, οἷον, ἐκ ἀμφιβεβητύμων, ἀλλ᾽ ἀποδεδειγμένον διὰ τῶν ἔργων, ὅτι ἀπὸ Θεοῦ ἦν. Demonstratum i.e. non dubitatum, sed demonstratum per opera, quod à Deo erat. Frigidum & jejunum videtur dicere hominem à Deo approbatum: non enim omninò attingit scopum loci.
units.tr: v. 22. "Jesus the Nazarene, a man demonstrated by God to you by powers and wonders, etc." [Ἰησοῦν τὸν Ναζωραῖον ἄνδρα ἀπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀποδεδειγμένον εἰς ὑμᾶς δυνάμεσι καὶ τέρασι]: "Jesus of Nazareth, a man shown by God to be among you (or to you) by the powers, wonders and signs which God did through him in the midst of you." The word "to be" (εἶναι) is understood. So Chrysostom reads the words in reverse order, "Jesus the Nazarene, a man shown by God to you by powers," adding "whom he sent from God," because he was sent by God. The Greek Scholiast also notes that "demonstrated" means not "doubtful" (ἐκ ἀμφιβεβητύμων) but "demonstrated through works," because he was from God. "Demonstrated," that is, not doubted but shown through the works that he was from God. It seems a flat and bare thing to say that the man was approved by God; for it does not altogether hit the point of the passage.

units.la: V 27. "Ὅτι οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψεις τὴν ψυχήν μου εἰς ᾅδην, &c. Quoniam non derelinques animam meam in Hade, neque dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem. Prius membrum spectare videtur animam, quæ non in statu mortis detenta erat, ἐν ταῖς ὠδῖσι τοῦ θανάτου, ut v. 24. i.e. ἐν δεσμοῖς, in vinculis ut Athanasius, Beza & alii, in receptaculis illis, ubi piorum animæ reservantur, donec coronam accipiant, ut Augustinus, sive in medio umbræ mortis, ubi animæ mortuorum erant, ut Irenæus, sive εἰς ᾅδην, quo eum descendisse vel migrasse edocti fumus Symbolo Apostolico, sive in Paradiso cum anima latronis, quæ omnia idem volunt. Non enim video cur non & in hoc sensu accipiatur Paradisus, ab Hebræa voce פרדס separavit, i.e. locus separatus, ut sunt amœnitatis causâ horti vel vivaria, in quibus ad voluptatem arbores & plantæ excoluntur; sive aluntur feræ, cujus amœnitatis gratiâ vox ista sensum hunc obtinuit apud Græcos & Hebræos, apud quos frequentissimè vocatur פרדס. Neque est terminatio vocis פרדס apud Hebræos adeò insolita, apud quos ejusmodi anomala sunt frequentia, ut eam opus sit debere Persis. Licet enim forte Nehemiae eam à Persis mutuari poterat, qui in aulâ vivebat Persicâ, Solomonem tamen certum est, qui eâdem voce usus est in Ecclesiaste. & in Cantic. multis retro ante Nehemiam seculis, Hebræâ scripsisse dialecto, nec quidem reor omnino usum esse Persicâ. Utcunque verò id sit, fas esse reor dicere, pios, qui in statu mortis sunt, esse in Paradiso, in quocunque loco separatos, atque in eo loco non esse relictam animam Christi. Posterius verò membrum spectare videtur corpus, quod non sensit corruptionem, ut cætera humana corpora; in quo sensu interpretatur Psalmistam Petrus, v. 31. &c. χαταλείψει &c. Quoniam non relicta est anima ejus in Hades, neque caro ejus vidit corruptionem. Planè distinguens inter animam & carnem, quasi de industriâ, ne quis hoc ad sepulchrum Christi tantùm spectare putet, ut quidam volunt, qui vocem άδης nihil aliud significare dicunt. Perversissimum verò est, ut Tertullianus de Carne Christi, ut carnem nominantes animam intelligamus, & animam significantes carnem interpretemur &c. Nec minus planè distinguit Athanasius, Χότε γάρ δύναται &c. Neque enim mors prevaluit ut sibi subjiceret humanam ejus animam, ut vinculis detineret, nec corruptio per tyrannidem invadens in ejus corpus vim suam exercebat ad putrefactionem. Recte Hilarius. Humanae ista lex necessitatis, ut consepultis corporibus ad inferos animae descendant. Quam descensionem Dominus ad consummationem veri hominis non recusavit. Et procul dubio iste fuit finis verborum Petri, ut probaret resurrectionem Christi, neque eum fuisse relictum in statu mortis. At verò sunt non pauci, qui prorsus negant ullum esse hujusmodi locum vel receptaculum animarum, affirmantes, piorum animas immediatè post separationem a corpore migrare in cœlos, etiam in tertium cœlum aliqui. Quorum ego affirmationem nec Scripturis, nec authoritate, nec ratione niti arbitror. Allegant inter alia, Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. At eo die non fuit Salvator in cœlo, nisi loquantur vel sentiant &#x E6;quivocè, nondum enim ascendit vel humano corpore vel anima, quantum Scriptura vel ratio docet. Fuit ergo Paradisus locus aliquis alius, nimirum Hades, in quo pro brevi tempore detenta est ejus anima, & in quem descendit, ut se hominem esse ostenderet, & in quo fuit eo die una cum ejus anima; anima etiam Latronis, ubi illa quidem cum reliquis piorum defunctorum animis (excepta Salvatoris) requiescit in ultimum diem resurrectionis. Recte Drusius, Paradisum a coelo distingui, quod ille sit receptaculum animarum post vitam, caelum autem recipiat post judicium extremum. Nec solebant (ut observavit Grotius) Christiani veteres hunc sive statum sive locum medii temporis inter hanc vitam & resurrectionem caeli nomine appellare. Urgent alii illud Ambrosii, Christum introitu suo aperuisse credentibus regnum caelorum, nec antea quidem Patres participes esse factos promissionis, a morte vero & ascensione Christi eos una cum eo ascendisse in coelos ibique consummatos, scilicet quoad animas in coelum receptas, quae ante ascensionem Christi non ascenderant. Fateor equidem Christum aperuisse credentibus regnum coelorum, (non tamen eorum sensu) clausum enim erat antea universo mundo, nisi Judaeis, nunc vero ab ejus passione & ascensione patet cuilibet intranti, ita ut cuivis hominum, qui in ipsum crediderit, liceat in id perrumpere. At vero, ut occurram argumento, ubinam erant obsecro Patrum animae, antequam cum Christo ascenderent, ut aiunt, in coelos? ubicunque enim illae fuerint, ratio suadet, nec Scriptura negat, eodem loci fuisse animam Christi, & ubi anima Christi, anima fuit & Latronis. Nondum vero ascenderant, nec certe erant in cruciatus loco, non enim Latroni fuisset solatium, quod opinor intendebat Christus, si dixisset ei, hodie mecum eris in cruciatus loco, erant ergo in loco tertio quietis aliquo. In quo si remanere dicamus omnium piorum defunctorum animas in novissimum diem, quid inde periculi, quid incommodi? Si, inquam, credamus, nec credamus amplius, unam omnibus manere resurrectionem in ultimo
units.tr: v. 27. "Because you will not leave my soul in Hades, etc. [Ὅτι οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψεις τὴν ψυχήν μου εἰς ᾅδην]: Because you will not leave my soul in Hades, nor will you give your Holy One to see corruption." The first clause seems to refer to the soul, which was not held in the state of death, "in the pangs of death" as in v. 24 [ἐν ταῖς ὠδῖσι τοῦ θανάτου], that is, "in bonds" [ἐν δεσμοῖς], in chains, as Athanasius, Beza and others take it; in those receptacles where the souls of the godly are kept until they receive their crown, as Augustine has it; or in the midst of the shadow of death, where the souls of the dead were, as Irenaeus has it; or into Hades, to which we are taught by the Apostles' Creed that he descended or went; or in Paradise with the soul of the thief. All these say the same thing. For I do not see why Paradise should not also be taken in this sense, from the Hebrew word פרדס [pardes], separated, that is, a separate place, as gardens or fish-ponds are set apart for pleasure, in which trees and plants are cultivated for delight, or wild animals are kept, for the sake of pleasure; and this word has taken on that meaning among the Greeks and Hebrews, among whom it is most often called פרדס. Nor is the ending of the word פרדס among the Hebrews so unusual, since among them such irregular forms are common, so that there is no need to say it was borrowed from the Persians. For although Nehemiah could perhaps have borrowed it from the Persians, since he lived at the Persian court, it is certain that Solomon, who used the same word in Ecclesiastes and in the Song of Songs, many centuries before Nehemiah, wrote in the Hebrew dialect, nor do I think he used Persian at all. However that may be, I think it is right to say that the godly who are in the state of death are in Paradise, in whatever place they are set apart, and that the soul of Christ was not left in that place. The second clause seems to refer to the body, which did not see corruption as the other human bodies do; and in this sense Peter interprets the Psalmist, v. 31, etc. "χαταλείψει": Because his soul was not left in Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. He clearly distinguishes between soul and flesh, as if on purpose, so that no one should think this refers only to the sepulchre of Christ, as some wish, who say that the word ᾅδης means nothing else. But it is most perverse, as Tertullian says of the Flesh of Christ, to take the flesh as meaning the soul, and to interpret the soul as meaning the flesh, etc. Athanasius likewise distinguishes quite plainly: "For death did not prevail so as to subject his human soul to itself, to hold it in chains, nor did corruption, invading by tyranny, exercise its force on his body to bring about putrefaction." Hilary rightly says: It is the law of human necessity that souls descend to the underworld together with the buried bodies. The Lord did not refuse this descent, in order to complete a true man. And without doubt this was the purpose of Peter's words, to prove the resurrection of Christ, and that he had not been left in the state of death. But there are not a few who utterly deny that there is any such place or receptacle of souls, affirming that the souls of the godly, immediately after separation from the body, migrate into the heavens, some even into the third heaven. I think their affirmation rests on neither Scripture, nor authority, nor reason. They allege, among other things, Today you will be with me in Paradise. But on that day the Saviour was not in heaven, unless they speak or think equivocally; for he had not yet ascended, either in his human body or in his soul, as Scripture or reason teaches. Paradise was therefore some other place, namely Hades, in which his soul was held for a short time, and into which he descended to show that he was a man, and in which he was on that day together with his soul; and the soul of the thief was there too, where it indeed rests with the other souls of the departed godly (except that of the Saviour) until the last day of resurrection. Drusius rightly distinguishes Paradise from heaven, since the former is the receptacle of souls after this life, whereas heaven receives them after the final judgment. Nor did the ancient Christians (as Grotius observed) usually call this state or place of the interval between this life and the resurrection by the name of heaven. Others press that saying of Ambrose, that Christ by his coming opened the kingdom of heaven to believers, and that the Fathers before did not share in the promise, but that from the death and ascension of Christ they ascended with him into the heavens and were there made perfect, that is, as to their souls received into heaven, which had not ascended before the ascension of Christ. I grant indeed that Christ opened the kingdom of heaven to believers (though not in their sense); for it was previously closed to the whole world except the Jews, but now since his passion and ascension it lies open to anyone who enters, so that it is lawful for any man who believes in him to force his way into it. But, to meet the argument directly: where, I beg you, were the souls of the Fathers before they ascended, as they say, with Christ into the heavens? For wherever they were, reason suggests, and Scripture does not deny, that the soul of Christ was in the same place, and where the soul of Christ was, there the soul of the thief was too. But they had not yet ascended, nor were they certainly in the place of torment; for it would not have been a comfort to the thief, as I think Christ intended, if he had said to him, Today you will be with me in the place of torment; they were therefore in some third place of rest. If we say that the souls of all the godly departed remain in that place until the last day, what danger or harm follows from this? If, I say, we believe this, and we no longer believe that there is one resurrection for all at the last

units.la: Sic
units.tr: Thus.

units.la: ultimo die, & patribus & nobis, in quo die nos cum illis perfecte consummabimur, interim vero universas piorum animas esse in manu Dei, ὡς ἀφειλόμενον αὐτοῖς τόπον, in loco iis debito, ut in Epistola Polycarpi ad Philippenses. Estque illud interim, si cum æternitate compares, millies millies vel puncto minus. Sed reprimo me. Quæstio ista severiorem forte disquisitionem postulat, prolixa magis quam ut his angustiis terminetur; Quæstio tamen, quam neque Scriptura usquam explicite, neq; generale aliquod Concilium in utramvis partem pro articulo fidei definivit, antequam id fecerat Convocatio Dublinensis 1615. Quæ tum pro articulo fidei statuit, Post finem huius vitæ animas filiorum Dei immediate recipi in cælis, &c. de industria forte ut occurrerent Romanorum Limbo. Neque hæc dixissem, nisi quòd adeò multi idque adeò mordicus teneant dogma istud pro articulo fidei, damnantes universos, qui aliter sentiunt ac ipsi, impietatis & hæresewς, atq; etiam hæc verba mihi ita viderentur explicita, ut quodammodo manu ducerent in sensum quem proposui, licet rarius eo nomine à quoquam animadversa. Placet mihi admodum modestia Calvini in hoc ipso argumento, ubi agens de animabus fidelium, earumque statu & loco post hanc vitam, Valde (inquit) Se torquent multi, disputando quem locum occupent piorum animæ, & an cœlesti fruantur gloria, necne, atqui stultum & temerarium est de rebus incognitis altius inquirere, quàm Deus nobis scire permisit: & alibi in locum Evangelii de Latrone & Paradiso. De loco Paradisi curiosè & argutè disputandum non est, nobis sufficiat, quicunque fide insiti sumus in Christi corpus, esse ejus vitæ participes, ac ita post mortem leatâ ac lætâ quiete fruituros, donec in solidum patefiat in Christi adventu caelestis vitae gloria. In qua sententia ego lubens acquiesco, tutum esse arbitrans quod sentio, vero simile cum Petro Martyre, rationi consonum, nec Scripturae absonum. Vide Usserium contra Jesuitam de Limbo Patrum versus finem, sive per totum: & Montacutium in Apparatu ad Origines Ecclesiasticas, pag. 49, 50. &c.
units.tr: At the last day, in which we and the fathers will be made perfect together with them. Meanwhile the souls of all the pious are in the hand of God, as a place owed to them [ὡς ἀφειλόμενον αὐτοῖς τόπον], in a place due to them, as in the Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians. And this meanwhile, if you compare it with eternity, is a thousand thousand times, or less than a point. But I hold myself back. This question would perhaps need a more rigorous inquiry, too long to be settled within these narrow limits. Yet neither Scripture anywhere states it explicitly, nor any general council defined it as an article of faith in either direction, until the Dublin Convocation of 1615 did so. That convocation then laid down as an article of faith, After the end of this life the souls of the sons of God are received immediately into heaven, etc., perhaps deliberately to meet the Limbo of the Romanists. I would not have said this, except that so many hold that doctrine so stubbornly as an article of faith, condemning as impious and heretical all who think otherwise, and except that these words seem to me so explicit that they would, in a way, lead one by the hand to the sense I have proposed, although this has rarely been noticed by anyone under that name. I am greatly pleased by the modesty of Calvin on this very subject, where, treating of the souls of the faithful and their state and place after this life, he says: Valde (he says) Many men torment themselves by disputing what place the souls of the pious occupy, and whether they enjoy heavenly glory or not; but it is foolish and rash to inquire into things unknown more deeply than God has permitted us to know. And elsewhere, on the passage of the Gospel about the Thief and Paradise: The place of Paradise is not to be disputed curiously and subtly; it is enough for us that whoever are engrafted by faith into the body of Christ are partakers of his life, and so after death will enjoy a quiet, joyful rest, until the glory of heavenly life is fully revealed at the coming of Christ. In this opinion I gladly rest, judging that what I think is safe, probable with Peter Martyr, consonant with reason, and not discordant with Scripture. See Ussher against the Jesuit on the Limbo of the Fathers, near the end or throughout; and Montagu in the Apparatus to the Origines Ecclesiasticae, pp. 49, 50, etc.

units.la: V. 30. Τὸ χῖ σάρκα ἀναστήσειν ἢ χεισὶν, &c. Τὸ, hoc loco sumitur τεχνικῶς, vel, ut dicunt, materialiter, & materiam denotat jurisjurandi quod juravit Davidi Deus, nempe τὸ ἀναστῆσαι χῖ σάρκα, &c. ex fructu lumbi ipsius resurgere facturum Christum in carne, ut sederet super solium ejus. Atque hoc ipsum est τὸ ζητούμενον, quod Apostolus probare contendit, nempe Christum resurrexisse in carne, quod ex contextu abunde manifestum est. Praescius enim locutus est de ἀναστάσεως τῆς χεισῶ, de resurrectione Christi. v.31, quod idem etiam affirmat versu immediate proximo. Ut omnino vox ἀναστῆσαι non debeat intelligi de Christi adventu, sed de resurrectione ejus in carne, atque ita affirmat Beza τὸ ἀναστῆσαι, melius praesenti argumento quadrare, si de resurrectione Christi accipiatur, quam si ad adventum referas. Si vero τὸ ἀναστήσειν melius quadrat resurrectioni, multo magis τὸ χῖ σάρκα ἀνασταῆσαι, in carne facturum resurgere. Τὸ χῖ frequenter hoc sensu usurpatur, ut χῖ τῶν Ἀντιοχείαν, in Antiochia, Act. 15.25, χῖ καιρόν, in tempore, Rom. 5.6. ἔμεινον χῖ χώραν, manserunt in agro. Phav, χῖ, ἀντὶ τῆς, ἐν. Hesych.
units.tr: Verse 30. That he would raise up Christ in the flesh [τὸ ἀναστήσειν τὸν Χριστὸν κατὰ σάρκα]. The article τὸ here is taken technically, or as they say materially, and denotes the matter of the oath which God swore to David, namely that he would raise up Christ in the flesh from the fruit of his loins, to sit upon his throne. And this very thing is the point at issue, which the Apostle labours to prove, namely that Christ rose again in the flesh, which is abundantly clear from the context: for foreseeing it, he spoke of the resurrection of Christ [ἀναστάσεως τοῦ Χριστοῦ], of the resurrection of Christ, in verse 31, which he also affirms in the verse immediately following. So the word ἀναστῆσαι ought by no means to be understood of the coming of Christ, but of his resurrection in the flesh. Beza likewise affirms that ἀναστῆσαι fits the present argument better if it is taken of the resurrection of Christ than if it is referred to his coming. But if ἀναστήσειν fits the resurrection better, much more does κατὰ σάρκα ἀναστῆσαι, to raise up in the flesh. The article τὸ is frequently used in this sense, as ἐν τῇ Ἀντιοχείᾳ [in Antioch], Acts 15:25; ἐν καιρῷ [in time], Rom. 5:6; ἔμειναν ἐν χώρᾳ [they remained in the field]. Phavorinus: χῖ, instead of τῆς, ἐν. Hesychius.

units.la: Cap. 3. v. 18, 19, 20, 21. Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς, ἃ προκατήγγειλε διὰ στόματος πάντων τῶν προφητῶν αὐτοῦ, παθεῖν, ἐπλήρωσεν οὕτω, (μετανοήσατε ἐν τῇ ὁπισσέφατε εἰς τὸ ἐξαλειφθῆναι ὑμῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας) ὅπως ἂν ἕλθωσι καιροὶ ἀνα-ψύξεως ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ κυρίου, καὶ ἀποστείλῃ τὸν προκεχειρισμένον ὑμῖν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, ὃν δεῖ οὐρανὸν μὲν δέξασθαι ἄχρι χρόνων ἀποκαταστάσεως πάντων. Deus autem, ea quae praenuntiavit per os omnium Prophetarum Christum perpessurum implevit ita (poenitemini igitur, & converti-mini, ut deleantur peccata vestra) ut venerint tempora refrigerii ab ira Domini, & miserit quis vobis praenunciatus est Jesum Christum, quem oportet quidem caelum recipere usque ad tempora consummationis omnium, quae Deus locutus est per os omnium sanctorum suorum a saeculo Prophetarum. Parenthesis ejusmodi frequenter intervenit in N. T. ut Joh. 1. 14. Luc. 1. 55. 2. 34, 35. Col. 3. 15, 16. Apoc. 2. 9. & alibi. ὅπως ἂν, ἀντὶ τοῦ ἵνα. Bud. & sic saepius vertitur in N. T. ut Matth. 6. 5. ὅπως ἂν φανῶσι, ut appareant. Luc. 2. 35. ὅπως ἂν ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν, ut revelentur, & alibi. Ἀπὸ προσώπου, recte ab ira: sic πρόσωπον Κυρίου ἐπὶ ποιοῦντας κακά, facies Domini super facientes malum. 1 Pet. 3. 12. Facies Domini, h.e. ira Domini. Drus. פְּנֵי enim apud Hebraeos significat faciem & iram. Χρόνων ἀποκαταστάσεως, tempora consummationis; ἀποκαταστάσεως τελείωσις. Hesych. & Phav. Sic Oecumenius, ἀποκαταστῆναι δεῖ, φησι, τὰ εἰς πέρας ἐλθεῖν ἅπαντα, ἢ τότε ἐλεύσονται: Oportet, inquit, consummari, & ad finem venire omnia, & tunc veniet; nempe judicare vivos & mortuos.
units.tr: Ch. 3, vv. 18, 19, 20, 21. But God, what he had foretold through the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he has thus fulfilled (repent therefore and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out), so that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and he may send the Jesus Christ who was appointed for you, whom heaven must indeed receive until the times of the restoration of all things. The Latin version renders this: God, having foretold by the mouth of all his prophets that Christ would suffer, has fulfilled it thus (repent, therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out), so that times of refreshment may come from the face of the Lord, and he may send Jesus Christ, who was preached to you, whom heaven indeed must receive until the times of the consummation of all things, which God has spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began. A parenthesis of this kind frequently occurs in the New Testament, as John 1:14; Luke 1:55; 2:34, 35; Col. 3:15, 16; Rev. 2:9, and elsewhere. ὅπως ἄν, instead of ἵνα [that]. Budaeus. And it is often so rendered in the New Testament, as Matt. 6:5, ὅπως ἂν φανῶσι, that they may appear; Luke 2:35, ὅπως ἂν ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν, that they may be revealed; and elsewhere. Ἀπὸ προσώπου, rightly rendered "from the wrath": so πρόσωπον Κυρίου ἐπὶ ποιοῦντας κακά, the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, 1 Pet. 3:12. "The face of the Lord," that is, the wrath of the Lord. Drusius: for פְּנֵי [pənê] among the Hebrews signifies both face and anger. Χρόνων ἀποκαταστάσεως, times of consummation; ἀποκαταστάσεως τελείωσις, Hesychius and Phavorinus. So Oecumenius: "It is necessary," he says, "that all things come to an end and be completed, and then he will come"; namely, to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: Ca. 7, v. 4. Καὶ ἐξελθὼν, μετὰ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ, μετῴκισεν αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν γῆν ταύτην &c. Et inde postquam mortuus est pater ejus, transtulit illum in hanc terram, in qua vos nunc habitatis. Haud parum vexavit Interpretes, Stephanum hic dicere, Deum transtulisse Abraham-mum mum è Charran post mortem Patris, eò quòd dicitur Gen. 12.4. Abrahamum exivisse è Charran anno ætatis 75. c. 11. 26. natum fuisse Tharæ 70. & v. 32. Tharam fuisse annorum 205 cùm moreretur; exinde enim sequitur, Tharam supervixisse decessum Abrahami è Charran 60 annos. Ut hunc ergo nodum solvant recentes ferè omnes & Chronologi & Interpretes, cæteris omnibus explosis sententiis, volunt Abrahamum fuisse natum Tharæ anno ætatis 130, & non 70, ut opinati sunt multi è veteribus; annis enim 130 si addas 75, quæ ætas erat Abrahami cùm egrederetur è Charran, incides in verum annum mortis Tharæ. Atque ut hanc opinionem tueantur, aiunt, non necesse est ut ex Gen. 11. 26. intelligatur Abraham esse natum Tharæ 70, at vero Tharam eo ætatis anno incœpisse esse patrem; non enim expressè dicitur eo ipso anno natum esse Abraham, at vero Tharam vixisse annos 70, & genuisse Abrahamum, Naborem, & Haranem, ex quo concludi nolunt Abrahamum fuisse fratrem natu maximum, quia prior nominatur, sed aiunt esse potius verisimile eum fuisse ætate minimum. Atque ut hanc sententiam adhuc firmiorem reddant, argumentum struunt ex suis suppositis, quo absurdum conantur impingere aliter sentientibus; viz. si Abrahamus fuerat filius natu maximus, tum Sara, uxor ejus, filia fratris sui Haranis, & nisi decennio ipso junior, Gen. 17. 17. necessario nata est Harae octavo ætatis anno, quod ridiculum foret dicere. Ut vero hoc argumentum prius diluam, primo, non video cur concedatur Saram fuisse filiam Haranis: neque enim adhuc finita est illa quæstio. Quis enim legit Gen. 20. 12. verè soror mea est de patre, sed non de matre, quia confidenter statuit Saram fuisse sororem Abrahæ, & & filiam Thara, sed non ex unâ eâdémque uxore? præsertim tam solenni affirmatione additâ, ut seipsum à suspicione falsiloquii liberaret. Unde Hieronymus post alteram verborum expositionem, addit, sed quia in Hebræo habet, Vere soror mea est, filia patris mei, sed non filia matris meæ, magis sonat quòd Abrahæ soror fuit, in excusationem ejus dicimus, nec dum illo tempore tales nuptiæ esse prohibitæ. Ut etiam Doctores Hebræi inter sex genera injustæ copulationis illud unum statuunt, cum sorore uterinâ. Immò Musculus magis adhuc rotundè agit; Omnia hæc commenta simplicitas Hebraica respuit; quid enim necesse est torqueri in re tam clarè expressâ? Verè, inquit, soror mea est, filia Patris mei, & nè uterina putetur, addit, & non filia matris meæ, ut manifestum sit natam esse Saram Terah patri Abrahæ ex aliâ uxore, quam eâ unde suscitulit Abrahamum. Addi potest ex Eusebio ὁ δὲ Ἀβραὰμ λαμβάνει τὴν γυναῖκα τῶν Σάρραν, Abrahamus vero a patre accipit uxorem suam Saram, non ab Harane. Atque hinc apparet quæstionem istam nondum esse finitam. Detur vero, Saram fuisse Ischam, & filiam Haranis, quid impedit quin Haran esset 40 annorum senex cum nasceretur Abrahamus? Et tum quàm facilè poterit Sara esse filia Haranis, & nisi decennio Abrahamo junior? nec absurdum sequatur illud, Haranem fuisse nisi octo annorum senem cum nata esset Sara? Nam licet Scriptura dicat, Tharam vixisse 70 annos, & genuisse Abrahamum, Naborem, & Haranem, non ergo necessario sequitur Tharam eo tempore incœpisse esse patrem, non magis quàm Tharam eo anno genuisse omnes, quod credo nemo sanus affirmaverit, vel Noab incœpisse esse patrem, cùm dicitur Gen. 5. 32. fuisse quingentorum annorum filius, & genuisse Sem, Cham, & Japhet. At certè est multo magis vero simile, Tharam incœpisse esse patrem circa 30 ætatis annum, & circa id tempus genuisse Haranem, quo tempore progenitores ejus incœperunt esse patres, & quo tempore Cainam (quem interposuit Lucas) ipsi nuperi Chronologi statuunt incœpisse gignere filios; Haranem aio, eò quòd ipse videtur frater natu maximus, si & Nahor & Abraham utrique duxerint filias ejus. Si verò Haran natus erat Thara 30, oportuit eum esse annorum 40, cùm nasceretur Abraham Thara 70; & si Sara nata esset Harani anno ætatis 50, quod adeò fas & aptum est conjicere, oportuit eam esse nonagenariam, cùm Abrahamus fuerit centenarius. Adeò ut argumentum illud ab absurdo utrovis modo concidat. Atque hujus opinionis, quæ mihi videtur satis probabilis, & valdè æqua, ansam Josephus præbuit, Antiq. Jud. lib. 1. ubi expressè affirmat Abrahamum esse natum Thara 70, seorsim verò habuisse fratres Nahorem & Haranem, nullo respectu ad eorum ætatem habito, quasi quovis alio tempore potuissent nasci, etiam antè patris 70. Mentio enim ibi fit eorum tantùm, quia in succeedente historiâ nominantur. Quod etiam, salvâ reverentiâ, pari modo intelligendum reor de Patriarchâ Noab, nempè, illum quingentesimo ætatis anno genuisse Semum, nec quidem eo anno incœpisse esse patrem, Semum verò habuisse fratres Japhet & Cham, qui quovis alio tempore potuerunt nasci, etiam longo fortè temporis spatio ante Noe quingentesimum, nominati tantùm Gen. 5. 32. ut sunt Nahor & Haran, Gen. 11. 26. eò quòd de iis fit mentio in sequenti historia. Argumenta pro utraque sententiâ sunt ejusmodi. Primò, Semum anno Noe quingentesimo fuisse natum arguit, eò quòd ætatem ejus, ut etiam Abrahami, oportuit esse fixam, in cujus progenie tendens ad Abrahamum civitatis Dei ordo dirigitur, ut est in titulo c. 10. Lib. 15, Aug. de Civit. Dei. Objicitur vero Semum non potuisse nasci Noæ quingentesimo, propterea quòd dicatur Gen. 11.10, Semum fuisse centum annorum filium, & genuisse Arphaxad בְּרֵאשִׁית duobus annis post diluvium, unde colligunt Noah genuisse Semum anno ætatis 502. Quod etiam monuit Scaliger Can. Isag. lib. 3 Sciant vero studiosi quosdam biennium plus quam nos ab Adam ad Exodum putare, idque propter natalem Arphaxad, qui contigerat anno secundo Diluvii. Nos non omisimus quidem illum annum, sed annum 500 Noæ, & 1656 Diluvii currentes accipimus. Demonstrationis gratiâ, pone natum esse Noab die primo mensis primi, (ut ineunte anno natum ferè omnes dicunt) & quingentesimo ætatis anno genuisse Semum, quatuordecim forte dies antequam expleretur annus, & tum oportuit Semum esse centum annorum filium, quatuordecim diebus antequam expleretur annus Noæ sexcentesimus, adeò ut, cùm exiccatum est Diluvium, & egressus est Noab ex arcâ, anno sexcentesimo primo vitæ suæ, secundo mense, & vicesimo septimo die mensis, Gen. 8 14. esset tum Semus centum annorum quatuordecim dierum, unius mensis, & viginti septem dierum, i.e. centum annorum & 71 dierum filius; quo vicesimo septimo die si Semus primùm (ut par est & fas conjicere) operam incœpit dare liberis post diluvium, potuit tum ab eo die nasci Arphaxad secundum tempus vitæ 280 dierum spatio, quibus si addas 71, reliquum ætatis Semi post centesimum jam numeratum, erunt in toto 351, adeò ut superetint centesimi anni vitæ Semi adhuc currentis, demendo 351 ex diebus 365 integro spatio anni, dies 14. Ideóque non importunè quingentesimum annum Noæ currentem accepit Scaliger, atque ὀγδοῆς dicitur secundùm planam Scripturæ literam. Et Semus erat centum annorum filius, & genuit Arphaxad secundo anno post diluvium. At verò objicitur, Arphaxad natum esse duobus annis post Diluvium, neque enim aliud significare volunt τὸ שנת. Quid verò velit τὸ שנת rectè, opinor, interpretati sunt LXX, δευτέρᾳ τους, quos secutus Augustinus & Scaliger, secundo anno Diluvii, sive post Diluvium. Si enim ab Orbe condito ad Diluvium, ut fatentur fere omnes, secundum computum Hebraicum numerantur anni 1656, & à Diluvio ad Abrahamum natum, posito eum natum Thare septuagesimo, 292, necesse est ut primus annus 292 annorum incipiat à Diluvio ingruente, & consequenter annum 1657 ab Orbe condito, in quo dicimus natum esse Arphaxad, oportet esse secundum post Diluvium; adeò ut neque etiam annum Diluvii 1656 importunè currentem acceperit Scaliger. Intellexit enim ille Diluvium incœpisse secundo mense anni 1656 à condito mundi, utrum verò id acciderit millesimo, sexcentesimo, quinquagesimo sexto vel septimo, unum idémque est nobis, quoad institutum nostrum, qui hoc tantum petimus, Arphaxad fuisse natum secundo anno post Diluvium, numerando à Diluvio ingruente, & non duobus completis annis post Diluvium exsiccatum. Si quis persistat adhuc dicere τὸ שנת non rectè explicari, præter ipsam demonstrationem in quæstionem vocat judicium LXX, & virorum, quos omnis ætas novit & agnoscet doctos, necnon morem loquendi apud Hebræos, de quo videre
units.tr: Chap. 7, v. 4. "And after his father was dead, he removed him into this land, &c." Stephen says that after his father was dead, God brought him into this land, in which you now dwell. This has greatly troubled the interpreters, since Gen. 12:4 says that Abraham left Haran in his seventy-fifth year; Gen. 11:26 says that Terah was seventy when Abraham was born; and v. 32 says that Terah was 205 years old when he died. From this it follows that Terah outlived Abraham's departure from Haran by sixty years. To untie this knot, nearly all the recent chronologists and interpreters, rejecting all other opinions, maintain that Abraham was born when Terah was 130, and not seventy, as many of the ancients thought. For if you add 130 years to 75, Abraham's age when he left Haran, you arrive at the true year of Terah's death. To defend this opinion they say that it is not necessary to understand from Gen. 11:26 that Abraham was born when Terah was seventy; rather, Terah began to be a father in that year. For it is not expressly said that Abraham was born in that same year; it says only that Terah lived seventy years and begat Abraham, Nahor and Haran. They do not wish to conclude from this that Abraham was the eldest brother because he is named first, but they say it is rather more probable that he was the youngest. To make this opinion firmer still, they build an argument from their own assumptions, by which they try to fasten an absurdity on those who think otherwise: namely, if Abraham was the eldest son, then Sarah, his wife, the daughter of his brother Haran, and not ten years younger than he (Gen. 17:17), must necessarily have been born when Haran was eight years old, which would be ridiculous to say. But to answer this argument first: I do not see why it should be granted that Sarah was the daughter of Haran, for that question is not yet settled. For who, reading Gen. 20:12, "she is truly my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother," can confidently hold that Sarah was the sister of Abraham and the daughter of Terah, but not from one and the same wife? Especially since the statement is made with such solemn affirmation, so that he might free himself from the suspicion of lying. Hence Jerome, after giving a second explanation of the words, adds: "But because the Hebrew has, 'Truly she is my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother,' it sounds more as though she was Abraham's sister; in his defence we say that such marriages were not yet forbidden at that time." Indeed the Hebrew doctors also count among the six kinds of unlawful union this one only: with a sister of the same mother. Musculus goes even further and bluntly: "Hebrew plainness rejects all these inventions; for why is it necessary to twist a matter so clearly expressed? Truly, she says, she is my sister, the daughter of my father; and lest she be thought to be of the same mother, he adds, 'and not the daughter of my mother,' so that it is plain that Sarah was born to Terah, the father of Abraham, by another wife than the one by whom he begot Abraham." It may also be added from Eusebius: "Abraham took Sarah as his wife from his father, not from Haran." From this it is clear that this question is not yet settled. But grant that Sarah was Iscah and the daughter of Haran: what prevents Haran from being a forty-year-old when Abraham was born? Then Sarah could easily be the daughter of Haran and ten years younger than Abraham, and would not the absurdity follow that Haran was no more than an eight-year-old when Sarah was born? For although Scripture says that Terah lived seventy years and begat Abraham, Nahor and Haran, it does not follow necessarily that Terah began to be a father at that time, any more than that Terah begat all of them in that year. No sane person, I believe, would affirm this, any more than that Noah began to be a father when it is said at Gen. 5:32 that he was five hundred years old and begat Shem, Ham and Japheth. But it is far more likely that Terah began to be a father about his thirtieth year, and that about that time he begat Haran, when his ancestors also began to be fathers, and at about the time when Cainan (whom Luke inserted) the recent chronologists themselves hold began to beget sons. I say Haran, because he himself seems to be the eldest brother, if both Nahor and Abraham married his daughters. But if Haran was born when Terah was thirty, he must have been forty when Abraham was born to Terah at seventy; and if Sarah was born to Haran in his fiftieth year, which is so right and fitting to conjecture, she must have been ninety when Abraham was a hundred. So the argument from absurdity collapses either way. The basis of this opinion, which seems to me quite probable and very fair, was supplied by Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 1, where he expressly affirms that Abraham was born when Terah was seventy, but that he had the brothers Nahor and Haran separately, without any regard to their age, as if they could have been born at any other time, even before their father's seventieth year. For mention is made of them there only because they are named in the following history. I think that, with due respect, the same should be understood of the patriarch Noah: namely, that he begat Shem in his five-hundredth year, but did not then begin to be a father, and that Shem had the brothers Japheth and Ham, who could have been born at any other time, even perhaps long before Noah's five-hundredth year, and are named only at Gen. 5:32, as Nahor and Haran are at Gen. 11:26, because they are mentioned in the following history. The arguments for each opinion are of this kind. First, that Shem was born in Noah's five-hundredth year is shown by the fact that his age, as also Abraham's, had to be fixed, since the order of the City of God is traced through his descent to Abraham, as stated in the title of chapter 10 of book 15 of Augustine's City of God. But it is objected that Shem could not have been born in Noah's five-hundredth year, because Gen. 11:10 says that Shem was a son of a hundred years and begat Arphaxad [בְּרֵאשִׁית] two years after the flood, from which they conclude that Noah begat Shem in his 502nd year. Scaliger also noted this in Canon Isagogicus, book 3: "Let the students know that some think it was two years more than we do from Adam to the Exodus, and that on account of the birth of Arphaxad, which fell in the second year of the Flood." We have not indeed omitted that year, but we take it as the five-hundredth year of Noah and the 1656th of the Flood as running. For the sake of demonstration, suppose that Noah was born on the first day of the first month (as nearly all say that he was born at the beginning of a year), and that he begat Shem in his five-hundredth year, perhaps fourteen days before the year was complete. Then Shem must have been a son of a hundred years fourteen days before Noah's six-hundredth year was complete. So when the Flood was dried up and Noah came out of the ark, in the six hundredth first year of his life, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month (Gen. 8:14), Shem was then a son of one hundred years, fourteen days, one month and twenty-seven days, that is, a son of one hundred years and seventy-one days. If from that twenty-seventh day Shem first (as is right and fitting to conjecture) began to devote himself to having children after the Flood, then Arphaxad could have been born from that day, within the space of 280 days, the second time of his life. If you add to these the 71 days, and the remainder of Shem's age after the hundredth year already counted, the total is 351, so that fourteen days of the hundredth year of Shem's life still remain to run, if you subtract 351 from the 365 days of the whole year. Therefore Scaliger did not unreasonably take Noah's five-hundredth year as running, and it is said [ὀρθῶς] according to the plain letter of Scripture: "And Shem was a son of a hundred years, and he begat Arphaxad the second year after the flood." But it is objected that Arphaxad was born two years after the Flood, for they wish the Hebrew שנת to mean nothing else. But what שנת rightly means, I think, the Seventy have interpreted: [δευτέρᾳ] the second, which Augustine and Scaliger followed, in the second year of the Flood, or after the Flood. For if from the creation of the world to the Flood, as nearly all admit, 1656 years are counted by the Hebrew reckoning, and from the Flood to the birth of Abraham, supposing that he was born when Terah was seventy, 292 years, then the first year of the 292 years must necessarily begin at the onset of the Flood, and consequently the year 1657 from the creation of the world*, in which we say that Arphaxad was born, must be the second after the Flood. So Scaliger was not unreasonable in taking the year of the Flood, 1656, as running. For he understood that the Flood began in the second month of the year 1656 from the creation of the world. Whether that happened in the thousandth, six hundredth, fiftieth-sixth or seventh year is all one to us, for our purpose, which asks only this: that Arphaxad was born in the second year after the Flood, counting from the onset of the Flood, and not after two completed years following the Flood's drying up. If anyone still persists in saying that שנת is not rightly explained, he calls into question, apart from the demonstration itself, the judgment of the Seventy and of men whom every age knows and will acknowledge as learned, as well as the manner of speaking among the Hebrews, on which it is possible to see what I have noted on Matt. 2:16. But if the phrase [בֵּן־שָׁנָה] is taken in the strict sense, as they wish, and rendered "two years old," then Arphaxad was born nearly two months within two completed years. And why should Moses not have spoken exactly, but in round numbers...

units.la: licet quæ animadvertimus in Matth. 2. 16. Quod si vero stricto, ut volunt, sensu accipiatur τὸ בֵּן־שָׁנָה, & reddatur duobus annis, erit Arphaxad natus duos fere menses intra duos expletos annos. Et quidni locutus fuerit Moses ἀκεῖβως, sed ὀλοκληρῶς, numero completo forte posito pro facto; ut etiam apud Demosthenem & Plautum talentum numerari videmus, ubi non exiguus drachmarum numerus deest vel superest. Est vulgatissima est hæc numerandi καταχρηστικός, ut observavit Scaliger. Imò apud Mosem certissimè frequens; quis enim imaginatur vixisse Patres omnes totos præcisè rotundos annos, nec ullos menses, vel ullos dies supra vel infra? Quid ergo juvat ita Ecclesiæ Dei turbare chronologiam, & Sacræ Scripturæ literam convellere, cum quod Scriptura dicat ita in promptu est demonstrare, & licitè fieri posse & probabiliter esse factum? Et si hæc sint vera, quomodo secundo loco dici potest, Noah incœpisse esse patrem quingentesimo ætatis anno? Si enim Semus erat natus Noæ quingentesimo ætatis anno, & Japhet erat natu major, ut rectè vertunt Pagninus, LXX, & Paraph. Chald. Gen. 10. 24. (recte aio; si enim voluisset Moses Semum ætate grandiorem, dixisset certius (אחי יפת הגדול) & non (אחי הגדול יפת) ac etiam Cham filius הקטן, minor, ut diserte nominatur, Gen. 9. 24. i. e. Japheto minor, quod etiam confirmat inter alios Josephus Antiq. Jud. l. 1. c. 7. ubi vocat Semum τρίτον tertium filiorum Noæ; & Schindlerus vir in sacris judicii non vulgaris, qui Chamum, ait, secundum filium Noæ, & non minimum sed Sem, (ut utar ipsius verbis) Pentaglot in voce (שם), quomodo, ut jam antea divi, dici potest Noah quingentesimo anno incœpisse esse patrem, cùm ita manifestè evincitur, & Iaphetum & Chamum esse antea natos? Neque verò est credibile, saltem non probabile, eum non antea incoepisse esse patrem, quam aetas jam incoeperat defecisse; multò magis sonat vero simile, eum incoepisse esse Patrem circa idem tempus quo etiam Progenitores sui incoeperunt gignere filios, forte circa centesimum & octogesimum aetatis annum, circa quod tempus Methuselah genuit Lamech, & Lamech genuit Noah. Neque verò si Noah quingentesimo incoeperit esse Pater, & Semus fortè filius tertius, vel natu minimus, potest ullo sensu dici Semum centesimo aetatis anno genuisse Arphaxad, duobus annis vel secundo anno post Diluvium, sed tertio, nisi quis velit omnes tres natos intra biennii spatium, quod mirum foret afferere. Sed nimia est haec digressio, etsi tamen necessaria. Ut redeam ergo ad rem ipsam, mihi videtur eorum ratiocinatio ita à ratione abhorrere, ut ei nullo modo possim acquiescere. Primò enim quòd Abrahamum volunt natum esse Tharæ 130, parùm est in se probabile. Cur enim adeò miraretur Abraham, ac si ratio certaret cum fide, filium sibi nasci centenario, si natus fuisset ipse patri suo aetatis anno 130? At verò objectionem istam (etsi revera sit ἀναπίπτωσις) nè flocci quidem faciunt. Mirum Patriarchæ, aiunt, non rectè intellectum: respiciebat enim uxorem suam tantùm, & non seipsum, cùm ita apud se loqueretur Abraham. Desierant Saræ fieri muliebria, in eo mirum; habuit verò Abraham filios ex uxore juvene 37 annos postea. Itáne verò? At quid tum respondent Paulo? Rom. 4. 19. Οὐ κατενόησε τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σῶμα ἤδη νενεκρωμένον, Non consideravit corpus suum jam emortuum: & Heb. 11. 12. Διὸ καὶ ἀφ' ἑνὸς ἐγεννήθησαν καὶ ταῦτα νενεκρωμένου, &c. Quocirca & ex uno [masculini generis] orti sint coque emortuo tanquam sideræ cœli? E quibus locis collatis concludit Estius, Satis ex his liquere, Scripturam non solum in Sara ponere miraculum, sed etiam in Abraham. Quid etiam Musculo? Certè negari non potest ista verba Abrahami exprimere quandam senilis & emortui corporis considerationem tam in Abrahamo quàm in Sara. Quid Ambrosio? Non dubito quod facias, ut & centum annorum seni dones filium, & Naturæ auctor Naturæ metas relaxes. Quid Chrysostomo? ἐξ φύσιν ἀνθρωπίνων τὰ ἐπαγγελλόμενα· καὶ ὁ πατριάρχης ὑπὸ τῆς γήρως λοιπὸν ἀνενέργητος ὢν, πρὸς παιδοποιίαν ἀχρηστος. Supra humanam naturam promissa; erat enim Patriarcha præ senectute propè impotens, & ad filiorum procreationem omnino inutilis. Quoad verò generationem filiorum ex secunda uxore 37 annos post ea, Quidni Naturæ Auctor Naturæ metas relaxet? Quidni Divino miraculo vires reparet & restituat jam emortui, & faciat eum revige cere, quem prædixerat futurum patrem multarum gentium? Secundò, nec cum ratione convenit, Mosem ætatem Abrahami, à qua pendet tota Chronologia Ecclesiæ Lei, velle ita in incerto relinquere, ut eam non liceret nisi per conjecturam expicari vel extorquere. Quem quæso in finem (verba sunt Langii in re quidem alia, ejusdem verò naturæ) hæc à Mose perscripta sunt, nisi ut temporum constaret ratio? Propter hoc ergo Moses tempora appositi, ut veritas manifestior esset. Ut verò hæc veritas manifestior quoad Chronologiam Ecclesiæ Dei, quod præcipuè hoc loco intendebat Moses, cujus ætatem oportuit esse magis accuratè certam, Abrahami an Tharæ? Notitia natalis Abrahami erat quidem necessaria, sed non ita erat mortis Tharæ. Quomodo con-stabit stabit etiam certa temporum ratio, quæ à conjectura, eâque parum probabili, certè disputabili tota pendet? Cùm verò habes tempus natalis & decessus Abrahami è Charran, habes certam rationem temporum, in qua poteris tutò acquiescere. Tertiò, Abrahamum non fuisse natum Thara 70, est contra sententiam veterum ferè omnium gentium. Testimonia libet aliquot hic apponere. Primum erit quod jam antea nominavi ex Josepho, Θάρρ ... μὲν ἐτῶν ἑβδομήκοντα ποιεῖται τὸν Ἀβραὰμ· Thara 70 genuit Abrahamum; & paulò post, Ἀβραὰμ δὲ ἦν ἀδελφὸς Ναχώρ ... Abrahamus verò habuit fratres Naborem & Haranem. Ex quo manifeste patet, quid Judæi senserint Josephi tempore, quicquid de eâ re recentiùs scripserint, & quod ipse opus suum senserit fixam statuere ætatem Abrahami per se separatim, de ætate Naboris & Haranis non solicitus. Aliud est testimonium Nicephori Patriarchæ ante Eusebii tempora; Θάρρα ... ὁ Θάρρα ... Thara septuagenarius genuit Abrahamum. Præter ipsius Eusebii judicium passim in suis Chronicis, necnon & Latinorum, ut colligere est, ex Augustin. de Civit. Dei, lib. 16. c. 10. & 15. & in Quæst. super Genesim. Nec est contemnendum testimonium & judicium docti Arabis, Gregorii Abul. Pharajii, Hist. Dynast. Tareh filius Nahor. Natus est illi Abraham, cum esset secundùm utramque simul sententiam 70 annorum, & ab hoc tempore convenit inter duos computos LXX & Hebraeorum. Quomodo verò convenit, si de tempore nativitatis Abrahami discrepat? Propter has ergo rationes & testimonia non possum assentiri judicio eorum qui Abrahamum volunt nasci Thara 130. Quid igitur restat, si natus sit Abrahamus Thara 70 secundum Scripturæ turæ literam, & egressus è Charran post mortem patris anno ætatis suæ 75, nisi ut mortuus sit Thara 145 annorum tantum senex? faciunt enim 70 & 75, 145. quod quidem multò magis convenit quàm Hebræa lectio. Vix enim credibile, Tharam supervixisse ætatem patris Nahor 57 annos, vixit enim ille nisi 148, cùm jam ætas hominum cœperit decrescere, nec quì quam succedentium Patriarcharum eam ætatem, viz. 205 annorum, attigerit, qui tamen omnes benedictionem & promissiones acceperunt, cùm dicatur Tharam servisse Diis alienis, Ios. 24.2. Et si creditur Suidæ, fuit ipse ἀγαλματοποιὸς, factor imaginum. Nec Scriptura de conversione ejus usquam explicitè quicquam dicit, licèt tamen charitas & ipsa ratio suadent credere, eum non in idolola ria perstitisse usque ad summam senectutem, quia egressus est cum Abrahamo è Chaldæorum Ur, ut iret in terram Chanaan, & cum eo simul commoratus est in Charan usque ad diem mortis; at non longævitatis tantæ supra patrem & posteros gratiam tamen apud Deum meruisse. Adeò ut lectio vulgaris ista, Tharam mortuum esse 205 annorum senem, sit fere æquè ἀνάτ, ac illa etiam in Hebræo, 2 Chron 22.2. (licèt tamen sint aliqui qui omnia salvent) Et regnavit Achaziab filius quadraginta duorum annorum, quo concesso, oportuit eum esse seniorem patre, cui successit, qui obiit natus annos quadraginta; quæ est etiam contra fidem Interpretum Syriac, Arab. & Græcorum, qui omnes legunt, ut etiam legitur parallelo loco, 2 Reg. 8.26. Regnavit Achaziab filius duorum & viginti annorum; nisi quod Romana Græca Editio legat tantùm εἴκοσι, viginti. Vel ut ista, quæ est etiam numeralis; Gen. 2.2. Complevitque Deus בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי In
units.tr: Although I have noted these things on Matth. 2. 16. But if the phrase bēn-šānāh [בֵּן־שָׁנָה] is taken in the strict sense they prefer and rendered "two years old," then Arphaxad was born about two months short of two completed years. And why should Moses not have spoken not exactly [ἀκριβῶς] but roundly [ὀλοκληρῶς], perhaps putting a complete number for the fact? So too in Demosthenes and Plautus we see a talent counted, although a small number of drachmas is missing or left over. This catachrestic [καταχρηστικός] manner of counting is very common, as Scaliger observed. Indeed in Moses it is certainly frequent. For who imagines that all the Patriarchs lived exactly round years, with no months or days above or below? Why then does it help to disturb the chronology of the Church of God and to shake the letter of Holy Scripture, when what Scripture says can readily be shown both to be lawful and to have probably happened? And if these things are true, how can it be said in the second place that Noah began to be a father in his five hundredth year? For if Shem was born in Noah's five hundredth year, and Japheth was the elder, as Pagninus, the Septuagint and the Chaldee paraphrast rightly render it (Gen. 10. 24) (rightly, I say; for if Moses had wished Shem to be the elder, he would have said more clearly אחי יפת הגדול and not אחי הגדול יפת), and also Ham is called the younger [הקטן], as is plainly named in Gen. 9. 24, that is, younger than Japheth. This is also confirmed, among others, by Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 1, chapter 7, where he calls Shem the third [τρίτον] of Noah's sons; and Schindler, a man of no ordinary judgement in sacred matters, who says that Ham was the second son of Noah, and not the least, but Shem (to use his own words) (Pentaglot, under the word שם). How, as I have said before, can it be said that Noah began to be a father in his five hundredth year, when it is so plainly shown that both Japheth and Ham were born earlier? Nor is it credible, or at least not probable, that he did not begin to be a father until his years had already begun to fail. Much more likely is it that he began to be a father at about the same time as his forefathers began to beget sons, perhaps about the hundred and eightieth year of age, at which time Methuselah begot Lamech, and Lamech begot Noah. Nor, if Noah began to be a father in his five hundredth year, and Shem was perhaps the third or the youngest son, can it in any sense be said that Shem begot Arphaxad in his hundredth year, two years or in the second year after the Flood, but rather in the third year, unless one wishes to say that all three were born within a span of two years, which would be a strange thing to assert. But this digression is excessive, though necessary. To return therefore to the matter itself, their reasoning seems to me to be so far from reason that I cannot in any way assent to it. For first, their claim that Abraham was born to Terah when he was 130 is in itself not very probable. For why would Abraham have wondered so much, as if reason contended with faith, that a son should be born to him at a hundred years old, if he himself had been born to his father in his 130th year? But that objection (though in truth it is a ἀναπίπτωσις, an evasion) they do not value even a little. The wonder, they say, is not rightly understood: for Abraham was looking only at his own wife, and not at himself, since he was speaking thus to himself. Sarah had ceased to have the ways of women; in that there is a wonder. But Abraham had sons by a young wife 37 years later. Really? But what do they then answer to Paul? Rom. 4. 19: Οὐ κατενόησε τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σῶμα ἤδη νενεκρωμένον, He did not consider his own body, already dead; and Heb. 11. 12: Διὸ καὶ ἀφ' ἑνὸς ἐγεννήθησαν καὶ ταῦτα νενεκρωμένου, etc. Wherefore there sprang even from one [of masculine gender] and him as good as dead, as the stars of heaven. From these places compared together Estius concludes: It is clear enough from these that Scripture places a miracle not only in Sarah but also in Abraham. What too of Musculus? Certainly it cannot be denied that those words of Abraham express a certain consideration of his aged and dead body, both in Abraham and in Sarah. What of Ambrose? I do not doubt that you would do it, that you would give a son to an old man of a hundred years and relax the limits of Nature, as Author of Nature. What of Chrysostom? Promises beyond human nature; for the Patriarch, by reason of old age, was almost impotent and altogether useless for begetting children. But as to his begetting children by a second wife 37 years afterwards, why should not the Author of Nature relax the limits of Nature? Why should He not by a divine miracle restore and renew the powers of one already dead, and make him vigorous again, who had foretold that he would be the father of many nations? Secondly, nor does it agree with reason that Moses, on whose age of Abraham the whole chronology of the Church of God depends, should wish to leave it so uncertain that it could be explained or extracted only by conjecture. To what end, I ask (these are the words of Lang, in a different matter but of the same nature), were these things written by Moses, unless that the reckoning of times might be known? Therefore Moses set down the times for this reason, so that the truth might be more manifest. But for this truth to be more manifest with regard to the chronology of the Church of God, which Moses especially intended in this place, whose age ought to have been more accurately certain, was it that of Abraham or that of Terah? The knowledge of Abraham's birth was indeed necessary, but not so the knowledge of Terah's death. How will a certain reckoning of times be established, which depends wholly on conjecture, and that a very doubtful one, certainly one open to dispute? But when you have the time of the birth and death of Abraham from Charran, you have a certain reckoning of times, in which you can safely rest. Thirdly, that Abraham was not born when Terah was 70 is contrary to the opinion of almost all the ancient peoples. I should like to set out a few testimonies here. The first will be that already mentioned from Josephus: Θάρρ ... μὲν ἐτῶν ἑβδομήκοντα ποιεῖται τὸν Ἀβραὰμ, Terah at seventy begot Abraham; and a little later, Ἀβραὰμ δὲ ἦν ἀδελφὸς Ναχώρ ..., Abraham had brothers, Nahor and Haran. From this it is plainly evident what the Jews thought in Josephus's time, whatever more recent writers have written on the matter, and that he himself thought that the age of Abraham should be fixed by itself separately, without being anxious about the ages of Nahor and Haran. Another testimony is that of Nicephorus the Patriarch, before the time of Eusebius: Θάρρα ... ὁ Θάρρα ..., Terah, aged seventy, begot Abraham. Besides the judgement of Eusebius himself, scattered through his Chronicles, and of the Latins, as may be gathered from Augustine, City of God, book 16, chapters 10 and 15, and in the Questions on Genesis. Nor is the testimony and judgement of the learned Arab, Gregory Abu'l-Faraj, in his History of the Dynasties, to be despised: Terah, son of Nahor. Abraham was born to him when he was seventy years old according to both opinions together, and from this time the two reckonings, of the Seventy and of the Hebrews, agree. But how does it agree if it differs about the time of Abraham's birth? For these reasons and testimonies, therefore, I cannot assent to the judgement of those who want Abraham to have been born when Terah was 130. What then remains, if Abraham was born to Terah when he was 70, according to the letter of Scripture, and went out from Charran after his father's death in his seventy-fifth year of age, except that Terah died as an old man of only 145 years? For 70 and 75 make 145, which agrees far better than the Hebrew reading. For it is scarcely credible that Terah outlived the age of his father Nahor by 57 years, since the latter lived only 148, when the age of men had already begun to decline, and none of the succeeding Patriarchs reached that age, namely 205 years, though all of them received the blessing and the promises, since Terah is said to have served other gods, Josh. 24. 2. And if one believes Suidas, he himself was an ἀγαλματοποιὸς, a maker of images. Nor does Scripture anywhere state explicitly anything about his conversion; yet charity and reason itself urge us to believe that he did not persist in idolatry until his extreme old age, because he went out with Abraham from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan, and remained with him at Charran until the day of his death; yet he did not merit so great a length of life, above his father and his posterity, in the favour of God. So that this common reading, that Terah died an old man of 205 years, is almost as absurd as that Hebrew reading in 2 Chron. 22. 2 (though there are some who save everything): And Ahaziah the son of forty-two years reigned, which being granted, he must have been older than his father, whom he succeeded, who died aged forty; which is also contrary to the faith of the Syriac and Arabic interpreters and of the Greeks, who all read it so, as is also read in the parallel place, 2 Kings 8. 26: Ahaziah the son of twenty-two years reigned; except that the Roman Greek edition reads only εἴκοσι, twenty. Or such as this, which is also a numeral: Gen. 2. 2, And God finished [בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי] on the seventh day his work which he had made.

units.la: In die septimo opus suum quod fecerat. Quisnam enim adeo Masora tenax, qui non in hoc loco agnoscit σφάλμα, & fatebitur deberi legi ב‎ ... ‎ Et perfecit Deus in die sexto opus suum quod fecerat, & requievit in die septimo, ut sequitur) ab omni opere suo quod fecerat; ut habent Codex Samaritanus, Syrus, & universi interpretes Graeci. Et quidni liceat eâdem lege & licentiâ, qua illi negant, Abrahamum natum esse Tharâ 70 secundum Scripturæ literam & receptam sententiam veterum colligere ac etiam æquè confidenter affirmare, Tharam fuisse cùm moreretur nisi 145 annorum senem, præsertim cùm in majorem fidem, præter rationem ipsam, habeamus testem apud Eusebium, plusquam mille & trecentorum annorum senem Chronologiam Samariticam, Θάρρα γενόμενος ἐτῶν ὁ γῶρα ἀ Ἀβρααμ ᾧ ἐπίσης ἔτη ὅς μίχεις ὅε ἔτως Ἀβραάμ. Tharâ cùm esset 70 annorum genuit Abrahamum, & supervixit annos 75, usque ad 75 annum Abrahami, cum quâ perfectè quadrat Pentateuchus Samaritanus; Gen. 11 32. Et fuerunt dies Tharae centum & quadraginta quinque anni, postea mortuus est Thara in Haran. Et quidni testis Samaritic sit testis bonæ fidei in re etiam ita probabili? Quid periculi, si admittatur mendum vel lapsus in Hebræo? Imò nonne est necesse, ut id fiat in locis suprà nominatis? Quod si ergo liceat & æquum sit emendare in iis, quidni idem fiat etiam in nomine Tharæ, sensu emendationem æquè postulante? Verba sunt incomparabilis Capelli, in Criticis suis sacris: Non pauca esse ἀδιάλλακτα ἄποργα in Bibliis Hebræis, quæ vix alià ratione solvi aut contiliari possunt, quam admittendo levem in sacro codice lapsum emendandum. Quod quo minùs hæc in hoc ipso loco ætatis Tharæ, cùm lectio ista Samaritani Codicis ita bellè conciliat Stephanum cum Mose, & Mosem cum seipso, (si enim cum eo legas Tharam fuisse tantum 145 annorum fuisse cum moreretur, apte congruunt, Abrahamum esse natum 70 anno Tharæ, & exiisse è Charran, ubi mortuus erat Thara anno ætatis 75, & Deum transtulisse eum post mortem patris in terram Chanaan) unicum tantùm equidem video obstaculum, quod etiam ibidem animadvertit incomparabilis vir. Religio est vel latum pilum à codicibus Hebraïs, ut Rabbinorum curâ nobis transmittuntur, recedere, vel ipsorum lectionem vitii arguere. Et si ita itaque sententia, præstat cum Scaligero nodum hunc solvendum relinquere, dum Elias venerit. Sciendum vero interim, dum nimis arctè adhæretur Masorethis, certissimum esse, Interpretes in innumeras impegisse inextricabiles controversias, quæ, si admittatur in illis mendum, vel ex Samaritano vel ex LXX facilè emendari & conciliari poterint sine ullo fidei præjudicio. Et quidni admittatur mendum vel varia lectio in Veteri, pari modo quo admittimus in Novo?
units.tr: On the seventh day he finished his work which he had made. For who is so devoted to the Masora that he does not recognise an error (σφάλμα) in this place, and admit that it must be read ב [bet] ... And God finished on the sixth day his work which he had made, and rested on the seventh day, as follows, from all his work which he had made; as the Codex Samaritanus, the Syriac, and all the Greek translators have it.
