And why should we not be allowed, by the same rule and licence by which they deny that Abraham was born when Terah was 70, to infer from the letter of Scripture and the view accepted by the ancients, and with equal confidence to affirm, that Terah was a man of only 145 years when he died? This is especially so since, apart from reason itself, we have for greater assurance a witness in Eusebius, who gives the Samaritan chronology as over thirteen hundred years old: Θάρρα γενόμενος ἐτῶν ὁ γῶρα ἀ Ἀβρααμ ᾧ ἐπίσης ἔτη ὅς μίχεις ὅε ἔτως Ἀβραάμ. Terah, when he was 70 years old, begot Abraham, and lived 75 years, until the 75th year of Abraham; with which the Samaritan Pentateuch agrees exactly; Gen. 11:32. And the days of Terah were 145 years; then Terah died in Haran. And why should the Samaritan witness not be a witness of good faith in a matter which is also so probable? What danger is there if a flaw or slip is admitted in the Hebrew? Indeed, is it not necessary that this be done in the places named above? If, then, it is lawful and fair to emend them, why should the same not be done also in the name of Terah, since the sense demands an emendation just as much? These are the words of the incomparable Capellus, in his Critica sacra: Not a few ἀδιάλλακτα ἄποργα in the Hebrew Bibles, which can hardly be resolved or reconciled in any other way than by admitting that a slight slip in the sacred codex must be emended. That this reading of the Samaritan codex reconciles so neatly, in this very place, the age of Terah, Stephen with Moses, and Moses with himself, is no reason to refuse it. (For if you read with it that Terah was only 145 years old when he died, the details agree well: Abraham was born in Terah's 70th year, and left Haran, where Terah had died, in the 75th year of his age, and God transferred him to the land of Canaan after his father's death.) I see indeed only one obstacle, which the same distinguished man also notes in the same place. It is a point of religion either to depart by the breadth of a hair from the Hebrew codices, as they have been handed down to us through the care of the rabbis, or to charge their reading with error. If that is the view, it is better to leave this knot to be untied with Scaliger, until Elijah comes. Meanwhile, it should be known that while we cling too tightly to the Masoretes, interpreters have fallen into countless inextricable controversies, which, if an error is admitted in those texts, could be easily emended and reconciled from the Samaritan or the LXX, without any prejudice to faith. And why should we not admit an error or a variant reading in the Old Testament, in the same way that we admit one in the New?

units.la: C. 7. v. 10. Καὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ χάριν καὶ σοφίαν ἐναντίον Φαραὼ βασιλέως Αἰγύπτου, καὶ κατέστησεν αὐτὸν &c. Et dedit ei gratiam & sapientiam in conspectu Pharaonis regis Ægypti, qui, ut vertit Beza, constituit eum præpositum super Ægyptum. Phrasi eadem quam animadvertimus Matth. 27. 10. & sæpius alibi.
units.tr: Chapter 7, verse 10. Καὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ χάριν καὶ σοφίαν ἐναντίον Φαραὼ βασιλέως Αἰγύπτου, καὶ κατέστησεν αὐτὸν &c. And he gave him grace and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and he set him, as Beza translates it, over Egypt as ruler. This is the same idiom we noted at Matt. 27:10 and often elsewhere.

units.la: V. 15, 16. Κατέβη ὁ Ἰακὼβ εἰς Αἴγυπτον καὶ ἐτελεύτησεν αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν. Καὶ μετετέθησαν εἰς Συχέμ, καὶ ἐτέθησαν ἐν τῷ μνήματι ὃ ὠνήσατο Ἀβραὰμ τιμῆς ἀργυρίου παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἑμμὼρ τοῦ Συχέμ. Et descendit Jacob in Ægyptum, & defunctus est ipse & patres nostri, translati sunt in Sichem, & positi sunt in sepulchro quod emit Abraham pretio argenti à filiis Emmor patris Sichem. Verfiu ista hunc locum variis fecit obnoxium erroribus. Primò enim implicat à connexione copulativæ [ x̧ ] Iacobum unà cum patribus deportatum sive translatum fuisse in Sichem, cùm ex Scriptura pateat Iacobum diu ante exitum ex Ægypto, deportatum & sepultum esse à Iosepho, & senioribus Israel in spelunca agri Macpelah, quam emerat Abraham cum agro in possessionem sepulchri ab Ephron Hethæo, Gen 50. 13. Proximo loco affirmare videtur, quod diserte est contrarium authoritati veteris, Abrahamum emisse locum sepulturæ à filiis Emmor patris Sichem, cùm quem ille emerat, ab Ephrone Hethæo emerit, Iacob verò à filiis Emmor. Ultimo loco necessariò innuit, patres reliquos sepultos fuisse in Sichem, cùm, siqua ratione fides, sepulti fuerint in eodem loco, in quo sepulti erant eorum patres, nempe in Hebrone. Nam, ut jam antea dixi, Iacob certè sepultus est in spelunca agri Macpelah, quam emit Abraham cum agro ab Ephron Hethæo in possessionem sepulchri (procul dubio pro familia suâ) prout ipse Iacob dixerat ad Iosephum, Non sepelias me in Ægypto, sed dormiam cum patribus meis, & auferes me de hac terra, condésque in sepulchro majorum meorum. Gen. 47. 30, 31. Ubi sepelierunt Abrahamum & Saram uxorem ejus, ubi sepultus est Isaac cum Rebecca conjuge sua, ubi & Lea condita jacet. Gen. 49. 31. Et ubi Iacob & Lea ambo sepulti sunt, & Iacobi patres & matres, etiam plusquam probabile est, & filios suos omnes etiam esse sepultos, Iosepho tantum excepto, qui sepultus est in Sichem, secundum juramentum quod cepit à filiis Israel, Gen. 50. 25. In parte agri quem emerat Iacob Jacob à filiis Emmor patris Sichem centum novellis ovibus, et fuit in possessionem filiorum Iosephi. Ios. 24. 32. Et quod huic conjecturæ omnino possit reponi, nil equidem reperio præter testimonium sancti Hieronymi, qui in Epitaphio Paulæ ait: fratres Iosephi sepultos esse in Sichem. Sed cum reverentiâ liceat tanti viri testimonio opponere illud Iosephi, qui lib. 2. Antiq. Iud. expressè affirmat, Iosephi fratres mortuos in Ægypto, et eorum corpora filios et nepotes in Hebronem (nempe in ipsum unam agri Macpelah, hæc est Hebron, qui confirmatus est Abrahæ in possessionem monumenti à filiis Heth, Gen. 23. 19, 20.) relata sepelivisse; Iosephi autem ossa translata esse in Chananæam per Hebræos cum ex Ægypto migrarent, sic enim jurejurando eos obstrinxerat Iosephus, secundum quod sepulta sunt in Sichem, ut jam antea dictum. Neque fuit ab officio vel ratione alienum, ut prius sepelirent Iosephi ossa in Sichem, vel honoris causâ, eò quòd fuerit totius Ægypti præfectus, atque inde ad Hebronem deportarent reliquorum patrum ossa sepelienda in Hebrone. Et si libranda testimonia, quamvis in quæstione fidei crediderim Hieronymo, in re tamen Historiæ, quæ etiam nationem suam tangit, & de qua de industriâ scripsit, fidem Iosepho potius adhibendam sentio, præsertim cum propius ad Scripturæ mentem & rationem accesserit. Ut ergo præveniatur, in quem tam sumus proni, error primus, verba verim in hunc modum verti, saltem intelligi, Et descendit Jacob in Ægyptum, x) ἐτελεύτησεν αὐτὸς, et defunctus est ipse, et patres nostri (repetendo ἐτελεύτησεν in plurali, quod necessario faciendum ut constructio fiat) defuncti sunt, et translati sunt in Sichem, i.e. Patres nostri, & non Jacob. Et ut concilicentur τὰ Συνόντα posteriora, verti velim & distingui in hunc modum : χ̀ ἐτέθησαν ἐν τῷ μνήματι ( ὃ ὠνήσατο Ἀβραὰμ παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἐμμὼρ τοῦ Συχέμ. Et posita sunt in sepulchro ( quod emit Abraham pretio argenti ) à filiis Emmor patris Sichem. Atque hâc versione, quæ certè est in se legitima quoad Grammaticam vel usum loquendi, nulla vis omninò hic veritati historiæ ; nec enim affirmat positos fuisse patres in sepulchro quod emit Abraham à filiis Emmor, quod adeò Scripturæ veteri est contrarium, nec sepultos fuisse in agro Sichem; sed potiùs innuit, ipsos priùs deportatos esse in Sichem, & deinde postquam Josephi ossa priùs ( ut par erat ) ibi fuissent condita, à Sichemis vel ab agro Sichem, quod unum & idem est, translatos esse & sepultos in sepulchro, quod emit Abraham pretio argenti, nempè ab Ephrone in Hebrone, secundum testimonium Josephi, rationem, & Scripturam. Neque est versio ista omninò insolens, vel nova Παρὰ enim cum Genitivo proprie significat motum à persona, χίνησιν ἀπὸ ἐωλῶν. Cùm ergo lectio vetus & versio sit ita dura & inconcinna, ut nullo modo possit conciliari, nisi crasâ aliquâ emendatione textus, sobriis & doctis perpendendum submitto, an non satius & magis æquum sit hanc interpretationem admittere, etsi magisteriali authoritate destitutam, quàm, ut solemus, fugere ad remedia ita violenta. Neque sum solus sine teste, adstipulatur nobis De Dieu, vir inter primos doctus, cùm dicat, Ἀδὰ τῷ ὑῶν Ἐμμὼρ τῶ Συχέμ, Non esse construendum cum ἀνήσατο, sed cum ἐτέθησαν, quam sententiam ob Josephi authoritatem agnoscit apud se potiorem esse.
units.tr: Verses 15, 16. Κατέβη ὁ Ἰακὼβ εἰς Αἴγυπτον καὶ ἐτελεύτησεν αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν. Καὶ μετετέθησαν εἰς Συχέμ, καὶ ἐτέθησαν ἐν τῷ μνήματι ὃ ὠνήσατο Ἀβραὰμ τιμῆς ἀργυρίου παρὰ τῶν υἱῶν Ἑμμὼρ τοῦ Συχέμ. And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers. And they were carried over to Shechem, and laid in the tomb which Abraham bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem. This version makes this passage open to various errors. First, by the connection of the copulative [x̧] it implies that Jacob was carried away and transferred to Shechem together with the fathers, although it is plain from Scripture that Jacob was carried off and buried long before the exodus from Egypt by Joseph and the elders of Israel in the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham had bought with the field as a burial place from Ephron the Hittite, Gen. 50:13. In the next place, it seems to affirm what is plainly contrary to the old authority, that Abraham bought a burial place from the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem, whereas he bought it from Ephron the Hittite, and Jacob bought it from the sons of Hamor. Last, it necessarily hints that the remaining fathers were buried in Shechem, whereas, if they were buried in the same place where their fathers lay, that is in Hebron, the faith would be kept. For, as I have said before, Jacob was certainly buried in the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite as a possession of a tomb (no doubt for his family), just as Jacob himself had said to Joseph: Do not bury me in Egypt, but I shall sleep with my fathers, and you shall carry me out of this land and lay me in the tomb of my ancestors, Gen. 47:30, 31. There they buried Abraham and his wife Sarah, there Isaac was buried with his wife Rebekah, and there Leah lies laid to rest, Gen. 49:31. And where Jacob and Leah were both buried, and the fathers and mothers of Jacob, it is also more than probable that all his sons were buried there too, except Joseph only, who was buried in Shechem, according to the oath he took from the children of Israel, Gen. 50:25. In the part of the field which Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem, for a hundred lambs, and it became the possession of the sons of Joseph, Josh. 24:32. As to what could be objected to this conjecture, I find nothing except the testimony of St. Jerome, who says in the Epitaph of Paula that the brothers of Joseph were buried in Shechem. But with reverence it is allowed to set against the testimony of so great a man that of Josephus, who in book 2 of the Antiquities of the Jews expressly affirms that the brothers of Joseph died in Egypt, and their bodies were carried by their sons and grandsons to Hebron (namely into the field of Machpelah, which is Hebron, and which was confirmed to Abraham as a possession of a tomb by the sons of Heth, Gen. 23:19, 20), and buried there. But the bones of Joseph were carried by the Hebrews into Canaan when they left Egypt, for so Joseph had bound them by oath, and according to that they were buried in Shechem, as said before. Nor was it against duty or reason that they first buried Joseph's bones in Shechem, either out of honour, because he had been prefect of all Egypt, and then carried the bones of the other fathers to be buried in Hebron. And if testimonies are to be weighed, although in a question of faith I have believed Jerome, in a matter of history, which also touches on his own nation and about which he wrote deliberately, I think faith is rather to be given to Josephus, especially since he comes closer to the mind and reasoning of Scripture. So, that the first error, into which we are so prone, may be forestalled, I wish these words to be translated and understood in this way: And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers (repeating ἐτελεύτησεν in the plural, which must be done for the construction to work), died, and were carried over to Shechem; that is, our fathers, and not Jacob. And so that the following words agree, I wish them to be translated and punctuated in this way: and they were laid (in the tomb which Abraham bought from the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem) in the tomb (which Abraham bought for silver) from the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem. By this translation, which is certainly correct in itself as regards grammar and idiom, there is no force at all against the truth of history. For it does not affirm that the fathers were laid in a tomb which Abraham bought from the sons of Hamor, which is so contrary to the old Scripture, nor that they were buried in the field of Shechem; rather, it hints that they were first carried to Shechem, and then, after Joseph's bones had first been laid there (as was fitting), were carried from Shechem, or from the field of Shechem, which is one and the same, and buried in the tomb which Abraham bought for a sum of silver, namely from Ephron in Hebron, according to the testimony of Josephus, reason and Scripture. Nor is this version wholly unusual or new, for παρά with the genitive properly signifies motion from a person, ἡ κίνησις ἀπὸ ἐωλῶν. Since, then, the old reading and version are so harsh and incongruous that they cannot be reconciled in any way except by some gross emendation of the text, I submit for the consideration of sober and learned readers whether it is not better and fairer to admit this interpretation, although it lacks magisterial authority, than, as we usually do, to flee to such violent remedies. Nor am I alone without a witness: De Dieu, one of the foremost scholars, supports us, when he says that ἀπὸ τῶν υἱῶν Ἐμμὼρ τοῦ Συχέμ should not be construed with ὠνήσατο but with ἐτέθησαν, a view which he considers, on account of Joseph's authority, to be the stronger.

units.la: V. 19. Οὗτος καταςοφισάμενος τὸ γένος ἡμῶν ἐκάκωσε τοὺς πατέρας ἡμῶν τοῦ ποιεῖν ἐκτιθέναι τὰ βρέφη αὐτῶν εἰς τὸ μὴ ζωογονεῖσθαι. Verba hæc plerumque non vertuntur commodè. Vix enim crediderim Hebræos ita omnem exuisse humanitatem, ut ipsi suos exponerent infantes ne servarentur vivi. Nec quicquam tale in Exodo narrat Moses, at Pharaonem præcepisse populo suo (obstetricibus Hebræis renuentibus exequi mandata ejus quoniam timebant Deum) diserte hisce verbis, omnem filium qui nascitur Hebræis εἰς τὸν ποταμὸν βίψατε projicite in flumen &c, Ita ut ad veriorem sensum concilientur hæc verba, credo ea multò rectiùs verti. Hic circumveniens genus nostrum afflixit patres nostros faciendo projici infantes eorum, ne servarentur vivi, vel ut vertit Interpres Arabicus, efficiendo ut infantes eorum projicerentur ne viverent. ἐκθετα enim apud Suidam ἐκθεμένα projecta, τὰ βρέφη ἔκθετα recte, faciendo projici. Reperire est eandem phrasim. 1. Reg. 17, 20. οὐ κεκάκωκας τὴν χήραν ... Tu afflixisti viduam faciendo mori filium ejus, ut etiam Ruth. 1. 6. ὅτι ἐπεσκέψατο Κύριος τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ τοῦ δοῦναι αὐτοῖς ἄρτους, Quod visitaverat Dominus populum suum dando eis panem, & Psal. 78. 18. ἐξεπείρασαν τὸν Θεὸν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις αὐτῶν τοῦ αἰτῆσαι βρώματα ταῖς ψυχαῖς αὐτῶν. Tentarunt Deum in cordibus suis petendo cibum animabus suis. Ac si ita vertatur, Luc. 1. 54. 55. commodiorem opinor reddet sensum, ἀντελάβετο Ἰσραήλ παιδὸς αὐτοῦ, & sublevavit filium suum Israel reminiscendo misericordiam &c. ut ibidem etiam, v. 76, 77. præibis enim ante faciem Domini parare vias ejus τοῦ δοῦναι γνῶσιν σωτηρίας &c. dando cognitionem salutis populo ejus in remissionem peccatorum.
units.tr: V. 19. "This man, dealing craftily with our race, mistreated our fathers, so that they made their infants be cast out so that they would not be kept alive" [Οὗτος καταςοφισάμενος τὸ γένος ἡμῶν ἐκάκωσε τοὺς πατέρας ἡμῶν τοῦ ποιεῖν ἐκτιθέναι τὰ βρέφη αὐτῶν εἰς τὸ μὴ ζωογονεῖσθαι]. These words are usually not translated well. I could hardly believe that the Hebrews had so put off all humanity that they themselves exposed their infants so that they would not be kept alive. Nor does Moses tell anything of the kind in Exodus. He says rather that Pharaoh commanded his people (when the Hebrew midwives refused to carry out his orders, because they feared God) in these express words: every son that is born to the Hebrews, cast into the river [εἰς τὸν ποταμὸν βίψατε], etc. So that these words may be brought into a truer sense, I think they ought to be rendered much more correctly: "This man, dealing craftily with our race, afflicted our fathers by causing their infants to be cast out, so that they would not be kept alive," or, as the Arabic interpreter renders it, "by bringing it about that their infants were cast out so that they would not live." For ἔκθετα in Suidas means "cast out," and τὰ βρέφη ἔκθετα is correctly rendered "by causing [them] to be cast out." The same phrase can be found: 1 Kings 17:20, "Hast thou afflicted the widow ... by causing her son to die" [οὐ κεκάκωκας τὴν χήραν], just as in Ruth 1:6, "that the Lord had visited his people by giving them bread" [ὅτι ἐπεσκέψατο Κύριος τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ τοῦ δοῦναι αὐτοῖς ἄρτους]; and Psalm 78:18, "They tempted God in their hearts by asking food for their souls" [ἐξεπείρασαν τὸν Θεὸν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις αὐτῶν τοῦ αἰτῆσαι βρώματα ταῖς ψυχαῖς αὐτῶν]. If it is translated in this way, Luke 1:54-55, I think, gives a more fitting sense: "He has helped Israel his servant [ἀντελάβετο Ἰσραὴλ παιδὸς αὐτοῦ], remembering his mercy, etc." So also in the same passage, verses 76-77: "For thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways [τοῦ δοῦναι γνῶσιν σωτηρίας], giving knowledge of salvation to his people for the remission of sins."

units.la: V. 45. Ἢ γὰρ εἰσήγαγον διαδεξάμενοι οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν, &c. Quod etiam patres nostri accipientes enter successivè alius ab alio introduxerunt cum Iesu in possessionem gentium. Διαδέχομαι, τὸ διὰ πολλῶν ἐξελθόντων ἀπ' ἄλλης εἰς ἄλλην ἐπὶ ἡμᾶς ἥκον διέχομαι. Phav.
units.tr: V. 45. "Which also our fathers, receiving it in succession, brought in" [Ἢ γὰρ εἰσήγαγον διαδεξάμενοι οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν, &c.]: that is, our fathers too, receiving it, successively one after another, brought it in with Jesus into possession of the nations. "Διαδέχομαι" means that the thing has come to us through many, passing from one to another; I receive it in succession. Phav.

units.la: C. 8. v. 33. Ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει αὐτοῦ ἡ κρίσις αὐτοῦ ἤρθη. In humiliatione ejus judicium ejus sublatum est. i. e. cum semel humiliaverat seipsum ad mortem crucis, Philip. 2. 8. non erat amplius obnoxius judicio hominum. Tunc enim ut sequitur quis enarrabit generationem ejus? quoniam tollitur à terra vita ejus. Sublata est enim vita ejus è potestate terrenorum judicum, adeò ut à generatione in generationem in æternum nunc victurus est invita hominum malitia. Non jam amplius moritur, mors illi ultrà non dominabitur. Rom. 6. 9. Atque hæc interpretatio facillimè aperatur ad textum Hebraicum.
units.tr: C. 8. v. 33. "In his humiliation his judgment was taken away" [Ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει αὐτοῦ ἡ κρίσις αὐτοῦ ἤρθη]. That is: once he had humbled himself to the death of the cross (Philippians 2:8), he was no longer subject to the judgment of men. For then, as it follows, who shall declare his generation? For his life is taken from the earth. For his life was taken out of the power of earthly judges, so that from generation to generation, for ever, he is now to live despite the malice of men. He now dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him (Romans 6:9). And this interpretation is most easily brought out from the Hebrew text.

units.la: C.10.v. 36, 37, 38. Τὸν λόγον, ὃν ἀπέστειλε τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ εὐαγγελιζόμενος εἰρήνην διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (οὗτός ἐστι πάντων κύριος) ὑμεῖς οἴδατε, τὸ γενόμενον ῥῆμα καθ' ὅλης τῆς Ἰουδαίας, ἀρξάμενον ἀπὸ τῆς Γαλιλαίας, μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα ὃ ἐκήρυξεν Ἰωάννης, Ἰησοῦν ἀπὸ Ναζαρὲθ, ὡς ἔχρισεν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεὸς, &c. Τὸ Iumitur τεχνικῶς, vel appositivè; ante 'Iesu cum Syro subaudi χρ. Ubiq; enim locus est Accusativo, si intelligas χρ. Verbum quod misit filiis Israel, annuncians pacem per Jesum Christum (hic est omnium Dominus) vos nostis, verbum scilicet quod fuit per totam Judæam, initium sumens à Galilæa post baptisma quod prædicavit Johannes de Jesu Nazareno, quomodo unxerit eum Deus spiritu sancto, &c. Vos nostis, i.e. firmâ accepistis, non ignoratis utpote rem adeò vulgatam.
units.tr: C. 10. v. 36, 37, 38. "The word which he sent to the children of Israel, preaching peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), you know, the word that was published throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached, concerning Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him, etc." [Τὸν λόγον, ὃν ἀπέστειλε τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ εὐαγγελιζόμενος εἰρήνην διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (οὗτός ἐστι πάντων κύριος) ὑμεῖς οἴδατε, τὸ γενόμενον ῥῆμα καθ' ὅλης τῆς Ἰουδαίας, ἀρξάμενον ἀπὸ τῆς Γαλιλαίας, μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα ὃ ἐκήρυξεν Ἰωάννης, Ἰησοῦν ἀπὸ Ναζαρὲθ, ὡς ἔχρισεν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεὸς, &c.]. The article "Τὸ" is used either technically or in apposition; with the Syrian, supply "Christ" (χρ.) before "Jesus." For the construction is always in the accusative if you understand χρ. The word which he sent to the sons of Israel, bringing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), you know, namely the word that was spread through all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John preached concerning Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit, etc. "You know," that is, you have firm knowledge of it; you are not ignorant, since the matter was so widely known.

units.la: C. 13. v. 20. Καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ὡς ἔτεσι τετρακοσίοις καὶ πεντήκοντα ἔδωκε κριτὰς ἕως Σαμουὴλ. ηλ. Porro quadringentis & quinquaginta annis dedit eis Iudices, ut Syrus, & Arabs, & alii. Verum locus iste, ut ait Scaliger, est crux Chronologorum, dicas & Interpretum, inter quos haud pauci tuentur hanc versionem, quâ usus est Syrus & Arabs; quam etiam pro viribus defendit Beroaldus, lib. 3. c. 4. nec sine applausu, addendo in sua computatione Chronologica annos Oppressorum numero annorum Iudicum, qui initium sumentes a tempore quo Cushan-rishathaim opprimere inceperit Israelem, Iud. 3. 8. faciunt exactum numerum quadringentorum & quinquaginta annorum usque ad Samuelem. Felix quidem & speciosa est inventio. Verum praeter exceptiones justas, quae huic computo possunt objici, eo quod tempus Seniorum, qui judicabant Israelem immediate post Iosuam, non in eo comprehenditur, quos negari non potest fuisse Iudices, etiamsi quam diu, non pater ex Scriptura; Eusebius, ait, Traditionem dedisse eis octodecim annos, Africanus triginta tribuit: verum quam longo vel brevi tempore utcunque fuerit, auget certe numerum quadringentorum & quinquaginta annorum, ita ut numerus iste non sit adeo exactus ut Beroaldus voluit; & praeterquam etiam quod viginti anni Samsonis, in quibus judicavit Israelem in diebus Philistinorum, in quorum manus dedit Deus Israelitas spatio quadraginta annorum, sint ex iis deducendi, quod computationem ejus etiam reddit vanam, si se sibi Beroaldus objectionem fecit nullâ arte diluendam; atque ea est hujusmodi, Posito, tempus ab exitu ex Ægypto usque ad inchoationem structurae templi, fuisse quadringentorum & octoginta annorum, ut dicitur 1 Reg. 6. 1. Qui numerus omnino retinendus, nisi totam sacram Chronologiam subvertere malimus, ut inquit Beza, si Iudicibus demus annos quadringen-tos & quinquaginta, Mosi in deserto quadraginta, Iosue octodecim, (nec quisquam dat pauciores Samueli & Sauli quadraginta, Davidi triginta, & Salomoni ante inchoatam structuram templi quatuor) erunt in toto (nec supputamus tempus Seniorum) 582 anni. Adeo ut secundum sui ipsius objectionem fit plane impossibile temporibus Iudicum tribuere 450 annos. Sed ut rem salvet, Ut Apostoli memorata supputatio intelligatur, animadvertendum ait, quosdam annos bis repeti, & iterato dici, quemadmodum afflictionum anni dicti sunt comprehendi debere, & ad eam summam referri quâ dicitur pax fuisse & quievisse terra a praeliis. De quo nihil solicitus Apostolus eam summam retulit, quam sigillatim sumpti omnes isti numeri, quos exposuimus eundem per singula capita libri Iudicum, constituunt. Sed has considerationes unquam in Apostoli mentem ascendisse vix credibile, multo minus Apostolum contra ipsam scientiae lucem voluisse numerare annorum summam, quae constare non potuit cum Scriptura Veteri. Egregium certe id fuisset scandalum Iudaeis, quibus non ignoti vel inobservati temporum erant computi. Cum ergo interpretatio ista tot exceptionibus sit obnoxia, sine injuria fas est aliam exquirere, neque occurrit nobis alia magis sana, quam eorum qui hic volunt intelligi, non quamdiu, sed quando Deus dedit illis Iudices, ideoque distinguunt & referunt verba illa [ χ̀ μ̓ᾶ τοῦτο ὡς ἔτεσι τετρακοσίοις χ̀ πεντήκοντα ] ad verba praecedentia, v. 17. nempe ad tempus quo Deus populi Israelis elegit patres eorum; adeo ut debuerint verba distingui & verti in hunc modum. Et post ea fere vel circiter quadringentis & quinquaginta annis, i. e. per Metaphesim, Metathesim, & fere vel circiter quadringentis & quinquaginta annis postea, dedit eis judices; in quo sensu legunt Lat. Vet. & Æthiop. Tempus vero hoc, in quo Deus potest dici elegisse patres quasi quadringentis & quinquaginta annis ante tempus Judicum ab iis computatur à nato Isaaco, in quo Deus vere dicitur elegisse Patres, Dixerat enim Abrahamo Deus, In Isaaco vocabitur semen tuum. Et ut computus iste magis fiat planus, à nato Isaaco aiunt ad natum Jacobum sunt anni 60, inde ad introitum in Ægyptum 130, inde ad exitum 210, inde ad introitum in terram Chanaan 40, inde ad distributionem terræ, quo tempore inceperunt esse Judices, 7, qui simul faciunt 447 annos, i. e. circiter vel fere 450, desunt enim solummodo tres. Et si computus incipiat ab anno præcedente, nempe ab Isaaco promisso, cùm diceret Abrahamo Deus, Sara uxor tua pariet tibi filium, vocabisque nomen ejus Isaac, & constituam pactum meum illi in fœdus sempiternum, & semini ejus post eum. Gen. 17. Quo tempore Deus forte dicitur æquè, si non magis proprie, elegisse patres, anni erunt 448, anno adhuc altero propiore ad numerum Apostoli, adeò ut defuerint tantùm duo. Reverendissimus vero & Doctissimus Usserius noster, à nato Isaaco ad distributionem terræ, (quod evenisse ait annis post electionem Patrum circiter 450) numerat annos 452, & alii propemodum, si non exactè 450. Ex quo fas opinor est conjicere, propter hanc temporis incertitudinem, Apostolum ejus circumstantiam expressisse particulâ indefinitâ, ὡς, circiter quadringentis & quinquaginta annis. Ideóque non inopportune Scaliger in notis in Euseb. Chronic. pag. 255 ait. Ego sapientissimè ab Eusebio dictum puto, ὁ Ἀπόστολον ἀν ἀκεὶ βολογούμενον εἰπεῖν, ἀλλὰ ἐνδοχῶς. ἐκδοχὴ καινοτέρα, ut sit numerus pro numero ex quotidiano usu, quo ὀλοχερῶς ἐκ ἀκειβῶς aliquam summam enunciamus. Sic apud Demosthenem & Plautum talentum nominari videmus, ubi non exiguus drachmarum numerus deest vel superest. Et vulgatissima est haec numerandi καταχρησις.
units.tr: C. 13. v. 20. "And after these things, for about four hundred and fifty years, he gave them judges until Samuel" [Καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ὡς ἔτεσι τετρακοσίοις καὶ πεντήκοντα ἔδωκε κριτὰς ἕως Σαμουήλ]. Moreover, "for four hundred and fifty years he gave them judges," as the Syriac and Arabic and others have it. But this passage, as Scaliger says, is the cross of chronologers, and of interpreters too, among whom not a few defend this version, which the Syriac and Arabic use; Beroaldus also defends it as far as he can, in book 3, chapter 4, and not without applause, by adding to his chronological reckoning the years of the oppressors to the number of the years of the judges, reckoning from the time when Cushan-rishathaim began to oppress Israel (Judges 3:8), and so making up the exact number of four hundred and fifty years down to Samuel. It is indeed a happy and attractive discovery. But apart from the fair objections that can be raised against this reckoning, namely that the time of the elders who judged Israel immediately after Joshua is not included in it, though it cannot be denied that they were judges, even if for how long is not clear from Scripture (Eusebius says tradition gave them eighteen years; Africanus assigns thirty), yet however long or short that time was, it certainly increases the number of four hundred and fifty years, so that this number is not as exact as Beroaldus wanted. Moreover, the twenty years of Samson, in which he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines, into whose hands God gave the Israelites for a space of forty years, must be deducted from it; and this too makes his computation vain. If Beroaldus raised an objection to himself that cannot be dissolved by any skill, it is of this kind: granting that the time from the exodus from Egypt to the beginning of the building of the temple was four hundred and eighty years, as 1 Kings 6:1 says, this number must certainly be retained, unless we prefer to overturn the whole sacred chronology. As Beza says: if we give the judges four hundred and fifty years, Moses in the wilderness forty, Joshua eighteen (and no one gives fewer), Samuel and Saul forty, David thirty, and Solomon four before the building of the temple was begun, there will be in all (not counting the time of the elders) 582 years. So that, by his own objection, it is quite impossible to assign four hundred and fifty years to the times of the judges. But to save the matter, "so that the aforementioned reckoning of the Apostle may be understood," he says, "it must be noted that some years are counted twice and said again, just as the years of afflictions are said to be included and referred to that sum in which the land is said to have had peace and rest from wars." Anxious about nothing of this, the Apostle reckoned that sum which all these numbers, taken separately, which we have set out, make up through the individual chapters of the book of Judges. But it is scarcely credible that these considerations ever came into the Apostle's mind, much less that the Apostle wished, against the very light of knowledge, to state a sum of years that could not agree with the Old Testament. That would certainly have been an extraordinary scandal to the Jews, to whom the reckonings of time were not unknown or unobserved. Since, therefore, this interpretation is liable to so many exceptions, it is lawful without wrong to seek another. Nor does any other more sound one occur to us than that of those who wish this to be understood not as "for how long," but as "when God gave them judges." So they distinguish and refer the words [καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ὡς ἔτεσι τετρακοσίοις καὶ πεντήκοντα] to the preceding words of verse 17, namely to the time when God chose the fathers of the people of Israel; so that the words ought to be divided and rendered in this way: "And after these things, about four hundred and fifty years, that is, by metaphesis or metathesis, [God chose the fathers], and about four hundred and fifty years afterwards he gave them judges." In this sense the old Latin and Ethiopic read. This time, in which God may be said to have chosen the fathers about four hundred and fifty years before the time of the judges, is reckoned by them from the birth of Isaac, when God truly is said to have chosen the fathers, for God had said to Abraham, "In Isaac shall thy seed be called." And to make this computation clearer, they say: "from the birth of Isaac to the birth of Jacob are sixty years; from there to the entry into Egypt, 130; from there to the exodus, 210; from there to the entry into the land of Canaan, forty; from there to the division of the land, at which time they began to be judges, seven; which together make 447 years," that is, "about" or "nearly 450," for only three are lacking. And if the computation begins from the year before, namely from the promise of Isaac, when God said to Abraham, "Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac, and I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him" (Genesis 17), at which time God is perhaps said, if not more properly, at least equally, to have chosen the fathers, the years will be 448, and with one more year nearer to the Apostle's number, so that only two are lacking. But our most reverend and most learned Ussher, "from the birth of Isaac to the division of the land" (which he says happened about 450 years after the election of the fathers), counts 452 years, and others nearly 450, if not exactly. From which, I think, it is permissible to conjecture that, because of this uncertainty of time, the Apostle expressed the circumstance with the indefinite particle ὡς, "about four hundred and fifty years." And so not inappropriately Scaliger, in his notes on Eusebius's Chronicle, page 255, says: "I think Eusebius said it most wisely: the Apostle would not have said it exactly but approximately, a more recent interpretation, so that the number is put for a number in ordinary usage, by which we state some sum roughly, not exactly" (ὁλοχερῶς, ἐκ ἀκειβῶς). Thus in Demosthenes and Plautus we see a talent named where a not small number of drachmas is missing or left over. And this figure of speech in counting is very common.

units.la: V. 27. Οἱ γὰρ κατοικοῦντες ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ, καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες αὐτῶν, τοῦτον ἀγνοήσαντες καὶ τὰς φωνὰς τῶν προφητῶν τὰς κατ' πᾶν σάββατον ἀναγινωσκομένας, κρίναντες, ἐπλήρωσαν. Vertendum per Hyperbaton, quasi legeretur, Οἱ δὲ κατοικοῦντες ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ, καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες αὐτῶν, τοῦτον κρίναντες, ἀγνοήσαντες καὶ τὰς φωνὰς τῶν προφητῶν τὰς κατὰ πᾶν σάββατον ἀναγινωσκομένας ἐπλήρωσαν. Qui enim habitabant in Ierusalem, & principes eorum hunc condemnantes, ignorantes etiam voces Prophetarum, quae unoquoque legebantur Sabbato, impleverunt. Similes implicitas & perplexas trajectiones videre est apud Demosthenem, quibus eum usum fuisse affirmat Stephanus ad venustatem sermoni concilandam, & apud Platonem, quale est illud in Phaedro, ἀληθῆ, ἔφη, λέγεις, ὦ Σωκράτης, ὦ Κέβης, Vera dicis O Cebes, inquit Socrates. Quod loquendi genus & imitari & affectare videtur Cicero; Nolo inquit mirari Africanus. O magnam inquit artem Brutus. Vide Bezam in Act. 24. 22. vide etiam Job 12 8.
units.tr: Vet. 27. For those who lived in Jerusalem, and their rulers, not recognising him, and the voices of the prophets read every Sabbath, judging him, fulfilled them [Οἱ γὰρ κατοικοῦντες ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ, καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες αὐτῶν, τοῦτον ἀγνοήσαντες καὶ τὰς φωνὰς τῶν προφητῶν τὰς κατ' πᾶν σάββατον ἀναγινωσκομένας, κρίναντες, ἐπλήρωσαν]. This should be rendered by hyperbaton, as if it read: "But those who lived in Jerusalem, and their rulers, judging this man, not recognising him and the voices of the prophets read every Sabbath, fulfilled them" [Οἱ δὲ κατοικοῦντες ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ, καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες αὐτῶν, τοῦτον κρίναντες, ἀγνοήσαντες καὶ τὰς φωνὰς τῶν προφητῶν τὰς κατὰ πᾶν σάββατον ἀναγινωσκομένας ἐπλήρωσαν]. "Qui enim habitabant in Ierusalem, et principes eorum hunc condemnantes, ignorantes etiam voces Prophetarum, quae unoquoque legebantur Sabbato, impleverunt." Similar tangled and perplexed transpositions can be seen in Demosthenes, which Stephanus says he used to make his style pleasing, and in Plato, such as that in the Phaedrus: "You speak the truth, O Socrates, said Cebes" [ἀληθῆ, ἔφη, λέγεις, ὦ Σωκράτης, ὦ Κέβης]. Cicero also seems to imitate and affect this manner of speaking: "I would not wish, said Africanus, to be admired"; "O what a great art, said Brutus." See Beza on Acts 24.22; see also Job 12.8.
1 Cor. 10. 27. Phil. 1. 21. Jac. 2. 1. 3. 3. and elsewhere.

units.la: V. 41. Ἴδετε οἱ καταφρονηταὶ καὶ θαυμάσατε καὶ ἀφανίσθητε, &c. Lucas nec Hebraea nec Graeca laudat καὶ πόλει, propriùs verò accedit ad Interpretes Graecos, quos salvo sensu contraxit. Apud eos enim legitur, Ἴδετε οἱ καταφρονηταὶ καὶ ἐπιλάβεσθε, καὶ θαυμάσατε θαυμάσια, καὶ ἀφανίσθητε. ἀφανίζοντες. Videte contemptores & resipiscite, & admiramini mirabilia, & disperdimini; ut Interpres. Hebræum verò, ראו בגוים והנשו והתמהו והתמהורתם הו Videte in gentibus (i. e. vos qui estis inter Gentes,) & aspicite, & attoniti estote, obstupescite, ut Pagninus. Ubi verbum תמהו, pro possibili errore literarum bis à Græcis videtur reddi; postquam enim pro vulgari lectione vertissent θαυμάσατε, opinantes, opinor, non bene convenire unam eandemque vocem repetitam, addiderunt etiam τὸ ἀφανίζοντες, existimantes forte pro תמהה, debuisse legi חכה, errore proclivi satis ob literarum similitudinem; quæ vox significat, latibulum quærite, & admodum quadrat cum voce ἀφανίζοντες; ἀφανίζειν enim apud Hesychium est σκεπάσαι, tegere, vel abscondere. Sic apud Plutarchum, ἀφανίζειν ὁ θέλει τὸ ἀληθὲς, non vult tegere veritatem; &, οἱ γὰρ ἔλαφοι κατευθύνουσι καὶ ἀφανίζουσι τὰ κέρατα, ὅταν ἐκπέσῃ τὸ κέρας, Cervi quando decidit cornu defodiunt, & abscondunt sub terra. Sic Job. 22. 20. vocem כחד quæ significat, abscondit, LXX vertunt ἀφανίζει; in quo sensu ἀφανιζόντες videtur hoc loco aptius verti. Videte contemptores, et obstupescite, vel et attoniti estote, & abscondimini, sive latibula vobis quærite. Est enim חבא, vel מחסה, proprie latibulum, vel receptaculum, ubi quis tutus est contra cæli, aliasve injurias, ut Schindlerus. Atque ita debere intelligi valdè innuit, quòd versio ista magis convenit cum scopo loci, quàm vel evanescite, vel disperdimini, quæ quid sibi velint non adeò est in promptu dicere; præcipuè si erratum fit à Masoretbis, legendo בנוים inter Gentes, pro בנרים καταφρονηταί, contemptores, ut est propter similitudinem literarum ד ו cerè pos-sibile fibl'e, & in hoc loco Habak. videtur plusquám probabi'le. Non enim alloquitur Propheta Gentes, sed Judæos, quos omnino tangit sequens sermo,super quos in ipsorum diebus superventura fuit devastatio, quam prænunciat, captivitas nempè Babylonica, de qua vide quid locutus fuerit Dominus 2 Reg. 21.13,14. Qui optimo etiam jure vocantur contemptores, qui perverterunt judicium, & lacerârunt legem Dei, ut vertunt aliqui, ideóque non sine causa jubentur aspicere, & attoniti mirari opus Domini,quod facturus erat in diebus eorum, & seipsos tegere à ventura irâ. Atque ne hoc factum jam in ipsos superveniat, Judæos hoc loco cavere jubet Apostolus, excidium Hierosolymæ horrendum præsignificans.
units.tr: Vet. 41. Behold, you despisers, and wonder, and perish, etc. Luke quotes neither the Hebrew nor the Greek with "and to the city", but he comes closer to the Greek Translators, whose sense he has condensed without loss. For they read: "Behold, you despisers, and take hold, and wonder at wonders, and perish" [Ἴδετε οἱ καταφρονηταὶ καὶ ἐπιλάβεσθε, καὶ θαυμάσατε θαυμάσια, καὶ ἀφανίσθητε]. The Vulgate translator reads: Behold, you despisers, and repent, and wonder at the wonders, and perish. The Hebrew, however, reads ראו בגוים והביטו והתמהו והתמהמהו, Behold among the nations (that is, you who are among the Gentiles), and look, and be astonished, be stupefied, as Pagninus has it. Here the word תמהו seems to have been rendered twice by the Greeks, through a possible error of letters. For after they had translated the common reading as θαυμάσατε, supposing, I think, that it did not fit well for one and the same word to be repeated, they also added τὸ ἀφανίζοντες, thinking perhaps that תמהו ought to be read as חכה, an error quite easy because of the similarity of the letters. This word means seek a hiding place, and agrees well with the word ἀφανίζοντες. For in Hesychius ἀφανίζειν means σκεπάσαι, to cover, or to hide. So in Plutarch, ἀφανίζειν ὁ θέλει τὸ ἀληθὲς means he does not wish to cover the truth; and οἱ γὰρ ἔλαφοι κατευθύνουσι καὶ ἀφανίζουσι τὰ κέρατα, ὅταν ἐκπέσῃ τὸ κέρας, when a stag's horn falls off, the stags bury it and hide it under the earth. So in Job 22.20, the LXX render the word כחד, which means hides, as ἀφανίζει; in this sense ἀφανιζόντες seems more fitting here. Behold, you despisers, and be stupefied, or be astonished, and hide yourselves, or seek for yourselves a hiding place. For חבא, or מחסה, properly means a hiding place or refuge, where one is safe against the sky or other injuries, as Schindler has it. That this is how it should be understood is strongly suggested, since this version agrees better with the purpose of the passage than vanish or perish, whose meaning is not at all easy to state. This is especially so if the error was made by the Masoretes, reading בגוים among the Gentiles instead of בגדים, despisers, which, because of the similarity of the letters ד and ו, is almost possible; and in this passage of Habakkuk it seems more than probable. For the Prophet does not address the Gentiles but the Jews, whom the following speech wholly concerns, and over whom the devastation he foretells was to come in their own days, namely the Babylonian captivity; on which see what the Lord said in 2 Kings 21.13, 14. They are rightly called despisers, since they perverted judgment and tore up the law of God, as some translate; and therefore they are not without cause bidden to look, and to marvel in astonishment at the work of the Lord which he was about to do in their days, and to hide themselves from the coming wrath. And so that this may not now come upon them, the Apostle bids the Jews in this passage to beware, foreshadowing the dreadful destruction of Jerusalem.

units.la: V. 48. Καὶ ὅσοι ἦσαν τεταγμένοι εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, Et crediderunt quotquot erant præordinati ad vitam æternam, ut Vetus, Ordinati ut Beza, eodem tamen sensu. Dura verò & insolens est illa versio, neque quadrat, ut haud pauci sentiunt, cum Scriptura. Quidni ergò, ut saltem locus iste nil momenti afferat tam controverso sensui, de quo nunquam erit, usque dum Elias venerit, disputandi finis, distinguantur & vertantur verba ista potiùs in hunc modum: ὅσοι ἦσαν τεταγμένοι, εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, Et crediderunt, quotquot convenerunt, in vitam æternam. Judæi seipsos indignos judicârunt vitâ æternâ, v. 46. Gentes autem audientes gavisæ sunt, et glorificabant verbum Domini, et crediderunt in vitam æternam quotquot convenerunt: τεταγμένοι, posito pro συντεταγμένοι, qua voce usus est Evangelista, v. 44. συνήχθη πᾶσα ἡ πόλις· συνήχθη, pene universa civitas convenit audire verbum Dei. Credere in vitam æternam. est articulus fidei, imò summa fidei, hæc est enim vita æterna, ut cognoscat te solum Deum verum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum. Ioh. 17. 3. Quoad interpretationem vocis τεταγμένοι, non est omnino nova, nec sine authoritate; vox enim Hebræa סדר, quæ à LXX frequenter vertitur συνάγω, & συναθροίζω, convenio, & congrego, vertitur ab iis quandoque τάττομαι, ut Exod. 29.43. ינעד ישמ לבני ישראל, וּ τάξομαι ἐκεῖ τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ. Et conveniam ibi filiis Israel, ut Pagninus. Est etiam τάσσω proprie, εἰς τάξιν καθίσῳ, in ordine colloco, adeo ut neque à sensu abhorreat, si reddatur, Et quotquot erant in ordine collocati (nempe ad audiendum verbum Dei) crediderunt in vitam æternam; vel, quotquot erant instructi, secundum vim vocis alteram, i. e. qui quod docuit Apostolus audiverunt. Nec possum aliter sentire, quin εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον necessario oporteat construi cum verbo ἐπίστευσαν, quicquid velit τὸ τεταγμένοι.
units.tr: Vet. 48. And as many as were ordained to eternal life believed, as the Old Version has it; "ordained", as Beza has it, with the same sense. But that rendering is harsh and strange, and, as not a few think, does not fit with Scripture. Why not, then, so that this passage at least contributes nothing of weight to a sense so disputed, on which there will be no end of debate until Elias comes, distinguish and translate the words in this way instead: ὅσοι ἦσαν τεταγμένοι, εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, "And as many as had gathered, believed unto eternal life." The Jews judged themselves unworthy of eternal life (v. 46). The Gentiles, however, hearing, rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and believed unto eternal life, as many as had gathered. Here τεταγμένοι stands for συντεταγμένοι, the word the Evangelist used at v. 44: συνήχθη πᾶσα ἡ πόλις, "almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God." To believe unto eternal life is an article of faith, indeed the sum of faith, for this is eternal life, that they know you the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17.3). As for the interpretation of the word τεταγμένοι, it is not altogether new, nor without authority. For the Hebrew word סדר, which the LXX often render as συνάγω and συναθροίζω, to gather and assemble, they sometimes render by τάττομαι, as in Exod. 29.43: ינעד ישמ לבני ישראל, and τάξομαι ἐκεῖ τοῖς υἱοῖς Ἰσραὴλ, "and I will meet there with the children of Israel," as Pagninus has it. Also τάσσω properly means εἰς τάξιν καθίσῳ, I set in order, so that it does not clash with the sense if it is rendered, "And as many as were set in order (namely to hear the word of God) believed unto eternal life"; or, "as many as were instructed," according to the other force of the word, that is, those who heard what the Apostle taught. Nor can I think otherwise, but that εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον must necessarily be construed with the verb ἐπίστευσαν, whatever the word τεταγμένοι means.

units.la: Cap. 14. v. 23. Χειροτονήσαντες δὲ αὐτοῖς &c. i. e. ut alii, καταστήσαντες, in quo sensu multoties occurrit apud Scriptores Græcos, Ethnicos & Ecclesiasticos. Cum constituissent illis Presbyteros, ut scribit Paulus Tito 1. 5. ut alii, ordinantes, vel cum ordinâssent illos, sensu hodierno Ecclesiastico. Ultra vero valeat interpretatio, non minima lis est. Ut dicam ego quod sentio liberè, non possum non profiteri, me totum in eorum sententiam ire, qui aiunt Lucam hoc loco velle, καταστήσαντες, constituentes, non verò ordinantes sensu Ecclesiastico hodierno. Non enim vel argumento, vel testimonio adhuc vincor, ut credam χειροτονίαν, per se tunc temporis, vel à multis post diebus, significasse χειροτονίαν vel καθίστασθαι, adeò ut omne quod affirmat Zonaras de acceptione verâ hujus vocis in initio Scholii in primum Apostolorum Canonem (quocunque fine vel impulsu) verissimum esse rear. Cujus verba, quia sententiam nostram ita plane exprimunt, (valeant quantum valere possunt) libet hic apponere. Νῦν μὲν χειροτονία καλεῖται, &c. Nunc quidem Chirotonia vocatur absolutio precum, sanctique Spiritus invocatio, dum sacerdotio quis initiatur & consecrationem sortitur, ex eo dicta, quòd Pontifex extendat manum, benedicens hominí ad sacra deligendo; sed ipsum suffragium quondam nominatum est Chirotonia. Nam cùm turbæ liceret in urbibus eligere sacrorum præfectos, conveniebat ipsa turba, & alii quidem hunc, alii deligebant illum; quatenus autem plurium suffragium vinceret, eligentes rursum solitos τείνειν τὰς χεῖρας, extendere manus, & per manus ita porrectas numerabantur, qui vel hunc vel illum delegissent; plurium verò calculis electum summo sacerdotio præfecêre. Chirotoniæ nomen hinc desumptum, quo sic etiam Synodorum Patres inveniuntur usi, suffragium nominantes Chirotoniam. Cujus exemplum profert ex Laodicensis Synodi canone quinto. Et hucusque Zonaras; ex quo, siqua fide, aperte arguitur vocem χειροτονίας sensu hodierno Ecclesiastico esse novam, saltem non in usu tempore Apostolorum. Ut hoc verò roberur pleniùs, missas faciendo authoritates universas suspectas, vel quæ in quæstionem vocari poterint, provocemus ad æquos judices, ad certa & probata testimonia à primævis Scriptoribus petenda, quorum sana & accepta est apud omnes authoritas. Et primò initium sumamus à Sancto Paulo, 2 Cor. 8. 19. ubi frater ille, cujus laus fuit in Evangelio, dicitur χειροτονηθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν, constitutus ab Ecclesiis socius peregrinationis Pauli, ubi vix credo quenquam velle sobriè afferere, cum ordinatum fuisse ab Ecclesiis sensu Ordinationis hodierno. Atque ab eo descendemus ad Scriptores proximos, quos omnes agnoscunt genuinos. Inter quos primâ vice occurrit Ignatius, apud quem in Epist. ad Philadelph. quæ habetur genuina, legimus verba illa. πρέπον ἐστὶν ὑμῖν ὡς ἐκκλησία Θεοῦ χειροτονῆσαι ἐπίσκοπον, Decet vos ut Ecclesiam Dei eligere sive constituere Episcopum, Ecclesiæ sci icet Antiochenæ; ubi certè nemo serio affirmaverit Episcopos intelligi, quasi ad Ecclesiam repræsentativam hæc dicta forent, cùm indefinitè scribat ad Philadelphenses, quos Ecclesiam vocat collectivè, & quibus dat præcepta singularia, nullo modo Episcopis propria sc lis. Et ab eo veniamus ad Scriptores Ecclesiasticos historicos primævos: in quibus plerumque, ni fallor, si non omninò, voces χειροτονία & χειροτονεῖν, electionem vel constitutionem, eligere vel constituere significant. Imò in quibusdam locis certò scio ita necessariò verti, & credo here'è ita jure deberi vel saltem legitimè posse in omnibus. Sic in Eusebio legimus, Hist. Ecclesiast. l. 6. c. 29. τῶν δὲ ἀδελφῶν ἁπάντων χειροτονίας ἕνεκα τῆς ἐκκλησίας συνηθροισμένων, omnibus enim fratribus electionis gratia in Ecclesia congregatis. Sic in Socrate, lib. 2. c. 6. Alexander Episcopus Constantinopolis diei ur esse mortuus, ἐδεῖτο εἰς τὸν αὐτὸν τόπον χειροτονηθῆναι, priusquam aliquem in suo loco constitui esset: & c. 26. ἐξώτερα πολλὰ φιλονεικία περὶ χειροτονίας ἐπισκόπου, ἄλλων ἄλλον ζητούντων, Magna fuit contentio circa electionem Episcopi, cùm alii alium, alii alium. Et in Theodoreto, lib. 4. c. 6. ἀλλὰ καὶ σύμψηφος τῆς χειροτονίας γεγένημαι. Non solum non contradixi, sed etiam tuæ electioni unà cum aliis suffragatus sum.
units.tr: Chap. 14, v. 23. Χειροτονήσαντες δὲ αὐτοῖς, etc. That is, as others have it, καταστήσαντες, a sense in which the word often occurs among Greek writers, both pagan and ecclesiastical: "When they had appointed elders for them," as Paul writes to Titus 1.5; or, as others have it, "ordaining", or "when they had ordained them", in the modern ecclesiastical sense. But which rendering is correct is no small dispute. To say freely what I think, I cannot but declare that I entirely go along with those who say that Luke in this passage means καταστήσαντες, "appointing", and not "ordaining" in the modern ecclesiastical sense. For I am not yet convinced, either by argument or by testimony, that I should believe that χειροτονία in itself, at that time or for many days afterwards, signified ordination or καθίστασθαι; so that I think everything that Zonaras affirms about the true meaning of this word at the beginning of his scholium on the first Canon of the Apostles (for whatever purpose or impulse) to be most true. Since his words express our view so plainly, let them have what weight they can; it pleases me to set them here: "Νῦν μὲν χειροτονία καλεῖται," etc. [Νῦν μὲν χειροτονία καλεῖται]. "Now indeed chirotony is called the completion of prayers and the invocation of the Holy Spirit, when someone is initiated into the priesthood and receives consecration; it is so called because the Bishop stretches out his hand, blessing the man chosen for sacred duties. But the vote itself was once called chirotony. For when the crowd was permitted in the cities to choose the presidents of sacred things, the crowd assembled, and some chose this man, others that. Then, as the vote of the majority prevailed, those choosing stretched out their hands again, as usual, and by the hands thus extended they were counted, those who had chosen this man or that; and the man chosen by the majority of votes they set over the chief priesthood. From this the name chirotony was derived, which the Fathers of the Synods are also found to have used, calling a vote a chirotony." He gives an example of this from the fifth canon of the Synod of Laodicea. And so far Zonaras. From him, if his good faith is to be trusted, it is plainly argued that the word χειροτονία in the modern ecclesiastical sense is new, at least not in use in the time of the Apostles. But to strengthen this more fully, setting aside all authorities that are suspect or that may be called into question, let us appeal to fair judges, to certain and proven testimonies to be sought from the earliest writers, whose sound and accepted authority is recognised by all. And first let us begin with St Paul, 2 Cor. 8.19, where that brother, whose praise is in the Gospel, is said to be χειροτονηθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν, "appointed by the Churches as companion of Paul's journey"; here I scarcely think anyone would soberly maintain that he was ordained by the Churches in the modern sense of ordination. And from there we shall descend to the nearest writers, all of whom are acknowledged to be genuine. Among them, the first to appear is Ignatius, in whose Epistle to the Philadelphians, which is held to be genuine, we read these words: It is fitting for you, as the Church of God, to choose a Bishop [πρέπον ἐστὶν ὑμῖν ὡς ἐκκλησία Θεοῦ χειροτονῆσαι ἐπίσκοπον], namely the Church of Antioch; where surely no one seriously affirms that Bishops are meant, as if these words were addressed to a representative Church, since he writes indefinitely to the Philadelphians, whom he calls a Church collectively, and to whom he gives singular precepts that are in no way peculiar to Bishops. And from him let us come to the earliest ecclesiastical historians: in whom, unless I am mistaken, the words chirotonia and chirotonein mostly, if not always, signify choosing or appointing, to elect or to appoint. Indeed in some places I know for certain that they must necessarily be so rendered, and I believe they rightly ought to be, or at least can legitimately be, in all places. Thus in Eusebius we read (Hist. Eccl. bk. 6, ch. 29): Since all the brothers had gathered in the Church for the sake of election [τῶν δὲ ἀδελφῶν ἁπάντων χειροτονίας ἕνεκα τῆς ἐκκλησίας συνηθροισμένων]. So in Socrates, bk. 2, ch. 6: Alexander, Bishop of Constantinople, is said to have died, and it was necessary to appoint someone in the same place before anyone else could be set in his place [ἐδεῖτο εἰς τὸν αὐτὸν τόπον χειροτονηθῆναι]; and ch. 26: there was much strife about the election of a Bishop, while some sought one and some another [ἐξώτερα πολλὰ φιλονεικία περὶ χειροτονίας ἐπισκόπου, ἄλλων ἄλλον ζητούντων]. And in Theodoret, bk. 4, ch. 6: But I was also a fellow voter in your election [ἀλλὰ καὶ σύμψηφος τῆς χειροτονίας γεγένημαι]: I not only did not oppose it, but also gave my vote together with the others for your election.

units.la: Multa occurrunt similia exempla in his Authoribus, & in Sozomeno, & apud Evagrium, lib. 3. c. 13. Pergamius dicitur ὑπὸ τῶν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ χειροτονηθέντων constitutus subrex Ægypti. Sic etiam habemus in Philone, in legatione ad Caium, χειροτονουμένοις ὑπὸ τῶν ἐπάρχων, constitutis Præfectis. Ut taceam Scriptores Ethnicos, inter quos habet insigne exemplum Maximus Tyrius, in quo Darium lascivien equus ἐχειροτόνησεν διὰ τὸ ἀέχλω, constituit principem. Adeo ut quantum est in me colligere è probatis veterum testimoniis, χειροτονεῖν plerumque, si non omnino, apud eos est ψηφίζειν vel αἱρεῖσθαι, eligere vel constituere. Faceor eadem vox occurrit in sensu Ordinationis hodierno in variis scriptis, quæ præ se ferunt antiquitatem valde magnam; Ut apud Apostolorum Canones, & quæ etiam prætenduntur Clementis constitutiones, quibus addi poterit ejusdem valoris χειροτονία ex Responsi ad orthodoxos. Sed cum de eorum singulis authoribus & antiquitate non immerito dubitetur inter eruditos, non est certè æquum ut suspecta eorum Authoritas imponat legem pro usu vocis aliorum testimoniis, quorum fides hunquam vocata est in dubium. Neque vero est probabile Lexicographos veteres nullam hujusmodi ordinationis mentionem facere, apud quos χειροτονούντες, καταστήσαντες, ἀλλὰ ἐμφανῶς, χειροτονία, ὀπλογή, χειροτονήσαντες ἀντὶ ψηφίζειν. Vel Lucam, quem omnes prædicant τὸ Ἑλληνικὸν ἐξ ἀπαρχῆς cum Sophronio, velle usurpare vocem in sensu nusquam apud eos cognito vel cognoscibili. Argumentis ergo & testimoniis hisce fretus, non possum non credere quin τὸ χειροτονεῖν ab antiquo significârit constituere tantùm & eligere, nec quid aliud. Vocem verò χειροτονήσαντες hoc loco nihil aliud vel ultrà denotare notare quàm constitutionem Presbyterorum, quæ facta est à Paulo & Barnaba, nec χειροτονίαν, nec χειροθεσίαν, consecrationem vel ordinationem, sensu hodierno Ecclesiastico. Prima istius sensus notio expressis verbis in Authore probato occurrit in Hieronymo, nec in ea parte commentariorum suspecto, Is. 6. 58. ubi χειροτονίαν dicit esse Ordinationem Clericorum, quæ non solùm ad imprecationem vocis, sed ad impositionem impletur manûs. Quæ vocis istius acceptio circa ista tempora primùm videtur increbuisse, (etsi nec tum universaliter nota) cum jam pridem variis tumultibus evenientibus inter populum ipsum, & populum & Clerum pro electione Episcoporum, populus in posterum prudenter exclusus est decreto Patrum, vox verò χειροτονίας remansit, ab ipsis assumpta & tractu temporis in suum usum, i. e. in consecrationis sensum substituta & accommodata. In summa, ne quis detorqueat sententiam nostram, sola mihi res est cum illis, qui volunt τὸ χειροτονεῖν hoc loco proprie & per se significare χειροτονίαν, nempe solemnem ordinationem cum precibus, jejunio, & impositione manuum. Hoc ego τὸ χειροτονεῖν hoc loco significare constanter nego. Hos Presbyteros, quos Apostoli vel elegerant vel constituerant in variis distantibus Ecclesiis, fuisse omnes consecratos cum precibus, jejunio, & impositione manuum non nego, sed potius firmiter credo. Licet forte tamen verba in hoc loco id neque evincant, nec quidem ferant, ut quidam volunt, qui pace sanctissimi viri beati Chrysostomi, non imprudenter vel incogitanter jejunium & preces hoc loco referant ad valedictionem Pauli & Barnabæ & non ad constitutionem Presbyterorum, quasi id tantum obiter narraretur, sensus verò esset secundum veram & rectam constructionem, batem, χειροτονήσαντες δὲ αὐτοῖς πρεσβυτέρους κατ' ἐκκλησίαν, προσευξάμενοι μετὰ νηστειῶν παρέθεντο αὐτοὺς τῷ Κυρίῳ, &c. Et cum constituis-sent illis Presbyteros per singulas Ecclesias, precatì cum jejunio commendárint eos Domino in quem credidérunt. Neque fuit ejusmodi valedictio omi-nino incongrua vel insolita. AEt. 20. 36. Paulus valedicturus Ephesiis, θεὶς πάντας αὐτοῖς προσηύξα-το, genuit cum omnibus illis: & 21. 5. valedi-cturus discipulis in Tyro, genuit cum eis positis genibus in littore. Quod si aliquando jejunarent, satis est & id probabile in negotio quod semper solenne fuit. Probabiliter etiam constitutio Presbyterorum in singulis Ecclesiis adeò distantibus, ut fuerunt Derbe, Lystra, Antiochia, & Iconium, non fuit unius diei opus, quod strenuè fuisse innuimur, si precatio cum jejunio referatur ad constitutionem Presbyterorum.
units.tr: Many similar examples occur in these authors, in Sozomen, and in Evagrius, book 3, chapter 13, where Pergamius is said to be made sub-king of Egypt by those chosen in Egypt [ὑπὸ τῶν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ χειροτονηθέντων]. So too we have in Philo, in the Embassy to Caius, appointed by the prefects [χειροτονουμένοις ὑπὸ τῶν ἐπάρχων]. I say nothing of the pagan writers, among whom Maximus of Tyre gives a notable example, where the neighing horse made Darius prince [ἐχειροτόνησεν διὰ τὸ ἀέχλω]. So that, as far as I can gather from the approved testimonies of the ancients, χειροτονεῖν among them means for the most part, if not altogether, ψηφίζειν or αἱρεῖσθαι, that is, to elect or to constitute. I admit that the same word occurs in the modern sense of ordination in various writings which show very great antiquity, as in the Apostolic Canons, and in the so-called Constitutions of Clement, to which may be added the χειροτονία of the same value from the Answer to the Orthodox. But since the authors and the antiquity of these works are not without reason doubted among the learned, it is certainly not fair that their suspect authority should dictate the usage of the word to the testimonies of others, whose trustworthiness has never been called into doubt. Nor is it probable that the ancient lexicographers make no mention of such an ordination, among whom the words χειροτονοῦντες and καταστήσαντες appear, but plainly χειροτονία, and χειροτονήσαντες in place of ψηφίζειν. Nor is it likely that Luke, whom all proclaim, with Sophronius, to be purely Greek from the beginning, would wish to use the word in a sense nowhere known or knowable among them. Relying therefore on these arguments and testimonies, I cannot but believe that τὸ χειροτονεῖν from of old signified only to constitute and to elect, and nothing more. The word χειροτονήσαντες in this place denotes nothing more or further than the constitution of elders made by Paul and Barnabas, not a χειροτονία, nor a χειροθεσία, a consecration or ordination in the modern ecclesiastical sense. The first notion of that sense occurs in plain words in an approved author, Jerome, and not in that part of his commentaries which is suspect, on Is. 6. 58, where he says that χειροτονία is the ordination of clergy, which is accomplished not only by the invocation of the voice but by the imposition of hands. This acceptance of the word seems to have first become common around these times (though even then it was not universally known), when, after various tumults had long arisen between the people and the clergy over the election of bishops, the people was prudently excluded for the future by a decree of the Fathers, but the word χειροτονία remained, taken over by the clergy and, in the course of time, turned to their own use, that is, substituted and adapted to the sense of consecration. In sum, so that no one may twist my view, my dispute is only with those who want τὸ χειροτονεῖν in this place to mean properly and in itself χειροτονία, namely a solemn ordination with prayers, fasting, and the imposition of hands. I constantly deny that τὸ χειροτονεῖν here means this. That these elders, whom the Apostles either chose or appointed in various distant churches, were all consecrated with prayers, fasting, and the imposition of hands, I do not deny, but rather firmly believe. Yet perhaps the words in this place do not prove this, nor even bear it, as some wish, who, with all respect for the most holy man, blessed Chrysostom, not unwisely or thoughtlessly refer the prayers and fasting in this place to the farewell of Paul and Barnabas and not to the constitution of the elders, as if this were mentioned only in passing, whereas the sense, according to the true and right construction, is: "And when they had appointed elders for them in each church, having prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord" [χειροτονήσαντες δὲ αὐτοῖς πρεσβυτέρους κατ' ἐκκλησίαν, προσευξάμενοι μετὰ νηστειῶν παρέθεντο αὐτοὺς τῷ Κυρίῳ]. Nor was such a farewell at all out of place or unusual. Acts 20. 36: Paul, about to bid farewell to the Ephesians, knelt down and prayed with them all [θεὶς πάντας αὐτοῖς προσηύξατο]; and Acts 21. 5: about to take leave of the disciples at Tyre, he knelt with them on the shore. And if they at some time fasted, that too is quite probable in a matter that was always solemn. Probably also the constitution of elders in individual churches so far apart as Derbe, Lystra, Antioch, and Iconium was not the work of one day, which the strenuous nature of the task suggests, if the prayer with fasting is referred to the constitution of the elders.

units.la: C. 15. v. 10. Νῦν οὖν τί πειράζετε τὸν Θεὸν, ἐπιθεῖναι ζυγὸν &c. Nunc ergo quid tentatis Deum, imponendo jugum cervici discipulorum, ut nec patres nostri potuerunt. AEt. 15. 19.
units.tr: Ch. 15, v. 10: "Now therefore why do you tempt God, putting a yoke on the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers were able to bear." Acts 15. 19.

units.la: V. 14. Συμεὼν ἐξηγήσατο καθὼς πρῶτον ὁ Θεὸς ἐπεσκέψατο, λαβεῖν ἐξ ἐθνῶν λαὸν τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ. Symeon narravit quomodo Deus primùm visitaverat, sumendo ex Gentibus populum nomini suo. Eadem est dictionis formula cum ea quæ præcesserit. Dictio est Elleiptica, & supplenda articulo τῷ, & præpositione quæ sensui maximè est congrua, aliquando δὲ, aliquando ἐπὶ; ut AEt. 27. 1. vel à simili.
units.tr: V. 14: "Symeon declared how God first visited, taking from the Gentiles a people for his name." The phrasing is the same as that which precedes. The expression is elliptical, and the article τῷ must be supplied, along with a preposition that best suits the sense, sometimes δὲ, sometimes ἐπὶ, as in Acts 27. 1, or by analogy.

units.la: C. 16. v. 10. Ὡς δὲ τὸ ὅραμα εἶδεν Παῦλος &c. Ut autem visionem viderat Paulum studuimus proficisci in Macedoniam. Mutantur personæ, unde liquet Lucam hoc tempore associatum esse Paulo, quod Gratus pri-mò mƺ observat factum 20. 5. At illud secundum erat tempus cum proficisceretur à Philippis Troada, nunc vero profecti sunt à Troade Philip-pos.
units.tr: Ch. 16, v. 10: "And when Paul had seen the vision, we sought to go into Macedonia." The persons change, whence it is clear that Luke had joined Paul at this time, which Gratus first observes happened at Acts 20. 5. But that was the second occasion, when he set out from Philippi to Troas; now they set out from Troas to Philippi.

units.la: C. 17. v. 8; 9. Ἐταράξαν δὲ τὸν ὄχλον καὶ τὰς πολιτάρχας ἀκούοντας ταῦτα, καὶ λαβόντες τὸ ἱκανὸν &c. i. e. per Hyperbaton. Commoverunt autem ipsa plebem & principes civitatis cum audirent, qui accipientes cautionem à Jasone & reliquis, dimiserunt illos. τὸ ἱκανὸν recte exponitur qui vel & ille, subaudiendo αὐτός, ut Matth. 27. 10. Act. 7. 10. & alibi.
units.tr: Ch. 17, vv. 8, 9: "They troubled the crowd and the rulers of the city when they heard these things, and when they had taken security from Jason and the rest, they let them go." This is by hyperbaton: they troubled the people and the rulers of the city when they heard these things, who, taking security from Jason and the others, released them. τὸ ἱκανὸν is rightly explained as he who also, supplying αὐτός, as in Matt. 27. 10, Acts 7. 10, and elsewhere.

units.la: V. 30. Τῆς μὲν οὖν χρόνος τῆς ἀγνοίας ὑπεριδὼν ὁ Θεὸς τανῦν ἀπαγγέλλει &c. Haec quidem tempora ignorantiae despiciens Deus nunc annuntiat omnibus hominibus, ut poenitentiam agant. Τὰς dicitur pro τοὺς. Despiciens, i. e. non respiciens, vel sine respectu praeteriens. In quo sensu vox illa saepius accipitur in Veteri, ut Deut. 22. 1. 3. & 4. & Job 31. 19. Misericordiam Dei nunc in praesenti in gentes praedicat, qui eos priorum temporum fivie perire in ignorantia non respiciens illos: ὑπεροψεῖ, καταφρονεῖ, Hesych.
units.tr: V. 30: "The times of ignorance God indeed overlooked, but now he declares to all men that they should repent." Τὰς is put for τοὺς. Overlooking, that is, not regarding, or passing by without regard. In this sense that word is more often used in the Old Testament, as in Deut. 22. 1, 3, and 4, and Job 31. 19. He now preaches God's mercy among the Gentiles, not regarding those who in former times were allowed to perish in ignorance: ὑπεροψεῖ, καταφρονεῖ [Hesychius].

units.la: C. 19. v. 9. Ἐν τῇ χολῇ τυράννου τινὸς: sic legit Rob. Steph. & non Τυράννου cum littera majuscula. In Schola cujusdam civitatis principis; τύραννός ἐστιν ἀρχῶν πόλεως, est civitatis princeps. Phav. Et in hoc sensu videntur Æthiop. & Arab. Interpretes hanc vocem intellexisse. Sic Esa. 13. & Jud. 16. saepius in eodem capite pro Hebraeo טְרָנוּ, apud LXX ἄρχοντες, Chaldaeus legit טְרַנָּא, tyranni. Adeo ut vox videatur Chaldaica. Eandem etiam habemus Dan. 3. 2. Esth. 9 3 Habak. 1. 10. Si nomen est proprium, cur addit τινὸς? Erasm. C. 20. v. 8. ἐν τῷ ὑπερῴῳ. Rectè in cœnaculo, ut Vetus. בעליה in superiore parte domus, à verbo עלה, ascendit, ad quam scalis ascendebatur, ubi antiquitùs cœnabatur, ὑπερῷον. Schind. ut etiam sæpe vertitur à LXX, & cœnaculum à Latino. sic Festus, Cœnacula dicuntur ad quæ scalis ascenditur.
units.tr: Ch. 19, v. 9: "In the school of a certain tyrant" [Ἐν τῇ χολῇ τυράννου τινὸς]. So Robert Stephanus reads, and not Tyrant with a capital letter. Tyrant is the ruler of a city; τύραννός ἐστιν ἀρχῶν πόλεως, is the prince of the city. Phavorinus. And in this sense the Ethiopic and Arabic translators seem to have understood the word. So in Isaiah 13 and Judges 16, often in the same chapter, the Hebrew [טְרָנוּ] is rendered by the Septuagint as rulers [ἄρχοντες], while the Chaldee reads [טְרַנָּא], tyrants. So the word seems to be Chaldean. We have the same in Dan. 3. 2, Esth. 9. 3, and Hab. 1. 10. If it is a proper name, why does he add "of a certain"? Erasmus. Ch. 20, v. 8: "in the upper room" [ἐν τῷ ὑπερῴῳ]. Rightly "in the upper room", as the Old Testament has it. [בעליה], in the upper part of the house, from the verb [עלה], to ascend, the place to which one went up by a stair, where they formerly dined, is ὑπερῷον. Schindler. It is also often rendered by the Septuagint, and cenaculum by the Latin. So Festus: cenacula are called those to which one ascends by a stair.

units.la: C. 21, v. 16. Συνῆλθον δὲ καὶ τῶν μαθητῶν ἀπὸ Καισαρείας σὺν ἡμῖν ἄγοντες παρ' ᾧ ξενισθῶμεν Μνάσωνί τινι Κυπρίῳ, ἀρχαίῳ μαθητῇ. Subaudiendum οἱ vel τινὲς τῶν μαθητῶν. Venerunt simul cum nobis quidam discipuli, vel quidam ex discipulis à Cæsarea, ducentes ad Mnasonem quendam Cyprium, antiquum discipulum, apud quem hospitaremur. Μνάσωνι pro πρὸς τὸν Μνάσωνα. Verbis enim quæ significant motum è loco Dativus sæpè additur pro Accusativo cum præpositione, ut ὁδὸς διὰ τῆς ἀγορᾶς τῇ πόλει, pro εἰς πόλιν. Miror verò cur interpretes quos vidi omnes vertant, adducentes secum Mnasonem, cùm neque sterit cum Grammatica vel sensu; multò est enim probabilius Mnasonem habitâsse, & jam fuisse Hierosolymis, apud quem staruebant hospitari.
units.tr: C. 21, v. 16. Some of the disciples also came with us from Caesarea, bringing with them one Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we might lodge. [Συνῆλθον δὲ καὶ τῶν μαθητῶν ἀπὸ Καισαρείας σὺν ἡμῖν ἄγοντες παρ' ᾧ ξενισθῶμεν Μνάσωνί τινι Κυπρίῳ, ἀρχαίῳ μαθητῇ.] We must supply οἱ or τινὲς τῶν μαθητῶν: some of the disciples came with us from Caesarea, bringing us to Mnason, a certain Cypriot and an early disciple, with whom we would stay as guests. The dative Μνάσωνι stands for πρὸς τὸν Μνάσωνα, since with verbs of motion from a place the dative is often used in place of the accusative with a preposition, as in ὁδὸς διὰ τῆς ἀγορᾶς τῇ πόλει for εἰς πόλιν. I am surprised, however, why all the translators I have seen render it "bringing Mnason with them", since this agrees neither with the grammar nor with the sense. It is much more probable that Mnason lived there and was already at Jerusalem, and that they were to stay as guests with him.

units.la: C. 22 v. 25. Ὡς δὲ προέτειναν αὐτὸν τοῖς ἱμᾶσι, Προτείνει, δι᾽ ἀνοι, Hesych. ut verò tradiderant eum flagellis. i. e. flagellandum, dixit astanti Centurioni Paulus, num hominem indemnatum & Romanum licet vobis flagellare? vix credo Apostolum distulisse sermonem suum ad Centurionem usque dum denudassent corpus & extendissent flagellandum, sed à prima facie flagellorum primam arripuisse occasionem se notum facere.
units.tr: C. 22, v. 25. When they had stretched him out with the thongs. [Ὡς δὲ προέτειναν αὐτὸν τοῖς ἱμᾶσι.] Hesychius: "to stretch out" (προτείνει). That is, they were about to scourge him. Paul said to the centurion who stood by: "Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman and uncondemned?" I scarcely believe that the Apostle postponed his speech to the centurion until they had stripped his body and stretched him out to be scourged. Rather, at the first sight of the whips, he seized the first opportunity to make himself known.

units.la: C. 25. v. 5. Οἱ δυνατοὶ ἐν ὑμῖν, nemo καταγορεῖν. Qui ergo possunt inter vos accusare descendant simul, & si quid est in vino crimen accusent eum.
units.tr: C. 25, v. 5. [Οἱ δυνατοὶ ἐν ὑμῖν.] Let no one ... [καταγορεῖν]. Vulgate: "Therefore let those among you who are able go down together, and if there is any crime in the man, let them accuse him."

units.la: C. 26. v. 16, Καὶ μαρτυρέω ἐν τε ὧδε ὧν τε εἶδες ὧν τε ὀφθήσομαί σοι, ἐξαιρούμενός σε &c. Ut constituam te ministrum & testem tum eorum quae vidisti, tum eorum quae à te videri faciam, cum eripiam te de populo (scilicet Judaico) & gentibus, ad quas nunc te mitto. ὀφθήσομαι opinor accipi in Hebraeorum Hiphil, ut in N.T. accipiuntur plurima.
units.tr: C. 26, v. 16. [Καὶ μαρτυρέω ἐν τε ὧδε ὧν τε εἶδες ὧν τε ὀφθήσομαί σοι, ἐξαιρούμενός σε &c.] That I may make you a minister and a witness both of the things which you have seen and of those in which I shall appear to you, rescuing you from the people (namely the Jews) and from the Gentiles, to whom I now send you. I think that ὀφθήσομαι is to be taken in the Hebrew Hiphil sense, as very many words are taken in the New Testament.

units.la: C. 27. v. 9. διὰ τὸ ἠὶ νηστείαν ἤδη παρελη-λυθέναι. Eo quod & jejunium praeterivisset. Non ingratum erit ipsero nec intempestivum suo loco hic apponere, quod animadvertit alibi Reverendissimus Usserius in suis Veteris Testamenti Annalibus. Cujus verba sunt hujusmodi. Unde plusquam veri simile sit, eodem ejectum Adamum fuisse die quo inductus in Paradisum fuerat. Quo quidem dies Mundi decimus esse videtur (Kalendis Novembribus anni Juliani proleptici respondens: quo deinceps ad memorabilis hujus casus memoriam conservandam (ut ratio consentaneum est) instituta est Expiationis solennitas & statum Jejunium (νηστείας nomine Act. 27. 9. καὶ Ἐξομολογῶ denotatum) in quo universi tam inquilini quam peregrini animas suas affligere jubebantur, adjuncta sanctione severissima. Omnis anima quae non jejunis afflicta eo ipso die excindetur è populis suis. [Lev. 16. 29. & 23. 29.] Quàm vero in periculosa navigatio post vel circa Kalendas Novembris non esse opus dicere.
units.tr: C. 27, v. 9. [Διὰ τὸ καὶ τὴν νηστείαν ἤδη παρελη­λυθέναι.] Because the fast had already gone by. It will not be unwelcome, nor out of place here, to set down what the most reverend Ussher observed in his Annals of the Old Testament. His words are of this kind: "Whence it is more than likely that Adam was cast out on the same day on which he had been brought into Paradise. This day seems to be the tenth of the world, corresponding to the first of November of the proleptic Julian year. From then on, to keep alive the memory of this memorable fall (as reason suggests), the solemnity of the Expiation was instituted, and a strict fast (denoted by the word νηστεία in Acts 27:9, and [ἐξομολογῶ]), in which all, both natives and strangers, were commanded to afflict their souls, with the most severe sanction attached: 'Every soul that is not afflicted by fasting on that very day shall be cut off from his people' [Lev. 16:29; 23:29]." How dangerous a voyage after, or about, the Kalends of November was, there is no need to say.

units.la: V. 21. Πλεῖν μὲν ἐν ... ; Et non comparâsse hanc procellam, sive tempestatem. Γ-ενες, ... εὐ-χερῶς ... ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ... , eò quòd plures pondus seu graviter. Suid. & in Pollucis Onomastico, ὀλεισὶς ἄνεμος, procellosus ventus.
units.tr: V. 21. [Πλεῖν μὲν ἐν ...] And that he had not gained this storm or tempest. [Γενες, ... εὐχερῶς ... ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ...], because more weight or heavily. Suidas, and in Pollux's Onomasticon: [ὀλεισὶς ἄνεμος], a stormy wind, a gusty wind.

units.la: In Epistolam ad Romanos.
units.tr: On the Epistle to the Romans.

units.la: ROM. c. 1. v. 17. Δικαιοσύνη γὰρ Θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ ἀποκαλύπτεται ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν. Verba haec, ni fallor, optime exponuntur per Metathesin, quasi scriberetur, Δικαιοσύνη γὰρ Θεοῦ ἐκ πίστεως ἐν αὐτῷ ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι εἰς πίστιν. Justitia enim Dei ex fide in ea revelatur in fidem, i.e. ut credatur. Ut enim haec justitia Dei ex fide demonstretur & credatur, est opus fere totius Epistolae. MetathesES ejusmodi in N. T. sunt frequentissimae. Quoad Phrasim, εἰς πίστιν, est omnino eadem cum ea quae praecessit v. 5. & quae sequitur, 16. 26. εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως, in obedientiam fidei, i.e. ut obediatur fidei inter Gentes. Qualis etiam est illa, 15. 18 εἰς ὑπακοὴν ἐθνῶν, in obedientiam Gentium, i.e. ut obedirent Gentes, ut utroque loco plerumque exponitur. Quid vero velit ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν, non bene convenit inter Interpretes.
units.tr: ROM. 1. 17. For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith [Δικαιοσύνη γὰρ Θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ ἀποκαλύπτεται ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν]. Unless I am mistaken, these words are best explained by metathesis, as if it were written: the righteousness of God is revealed from faith in it, to faith [Δικαιοσύνη γὰρ Θεοῦ ἐκ πίστεως ἐν αὐτῷ ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι εἰς πίστιν]. For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith, to faith, that is, so that it may be believed. For nearly the whole Epistle is the work of showing that this righteousness of God comes from faith and is to be believed. Transpositions of this kind are very frequent in the New Testament. As for the phrase εἰς πίστιν [to faith], it is exactly the same as the one that came before at v. 5, and the one that follows at 16. 26, εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως [to the obedience of faith], that is, so that the faith may be obeyed among the Gentiles. So too is the phrase at 15. 18, εἰς ὑπακοὴν ἐθνῶν [to the obedience of the Gentiles], that is, so that the Gentiles might obey, as it is mostly explained in both places. But what ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν [from faith to faith] is meant to mean is not well agreed upon among the interpreters.

units.la: C. 2. v. 15. Τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου, Opus legis scriptum in cordibus. Opus legis est accusare, vel excusare. Atque id facit conscientia in uniuscujusque corde.
units.tr: C. 2. v. 15. The work of the law written in their hearts [Τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου, Opus legis scriptum in cordibus]. The work of the law is to accuse or to excuse, and conscience does exactly this in the heart of each person.

units.la: C. 3. v. 5. ᾿Ει δὲ ἡ ἀδικία ἡμῶν Θεοῦ δικαιοσύνην συνίστησι, τί ἐροῦμεν; μὴ ἄδικος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ἐπιφέρων τὴν ὀργὴν; (κατὰ ἄνθρωπον λέγω, μὴ γένοιτο· ἐπεὶ πῶς κρινεῖ ὁ Θεὸς τὸν κόσμον;) εἰ γὰρ ἡ ἀλήθεια τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ ψεύσματι ἐπερίσσευσεν εἰς τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ, τί ἔτι κἀγὼ ὡς ἁμαρτωλὸς κρίνομαι; καὶ μὴ (καθὼς βλασφημούμεθα, καὶ καθὼς φασί τινες ἡμᾶς λέγειν) ὅτι ποιήσωμεν τὰ κακὰ ἵνα ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀγαθά; ὧν τὸ κρίμα ἔνδικόν ἐστι. Si vero iniquitas nostra Dei justitiam commendat, quid dicemus? Nonne injustus est Deus qui infert iram? (secundum hominem loquor, absit; tum enim quomodo Deus judicabit mundum?) Si enim veritas Dei in meo mendacio abundavit ad ejus gloriam, cur ego tanquam peccator judicor, & non (sicut blasphemamur, & sicut quidam nos aiunt dicere) quoniam fecerimus mala ut venirent bona? quorum judicium justum est. Si enim in judicium vocarentur, eo quod fecerint mala ut venirent bona, κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον possint dicere, se non oportere judicari ut peccatores, sed absolvi potius, si non remunerari, eo quod fecissent quod tendebat ad Dei gloriam. At si hoc daretur, quomodo judicaret Deus mundum? si nimirum hoc praetextu evadere possent impii judicium Dei, nullus relinqueretur judicandus. Versio est certe in se legitima. Particula μὴ saepius in N. T. vertitur nonne, ut Matth. 12, 23. Job. 4. 29. 18. 17, & 25. & alibi, ut etiam in hoc ipso loco vertit Grotius. Parum interest quoad sensum, si vertatur, num injustus est Deus? Vide eandem dicendi formulam 9. 14.
units.tr: C. 3. v. 5. But if our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is not God unjust who inflicts wrath? (I speak in human terms [κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον], God forbid; for how then would God judge the world?) For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner?
