And why not (as we are slandered, and as some say that we say) "Let us do evil that good may come"? Their condemnation is just [Ei δὲ ἡ ἀδικία ἡμῶν Θεοῦ δικαιοσύνην συνίστησι, τί ἐροῦμεν; μὴ ἄδικος ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ἐπιφέρων τὴν ὀργήν; (κατὰ ἄνθρωπον λέγω, μὴ γένοιτο· ἐπεὶ πῶς κρινεῖ ὁ Θεὸς τὸν κόσμον;) εἰ γὰρ ἡ ἀλήθεια τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ ψεύσματι ἐπερίσσευσεν εἰς τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ, τί ἔτι κἀγὼ ὡς ἁμαρτωλὸς κρίνομαι; καὶ μὴ (καθὼς βλασφημούμεθα, καὶ καθὼς φασί τινες ἡμᾶς λέγειν) ὅτι ποιήσωμεν τὰ κακὰ ἵνα ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀγαθά; ὧν τὸ κρίμα ἔνδικόν ἐστι]. If indeed our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust who inflicts wrath? (I speak in human terms, God forbid; for how else would God judge the world?) For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner? And why not (as we are slandered, and as some say we say) that we should do evil so that good may come? Their condemnation is just. For if men were called to judgment because they had done evil so that good might come, they could say, in human terms, that they ought not to be judged as sinners but rather absolved, if not rewarded, since they had done what tended to the glory of God. But if this were allowed, how would God judge the world? Clearly, if the wicked could escape the judgment of God by this pretext, no one would be left to be judged. The translation is certainly legitimate in itself. The particle μὴ is often rendered nonne [is it not?] in the New Testament, as at Matth. 12. 23, Job. 4. 29, 18. 17, 25, and elsewhere; Grotius also renders it so in this very passage. It makes little difference to the sense whether it is rendered num injustus est Deus? [is God then unjust?]. See the same form of speech at 9. 14.

units.la: C 4 v. 6 Καθάπερ καὶ Δαβὶδ λέγει τὸν μακαρισμὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου &c. Post λέγει, subaudi τίνι, nempe τίνι τὸν μακαρισμόν. Sicut & David dicit de beatitudine hominis cui Deus imputat putat justitiam sine operibus. Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates &c. Ubique locus est Accusativo, si intelligas τι ut Grammatici. Vide Animad. in Act. 10. 36. & Rom. 10. 5.
units.tr: C. 4. v. 6. Just as David also speaks of the blessedness of the man [Καθάπερ καὶ Δαβὶδ λέγει τὸν μακαρισμὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου] &c. After λέγει, supply τίνι, namely τίνι τὸν μακαρισμόν [of whom he speaks the blessing]. Thus: as David also speaks of the blessedness of the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works. Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven &c. The place is everywhere in the accusative, if you understand τι as the grammarians do. See my Animadversiones on Acts 10. 36 and Rom. 10. 5.

units.la: C. 5. v. 7. Τοῦ γὰρ τὰ ἀγαθὰ τάχα τις καὶ τολμᾷ ἀποθανεῖν. Pro bono forsitan quis audeat mori. Pro bono, i.e. pro eo qui personaliter bonus huic vel illi homini. i.e. pro amico, μίαν ὁ τοιαύτην ἀγάπην ἔχει, &c. nemo majorem habet hoc amorem, quàm ut animam ponat pro amicis suis. Joh. 15. 13. ut exempla rara docent, nec ultra tendit humanus amor. Commendat autem in nos amorem Deus, quòd Christus pro nobis mortuus est, cùm peccatores essemus, v. 8 etiam cùm inimici, v. 10. Peccatores enim & inimici idem valent. Hic est amor qui cognitionem excedit. Eph. 3. 5.
units.tr: C. 5. v. 7. For scarcely would anyone die for a righteous man, though for a good man perhaps someone would dare to die [Τοῦ γὰρ τὰ ἀγαθὰ τάχα τις καὶ τολμᾷ ἀποθανεῖν]. For a good man, that is, for one who is personally good to this or that person; that is, for a friend, [μίαν ὁ τοιαύτην ἀγάπην ἔχει], since such love is had by no one. No one has greater love than this, that he lay down his life for his friends (John 15. 13). As rare examples show, human love does not go any further. But God commends his love toward us, in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners (v. 8), and even while we were enemies (v. 10). For sinners and enemies mean the same thing. This is the love that surpasses knowledge. Eph. 3. 5.

units.la: V. 12, 13, 14. &c. Διὰ τοῦτο, ὥσπερ δι' ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἡ ἁμαρτία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε, καὶ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὁ θάνατος, καὶ οὕτως εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους ὁ θάνατος διῆλθεν, ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον. Ἄχρι γὰρ νόμου ἁμαρτία ἦν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ. Ἁμαρτία δὲ οὐκ ἐλλογεῖται μὴ ὄντος νόμου· ἀλλὰ ἐβασίλευσεν ὁ θάνατος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ μέχρι Μωσέως· καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς μὴ ἁμαρτήσαντας ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παραβάσεως Ἀδὰμ, ὅς ἐστι τύπος τοῦ μέλλοντος. Non] acquiescendum reor anan-tapodotis, si quo modo illaeso sensu possint expediri. Neque verò assentior iis, qui volunt versum 18 & 19 respondere 12, atque eo modo evadere anantapodosin. Placet potiùs eorum sententia, qui vertunt καὶ ὥσπερ, etiam ita, vel quod planius frequenti metatbesi, ita quoque, ut Interpres Syrus, & Arabicus, & alii recentiores; qua versione non modò non laeditur, sed etiam magis perficitur sensus & syntaxis, sumendo τὸ ὡς, hoc loco, quod quod de priore notavit Erasmus non ita opportune, reddititè, & non copulativè, ut in oratione Dominicâ, ὡς ἐν οὐρανῷ, καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ut in coelo etiam in terra. Atque hoc modo non video quin haec verba sint in se completa admodum & persecta. Propterea sicut per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, & per peccatum mors, ita quoque mors in omnes homines pertransiit, eò quòd omnes peccaverunt. Usque enim ad legem peccatum erat in mundo. Peccatum verò non imputatur ubi non est lex. Imò regnavit mors ab Adamo usque ad Mosen, etiam in eos qui non peccaverunt secundum similitudinem transgressionis Adami, qui typus est futuri. Videtur Apostolus tacitè quorundam objectioni occurrere, quos negare innuitur omnes fuisse peccatores, quod jam antea affirmaverat. Ideòque forte sophisticè arguebant, Christum non esse mortuum pro omnibus. Est enim peccatum transgressio legis; non verò poterant illi legem transgredi qui non habebant, lex enim fuit a Mose. Joh. 1, 17. Ut ergo objectionem horum praeoccuperet, hoc argumento utitur. Sicut per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, & per peccatum mors; diâ τοῦτο, propterea pari modo & jure mors in omnes homines pertransiit, eò quòd omnes peccaverunt. Ita ut verissimum sit quod asserit. A lapsu Adami usque ad legem, i. e. ante legem certè Mosaicam, neque enim de alia lege disserit per totam Epistolam, peccatum erat in mundo. Ultrà verò objicitur; peccatum autem non imputatur ubi non est lex; lex enim operatur iram. c. 4,5. Imò etiam & imputatum est peccatum; regnavit enim mors ab Adamo usque ad Mosem, ergo ante legem peccarum & fuit in mundo, & etiam imputatum est. Mortuos esse argumentum est peccâsse, & peccatum sum imputari, nam stipendium peccati mors 6. 23. Ideóque quia mors pertransiit in omnes, necessa-rió statuendum omnes homines peccavisse, & poenæ mortis factos esse obnoxios, etiam eos qui non peccaverunt secundum similitudinem trans-gressionis Adams, in ipsos enim regnavit mors infantes, qui non peccaverunt nisi in Adamo, qui typus erat futuri hominis, subaudito ἀντιτύπου. Repræsentavit enim ille in persona sua totum genus hominum, etiam & infantium, qui ex ipso erant oriundi. Atque eo nomine & sensu appositè dicitur Adamus hoc loco τύπον τῆ̃ς μέλλοντος. Scio equidem universos interpretes & veteres & recentes Christum intelligere qui futurus erat; sed si exactius examinetur locus, longe ist*e* nullam aut vix ullam habet cohærentiam cum contextu. Et si loquamur sensu idoneo, non potest Adamus dici typus Christi; Typus enim est expressa figura cuiquam repræsentat, τύπος respondet τῷ ἀντιτύπῳ, ut sigillo cera. Necesse est ut ejus, quod bonum est, typus sit etiam bonus, ejus vero, quod malum est, typus etiam malus, alioquin non esset typus. Est etiam disparitas inter Christum & Adamum toto cœlo. Quod si dispar aliquid potest esse typus, si quod nigrum est potest dici typus ejus quod album est, vel curvum recti, non est quod plura dicam. Si ergo velimus loqui proprie, Adamus verius & rectius dicitur typus progeniei suæ, quæ ex eo futura erat: & quam virtualiter repræsentavit in persona suâ, quæ etiam per peccatum ejus obnoxia facta est peccato & pœnæ mortis. Atque ex his verbis in hunc modum expositis fortissimum credo argumentum struni pro originali peccato. Omnes enim homines in Adamo facti sunt obnoxii mortis & peccato causæ mortis, omnes enim Adami transgressionis participes ticipes facti sunt in ejus lumbis existentes, omnes denique immunditiem naturæ ab eo contraxerunt, qui filios genuit in imaginem suam, Gen. 5. 3. Omnes ergo eodem tenentur reatu cum Adamo, morte nque promerentur qui ex eo geniti. Neque sum omninò sine teste. Favet versio vel Paraphrasis Æthiopica, cujus verba sunt hujusmodi. Veruntamen dominata est mors propter ea ab Adamo usque ad Mosem, tam in iis qui peccaverunt, quam in iis qui non peccaverunt, per illud peccatum Adami, eo quòd unusquisque in similitudine Adami creatus est, & quia Adamus typus fuit illius qui erat venturus. E quibus verbis mihi pronum est intelligere, aperte eum dicere, Mortem in omnes, etiam in infantes dominatam esse propter peccatum Adami, propter has duas causas, & quia unusquisque in similitudine Adami creatus est,& quia Adamus typus fuit illius qui erat venturus. Quæ causæ etsi videntur duæ, sunt revera tamen una eademque. Est enim altera alterius redditio & explanatio. Idem enim est, Adamum typum esse posterorum qui venturi erant, & posteros Adami vel venturos in similitudine ejus esse factos. Dicere vero, quòd dominata est mors in omnes per peccatum Adami, quia Adamus erat typus Christi, præterquam quod sit ἀχόλυθον, est etiam ἀνόητον. Si vero dicas dominatam esse mortem in omnes per peccatum Adami, quia Adamus erat posterorum typus, i. e. qui in sua persona repræsentavit universum genus hominum, qui ex ipso erant futuri, appositè respondet scopo loci, facillimúmque cuivis homini primo intuitu apprehendere; neque vero est in ullo sensu necessarium, ut hoc loco Adamus dicatur typus Christi. Concluserat his ultimis verbis, quòd voluit Apostolus, omnes homines sub peccato, utpote qui in Adamo primo typo peccaverunt, atque inde morti facti sunt obnoxii. At tum demum progreditur v. 15: sermone discretivo, 'Ἀλλ' ὡς' &c. Ad copiosam satis etiam sine his verbis manifestationem disparitatis inter offensam Adami & Gratiam Dei in Christo. Quomodo etiam typus dicatur typus per antithesim, quod ita constanter aiunt, ingenuè fateor non intelligo, neque credo similem typum reperiri in toto sacro codice. Atque hac versione & interpretatione fundicus everti reor turrem illam confusionis, quam, fundamentum ponens in hoc ipso loco, sibi struxit luxurians ille calamus, qui fabricavit sibi novum genus hominum quos PraAdamitas vocat, qui tam fidenter ausus est omnia sacra ventilare. Ultrà per me licet qui vult respondeat, melius verò & pro sapientia fiet, si nemo id muneris in se suscipiat. praestat enim vanas & inutiles quæstiones silentio conspire, quam perscrutando & agitando, praesertim in hac ætate, ἀναςωπυρεῖν.
units.tr: Vers. 12, 13, 14, etc. "Therefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin, so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned" [Διὰ τοῦτο, ὥσπερ δι' ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἡ ἁμαρτία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε, καὶ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὁ θάνατος, καὶ οὕτως εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους ὁ θάνατος διῆλθεν, ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον]. "For until the law sin was in the world. But sin is not imputed where there is no law. Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression, who is the figure of the one to come" [Ἄχρι γὰρ νόμου ἁμαρτία ἦν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ. Ἁμαρτία δὲ οὐκ ἐλλογεῖται μὴ ὄντος νόμου· ἀλλὰ ἐβασίλευσεν ὁ θάνατος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ μέχρι Μωσέως· καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς μὴ ἁμαρτήσαντας ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παραβάσεως Ἀδὰμ, ὅς ἐστι τύπος τοῦ μέλλοντος]. I think we should not rest content with the anantapodoton, if the sense can be unravelled without harm. Nor do I agree with those who want verse 18 and 19 to answer to verse 12, and so escape the anantapodoton. I prefer the opinion of those who render καὶ ὥσπερ as "so also" or, more plainly by the common metathesis, "thus also", as the Syriac and Arabic interpreters and other more recent ones do. By this rendering the sense and syntax are not only not harmed but made more complete, if τὸ ὡς is taken here as quod, as Erasmus rightly noted of the earlier text, though not so aptly; it is rendered as a relative, not as a conjunction, as in the Lord's Prayer, ὡς ἐν οὐρανῷ, καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, "as in heaven, so also on earth". In this way I do not see why these words should not be complete and perfect in themselves. Therefore, just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, so also death passed through to all men, because all have sinned. For until the law sin was in the world. But sin is not imputed where there is no law. Indeed death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin according to the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a type of the one to come. The Apostle seems tacitly to meet the objection of certain people, who are implied to deny that all were sinners, which he had already affirmed. Therefore they perhaps argued sophistically that Christ did not die for all. For sin is the transgression of the law, but those who did not have the law could not transgress it, since the law came by Moses (John 1:17). So, to forestall their objection, he uses this argument: just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, (διὰ τοῦτο), so by the same measure and right death passed upon all men, because all have sinned. Thus what he asserts is entirely true: from the fall of Adam until the law, that is, certainly before the Mosaic law (for he does not discuss any other law throughout the whole Epistle), sin was in the world. Moreover it is objected: but sin is not imputed where there is no law, for the law works wrath (Rom. 4:15). Indeed sin was also imputed, for death reigned from Adam to Moses; therefore before the law sin was committed and was in the world, and was also imputed. That they are dead is the proof that they sinned, and that sin is imputed, for the wages of sin is death (Rom. 6:23). Therefore, since death passed upon all, it must necessarily be held that all men sinned and became liable to the penalty of death, even those who did not sin after the likeness of the transgression of Adam. For death reigned over infants, who did not sin except in Adam, who was a type of the coming man, understood antitype. For he represented in his own person the whole human race, including the infants who were descended from him. And in this name and sense Adam is fittingly called here a type of the one to come. I know indeed that all interpreters, both ancient and recent, understand Christ who was to come; but if the passage is examined more exactly, that interpretation has little or no coherence with the context. And if we speak in a fitting sense, Adam cannot be called a type of Christ; for a type is a clear figure presented to someone, and τύπος answers to τὸ ἀντίτυπον, as wax to a seal. It is necessary that a type of what is good be itself good, and a type of what is evil be evil too, otherwise it would not be a type. There is also a difference between Christ and Adam as wide as heaven and earth. But if something unlike can be a type, if what is black can be called a type of what is white, or what is crooked of what is straight, there is no need to say more. If therefore we wish to speak properly, Adam is more truly and rightly called the type of his posterity, which was to come from him, and whom he represented virtually in his own person, and who were also made liable to sin and the penalty of death through his sin. And from these words so expounded I believe a very strong argument is built for original sin. For all men were made liable to death and to sin, the cause of death, in Adam; all became partakers of Adam's transgression, being in his loins; finally all drew from him the uncleanness of nature, he who begat sons in his own image (Gen. 5:3). All therefore are bound by the same guilt as Adam, and deserve death, those who were born of him. Nor am I entirely without a witness. The Ethiopic version or paraphrase favours me, whose words are of this kind: Yet death has reigned from Adam until Moses, both over those who sinned and over those who did not sin, through that sin of Adam, because each one was created in the likeness of Adam, and because Adam was a type of the one who was to come. From these words it is easy for me to understand that it plainly says that death has reigned over all, even infants, on account of the sin of Adam, for these two reasons: because each one was created in the likeness of Adam, and because Adam was a type of the one who was to come. Although these causes seem two, they are really one and the same, for the one is the restatement and explanation of the other. For it is the same thing to say that Adam was a type of the posterity who were to come, and that the posterity of Adam, or those who were to come, were made in his likeness. But to say that death has reigned over all through the sin of Adam because Adam was a type of Christ, besides being inconsequent, is also senseless. But if you say that death has reigned over all through the sin of Adam because Adam was a type of the posterity, that is, one who in his own person represented the whole human race that was to descend from him, this fits the aim of the passage aptly, and is most easily grasped by anyone at first sight; nor is it in any sense necessary here that Adam should be called a type of Christ. By these last words the Apostle concluded what he meant: that all men are under sin, as those who in Adam, the first type, sinned, and were thereby made liable to death. But then at verse 15 he goes on with a discriminating statement, "But not as the offence..." [Ἀλλ' ὡς]. Even without these words there is a sufficiently full showing of the difference between the offence of Adam and the grace of God in Christ. How Adam is called a type by antithesis, as they constantly say, I frankly confess I do not understand, nor do I believe a similar type can be found in the whole sacred volume. And by this version and interpretation I think that tower of confusion is utterly overthrown from its foundations, which that wanton pen built for itself, laying its foundation in this very passage, the pen that fabricated for itself a new race of men whom it calls Pre-Adamites, and that boldly dared to toss up all holy things. Let whoever wishes respond further at his own discretion; but it would be better and wiser if no one took up this task upon himself. For it is better to pass over vain and useless questions in silence than to probe and stir them up, especially in this age, to fan them into flame [ἀναζωπυρεῖν].

units.la: C. 7. v. 6. Νυνὶ δὲ καταργήθημεν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου ἀποθανόντος ἐν ᾧ κατειχόμεθα. i. e. per frequentissimam trajectionem, Νυνὶ δὲ καταργήθημεν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου ἐν ᾧ κατειχόμεθα ἀποθανόντος. Et quid magis obvium vel scopo loci magis appositum? Nunc vero soluti sumus à lege in qua detinebamur mortuâ. Neque verò est obscurum sine trajectione dicere: Nunc verò soluti sumus à lege quæ est mortua in qua detinebamur. Atqui Paulus numquam dicturus fuit legem Dei esse mortuam, ut Doctissimus Beza. Et quidni ita dicat Paulus? intelligens tamen interim quod ne unus quidem apex praeteribit à lege Dei donec omnia fiant. Matth. 5. 18. Legem verò esse mortuam in τῷ ἐνεργείᾳ in ipso exemplo excemplo ostendit, ut Chrysostomus: Lex enim dominatur in hominem quamdiu viuit, ut rectissime Erasmus, v 1. Addens ultra, In conferenda similitudine Paulus legem Viri loco posuit & hominem uxoris vice. Ut mortuo Viri liberatur Uxor, ita antiquata lege liberatur prius abmaxime legi. Legem autem vivere dicit quamdiu valet, mortuam esse posteaquam desiit habere vigorem. Quo nihil potuit dici rectius. Sic Vatablus, vivit, jubendi lex. Et Sic Grotius: Quamdiu lex vivit, quamdiu extincta non est. Lex enim abrogata mortua est. 1. vim obligandi non habet. Atqui in hoc luto haeserunt diu multi fallor interpretes.
units.tr: Chap. 7, verse 6: "But now we have been released from the law, that being dead wherein we were held" [Νυνὶ δὲ καταργήθημεν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου ἀποθανόντος ἐν ᾧ κατειχόμεθα]. That is, by a very frequent transposition: "But now we have been released from the law wherein we were held, it being dead" [Νυνὶ δὲ καταργήθημεν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου ἐν ᾧ κατειχόμεθα ἀποθανόντος]. What could be more obvious, or better suited to the purpose of the passage? "But now we are released from the law in which we were held, being dead." Nor is it obscure to say without transposition: "But now we are released from the law which is dead, in which we were held." Yet Paul would never have said that God's law is dead, as the most learned Beza observes. Why should Paul not say it, though, when he understood that "not one jot or tittle shall pass from the law of God until all things are fulfilled" (Matth. 5. 18.)? He shows that the law is dead in its operation, in the very example itself, as Chrysostom does: "For the law rules over a man as long as he lives," as Erasmus rightly says (v. 1). Adding further: "In comparing the likeness, Paul put the law in the place of the husband and the man in the place of the wife. As the wife is freed by the husband's death, so she is freed from the law, which has been made obsolete." He says the law lives as long as it has force, and is dead once it has ceased to have power. Nothing could be said more rightly. So Vatablus: the law lives as a law of commanding. And so Grotius: the law is alive as long as it is not extinguished; for an abrogated law is dead, and no longer has the force of binding. Yet many interpreters, I think, have long stuck fast in this mire.

units.la: V. 24. Ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος· τίς με ῥύσεται ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου; Optime exponitur per metathesin, quasi legeretur, τίς με ῥύσεταί ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου τοῦ σώματος τούτου; Infelix ego homo; quis me liberabit a morte huius corporis, quod tam miserè detinetur sub lege peccati, quae est in membris meis? A morte, sive secundâ & aeternâ, statutum enim est hominibus semel mori, à quâ morte non est liberatio expectanda. Perinde ac si diceret, Quis me liberabit ab aeternâ condemnatione, qui sum ita captivus factus & venundatus sub peccato? Atque hunc esse sensum innuunt sequentia. Εὐχαριστῶ τῷ Θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ &c. Quae verba supplenda sunt, reddidit vel responderi, cum Valla, & aliis, Gratias ago Deo, αὐτὸς με ῥύσεται, ipse me liberabit per Iesum Christum, & tum demum sequitur, c. 8. 1. Nulla ergo est condemnatio iis qui sunt in Christo Iesu &c. Lex enim Spiritus vitae in Christo Iesu liberavit me à lege peccati & à morte, (non mortis, ut plerumque exponitur) ut legitimè poterit verti, & etiam legit Interpres.
units.tr: V. 24: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" [Ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος· τίς με ῥύσεται ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου;] This is best explained by a metathesis, as if it read: "Who will deliver me from the death of this body?" [τίς με ῥύσεταί ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου τοῦ σώματος τούτου;] Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the death of this body, which is so miserably held under the law of sin that is in my members? From death, namely the second and eternal death, for it is appointed for men once to die, and from that death there is no deliverance to be expected. It is as if he said: "Who will deliver me from eternal condemnation, I who am made so captive and sold under sin?" The words that follow indicate this sense: "I thank God through Jesus Christ" [Εὐχαριστῶ τῷ Θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ], etc. These words must be supplied, as Valla and others do: "I give thanks to God; he himself [αὐτὸς με ῥύσεται] will deliver me through Jesus Christ." Then at last follows chap. 8. 1: "There is therefore no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus," etc. For "the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and from death" (not "of death," as is commonly rendered). This can legitimately be translated thus, and the Ethiopic translator also so reads it.

units.la: {*} ... terpres Æthiopicus. Metathesei ejusmodi sunt in N.T. abunde familiares. Vide Animad. in AE. 13.27. & 2 Cor. 4.4.
units.tr: ... the Ethiopic translator. Transpositions of this kind are abundantly familiar in the New Testament. See my Animadversions on Acts 13. 27 and 2 Cor. 4. 4.

units.la: Cap. 8. v. 3 Τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον τῆς νόμου ἐν ᾧ ἠσθένει διὰ τῆς σαρκὸς, ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ υἱὸν πέμψας ἐν τῷ ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας, καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας κατέκρινε τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐν τῇ σαρκί. Vertendum per Metathesin. In eo enim quod impossibile legis infirmum erat propter carnem, Deus filium suum misit in similitudine peccatricis carnis, qui, sive & ille hostia pro peccato damnavit peccatum in carne. Ante πέμψας subaudi verbum substantivum ὢν, ut χ̀ ἐκλεξάμενος, & elegit. Luc. 6. 13. & εὑρόντες γὰρ, invenimus enim. AE. 24. 5. quâ nihil familiarius phrasi, qualis occurrit apud Lucam 1.22. Καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν διδάσκων αὐτοῖς, & ipse inmuebat illis. σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας, peccatricis carnis, ut vertimus τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τῆς δόξης, Gloriosum Evangelium, 2 Cor. 4. 4. & similia. Τὸ περὶ ἁμαρτίας necessario exponitur qui vel & ille, ut saepius facit Beza & Anglicus, idque valde licitè, ut videre est in Animad. Matth 27. 10. Job. 15. 6. AE. 2 2. 7. 10. & alibi. Non enim Deus Pater, nisi loquamur promiscuè, sed quem misit filius [verbum caro factum] pro peccato hostia damnavit peccatum in carne. περὶ ἁμαρτίας, ὀρθῶς vertitur, hostia pro peccato, ut exponunt Interpretes περὶ ἁμαρτίας Heb. 10.6. & Psal. 40. 6. de quo etiam vide apud LXX, Lev. 6. 30. & 16. 27. In Hebraeo enim חטאת vel חטאות, est peccatum & sacrificium expiationis pro peccato, Num. 8 8. Lev. 6 25. Exod. 29. 14. & alibi: ut etiam dicitur Hos. 4. 8. Peccata populi mei comedunt, i.e. sacrificia pro peccatis populi, contra mandatum Dei. Lev. 6. 30. & 16. 27. & 2 Cor. 5. 21. Eum qui non noverat peccatum pro nobis peccatum facit, ut nos essemus iustitia Dei in ipso. Hostiam pro peccato nostro. Parallelum huius loci, ut animadvertit Origenes, est Heb.9.26. νυνὶ δὲ ἅπαξ ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων εἰς ἀθέτησιν τῆς ἁμαρτίας διὰ τῆς θυσίας αὐτοῦ πεφανέρωται. In consummatione saeculorum per oblationem sui, i. e. pro peccato factus hostia, ad destructionem, i.e. ad condemnationem peccati apparuit. Cui etiam potest addi Heb. 7. 18. Ἀθέτησις μὲν γὰρ γίνεται προαγούσης ἐντολῆς διὰ τὸ αὐτῆς ἀσθενὲς καὶ ἀνωφελές. Priore enim loco damnavit & destruxit peccatum per immolationem sui, posteriore vero abolevit & damnavit legem propter ejus infirmum & inutile. Atque haec versio huius loci est in sollegitima, utrum sit accommoda, judicet aequus Lector.
units.tr: Chap. 8, v. 3: "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh" [Τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον τοῦ νόμου ἐν ᾧ ἠσθένει διὰ τῆς σαρκὸς, ὁ Θεὸς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ υἱὸν πέμψας ἐν τῷ ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας, καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας κατέκρινε τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐν τῇ σαρκί]. This must be rendered by a transposition: "For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weak because of the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and as a sin offering, condemned sin in the flesh." Before πέμψας understand the substantive verb ὢν, as in ἐκλεξάμενος, "and chose" (Luke 6. 13), and εὑρόντες γὰρ, "for having found" (Acts 24. 5), a phrase as common as any found in Luke 1. 22: "And he was teaching them" [Καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν διδάσκων αὐτοῖς]. "Sinful flesh" [σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας] means "sinful flesh," as we translate "the glorious gospel" [τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τῆς δόξης] (2 Cor. 4. 4) and similar phrases. Περὶ ἁμαρτίας must necessarily be explained as "even as" or "as a sin offering," as Beza and the English translators often do, and quite legitimately, as may be seen in my Animadversions on Matth. 27. 10, John 15. 6, Acts 2. 7, 10 and elsewhere. For it is not God the Father who is meant (unless we speak loosely), but the one whom he sent, the Son [the Word made flesh], who as a sin offering condemned sin in the flesh. περὶ ἁμαρτίας is rightly rendered "a sin offering," as the interpreters explain περὶ ἁμαρτίας in Heb. 10. 6 and Ps. 40. 6; see also the Septuagint, Lev. 6. 30 and 16. 27. For in Hebrew חטאת or חטאות means both sin and the sacrifice of atonement for sin (Num. 8. 8; Lev. 6. 25; Exod. 29. 14 and elsewhere), as also in Hos. 4. 8: "They eat the sins of my people," that is, the sacrifices for the sins of the people, contrary to God's command. Compare Lev. 6. 30 and 16. 27, and 2 Cor. 5. 21: "He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might be the righteousness of God in him," a sacrifice for our sin. The parallel to this passage, as Origen observes, is Heb. 9. 26: "But now once, at the end of the ages, he has appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself" [νυνὶ δὲ ἅπαξ ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων εἰς ἀθέτησιν τῆς ἁμαρτίας διὰ τῆς θυσίας αὐτοῦ πεφανέρωται]. That is, at the consummation of the ages, by the offering of himself, that is, made a sin offering, he appeared for the destruction, that is, the condemnation, of sin. To this may also be added Heb. 7. 18: "For there is an annulling of the former commandment because of its weakness and unprofitableness" [Ἀθέτησις μὲν γὰρ γίνεται προαγούσης ἐντολῆς διὰ τὸ αὐτῆς ἀσθενὲς καὶ ἀνωφελές]. In the former passage he condemned and destroyed sin by offering himself; in the latter he abolished and condemned the law because of its weakness and unprofitableness. Whether this rendering of the passage is suitable, let the fair reader judge; it is not, I think, unsuitable.

units.la: V. 19. &c: Ἡ γὰρ ἀποκαραδοκία τῆς κτίσεως τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν τῶν υἱῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀπεκδέχεται (τῇ γὰρ ματαιότητι ἡ κτίσις ὑπετάγη οὐχ ἑκοῦσα, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸν ὑποτάξαντα) ἐφ' ἑλπίδι ὅτι καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ κτίσις ἐλευθερωθήσεται ἀπὸ τῆς δουλείας τῆς φθορᾶς εἰς τὴν ἐλευθερίαν τῆς δόξης τῶν τέκνων τοῦ Θεοῦ. Οἴδαμεν γὰρ ὅτι πᾶσα ἡ κτίσις συνστενάζει καὶ συνωδίνει ἄχρι τοῦ νῦν. Creatio enim i. e. mundus avidè expectat revelationem filiorum Dei, (vanitati enim subjectus est mundus non volens sed propter eum qui subjecit eum) in spe quod & ipse mundus liberabitur ex servitute corruptionis in libertatem gloriae filiorum Dei. Scimus enim quod totus mundus ingemiscit, & est in dolore partûs usque ad praesens. Veteres plerumque & recentes hunc locum totum intelligunt per Prosopopoeiam dictum de creatura irrationali, quae liberabitur in statum incorruptibilitatis in ultimo die. Ego vero cum Augustino magis sententia per vocem κτίσεως hominem intelligi, neque sensum gemendi & dolendi esse in arboribus, quem secutus Cajetanus vult κτίσιν hoc loco significare τὴν κτῖ- σιν, frequenter enim sunt in N.T. ὁ κόσμος, ἡ κτίσις, & τὰ ἔθνη eadem. Saepius etiam Gentes distincte vocantur mundus, in oppositione ad Ecclesiam Dei, quae de mundo non esse dicitur, κόσμου τῆς ἐν ἀπιστίᾳ ἐν ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀνθρώπους λέγει ὁ Ἀπόστολος. Phavor. Potuit quidem irrationalis creatura aliquo sensu expectare liberationem à servitute corruptionis, nullo vero opinor sensu poterant expectare liberationem in libertatem gloriae filiorum Dei. Perinde ergo sensus est ac si dixisset, cum aio passiones hujus temporis non esse dignas ad gloriam quae revelanda est in nobis, non est quod objici ut quisquam vestrum, hoc nihil ad nos Romanos pertinere, promissa enim facta esse semini Abraham. Imò etiam dico vobis, in vobis etiam revelandam esse gloriam, quae futura est sive aeterna sive Evangelica. Nolo enim vos ignorare, Gentes universas, in quibus vos estis, 1;6. & 9.24. avide expectare quando patefient filii Dei per praedicationem gloriae Evangelii, cum manifestabuntur fideles ex omni natione qui in Christum credunt, qui soli vocantur proprie filii Dei, in spe quod & ipsae liberabuntur ex servitute corruptionis, à mancipiis peccati & erroris in libertatem gloriae filiorum Dei, i. e. Evangelii, in quam vocati sunt fideles, ut sint ab errore immunes, nec amplius servi peccati; i. e. quod & ipsae sient participes ejusdem Evangelii cum sanctis. Subjectus enim factus est mundus vanitati, i e. corruptioni erroris & peccati, non per se volenter, sed per eum qui peccato suo subjecit eum, scilicet Adamum, vel per eum qui ex voluntate sua propter peccatum subjecit eum, nempe Deum. Scimus enim quòd πᾶσα κτίσις, totus mundus, cnixe enixè hac spe laborat etiam in dolore partus usquè ad τὸ νῦν, nunc præsens tempus Evangelii, (non dicit εἰς τὸ τέλος, ad finem mundi, ut interpretatur Scholiast. Græc.) ut participes etiam fiant ejusdem gloriæ cum filiis Dei. Quibus tamen id hactenus negatum est, etsi universa Philosophia videtur hoc mysterio quasi in partu laborâsse, de summo bono perpetuo litigans, nec tamen unquam attingens scopum. Gentes expectâsse revelationem Evangelii monuit Prophetia ab antiquo. Gen. 49. 10. Et ipse erit expectatio gentium, ut est in Veteri. Isa. 42. 4. Et legem ejus Insulæ expectabunt: & Hagg. 2. 7. ubi é hebraeo vocatur Desiderium Gentium. Evangelium vocatur ἡ δόξα τοῦ Θεοῦ, gloria Dei. 2 Cor. 4. 6. & ἡ δόξα τοῦ μυστηρίου ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, gloria mysterii inter gentes. Col. 1. 27. Φθορὰ est corruptio, quæ vitiat mores, ἀλλοίωσις δ' φθορᾶς est servitus corruptionis, quæ contracta & derivata est ab Adamo, servitus peccati, ut ἀλλὰς δ' φθορᾶς servos corruptionis. Apostolus intelligit iniustos, quos Deus servat in ultimum judicium. 2 Pet. 2. 19. Est etiam μεταισθησις apud Phavorinum φθορὰ, πεζὰ γὰρ ἀνόητον, ἡ βουλὴ ἀνυπόστατος, negotium insipiens, & consilium instabile, quale est servitus peccati, & cultus Idolorum, quibus subjectæ erant gentes.
units.tr: V. 19, etc.: "For the earnest expectation of the creation waits for the manifestation of the sons of God. For the creation was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now" [Ἡ γὰρ ἀποκαραδοκία τῆς κτίσεως τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν τῶν υἱῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἀπεκδέχεται, τῇ γὰρ ματαιότητι ἡ κτίσις ὑπετάγη οὐχ ἑκοῦσα, ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸν ὑποτάξαντα, ἐφ' ἑλπίδι ὅτι καὶ αὐτὴ ἡ κτίσις ἐλευθερωθήσεται ἀπὸ τῆς δουλείας τῆς φθορᾶς εἰς τὴν ἐλευθερίαν τῆς δόξης τῶν τέκνων τοῦ Θεοῦ. Οἴδαμεν γὰρ ὅτι πᾶσα ἡ κτίσις συνστενάζει καὶ συνωδίνει ἄχρι τοῦ νῦν]. The creation, that is, the world, eagerly awaits the revelation of the sons of God; for the world was made subject to vanity, not willingly but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the world itself will be freed from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole world groans together and is in travail until now. Most ancient and modern interpreters mostly understand this whole passage as a prosopopoeia, spoken of irrational creation, which will be freed into a state of incorruptibility on the last day. But I, with Augustine, think rather that by "creation" (κτίσις) man is meant, and that the sense is not that trees groan and suffer, as Cajetan, following that view, wants the word κτίσις here to signify τὴν κτῖσιν. For in the New Testament ὁ κόσμος, ἡ κτίσις, and τὰ ἔθνη are frequently the same. Also, the Gentiles are often called distinctly "the world," in opposition to the Church of God, which is said not to be of the world; the Apostle speaks of "the men of this world who are in unbelief and in sin," as Phavorinus has it. Irrational creation could indeed in some sense expect deliverance from the bondage of corruption, but in no sense, I think, could it expect deliverance into "the liberty of the glory of the children of God." The sense, therefore, is as if he had said: "I affirm that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." Let none of you object, as if this had nothing to do with us Romans, since the promises were made to the seed of Abraham. Indeed I tell you further, that the glory which is to come, whether eternal or evangelical, will be revealed in you too. For I would not have you ignorant that the Gentiles in whom you are (Rom. 1. 6; 9. 24) eagerly expect when the sons of God will be made manifest through the preaching of the glory of the Gospel, when the faithful of every nation who believe in Christ will be made manifest, those alone who are properly called the sons of God, in the hope that they too will be delivered from the bondage of corruption, from the slaves of sin and error, into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God, that is, of the Gospel, into which the faithful are called, so that they may be free from error and no longer slaves of sin; that is, that they too may become partakers of the same Gospel with the saints. For the world was made subject to vanity, that is, to the corruption of error and sin, not willingly on its own part, but by him who subjected it through its sin, namely Adam, or by him who of his own will subjected it on account of sin, namely God. For we know that the whole creation, the entire world, labours earnestly in this hope, even in the pain of childbirth, until now, that is, the present time of the Gospel (he does not say "until the end," as the Greek scholiast interprets it), so that they too may become partakers of the same glory with the sons of God. Yet this has so far been denied them, although all philosophy seems to have laboured in this mystery as if in childbirth, disputing about the highest good perpetually, yet never reaching its goal. The prophecy from of old warned that the Gentiles would expect the revelation of the Gospel: Gen. 49. 10, "And he shall be the expectation of the nations," as in the Old Testament; Isa. 42. 4, "And the isles shall wait for his law"; and Hagg. 2. 7, where from the Hebrew it is called "the Desire of the Gentiles." The Gospel is called "the glory of God" (2 Cor. 4. 6), and "the glory of the mystery among the Gentiles" (Col. 1. 27). Φθορά is corruption, which taints morals; the bondage of corruption (ἀλλοίωσις δ' φθορᾶς) is the slavery of sin, contracted and derived from Adam, as the slaves of corruption (ἀλλὰς δ' φθορᾶς) are. The Apostle means the unrighteous, whom God reserves for the final judgment (2 Pet. 2. 19). Phavorinus also gives φθορὰ as a change of mind: "foolish business" and "an unstable counsel," such as the servitude of sin and the worship of idols, to which the Gentiles were subjected.

units.la: C 9. v. 10, 11. Ἐπαγγελίας γὰρ ὁ λόγος οὗτος, κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοῦτον ἐλεύσομαι, καὶ ἔσται τῇ Σάρρᾳ υἱὸς, οὐ μόνον δὲ, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ῥεβέκκα ἐξ ἑνὸς κοίτην ἔχουσα Ἰσαάκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν· μήπω γὰρ γεννηθέντων &c. ἐξ ἔργων αὐτῆς &c. Ante participium ἔχουσα subaudiendum verbum sui, quod unaquaque fere occurrit pagina. Promissionis enim verbum hoc est, secundum tempus hoc veniam, & erit Sarae filius, non solum vero, sed & Rebecca ex uno sive altero altero concubitum habuit Isaac patris nostri: di-cuum enim est ei nondum natis &c, major serviet minori. Ecce alterum promissionis verbum, adeo ut ἐξ ἑτέρας intelligendum sit, ex altero promissionis verbo. Concubitum habuit, est mos loquendi in Veteri, apud Graecos Interpretes familiaris, tantum est ac si diceres, concepit sive facta est gravida. Num. 5. 20. Vir dicitur κοιτὴν δώσει ἐν γυναικί, concubitum dare in mulierem; recte ergo pari ratione in hoc loco dicitur, Ῥεβέκκα κοιτὴν τοῦ ἔχειν ἐκ τοῦ Ἰσαάκ, Rebecca retinuit semen, sive concubitum patris nostri Isaac; i. e. ex eo concepit sive facta est gravida. Videre est eandem phrasin in Lev. 18. 23. & alibi. Ita ut non omnino fit necesse pronunciare cum Beza, Est itaque depravatus hic locus à quopiam Graecae linguae prorsus ignaro, cùm ita familiaris conciliatio sit ad manum. Ut verbo dicam quod res est, nimis multa imputantur sacris scriptoribus & Apographis eorum sphalmata, cùm inadvertentia vel incuria interpretum sit in vitio. Κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ζωῆς, verba sunt LXX, quos secutus Paulus. Atque illi certè legerunt פּ pro פּ; ideóque verterunt τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ζωῆς, pro τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ζωῆς, secundum tempus vitae, quam lectionem veriorem esse & ratio suadet, & codicis Hebraei autoritas. Gen. 18. 10. & 14. ἑτέρῳ in sensu nostro est abundè frequens, LXX usurpant pro אחר altero. Gen. 43. 13. Psal. 108. 14. Reperire est etiam in eodem sensu, 1 Cor. 4. 6. & apud Authores Ethnicos, ut docet Stephanus.
units.tr: Chap. 9, vv. 10, 11. "For this is the word of promise: At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son; and not only so, but Rebecca also, having conceived by one, even by Isaac our father" [Ἐπαγγελίας γὰρ ὁ λόγος οὗτος, κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοῦτον ἐλεύσομαι, καὶ ἔσται τῇ Σάρρᾳ υἱὸς· οὐ μόνον δέ, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ῥεβέκκα ἐξ ἑνὸς κοίτην ἔχουσα Ἰσαὰκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν]; "for when they were not yet born, etc.... of works, etc." Before the participle ἔχουσα the verb "was" must be understood, as it is on almost every page. For the word of promise is this: "At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son"; not only that, but Rebecca also conceived by one, that is, by the other word of promise, from Isaac our father, for it was said to her, "The elder shall serve the younger" [Gen. 25.23], while the children were not yet born. Here is the second word of promise, so that ἐξ ἑτέρας must be understood as "by another word of promise." The phrase "had concubitum" is a manner of speaking common in the Old Testament and familiar among the Greek interpreters; it means no more than "conceived" or "became pregnant." Num. 5. 20. says of a husband that he will "give concubitum in a woman" [κοιτὴν δώσει ἐν γυναικί]; so in the same way in this place it is said that Rebecca "had concubitum from Isaac" [Ῥεβέκκα κοίτην ἔχουσα ἐκ τοῦ Ἰσαάκ], that is, she retained the seed, or "had the concubitum of our father Isaac," i.e., she conceived from him, or became pregnant. The same idiom can be seen in Lev. 18. 23. and elsewhere. So there is no need to say with Beza, "This place has therefore been corrupted by someone entirely ignorant of the Greek language," when so familiar a reading lies to hand. To put it plainly, far too much is charged to the sacred writers and their copyists as errors, when the fault lies with the carelessness or negligence of the translators. Κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ζωῆς ["according to the time of life"] are the words of the LXX, whom Paul followed. And they certainly read one letter for another in the Hebrew, and so rendered it as τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ζωῆς, "according to the time of life," for the reading which is truer, reason and the authority of the Hebrew manuscript both suggest. In Gen. 18. 10. and 14., ἑτέρῳ in our sense is quite frequent; the LXX use it for the Hebrew אחר, "other." Gen. 43. 13. and Ps. 108. 14. It can also be found in the same sense in 1 Cor. 4. 6., and among the Gentile authors, as Stephanus shows.

units.la: V. 22. Εἰ δὲ Σιλὰν ὁ Θεὸς &c. Nil opus est Anantapodoto vel supplemento; loci cohaerentia per se plana est & expedita, incipiendo sensum à versu 20. Μεγάλη ὁ ἄνθρωπε, &c. &c. Atqui O homo, tu quis es qui contra respondeas Deo, si Deus volens ostendere iram, & notam facere potentiam suam, sustinuit in mul-tâ patientiâ vasa irae? verbis intermediis, μὴ ἐρεῖ τὸ πλάσμα; num dicet figmentum, &c? usque ad, εἰ δὲ θέλων, si Deus volens, parenthesi includendis. Conjunctio δὲ vel παρέλκει vel est expletiva.
units.tr: V. 22. "But if God..." [Εἰ δὲ Σιλὰν ὁ Θεὸς]. There is no need for anacoluthon or supplement; the connection of the passage is plain and clear in itself, if the sense is taken up from verse 20: "But O man, who are you to answer back against God? If God, willing to show wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath?" The intervening words, "Will the thing formed say [μὴ ἐρεῖ τὸ πλάσμα]? Will it say, etc.," up to "if God, willing [εἰ δὲ θέλων]," should be enclosed in parentheses. The conjunction δὲ is either superfluous or merely expletive.

units.la: V. 24. Οὺς κὴ ἐκάλεσεν, ἡμᾶς ἃ μόνον ἐξ Ἰουδαίων, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐξ ἐθνῶν. Vulgaris est trajectio, pro ἃ μόνον ἡμᾶς ἐξ Ἰουδαίων, i. e. Variato vulgari commate, ut supra. Quos etiam vocavit, non solum nos ex Iudeis, sed etiam eos qui sunt ex gentibus. Subintelli-gendo, τὰς. i. e. Non solum nos Iudaeos, sed etiam Gentes.
units.tr: V. 24. "Whom he has called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles" [Οὓς καὶ ἐκάλεσεν, ἡμᾶς οὐ μόνον ἐξ Ἰουδαίων, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐξ ἐθνῶν]. This is the common transposition for οὐ μόνον ἡμᾶς ἐξ Ἰουδαίων, that is, with the usual punctuation changed, as above: "Whom also he called, not only us from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles." Supplying τὰς ("those"), the meaning is: not only us Jews, but also the Gentiles.

units.la: C. 10. v. 5. Μωϋσῆς γὰρ γράφει τὴν δικαιοσύ-νὴν τὴν ἐκ τοῦ νόμου, ὅτι &c. Formula est loquendi omnino eadem cum ea quae praecessit. 4. 6. adeò ut hic etiam subaudiendum χρ. Moses enim scribit de justitia quae est ex lege, quòd qui ea fecerit per ea vivet. Quale est etiam, ὃν ἐγεγράφε Μωσῆς, de quo scripsit Moses: ut Syrus & Beza, subaudiendo κατὰ. Joh. 1. 45.
units.tr: C. 10. v. 5. "For Moses writes of the righteousness which is of the law, that..." [Μωϋσῆς γὰρ γράφει τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ τοῦ νόμου, ὅτι]. The formula of speech is entirely the same as the one that went before, at 4. 6., so that here too something must be understood, as the same abbreviation indicates. "For Moses writes of the righteousness which is of the law, that the man who does those things shall live by them." The same is true of ὃν ἐγεγράφει Μωϋσῆς, "of whom Moses wrote," as the Syriac and Beza render it, understanding κατὰ ("concerning"). John 1. 45.

units.la: C. 11. v. 2. Ὡς ἐντυγχάνει τῷ Θεῷ χρ τῷ Ἰσραὴλ. Quomodò conqueritur Deo contra Is-raelem. In quo sensu vox ἐντυγχάνει occurrit, 1 Mac. 8. 3. 10. 63. & 11. 25. Est enim ἐντυγχάνει προσέρχεται. Hesych. & peculiariter προσ-έρχεσθαι dicuntur qui supplices accedunt. Steph. Accedere verò licet Deo utrovis modo vel per intercessionem vel per querelam. Non verò idonè vertit Anglicus, How he maketh intercession to God against Israel, Intercedimus enim pro vel propter, sed non contra aliquem.
units.tr: C. 11. v. 2. "How he pleads with God against Israel" [Ὡς ἐντυγχάνει τῷ Θεῷ κατὰ τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ]. The word ἐντυγχάνει occurs in this sense at 1 Macc. 8. 3., 10. 63., and 11. 25., for it means "approaches" [προσέρχεται], as Hesychius explains, and those who approach as suppliants are said particularly to προσέρχεσθαι, as Stephanus notes. One may approach God in either way, whether by intercession or by complaint. The English version does not translate it properly: "How he maketh intercession to God against Israel." For we intercede for or on behalf of someone, but not against him.

units.la: C. 11. v. 21. Ei γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς τῶν κατὰ φύσιν κλά-δων οὐκ ἐφείσατο, μήπως οὐδὲ σοῦ φείσεται. Quid opus est supplemento? ὀρθῶς dicitur pro more loquendi אם LXX in Vetere. Cujus etiam videre est exemplum
units.tr: C. 11. v. 21. "For if God did not spare the natural branches [Εἰ γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς τῶν κατὰ φύσιν κλάδων οὐκ ἐφείσατο], lest perhaps he will not spare you either [μήπως οὐδὲ σοῦ φείσεται]." What need is there of a supplement? ὀρθῶς ("rightly") is used in place of the Hebrew idiom אם, as the LXX do in the Old Testament, of which an example may be seen

units.la: 2 Tim. 2. 25. exponendo μήπως ut μήποτε, forte. Si enim Deus naturalibus ramis non pepercit, forte neque tibi parcet.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 2. 25., where μήπως is explained as μήποτε, "perhaps": "For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps neither will he spare you."

units.la: C. 12. v. 19. Ἀλλὰ δότε τόπον τῇ ὀργῇ, μὴ ἑαυτοὺς ἐκδικοῦντες, ut immediate praecedit. Nolite vosmet ipsos ulcisci, sed date locum ultioni, i.e. Ministro Dei, qui est ἔκδικος εἰς ὀργὴν, vindex ad ultionem ejus qui malum fecerit. 13. 4. Scriptum est enim ut proximè sequitur, ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις, ἐγὼ ἀνταποδώσω, λέγει Κύριος, Mihi vindicta, ego rependam, dicit Dominus. Sic etiam 3. 5. ὁ ἀποφέρων τλὼ ὀργὴν, Anglicus vertit, who taketh vengeance, qui infert vindictam; ut docemur etiam Eph. 4. 26. nullo modo dare locum τῷ διαβόλῳ, Diabolo, nempe iracundiæ, ut patet ex contextu. Sic Plutarch. περὶ ἀοργησίας. Δεῖ ἢ μήτε παίζοντας τῇ ὀργῇ δίδωμι τόπον. Non decet vel ludentes dare locum iracundiæ.
units.tr: C. 12. v. 19. "But give place to wrath [Ἀλλὰ δότε τόπον τῇ ὀργῇ], not avenging yourselves," as immediately precedes. "Do not avenge yourselves, but give place to wrath, that is, to God's minister, who is the avenger [ἔκδικος εἰς ὀργήν] for the wrath of him who does evil" (Rom. 13. 4.). For it is written, as immediately follows: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord" [ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις, ἐγὼ ἀνταποδώσω, λέγει Κύριος]. So too in 3. 5. the one who "brings wrath" [ὁ ἐπιφέρων τὴν ὀργήν] is rendered by the English, "who taketh vengeance," that is, "who brings vengeance"; as we are taught also at Eph. 4. 26., that we must in no way give place to the devil [τῷ διαβόλῳ], namely to anger, as is clear from the context. So Plutarch, in his work on freedom from anger: "It is not fitting [δεῖ] even when joking to give place to anger." That is, "It is not right even for those who are playing to give place to anger."

units.la: C. 14. v. 1. Μὴ εἰς διαχρίσεις διαλογισμῶν. Infirmum fide assumite non ad dijudicationes cogitationum: i. e. non ut dijudicetis vel discriminetis interiores cogitationes, si quid aliter ex infirmitate fidei sentiat ac vos ipsi sentitis. Temerarias censuras prohibet Apostolus, ut Hieronymus: Quod sequentia abundè indicant. Nec verò significans vel omninò apposita est interpretatio eorum, quæ vertit vel ad dubias disputationes, vel ad certamina disputationum. Præterquam etiam quòd διαλογισμὸς in N. & V. T. plerumque accipitur pro cogitatione hominis secum ratiocinantis, ut recte observavit Stephanus.
units.tr: C. 14. v. 1. "Receive the weak in faith, not to disputes over thoughts" [Τὸν δὲ ἀσθενοῦντα τῇ πίστει προσλαμβάνεσθε, μὴ εἰς διακρίσεις διαλογισμῶν]. That is, do not so judge or discriminate the inward thoughts of another, if he feels differently from you out of weakness of faith. The apostle forbids rash censures, as Jerome says, and the following words sufficiently show this. Nor is the rendering "to doubtful disputations" or "to contests of disputes" either meaningful or at all appropriate, apart from the fact that διαλογισμός in the New and Old Testaments is mostly taken to mean the thought of a man reasoning with himself, as Stephanus rightly observed.

units.la: C. 16. v. 25. Τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ &c. Cur hæc Doxologia hodie attexatur ad calcem hujus capitis, non possum non mirari, cum fere apud omnes ex confesso sit, hos versus in omnibus antiquis exemplaribus, ut etiam remanent apud Graecos Patres, scriptos reperiri in fine capitis decimi quarti, excepto codice Alexandrino, qui ex abundanti forte cautela legit in utroque loco. Quantum vero de hac re liceat conjicere, mihi ita se habere videtur. Vulgaris erat opinio apud Veteres, quae ab Hieronymi verbis in hunc locum est & in posteros derivata, Marcionem haereticum capita 15. & 16. tota diffecuisse, quoniam contra sententiam ejus adeo faciebant, & deinde appositae, ut celaret fraudem, hanc doxologiam ad finem capitis 14, post verba illa, Omne quod non est ex fide est peccatum, eo nomine quod ibi Epistolam finiri voluerit. At hoc ab eo factum ego quidem valde dubito, licet non negarim quin id totum tentaret dissecare. Orthodoxos vero eorumque posteros hac opinione ductos, ut ex suo zelo Marcioni occurrerent, consulto potius credo hanc doxologiam ab eo loco, ubi non erat affixa fraude Marcionis, sed ab ipso Apostolo, removisse ad finem capitis 16. ut ita includerent omne quod Marcion voluit expungi, e suo loco aio ea causa removisse; non enim conjicere est quo alio fine id factum fuerit. Licet tamen doxologiae, quod non animadverterunt quicunque id fecerint, in fine epistolarum Pauli non sunt omnino usitatae. Cui semper solenne fuit in fine Epistolae alia salutatione uti. Quod est signum in omni Epistola, ita scribo, Gratia Domini &c. 2 Thes. 17. 18. Ideoque miror magis cur id factum fuerit, vel cur hodie factum remanet; facimus enim Apostolum sibi ipsi contradicere. Neque vero est fini capitis 16 omnino apposita, nullam enim habet cum contextu cohærentiam, cùm interim aptissimè connectatur ad calcem capitis 14, ubi cùm de periculo dubitantis animi jam fere toto capite disceptaverat, perappositè succedit hæc doxologia, Τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ &c. At gloria Deo qui potis est stabilire vos secundum vel per Evangelium meum &c. Ut enim Chrysostomus, & alii interpretes Graeci animadverterunt in hunc locum, ἐν τῷ Παύλῳ εἰς ἐυχὰς χ̀ ἀξολογίας καταλλείειν τὸν ἀθρωπον: Mos erat Paulo cum voto & doxologia concludere exhortationem. Cùm ergo celsaverit causa, vel certè notitia ejus, ob quam hi versus pio fortasse zelo in initio rejecti fuerint ad finem capitis 16, ut omne quod Marcion dissecari voluit reincluderent, non piaculum imò non ingratum animo meo hodie fecerit, quisquis eos in suum locum remiserit ad calcem capitis 14, post verba illa, πᾶν δὲ ὃ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως ἁμαρτία ἐστίν.
units.tr: C. 16. v. 25. "Now to him who is able [Τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ]..." I cannot but wonder why this doxology is today appended at the end of this chapter, since it is almost universally agreed that these verses are found in all the ancient copies, as they also remain among the Greek Fathers, written at the end of chapter fourteen, except in the Alexandrian codex, which perhaps from excessive caution reads them in both places. As far as one may conjecture about this matter, it seems to me to have been as follows. It was the common opinion among the Ancients, derived from the words of Jerome on this passage, that Marcion the heretic had cut off chapters 15 and 16 entirely, because they were so much against his opinion; and that then, to conceal the fraud, he had put this doxology at the end of chapter 14, after those words, "Whatever is not of faith is sin," on the ground that he wished the Epistle to end there. But that Marcion did this I greatly doubt, although I would not deny that he tried to cut away all of it. The orthodox, and their successors led by this opinion, so as to counter Marcion with their own zeal, I believe deliberately removed this doxology from the place where it was not attached by Marcion's fraud, but by the Apostle himself, to the end of chapter 16, so that they might thus include everything that Marcion wished to be expunged. I say they removed it from its place for that reason, for it is not possible to conjecture for what other purpose it was done. Yet doxologies, which those who did this did not notice, are by no means customary at the end of Paul's epistles. He always had the custom of using another form of greeting at the end of an Epistle. This is the sign in every letter: "So I write: The grace of the Lord..." (2 Thess. 3. 17, 18.). So I wonder all the more why this was done, or why it remains done today, for we make the Apostle contradict himself. Nor is the doxology in fact suitable at the end of chapter 16, for it has no coherence with the context, whereas it connects very aptly at the end of chapter 14, where, having nearly finished the whole chapter on the danger of a doubting mind, the doxology follows most fittingly: "Now to him who is able [Τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ] to establish you according to my gospel..." For, as Chrysostom and other Greek interpreters have noted on this passage, "It was Paul's custom to conclude an exhortation with prayer and doxology" [ἐν τῷ Παύλῳ εἰς εὐχὰς καὶ ἀξιολογίας καταλήγειν τὸν λόγον]. Since, then, the reason for which these verses were perhaps rejected in the beginning, out of pious zeal, to the end of chapter 16, so that they might reinclude everything Marcion wished to cut away, has been hidden, I think it is no wrong, indeed no unwelcome thing to my mind, that whoever has sent them back to their proper place at the end of chapter 14, after the words "whatever is not of faith is sin" [πᾶν δὲ ὃ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως ἁμαρτία ἐστίν], has done so.

units.la: In primam Epistolam ad Corinthios.
units.tr: In primam Epistolam ad Corinthios.

units.la: 1 COR. c. 2. v. 2. Οὐ γὰρ ἔκρινά τι εἰδέναι ἐν ὑμῖν, εἰ μὴ Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν &c. Non enim decrevi vel necessarium duxi, eos qui in vobis vel inter vos sunt, i.e. vos aliquid scire nisi Jesum Christum eumque crucifixum. Το ἐν ὑμῖν diction em esse reor Elleipdicam, ἀντὶ τῆς τὴς ἐν ὑμῶν. Qualis est illa in Z. V. ויהרנ במשמניה, ἀπίκτειναν ἐν τοῖς πίο-σιν αὐτῶν, Ꝝ occidit in pinguibus, i. e. ut Lat. pingues eorum, Psal. 78. 31. ἐν τοῖς πίοσιν, posito pro τὰς πίονας αὐτῶν, במשמניה pro משמניה, the fattest of them, ut est in Anglico, Et illa etiam in Hebræo solo, ראו בנוים, videte inter gentes vel in gentibus, i.e. Videte O gentes, vel vos qui estis inter gentes, ut plerumque exponitur Habak. 1. 5. Similis occurrit etiam in Novo. Joh. 16. 17. εἶπον οὖν ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν, dixerunt ergo ex discipulis, i. e. discipuli, ut Vetus. Et Luc. 21. 16. καὶ θανατώσουσιν ἐξ ὑμῶν, Ꝝ morte afficient ex vobis, ut Interlincaris, i. e. ut alii, trucidabunt vos. Neque opinor voluit Apostolus intelligi quid sibi, sed quid Corinthiis necessarium foret scire, ideòque se venisse ait non in sublimitate sermonis vel sapientiæ &c. Nihil enim voluit eos scire, nisi Jesum Christum eúmque crucifixum.
units.tr: 1 COR. ch. 2, v. 2. "For I determined not to know anything among you, save Jesus Christ, etc." [Οὐ γὰρ ἔκρινά τι εἰδέναι ἐν ὑμῖν, εἰ μὴ Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν &c.] For I did not decide, or did not think it necessary, that those who are among you or in your midst should know anything except Jesus Christ and him crucified. I think that ἐν ὑμῖν is an elliptical expression for τῆς ἐν ὑμῖν, as in that phrase in Z. V. [ויהרנ במשמניה], and he slew in their fat [ἀπίκτειναν ἐν τοῖς πίοσιν αὐτῶν], meaning he struck down in the fat ones, that is, as the Latin has it, pingues eorum, Psal. 78. 31. The ἐν τοῖς πίοσιν stands for τὰς πίονας αὐτῶν, and [במשמניה] stands for [משמניה], the fattest of them, as it is in English. There is also a similar construction in the Hebrew alone, [ראו בנוים], videte inter gentes or in gentibus, that is, Look, O nations, or you who are among the nations, as it is commonly explained at Habak. 1. 5. A similar usage also occurs in the New Testament, John 16. 17.: εἶπον οὖν ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν, so some of the disciples said, that is, the disciples, as the Old Latin has it. And Luke 21. 16.: καὶ θανατώσουσιν ἐξ ὑμῶν, they will put some of you to death, as the Interlinear has it, that is, they will slay you, some of you. I do not think the Apostle wished to be understood as to what he himself knew, but as to what it was necessary for the Corinthians to know; and therefore he says that he came not in excellence of speech or of wisdom, etc. For he wished them to know nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified.

units.la: V. 6. Σοφίαν δὲ λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις: Sapientiam loquimur in sacris. Non de personis, quos sequenti capite infantes in Christo vocat, adeò procul à perfectione aberant, sed de rebus loquitur per totum caput. Phrasis est hujus loci peculiaris. Sermo noster, &c. non est ἐν πειθοῖς, in suasoriis humanæ sapientiæ, sed ἐν ἀπολείξει, in demonstratione Spiritūs, ἐν μυστηρίῳ in mysterio, ἐν διδακτοῖς &c. in iis quæ edocti sumus à Spiritu sancto, quæ oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit, σοφίαν λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις, Sapientiam loquimur in sacris: τέλεια, ἱερά. Hesych. τέλεια, ἱερά dicebant eximia vel sanctiora. Bud. Com. Ling. Gr.
units.tr: V. 6. "But we speak wisdom among the perfect" [Σοφίαν δὲ λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις]: we speak wisdom among the mature. He is not speaking of persons whom in the following chapter he calls babes in Christ, for they were far from perfection; he is speaking of things throughout the whole chapter. The phrase in this place is peculiar. Our word, etc., is not in persuasive words [ἐν πειθοῖς] of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit [ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος], in mystery [ἐν μυστηρίῳ], in teachings [ἐν διδακτοῖς], etc., in those things which we have been taught by the Holy Spirit, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man. So σοφίαν λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις, we speak wisdom among the perfect, that is, among the sacred: τέλεια, ἱερά. Hesychius: τέλεια, ἱερά, they used to call the excellent or more sacred things [τέλεια] . Budaeus, Commentaries on the Greek Language.

units.la: C. 3, v. 12, 13. &c. Εἰ δέ τις ἐποικοδομεῖ &c. Sensus hujus loci est hujusmodi; Quod si quis minister
units.tr: C. 3, v. 12, 13, etc. "But if anyone builds upon this foundation" [Εἰ δέ τις ἐποικοδομεῖ &c.]. The sense of this passage is as follows: If any minister

units.la: Bud. Com. Ling. Gr. minister Evangelii superaedificaverit super hoc fundamentum. i. e. Iesum Christum, aurum, argentum, vel lapides pretiosos, doctrinam nempe de fide puram, solidam, & stabilem, sive foenum, ligna, vel stipulam, i e. doctrinam levem, caducam, & momentaneam, qualiscunque ea fuerit, dies manifestabit, cum ignis probationis venerit, quale sit cuiuscunque opus, τὸ πῦρ δοκιμάσει ignis. i e persecutio probabit. In eo die qui aedificati sunt in pura, solida, & stabili doctrina, manebunt firmi; atque inde Minister mercedem accipiet, perseverantiam nempe eorum quos in fide stabilivit. Qui vero tincti sunt principiis laxis, & minus firmiter radicati, cum supervenerit probatio persecutionis, deficient animis, & desciscent a fide, atque ita Minister perdet operam suam, αὐτὸς ζημιοῦται, ὅτι ᾧ οἷς διὰ πυρὸς, ipse vero servabitur, ita vero ut ipse per ignem evadat. i.e. si in igne persecutionis firmus ipse manserit. Τὸ πῦρ & πύρωσις passim in Scriptura significant probationem afflictionum & persecutionis. Quid vero velit μισθὸν λήψεται, mercedem accipiet, & ζημιοῦσθαι, operam perdet, clare indicant Iohannes, Ep. 2. ubi cum prius monuisset Electam Dominam & liberos eius multos impostores ingressos esse in mundum, Attendite vos ipsos addit, ne perdamus quae operati sumus, sed ut μισθὸν πλήρη ἀπολάβωμεν, mercedem plenam accipiamus. Et Paulus, ubi in Epistola ad Philippenses, 2. 16. hortatur eos λόγον ζωῆς ἐπέχειν, verbum vitae firmiter tenere, ut gloriari possit in die Christi, se non frustra cucurrisse, nec in vanum laborasse, i.e. operam perdidisse. En mercedem Pauli, ut gloriari possit propter eorum perseverantiam in die Christi.
units.tr: Budaeus, Commentaries on the Greek Language. minister of the Gospel builds upon this foundation, that is, Jesus Christ, with gold, silver, or precious stones, that is, pure, solid and stable doctrine concerning faith; or with hay, wood, or stubble, that is, light, perishable and momentary doctrine, whatever it may be, the day will declare it, when the fire of trial comes, of what sort each man's work is [τὸ πῦρ δοκιμάσει], the fire, that is, persecution will test it. On that day those who have been built up in pure, solid and stable doctrine will remain firm; and then the minister will receive a reward, namely, the perseverance of those whom he has established in the faith. But those who have been imbued with loose principles and less firmly rooted, when the test of persecution comes upon them, will lose heart and fall away from the faith, and so the minister will lose his labour [ζημιωθήσεται], but he himself will be saved, yet so as to pass through the fire, that is, if he himself remains firm in the fire of persecution. Fire and burning [τὸ πῦρ, πύρωσις] everywhere in Scripture signify the testing of afflictions and persecution. What is meant by he will receive a reward [μισθὸν λήψεται] and he will suffer loss of his labour [ζημιοῦσθαι] is clearly shown by John, 2 Ep., where, having first warned that the elect lady and her children many deceivers have entered into the world, he adds, Take heed to yourselves, that we lose not what we have wrought, but that we may receive a full reward [μισθὸν πλήρη ἀπολάβωμεν]. And Paul, in his Epistle to the Philippians, 2. 16., exhorts them to hold fast the word of life [λόγον ζωῆς ἐπέχειν], so that he may glory in the day of Christ that he has not run in vain nor laboured in vain, that is, has not lost his labour. Behold Paul's reward: that he may glory on account of their perseverance in the day of Christ.
Chapter 5, verses 12, 13.

units.la: Τί γὰρ μοι ἐσὶ τοὺς ἔξω κρίνειν; τὴν ἑαυτῶν ὑμεῖς κείνετε, τὸς δὲ ἔξω ὁ Θεὸς κείνει, κ᾿ ἐξαρεῖτε τὸ πονηρὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν. Nè quis miretur lectionem, sciat, puncto aliquos distinxisse post κ᾿, ante Theophylacti tempora, ut ipse monet, & κείνει pro κείνει, & τὸ πονηρὸν pro ἡ πονηρὸν, legisse Theodoretum, ut etiam legit Graeca Editio Aldi impressa cura Asulani. Venet. 1518. Quod opinor multo magis convenit scopo loci quàm hodierna lectio. Quid enim mihi eos etiam qui foris sunt judicare? Non omnino. Eos qui intus sunt judicate vos; eos vero qui extra sunt judicabit vel judicet Deus, & tolletis malum è vobis ipsis. Quasi diceret; Nil nostrâ interesse judicare eos qui extra Ecclesiam sunt, judicate verò vos eos qui intrà sunt, & sic demum auferetis malum è vobis, i. e. vos ipsi insontes eritis mali. Eos verò qui extra Ecclesiam sunt, æquum est relinquere judicio Dei. Atque ista certè lectio in neutro genere optime congruit cum usu ejusdem dictionis in Vetere, unde eam mutuarum esse Apostolum, non est quod quis dubitet. Sic sensit Chrysostomus, ἀμνημόνευσε τ' ῥήσεως ἐν τῇ παλαιᾷ, Meminit dictionis in Vetere, Sic Theodoretus, Μωσαϊκῷ τύπῳ μαρτυρίαν, Mosaicum opposuit testimonium. Verum phrasim istam nullam aliam ferre lectionem in Vetere vel sensum, quàm in neutro genere, manifestum erit cuivis qui examinaverit locorum circumstantias ferè ubicunque occurrit. Pro exemplo, ubi de puellâ agitur, in qua non inventa fuit virginitas. Deut. 22,21. Ipsa lapidibus obruetur, & morietur, κ᾿ ἐξαρεῖς τὸ πονηρὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν, & auferes malum è medio tui, ut Vetus. In quo loco malum significat reatum, ut Deut. 21. 9. Et qui nuperrimus est in Grammatica novissimus agnoscet solæcismum in Editione Romana, quæ in hoc loco legit τ πνεῦμα, ut etiam v. 22. & 24. ejusdem capitis, in quibus utrisque locis lectio est æquè incongrua, licèt prudenter ab emendatione cautum est in Bibliis nostris Polyglottis, ne ansam cavillandi Romani inde arriperent. ὑγὶ, ὑδαμῶς nequaquam vel non omnino. Hesych. & Phavor.
units.tr: "For what have I to do with judging those outside? Do not you judge those within; but those outside God judges, and you shall take away the evil from among yourselves" [Τί γὰρ μοι ἐστὶ τοὺς ἔξω κρίνειν; τοὺς ἔσω ὑμεῖς κρίνετε, τοὺς δὲ ἔξω ὁ Θεὸς κρίνει, καὶ ἐξαρεῖτε τὸ πονηρὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν.] Lest anyone be surprised at the reading, let him know that some, before the time of Theophylact, as he himself observes, placed a point after καί, and read κρίνει for κρίνει and τὸ πονηρὸν for ὁ πονηρός, as Theodoret read, as also the Greek edition of Aldus, printed under the care of Asulanus, Venice, 1518. This, I think, fits the purpose of the passage much better than the present reading. For what have I to do with judging even those who are outside? Not at all. Do you judge those who are inside; but God will judge, or let God judge, those who are outside; and you will remove the evil from yourselves. As if he were saying: it is no concern of ours to judge those outside the Church; but do you judge those who are within, and so at last you will take away the evil from yourselves, that is, you yourselves will be free of evil. Those outside the Church, however, it is right to leave to the judgement of God. And this reading in the neuter gender certainly agrees very well with the usage of the same expression in the Old Testament, from which there is no reason to doubt that the Apostle borrowed it. So Chrysostom understood it: ἀμνημόνευσε τῆς ῥήσεως ἐν τῇ παλαιᾷ, he recalled the expression in the Old; so Theodoret: Μωσαϊκῷ τύπῳ μαρτυρίαν, he set against it the testimony of the Mosaic type. But that this phrase admits no other reading or sense in the Old Testament than the neuter gender will be plain to anyone who examines the circumstances of the passages where it nearly always occurs. For example, where it concerns a girl in whom virginity was not found, Deut. 22. 21.: She shall be stoned with stones and die, καὶ ἐξαρεῖς τὸ πονηρὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν, and you shall remove the evil from the midst of you, as the Old Latin has it. In that place evil means guilt, as at Deut. 21. 9. And whoever is the most recent and newest expert in Grammar will recognise a solecism in the Roman Edition, which in this place reads τὸ πνεῦμα, as also in vv. 22 and 24 of the same chapter, in both of which places the reading is equally incongruous; although our Polyglot Bibles have prudently refrained from correcting it, lest the Romanists should seize on it as an occasion for mockery. ὑγί, ὑδαμῶς: in no way, or not at all. Hesychius and Phavorinus.

units.la: C 6. v. 1. Πεῷγμα ἔχων, negotium habens, i e. item, in quo sensu τὸ πεῷγμα passim accipitur apud Græcos, sicut & negotium apud Latinos.
units.tr: C. 6, v. 1. Having a matter [Πρᾶγμα ἔχων], having business, that is, a case, in which sense τὸ πρᾶγμα is commonly used among the Greeks, just as negotium is among the Latins.

units.la: V. 2. ᾿Αξιοι ἐστε κεριτηλίων ἐλαχίστων; Indigni estis ut de minimis judicetis? ut Vetus. Indigni estis minimis judiciis? ut Beza. Sed neque id satis plane; non enim intendit actum judicii, sed locum. κριτήριον enim apud Authores nusquam significat judicium, i. e judicandi Actum, sed sedem ubi judicium agitur. Atque idem est eum voce δικαστήριον, in quo sensu usurpatur Jud. 5. 9. Dan. 7. 10. Susan. 49. Jac. 2. 6. Expressius ergo ad vim vocis redditur, Indigni estis minimis subselliis? Subsellia enim dicuntur in quibus minutiora judicia exercentur, secundum Asco- pium.
units.tr: V. 2. "Are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters?" [Ἄξιοί ἐστε κριτηρίων ἐλαχίστων;] Are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? as the Old Latin has it; Are you unworthy of the smallest judgements? as Beza has it. But this is not quite exact either; for he is not referring to the act of judging but to the place. κριτήριον in the authors never means judgement, that is, the act of judging, but the seat where judgement is held. And the same is true of the word δικαστήριον, in which sense it is used at Jude 9, Dan. 7. 10, Susanna 49, James 2. 6. A more precise rendering that matches the force of the word would therefore be: Are you unworthy of the smallest courts? For subsellia [benches] is the name given to the places where the lesser judgements are conducted, according to Asconius.

units.la: V. 4. Βιωτικὰ μὲν ἔν κεῤῥινεῖα &c. Vulgaris [Seculária igitur judicia si habeatis, contemptibiles qui sunt in Ecclesia illos constituite] est neque mori loquendi apud Græcos, neque sensui, nec syntaxi accommoda. In hac enim versione opinor Interpretes judicia intelligere lites de rebus hujus vitæ: at κεῤῥinεον, ut modo dixi, nusquam apud Authores in isto sensu reperitur. Quod si dicant velle eos tribunalia, plane aiunt quod Apostolus diserte negat, increpans eo nomine quòd non haberent, sed potiùs vellent judicari coram infidelibus. Ipsa etiam illatio non est adeo adeò sensui conformis, quin satis causæ sit ἐπιχεὶν, & melius inquirendi in hanc versionem. Quæ facillimè restituitur in commodiorem sensum & syntaxin, idque sine vi vel solœcismo, variatis tantum punctis per Hyperbaton. Βαπτὰ μὴ ἐν κειτήεια, ἐὰν ἔχετε τὸς ἐξουδενωμένος ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τούτους, καθίζετε. Secularia igitur subsellia, si habeatis hos contemptibiles in Ecclesia, constituite. Hyperbata ejusmodi sunt in N.T. frequentissima, ut alibi sæpius memoravimus. Perinde est ac si diceret: Quid? num judicio vultis experiri apud infideles, quos contemptibiles habetis in Ecclesia? num iniquos & impios sinetis judicare inter vos, quos vos ipsi olim judicabitis? An ignoratis fore ut Angelos judicetis? & non secularia judicabimus? constituite ergo inter vos ipsos judices, constituite vobis tribunalia, ad pudorem vestrum dico. Itane, non est inter vos sapiens? ne unus qui possit judicare inter fratres? Procul absit ab Apostolo, ut jubeat constituere homines contemptibiles in loco judicii, nihil minus; imo exprobrat, quod adeo indigne de seipsis æstimârint, ut provocarent ad judicia infidelium, quasi non esset ne unus quidem sapiens inter ipsos, certè eo ipso nomine satis innuens, sapientem esse oportere, & non contemptibilem quemvis, qui constitueretur judex in Ecclesiâ. Durissima est etiâ phrasis illa, τὸς τούτους καθίζετε, neque Hebraismo salvari credo; quòd si verus esset Hebraismus, legi oportuit, τὸς ἐξουδενωμένος ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ αὐτὸς καθίζετε, & non τούτους. Quoad phrasim, καθίζειν κειτήειον, eadem est ac τὸ καθίζειν ἀτιμασμένον in Aristophane & Libanio. Sed altius radices egit inveterata opinio, quàm ut amoveatur nisi authoritate aliquâ magisteriali, vel invaluit supina incuria. Atque hoc factum etiam prophanis scriptoribus commune. Quomodo enim aliter fieri potuit, tam stupendam versionem nec in hodiernum usque diem emendatam praeterire, idque in re momenti, in primo limine Ptolomæi, in ipsa Geographiæ definitione, nisi fato quodam essent occæcati Interpretes, in errorem ducti importunâ duarum vocum connexione, legendo διαξεγαφῆς conjunctim, pro διὰ γεγαφῆς divisim? Eo quòd ab antiquo nulla adscriberentur puncta vel commata vel accentus. Ἡ γεωγραφία μίμησις δέ διαγεγραφῆς τῶ καταλειμμένῳ τ' γῆς μέρες ὅλα &c. Geographia est imitatio picturæ totius partis terræ cognitæ &c quod certè, quicquid aiunt, est insignificans, pro Ἡ γεωγεγραφία μίμησις δὲ διὰ γεγραφῆς &c Geographia est imitatio per picturam, per descriptionem, sive in tabula totius partis terræ cognitæ. Nomen ipsum Geographiæ quid aliud significat quàm descriptionem terræ?
units.tr: Verse 4: Βιωτικὰ μὲν ἔν κεῤῥινεῖα &c. The Vulgate rendering [Seculária igitur judicia si habeatis, contemptibiles qui sunt in Ecclesia illos constituite] is neither an idiomatic way of speaking in Greek, nor suited to the sense or the syntax. I think the translators here understand judicia to mean lawsuits about the affairs of this life. But κεῤῥinεον, as I have just said, is nowhere found in that sense in the authors. And if they say that the word means courts of law, they assert what the Apostle plainly denies, rebuking the Corinthians precisely because they had no such courts and preferred to be judged before unbelievers. The inference itself also does not fit the sense well enough to excuse the attempt, and there is good reason to seek a better reading than this version. The text is easily restored to a more suitable sense and syntax, without force or solecism, merely by changing the punctuation and reading a hyperbaton: Βαπτὰ μὴ ἐν κειτήεια, ἐὰν ἔχετε τὸς ἐξουδενωμένος ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τούτους, καθίζετε. Secular matters, then, if you have these contemptible people in the Church, set them up as judges. Hyperbata of this kind are very frequent in the New Testament, as I have often noted elsewhere. The sense is this: What is this? Do you wish to test your cause before unbelievers, those whom you hold in contempt in the Church? Will you allow the unjust and the impious to judge among you, when you yourselves will one day judge them? Do you not know that we shall judge angels? And shall we not judge secular matters? Set up, then, judges among yourselves, set up courts for yourselves, I say to your shame. Is it so, that there is not a wise man among you? Not even one who can judge between brothers? Far be it from the Apostle to order that contemptible men be set up in the place of judgment; quite the reverse. He rebukes them for valuing themselves so unworthily that they appealed to the courts of unbelievers, as if there were not even one wise man among them. Clearly by this very reproach he implies that the one who is appointed judge in the Church ought to be wise and not just any contemptible person. The phrase τὸς τούτους καθίζετε is also very harsh, and I do not believe it can be saved as a Hebraism; for if it were a true Hebraism, it ought to read τὸς ἐξουδενωμένος ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ αὐτὸς καθίζετε, and not τούτους. As for the phrase καθίζειν κειτήειον, it is the same as τὸ καθίζειν ἀτιμασμένον in Aristophanes and Libanius. But the long-established opinion has taken such deep root that it can be removed only by some magisterial authority, or else supine carelessness has prevailed. This has happened among profane writers too. For how else could so remarkable a mistranslation have escaped correction down to the present day, and that in a matter of importance, at the very threshold of Ptolemy, in the very definition of Geography, unless the interpreters had been blinded by some fate and misled by the awkward joining of two words, reading διαξεγαφῆς as one word instead of διὰ γεγαφῆς as two? This happened because from antiquity no points, commas or accents were written. Ἡ γεωγραφία μίμησις δέ διαγεγραφῆς τῶ καταλειμμένῳ τ' γῆς μέρες ὅλα &c. Whatever they say, this is meaningless; it should read Ἡ γεωγεγραφία μίμησις δὲ διὰ γεγραφῆς &c., Geography is an imitation by painting, by description, or on a map, of the whole known part of the earth. What else does the very name of Geography mean but a description of the earth?

units.la: C. 7. v. 14. Ἐπεὶ ἄρα τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν ἀκάθαρτά ἐστι. Alioquin [nisi parentum alteruter esset fidelis] liberi vestri essent immundi, i. e manerent Ethnici: νῦν δέ, nunc vero [quoniam parentum alter est fidelis] ἁγία ἐστίν, sancti sunt, i.e. reputantur membra Ecclesiæ Christianæ. Et in hac notione credo Apostolum sæpius usurpare vocem ἅγιος, ut in initio hujus Epistolæ, τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ τοῦ Θεοῦ τῇ οὔσῃ ἐν Κορίνθῳ, κλητοῖς ἁγίοις, Ecclesiæ Dei quæ est Corinthō, iis qui vocantur sancti, & Eph. 1. 1. τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ, sanctis qui sunt Ephesi. Ecclesia enim & sancti sunt sæpius apud Apostolum Synonyma, ut apparet etiam alibi, manifestissimè vero 2 Cor. 1. 1. Ecclesiæ Dei, quæ est in Corintho cum omnibus Sanctis qui sunt in universâ Achaiâ. Corinthus vero erat Metropolis Achaiæ. Qui enim pomœu de-derant derant Christo in Primitivâ Ecclesiâ dicebantur sancti, ut recte Drusius. Non quòd omnes, qui essent in Ecclesia Corinthi vel Ephesi, erant revera sancti, sed quia membra erant visibilia Ecclesiæ, ideo vocabantur sancti, & ob eam causam liberi eorum ex alterutro parente fideli, qui fuit vocatus sanctus, participes facti sunt Baptismi, quemadmodum filius Proselytæ factus est particeps circumcisionis, etiam infans octiduanus. Et li liberi eorum qui vocantur sancti, cùm sint etiam ipsi sancti, non capaces sint Baptismi, in quo præcellunt sancti immundis? quid inde habent commodi, eò quòd vocentur vel reputentur sancti? An id tantùm habent commodi, quòd nati sint in fœdere? Imò, si nati sunt in fœdere, debentur iis etiam jura fœderis, pari modo quo liberi proselytæ in Judaicâ Ecclesiâ fruebantur jure circumcisionis. Et si ante Baptismi collationem moriantur, forte quàm primum nati, si nascuntur sancti, quis interdicet illis jus ad regnum Dei? Omnem alienigenam Judaei vocabant ἄνθρωπον ἀνάγαστον, hominem immundum. Act. 10. 28. & 2 Cor. 6. 17.
units.tr: Chapter 7, verse 14: Ἐπεὶ ἄρα τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν ἀκάθαρτά ἐστι. Otherwise [unless one of the parents were a believer], your children would be unclean, that is, would remain Gentiles. But now [since one of the parents is a believer] they are holy, ἁγία ἐστίν, that is, they are reckoned members of the Christian Church. I believe the Apostle often uses the word ἅγιος in this sense, as at the beginning of this Epistle: τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ τοῦ Θεοῦ τῇ οὔσῃ ἐν Κορίνθῳ, κλητοῖς ἁγίοις, to the Church of God which is at Corinth, to those who are called saints; and Ephesians 1:1: τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ, to the saints who are at Ephesus.
