For with the Apostle, the Church and the saints are often synonyms, as appears also elsewhere, and most clearly in 2 Corinthians 1:1: To the Church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia. Corinth, moreover, was the metropolis of Achaia. Those who had professed faith in Christ in the primitive Church were called saints, as Drusius rightly says. Not that all who were in the Church at Corinth or at Ephesus were truly saints, but because they were the visible members of the Church, they were therefore called saints. For this reason their children, through one believing parent who was called holy, were made partakers of baptism, just as the son of a proselyte was made a partaker of circumcision, even an infant of eight days old. And if their children, who are called saints, are themselves also saints, why should they not be capable of baptism, in which the saints excel the unclean? What advantage do they gain from being called or reckoned saints? Do they gain only this, that they were born within the covenant? Indeed, if they were born within the covenant, the rights of the covenant are also owed to them, in the same way as the children of proselytes enjoyed the right of circumcision in the Jewish Church. And if they die before the conferring of baptism, perhaps as soon as they are born, if they are born holy, who will deny them a right to the kingdom of God? The Jews called every foreigner ἄνθρωπον ἀνάγαστον, an unclean man. Acts 10:28; 2 Corinthians 6:17.

units.la: V 16. 17. Ἡ τί ὄιδας, ἀνερ, εἰ γυναῖκα σώσεις; εἰ μὴ ἐκάσῳ ὡς ἐμέρισεν ὁ Θεὸς, &c. Græcus Scholiastes legit, ἢ μή; idonee connectens verba ista priori versui, ἢ τί ὄιδας, ἀνερ, εἰ γυναῖκα σώσεις, ἢ μή; ἑκάσῳ &c. At quid opus est variare lectionem? vulgaris cum distinctione sola sufficit: ἢ τί ὄιδας, ἀνερ, εἰ γυναῖκα σώσεις, εἰ μή; ἑκάσῳ &c. Quid nosti, O vir, utrum uxorem servabis, utrum non? Unicuique ut sortitus est Deus, unumquemque ut vocavit Dominus, ita ambulet.
units.tr: Verses 16, 17: Ἡ τί ὄιδας, ἀνερ, εἰ γυναῖκα σώσεις; εἰ μὴ ἐκάσῳ ὡς ἐμέρισεν ὁ Θεὸς, &c. The Greek scholiast reads ἢ μή, joining these words appropriately to the preceding verse: ἢ τί ὄιδας, ἀνερ, εἰ γυναῖκα σώσεις, ἢ μή; ἑκάσῳ &c. But why need the reading be changed? The ordinary text with the one punctuation is enough: ἢ τί ὄιδας, ἀνερ, εἰ γυναῖκα σώσεις, εἰ μή; ἑκάσῳ &c. For what do you know, O man, whether you will save your wife? Or what do you know, O wife, whether you will save your husband? Only, as the Lord has distributed to each, as God has called each, so let him walk.

units.la: V. 23. Τιμῆς ἠγοράσθητε, μὴ γίνεσθε δοῦλοι ἀνθρώπων. Pretio empti estis, nolite fieri servi hominum. minum. Hæc punctatio & versio videntur respicere redemptionem per Christi sanguinem, & verbatim implicant doctrinam expresse contrariam ei, quam modo docuerat. Quasi quoniam redempti essent per Christi sanguinem, non oporteret eos diutius esse servos, cum verbis proxime praecedentibus jubeat eos non curare, si vocati essent ad Christianismum cùm essent servi, sed in qua vocatione vocati sunt in ea manere. Adeò ut aliquis alius sensus exquirendus magis appositus, qui forte legendo priora verba interrogative potest esse hujusmodi. Τιμῆς ἠγοράσθητε, μὴ γίνεσθε δοῦλοι ἀνθρώπων. Pretio redempti estis? nolite fieri servi hominum. Non loquitur de redemptione a captivitate Satanæ vel peccati, sed a servitio humano, ut colligere est ex contextu, qui nihil habet commune cum redemptione spirituali. Cohærentia enim est hujusmodi. Servus vocatus es? nè sit tibi cura; Pretio redempti estis? nolite fieri servi hominum; sed si potes etiam liber esse, magis utere, ut 21. Unusquisque in quo vocatus est, in hoc maneat apud Deum. Continuationem suadet in eo statu, in quocunque quis vocatus est ad Christianismum, dat interim libertatem sese redimendi. Unicum vero monendum ultra: 'Ἀνθρώπων, intelligendum reor, ἀπίστων, ut antea, ubi ἀνὴρ ὁ ἄπιστος, maritus infidelis, dicitur sanctificari ἐν τῇ γυναικί, in uxore, & ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄπιστος, uxor infidelis dicitur sanctificari ἐν τῷ ἀνδρὶ, in marito, subaudiendum est γυναικὶ τῇ πιστῇ, uxore fideli, & ἀνδρὶ πιστῷ, marito fideli, ut legunt quaedam exemplaria Græca, & Latinus vetus. Non dissuadet ab omni servitio, sed, ut antea monuit in impari conjugio, idem hoc loco monet in impari servitio. Ac si diceret, An vocatus es ad fidem Christi, cùm sis ipse servus viri infidelis, noli propterea anxius esse, esto vero contentus eo statu, nisi poteris te honeste liberare, ne nomen Domini & doctrina blasphemetur, 1 Tim 6.1.
units.tr: Verse 23: Τιμῆς ἠγοράσθητε, μὴ γίνεσθε δοῦλοι ἀνθρώπων. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men. This punctuation and version seem to refer to redemption by the blood of Christ, and in wording they imply a doctrine expressly contrary to the one he had just taught. It would be as if, because they had been redeemed by the blood of Christ, they ought no longer to be slaves, although in the words immediately preceding he bids them not to be concerned if they were called to Christianity while they were slaves, but to remain in the calling in which they were called. So another sense must be sought, one that fits better, which may perhaps be found by reading the preceding words as a question, as follows: Τιμῆς ἠγοράσθητε, μὴ γίνεσθε δοῦλοι ἀνθρώπων. Were you bought with a price? Do not become slaves of men. He is not speaking of redemption from the captivity of Satan or of sin, but from human servitude, as can be gathered from the context, which has nothing in common with spiritual redemption. The connection is of this kind: Were you called as a slave? Let it not trouble you. Were you bought with a price? Do not become slaves of men; but if you can also be free, use it rather, as in verse 21: Let each one remain before God in the calling in which he was called. He urges continuance in the state in which anyone has been called to Christianity, and in the meantime he allows the freedom of ransoming oneself. One thing more must be noted: I think ἀνθρώπων should be understood as ἀπίστων, as before, where the unbelieving husband, ἀνὴρ ὁ ἄπιστος, is said to be sanctified ἐν τῇ γυναικί, in the wife, and the unbelieving wife, ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄπιστος, is said to be sanctified ἐν τῷ ἀνδρὶ, in the husband; so one must supply γυναικὶ τῇ πιστῇ, a believing wife, and ἀνδρὶ πιστῷ, a believing husband, as some Greek copies and the old Latin read. He does not dissuade from all servitude but, as he had earlier advised in an unequal marriage, here he advises the same in unequal servitude. It is as if he said: Were you called to the faith of Christ while you are yourself the slave of an unbelieving master? Do not be anxious on that account; be content in that state, unless you can honourably free yourself, lest the name of the Lord and the doctrine be blasphemed, 1 Timothy 6:1.

units.la: V. 26. Διὰ τὸ ἐνεστῶσαν ἀνάγκην. Haec verba aliqui volunt respicere Luc. 21. 23. quasi de desolatione, quam futuram ibi praedixit Jesus, intelligeret hoc loco Paulus. Sed ista ἀνάγκη μεγάλη, tribulatio magna, de qua Lucas, futura erat ὅτι ἔσται γῆς ἐπὶ τῆς λαοῦ τούτῳ, in hac terra & in populo isto, nempe in terra Judaea, & in populo Judaeorum, nec de ullo alio populo vel gente praedixit ibi Jesus. Adeo ut non foret omnino rationi consonans interpretari, Paulum velle Corinthios a conjugio abstinere propter illam tribulationem, quae tam longe a suis distabat finibus, nec immediate tangebat eos. Alii majore fateor cum ratione de persecutionibus intelligunt quae instabant: sed si contextum animadvertamus serio, intelligendum potius reor, propter praesuram imminentem incommodorum, quae conjugium p'erumque comitantur, de quibus postea Apostolus. Διὰ τὰς ἐν αὐτῷ συνοχλίας ἢ τὰ τοιαῦτα χαλεπά. Propter ejus difficultates conjugiique molestias. Theophylact.
units.tr: V. 26. Διὰ τὸ ἐνεστῶσαν ἀνάγκην. Some want these words to refer to Luke 21:23, as if Paul meant the desolation that Jesus foretold there. But that great distress, a great tribulation, of which Luke speaks, was to come ὅτι ἔσται γῆς ἐπὶ τῆς λαοῦ τούτῳ [that there shall be great distress upon the land and wrath upon this people], in this land and upon this people, namely in the land of Judaea and upon the Jewish people. Jesus did not foretell there any distress for any other people or nation. So it would not be at all reasonable to explain that Paul wanted the Corinthians to abstain from marriage because of that tribulation, which was so far from their borders and did not touch them directly. Others, I admit, understand it with better reason as the persecutions that were then threatening. But if we attend seriously to the context, I think it should rather be understood as because of the imminent pressure of the troubles that usually accompany marriage, of which the Apostle speaks afterwards. (Διὰ τὰς ἐν αὐτῷ συνοχλίας ἢ τὰ τοιαῦτα χαλεπά [because of the distresses in it, or such hardships].) Because of its difficulties and the burdens of marriage. Theophylact.

units.la: V. 29. &c. Per parenthesim & trajectionem exponendum, τοῦτο δὲ φημι ἀδελφοί (ὅτι ὁ καιρὸς συνεσταλμένος τὸ λοιπὸν ἐστιν) ἵνα καὶ οἱ ἔχοντες γυναῖκας ὡς μὴ ἔχοντες ὦσι, καὶ οἱ κλαίοντες ὡς μὴ κλαίοντες, καὶ οἱ χαίροντες ὡς μὴ χαίροντες &c. σχῆμα γὰρ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου. Hoc autem dico fratres, (quoniam quod remanet breve est tempus) ut & qui habent uxores sint tanquam non habentes, & qui flent tanquam non flentes, & qui gaudent tanquam non gaudentes, &c. praeterit enim figura hujus mundi. Τὸ λοιπὸν, non male intelligitur, τὸ ὑπολειπόμενον τῆς ζωῆς, Quasi diceret, Hoc autem dico vobis, quoniam tam breve est tempus vitæ, adeóque cito pede transeat mundus, ne soliciti sitis nimium, ut postero monet versu, sive propter tristitia sive propter delectabilia huius mundi.
units.tr: V. 29 and following. This should be explained by parenthesis and transposition: τοῦτο δὲ φημι ἀδελφοί (ὅτι ὁ καιρὸς συνεσταλμένος τὸ λοιπὸν ἐστιν) ἵνα καὶ οἱ ἔχοντες γυναῖκας ὡς μὴ ἔχοντες ὦσι, καὶ οἱ κλαίοντες ὡς μὴ κλαίοντες, καὶ οἱ χαίροντες ὡς μὴ χαίροντες, &c. σχῆμα γὰρ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου [But this I say, brothers (because the time is short from now on), that those who have wives should be as though they had none, and those who weep as though they did not weep, and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, etc.; for the form of this world is passing away]. But I say this, brothers (since the time that remains is short), so that those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who weep as though they did not weep, and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, etc., for the form of this world passes away. The phrase τὸ λοιπὸν [the rest] may well be understood as τὸ ὑπολειπόμενον τῆς ζωῆς [the remainder of life]. It is as if he said: I tell you this, because the time of life is so short and the world passes away so quickly, do not be overly anxious, as he warns in the next verse, whether because of sorrows or because of the pleasures of this world.

units.la: V. 35. Τοῦτο δὲ πρὸς τὸ ὑμῶν συμφέρον λέγω, οὐχ' ἵνα βρόχον ὑμῖν ἐπιβάλω, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ εὔσχημον καὶ εὐπάρεδρον τῷ Κυρίῳ, ἀπερισπάστως. Hoc vero dico ad utilitatem vestram, sive ad id quod vobis sit conveniens, non ut vinculum vobis imponam, sed ad id quod honestum est, et decorum Domino, sine violenta abstractione, nempe in verba mea: ἀπερισπάστως, μὴ εἰας ἀφαιρεῖσθαί τι. Vi aliquid abripere. Suid. οὐχ' ἵνα ἀναγκάσω ὑμᾶς χαίρειν καὶ μὴ χαίρειν παρασχεῖν. Non ut cogam vos et volentes et nolentes in virginitate degere. Τῷ δὲ ἀνάγκην Θεόν χαλεῖ: Necessitatem enim sive compulsionem vocat vinculum. Schol. Græc. Ἀπερισπάστως, sine violenta abstractione, i. e. sine compulsione. Non ut vi aliquâ vos traham in verba mea. Θεόχω, ἀξίως. Hesych. ἀπερισπάστως, ad verbum, sermone Gallico, bien-séant, quod tenè assidet: ἀξίως τῷ Θεῷ, digna Deo. Job. 3. 6.
units.tr: V. 35. Τοῦτο δὲ πρὸς τὸ ὑμῶν συμφέρον λέγω, οὐχ' ἵνα βρόχον ὑμῖν ἐπιβάλω, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸ εὔσχημον καὶ εὐπάρεδρον τῷ Κυρίῳ, ἀπερισπάστως [I say this for your own good, not to throw a noose around you, but for what is seemly and fitting for the Lord, without distraction]. I say this for your benefit, not to lay a snare upon you, but for what is honourable and becoming to the Lord, without violent distraction, namely in my words. ἀπερισπάστως [without distraction] means: μὴ εἰας ἀφαιρεῖσθαί τι [do not allow anything to be snatched away]. Snatched away by force. Suidas. οὐχ' ἵνα ἀναγκάσω ὑμᾶς χαίρειν καὶ μὴ χαίρειν παρασχεῖν [not that I should force you to be willing or unwilling in virginity]. Not that I should compel you to live in virginity whether willing or unwilling. The Greek scholia say: he calls compulsion or constraint a noose. ἀπερισπάστως, without violent distraction, that is, without compulsion. That is, I do not draw you by any force into my words. Θεόχω [seemly], ἀξίως [worthily]. Hesychius. ἀπερισπάστως, in the French idiom, bien-séant, what sits well and holds firmly: ἀξίως τῷ Θεῷ [worthy of God], fit for God. Job 3:6.

units.la: C. 9 v. 17. 18. Εἰ γὰρ ἑκὼν τοῦτο πράσσω, μισθὸν ἔχω· εἰ δὲ ἄκων οἰκονομίαν πεπίστευμαι, τίς μού ἐστιν ὁ μισθός; Ἵνα εὐαγγελιζόμενος, &c. Si enim volens hoc facio mercedem habeo: sin invito dispensatio est concredita, quæ mihi tandem est merces? ut evangelium prædicans sine sumptu faciam evangelium, ne utar potestate mea in evangelio. Ac si diceret, si volens prædicavero merces mihi debita est, eamque jure poteram exigere. Dignus enim est operarius mercede sua. Luc. 10. 7. & qui attendit ad altare participat cum altari, ut suprà, v. 13. εἰ δὲ ἀ-
units.tr: C. 9 v. 17, 18. Εἰ γὰρ ἑκὼν τοῦτο πράσσω, μισθὸν ἔχω· εἰ δὲ ἄκων οἰκονομίαν πεπίστευμαι, τίς μού ἐστιν ὁ μισθός; Ἵνα εὐαγγελιζόμενος, &c. [For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me. What then is my reward? That in preaching the gospel, etc.] For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a dispensation has been committed to me. What then is my reward? That preaching the gospel I may make the gospel without charge, so as not to use my power in the gospel. It is as if he said: if I preach willingly, a reward is owed to me, and I could rightly demand it. For the labourer is worthy of his wages. Luke 10:7. And he who attends to the altar shares with the altar, as above, v. 13. εἰ δὲ ἀ-

units.la: I
units.tr: I

units.la: ἀκων οἰκονομίαν πεπίστευμαι, si vero nolenti vel invito dispensatio mihi est concredita (ut fuit Paulo Act. 9. & 26.) quae mihi merces tunc est debita si evangelium praedicavero? certe nulla: oportet vero ut evangelium praedicem, quam fieri poterit, sine onere vel sumptu, & non utar potestate quam habeo ex evangelio vivere, Necessitas enim mihi incumbit, imo vae mihi si non praedicavero. v. 16. Delendo comma post ἀκων, melius ut opinor perficitur & completur sensus. καταχρῶμαι usurpatur saepius pro simplici χρῶμαι. ut etiam apud Latinos abuti pro uti.
units.tr: ἀκων οἰκονομίαν πεπίστευμαι [but if unwillingly a stewardship has been entrusted to me]: if a dispensation is entrusted to me against my will (as it was to Paul, Acts 9 and 26), what reward is then owed to me if I preach the gospel? Certainly none. But I must preach the gospel, as far as I can, without burden or charge, and not use the power I have to live from the gospel. For necessity is laid upon me, indeed woe is me if I do not preach (v. 16). I think the sense is more perfectly and fully expressed if the comma after ἀκων is deleted. καταχρῶμαι [to use up/abuse] is often used for the simple χρῶμαι [to use], just as in Latin abuti is used for uti.

units.la: C. 11. v. 7. Γυνὴ δὲ δόξα ἀνδρὸς ἐστι. Mulier vero imago viri est. Vir quidem non debet velare caput, εἰκὼν γὰρ δόξα Θεοῦ ὑπάρχων, quoniam sit figura & imago Dei. Mulier vero imago viri est. Vox ‎אִשָּׁה, quae apud Hebraeos est imago quae ab alia re deducta est, à LXX vertitur δόξα, Num 12. 8. Psal. 17. 15. Sic δόξα, imago vel gloria. Phavo.
units.tr: C. 11 v. 7. Γυνὴ δὲ δόξα ἀνδρὸς ἐστι [But the woman is the glory of the man]. Woman is the image of man. The man indeed ought not to cover his head, being the image and glory of God, since he is the figure and image of God. But the woman is the image of the man. The word ishah [אִשָּׁה], which among the Hebrews is an image derived from another thing, is rendered δόξα [glory] by the Seventy: Num. 12:8; Ps. 17:15. So δόξα means image or glory. Phavorinus.

units.la: V. 10. Διὰ τῆτο ὀφείλει ἡ γυνὴ ἐξουσίαν ἔχειν ὅτι ἡ κεφαλὴ διὰ τὰς Ἀγγέλους. Propter hoc debet mulier potestatem habere in capite per ve propter Angelos. Habere, i. e. tenere, aestimare, vel agnoscere, in quo sensu habere accipitur apud Latinos, ut τὸ ἔχειν apud Graecos. In capite est in viro, versu enim tertio vir vocatur caput mulieris, & Eph. 5. 22, 23. mulieres jubentur viris suis esse subdita, i. e. potestatem agnoscere in viris suis, ὅτι ὁ ἀνὴρ κεφαλὴ τῆς γυναικός: quoniam vir est caput mulieris. Vis interpretationis & argumenti est a verbis praecedentibus hujusmodi. Vir non est ex muliere, sed mulier ex viro, neque creatus est vir propter mulierem, sed mulier propter virum. Διὰ τοῦτο, Ergo debet mulier agnoscere potestatem in viro. Cujus omnino simile occurrit argumentum 1 Tim. 2: 12, 13: Mulier in silentio discito cum omni subjectione, mulierem enim non docere permitto, neque dominari in virum, sed esse in silentio. Adam enim prior formatus est, deinde Eva. Cum ergo argumenta sint eadem, quid ultra dubiremus, quin unus & idem sit locorum sensus, cum id ferat verborum usus & constructio? Quoad enim expositionem eorum, qui ἐξουσία volunt poni μετωνυμικῶς pro velamine, subjectionis signo, est opinor violenta & coacta nimis, quàm ut licitè (dictum sit cum venia) admitti debeat. Praeterquam etiam quòd non cohaereat apte cum scopo loci, cujus connexio est hujusmodi: Quoniam vir non est ex muliere, &c. Ergo debet mulier potestatem agnoscere in capite, verum tamen neque est vir sine muliere, neque mulier sine viro, &c. Quibus verbis posterioribus mitigare videtur Apostolus injunctionem quae praecesserat, ne videatur severa nimis. Ac si diceret, verum est quidem, Quia vir non factus est ex muliere, sed mulier ex viro, & quia vir non creatus est propter mulierem, sed mulier propter virum, ergo debere mulierem agnoscere potestatem in capite, i.e. in viro, jure hoc creationis, veruntamen neque est vir sine muliere, neque mulier sine viro per Dominum. Nam sicut mulier est ex viro, sic etiam vir est ex muliere, omnia verò ex Deo. Plane innuens tale ad invicem esse relationis vinculum, quoniam alter sine altera esse nequit, ut virum nullo modo deceat suae potestati quamvis a Deo jure creationis sibi datae nimium vendicare vel indulgere, sed ea uti cum modestiâ & sobrietate. Atque haec est necessaria hujus loci cohaerentia. Quid verò huc attinet mulieris gestatio velaminis in capite, non equidem video. Quoad verba, διὰ τὸς Ἀγγέλους, per vel propter Angelos, nihil opinor pinor aliud denotant, quam mulierem debere agnoscere potestatem in viro per vel propter ipsum Deum, qui per ministerium Angelorum in hoc ordine creavit illos, & non longo post creationem tempore imposuit etiam mulieri expressis verbis hanc legem subjectionis ⸿ cujus meminit Apostolus 1 Cor.14. 34.ubi mulier jubetur subjici, ⸿ Ὡς ⸿ ὁ νόμος λέγει, ut etiam lex dicit: Quam legem consentiunt universi ipsam esse quae occurrit Gen. 3. 16. ⸿ αὐτός σε κυριεύσει: & ipse in te dominabitur. Atque haec certe data est per ministerium Angelorum, ut fuit etiam Mosaica, Act. 7. 53. Gal. 3. 19. & Heb. 2. 2. Omnia enim Dei opera ad extra fiunt per eorum ministerium; non enim potest recte Deus dici habere os vel manus, vel loqui, vel praeire vel proprie quicquam agere; ideoque frequens est adscribere Angelis quod soli debetur Deo, quoniam ut ministri mandata ejus exequuntur; atque hinc non raro promiscue vocantur Angeli nomine Dei, & Deus nomine Angelorum. E. g. Act.7. 35 dicitur, ἐν χειρὶ Ἀγγέλου, per manum Angeli, qui apparuit ei in rubo: at vero ille Angelus vocatur Deus, Exod. 3. 6. & 12. Sic etiam infra in eodem capite, μετὰ τοῦ Ἀγγέλου, qui fuit cum Angelo qui locutus est ei in monte Sina. At vero etiam hic Angelus Exod. 19. saepius dicitur fuisse Deus, & 23. εἰς διαταγὰς Ἀγγέλων per ordinationes Angelorum, quomodo etiam dicitur Gal. 3. 19. ὁ νόμος διατεταγμένος διὰ Ἀγγέλων, lex ordinata per Angelos, cum dicatur Exod. 20.1. & locutus est Elohim. Sic etiam dicitur Gen.48. 15. Ὁ Θεὸς Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ, ὁ Θεὸς ὁ τρέφων με, ὁ ἄγγελος ὁ ῥυόμενός με, &c. Deus Abrahami & Isaaci, Deus qui nutrivit me, Angelus qui liberavit me, &c. Ut etiam Jud. 13. 21. & 23. Manoah vocat Angelum Dei Deum, um, scivit enim quòd fuit Angelus Dei, & statim dicit moriemur quia vidimus Deum. Atq; ex his exemplis, quibus addi multò plura poterant, manifestum est, non omnino esse rarum, sed abundè frequens, adscribere Angelis quæ Deus per eorum ministerium facit, ideóque nec esse novum, si Apostolus hoc loco dicat, mulierem debere agnoscere potestatem in viro per vel propter Angelos, eo nomine intelligens ipsum Deum. In summa, hæc interpretatio tam genuine fluit à verborum ordine, atque adeò non opus habet peregrino auxilio ad sui explicationem, ut confidam admodùm eam esse germanam atque ipsam veram.
units.tr: V. 10. Διὰ τοῦτο ὀφείλει ἡ γυνὴ ἐξουσίαν ἔχειν ὅτι ἡ κεφαλὴ διὰ τὰς Ἀγγέλους [Therefore the woman ought to have authority on her head because of the angels]. For this reason a woman ought to have power over her head, because of the angels. To have, that is, to hold, to esteem, or to acknowledge; in this sense habere is taken in Latin as τὸ ἔχειν [to have] in Greek. On her head means in the husband, for in verse 3 the husband is called the head of the woman, and at Eph. 5:22, 23 wives are commanded to be subject to their husbands, that is, to acknowledge authority in their husbands, ὅτι ὁ ἀνὴρ κεφαλὴ τῆς γυναικός [for the husband is the head of the wife]. The force of the interpretation and argument comes from the preceding words, as follows: man is not from woman, but woman from man; nor was man created for woman, but woman for man. Therefore (διὰ τοῦτο) the woman ought to acknowledge authority in the man. A wholly similar argument occurs at 1 Tim. 2:12, 13: "Let a woman learn in silence with all subjection; for I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to rule over a man, but to be in silence; for Adam was formed first, then Eve." Since the arguments are the same, why should we doubt that the sense of both passages is one and the same, when the usage and construction of the words allow it? As for those who want ἐξουσία [authority] to be taken metonymically for a veil, a sign of subjection, that interpretation seems to me too forced and strained to be admitted, with respect be it said. Besides, it does not fit well with the purpose of the passage, whose connection runs thus: since man is not from woman, etc., therefore the woman ought to acknowledge authority on her head; yet neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, etc. By these latter words the Apostle seems to soften the command that went before, lest it seem too severe. It is as if he said: it is true that, since man was not made from woman but woman from man, and since man was not created for woman but woman for man, therefore the woman ought to acknowledge authority on her head, that is, in her husband, by the right of creation; nevertheless, neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as woman is from man, so also man is from woman; but all things are from God. This plainly implies that there is such a bond of mutual relation that one cannot exist without the other, so that it does not befit the man to claim too much for his authority, though it was given him by God by the right of creation, but he should use it with moderation and sobriety. This is the necessary coherence of the passage. But what the woman's wearing of a veil on her head has to do with this, I certainly do not see. As for the words διὰ τὰς Ἀγγέλους [because of the angels], I think they mean nothing else than that the woman ought to acknowledge authority in the man because of God himself, who through the ministry of angels created them in this order, and not long after creation imposed this law of subjection on the woman in express words, which the Apostle mentions at 1 Cor. 14:34, where women are commanded to be subject, ὡς ὁ νόμος λέγει [as the law says], as the law also says. All agree that this is the law found at Gen. 3:16, αὐτός σε κυριεύσει [he shall rule over you], and he shall rule over you. This law was certainly given through the ministry of angels, as the Mosaic law was too (Acts 7:53; Gal. 3:19; Heb. 2:2). For all God's works ad extra are done through the ministry of angels; for God cannot properly be said to have a mouth or hands, or to speak, or to go before, or strictly to do anything. Therefore it is frequent to ascribe to angels what is due to God alone, since as ministers they carry out his commands; hence angels are often called by the name of God, and God by the name of angels. For example, Acts 7:35 says ἐν χειρὶ Ἀγγέλου [by the hand of an angel], by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush; yet that angel is called God, Exod. 3:6 and 12. So also later in the same chapter, μετὰ τοῦ Ἀγγέλου [with the angel], who was with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai. Indeed in Exodus 19 this angel is often said to be God, and in 23, εἰς διαταγὰς Ἀγγέλων [by the ordinances of angels], by the ordinances of angels, as also at Gal. 3:19, ὁ νόμος διατεταγμένος διὰ Ἀγγέλων [the law ordained through angels], the law ordained through angels, whereas at Exod. 20:1 it is said, and God (Elohim) spoke. Likewise at Gen. 48:15: ὁ Θεὸς Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ, ὁ Θεὸς ὁ τρέφων με, ὁ ἄγγελος ὁ ῥυόμενός με, &c. [the God of Abraham and Isaac, the God who has fed me, the angel who has redeemed me, etc.], the God of Abraham and Isaac, the God who fed me, the angel who delivered me, etc. So too at Judg. 13:21 and 23, Manoah calls the angel of God God, for he knew that it was an angel of God, and at once says, we shall die because we have seen God. From these examples, to which far more could be added, it is clear that it is not at all rare but quite frequent to ascribe to angels what God does through their ministry. So it is no novelty if the Apostle here says that the woman ought to acknowledge authority in the man because of the angels, meaning by that name God himself. In sum, this interpretation flows so naturally from the order of the words, and so needs no foreign help to explain it, that I am confident it is genuine and the true one.

units.la: V. 21. "Ἑκαστος γὰρ τὸ ἴδιον δεῖπνον προλαμβάνει, ἐν τῷ φαγεῖν ὃς μὲν πεινᾷ, ὃς δὲ μεθύει. In plerisque, si non in omnibus codicibus, distinguitur commate post φαγεῖν. Versio verò ista, propriam cænam præsumit in edendo, durius sonat, ideóque arbitror meliùs distingui, ut supra, post προλαμβάνει, Unusquisque enim præsumit cænam propriam, & in edendo sive inter edendum, i. e. cùm edant cœnam Domini, hic quidem esurit, ille verò satur est. Quoad trajectionem: sunt frequentes adeò trajectiones ejusmodi in N. T. ut non possim non attonitus mirari quenquam in ea hærere, præsertim cùm magis accommodum reddat sensum, & etiam tollat insolentiam phrasis. In summa sensus & cohærentia est ejusmodi. Cùm igitur convenitis in unum, i. e. in Ecclesia, non est, quod facitis, Dominicam cœnam edere; unusquisque enim suam privatim accipit, priusquam alii convenerint, atque hinc in edendo alius esurit, alius satur est. Opulenti quidem qui cœnam suam secum ferunt, saturantur, pauperes verò, οἱ μὴ ἔχοντες subaudi Δεῖπνον, qui non habent cœnam, esuriunt. Mos videtur tur fuisse Corinthiis ditioribus anteverterre coenam Dominicam edendo propriam per se privatim, priusquam convenirent pauperes. Sed hoc non fuit Dominicam coenam edere, quae vocatur κοινωνία τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ, communio sive communicatio corporis Christi, 1 Cor. 10. 16. ideoque pergit Apostolus increpare, An non domos habetis in quibus edatis & bibatis? aut Ecclesiam Dei contemnitis, & pudefacitis eos qui non habent [coenam?] Quid dicam vobis? laudabo vos in hoc? non laudo. Et sic tandem post sermonem alium de coena Domini, usque ad v. 33. rursus ad hunc redit, quem brevi concludit monitu, Itaque fratres mei, cum convenitis ad edendum, coenam nemo Domini. Expectate alius alium, quod si quis esurit, domi edat, ne ad condemnationem conveniatis: μὴ εἰς κρίμα συνέρχησθε. Hesych.
units.tr: V. 21. "For each one takes his own supper beforehand in eating [Ἕκαστος γὰρ τὸ ἴδιον δεῖπνον προλαμβάνει, ἐν τῷ φαγεῖν ὃς μὲν πεινᾷ, ὃς δὲ μεθύει]." In most manuscripts, if not all, the comma comes after φαγεῖν. The Vulgate rendering, "anticipates his own supper in eating," sounds harsh, so I think it is better punctuated, as above, after προλαμβάνει: "For each one takes his own supper beforehand, and in eating one is hungry, another is drunk." As for the transposition, such transpositions are so frequent in the New Testament that I cannot but wonder that anyone should stick at this one, especially since it makes the sense more suitable and removes the strangeness of the phrase. In short, the sense and connection are as follows. "When therefore you come together into one place," that is, into the Church, "what you are doing is not eating the Lord's supper; for each one takes his own private meal before the others have assembled, and so, in eating, one is hungry and another is full." The wealthy, who bring their own meals with them, are satisfied, but the poor, "those who do not have" (supply "supper"), go hungry. It seems that the wealthier Corinthians had the custom of anticipating the Lord's supper by eating their own food privately before the poor came together. But this was not "eating the Lord's supper," which is called "the communion of the body of Christ" [κοινωνία τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ], "communion or sharing in the body of Christ," 1 Cor. 10.16. Therefore the Apostle goes on to rebuke them: "Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing [supper?]? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you in this? I do not praise you." And so, after another discourse on the Lord's supper, down to v. 33, he returns to this point and briefly sums it up with an admonition: "So, my brothers, when you come together to eat, let no one [eat] the Lord's supper. Wait for one another; but if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for condemnation" [μὴ εἰς κρίμα συνέρχησθε]. Hesychius.

units.la: C. 12. v. 7. πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον. prout fuerit expediens.
units.tr: C. 12. v. 7. "for the common good" [πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον], as it is expedient.

units.la: V. 11. Διαιρῶν ἰδίᾳ ἑκάστῳ καθὼς βούλεται, i. e. ἰδίᾳ χαρίσματα: Distribuens suam cuique donatum unicuique prout vult, ὅτι Δεσπότης ὁ Θεὸς, ut Dominus & Deus. Theophylact. Heb. 2. 4. vocantur μερισμοὶ πνεύματος ἁγίου κατὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ θέλησιν. Distributiones Spiritus sancti secundum suam ipsius voluntatem.
units.tr: V. 11. "Distributing to each one his own gifts as he wills" [Διαιρῶν ἰδίᾳ ἑκάστῳ καθὼς βούλεται], that is, his own gifts. "Distributing to each one his own as he wills," because God is Lord, as Lord and God. Theophylact. In Heb. 2.4 they are called "distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will" [μερισμοὶ πνεύματος ἁγίου κατὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ θέλησιν].

units.la: V. 19. Μὴ πάντες δυνάμεις; Num omnes sunt virtutes? ut vulgo. Inepta certe dictio. Rectius verba ista connectuntur & distinguuntur cum sequentibus, v. 30 μὴ πάντες δυνάμεις· μὴ πάντες χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων ἔχουσι; num omnes habent virtutes, num omnes habent dona curationum? repetendo τὸ ἔχειν ἀπὸ τῆς κοινῆς. Virtutes, i. potestatem etiam vel morte puniendi, & miracula edendi.
units.tr: V. 19. "Are all powers?" [Μὴ πάντες δυνάμεις;] As commonly read, "Are all miracle-workers?" Certainly an awkward expression. These words are more rightly connected and punctuated with what follows, v. 30: "Are all powers? Do all have gifts of healings?" [μὴ πάντες δυνάμεις· μὴ πάντες χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων ἔχουσι;], repeating the verb "to have" [τὸ ἔχειν] from the common clause. "Powers" means the power even to punish by death, and to work miracles.

units.la: C. 14, v. 2 Ὁ γὰρ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ οὐκ ἀνθρώποις πνεῦμα λαλεῖ, ἀλλὰ τῷ Θεῷ· οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἀκούει, πνεῦ- μα δὲ λαλεῖ μυστήρια. Qui loquitur lingua, i. e. peregrina, non hominibus loquitur, sed Deo, nemo enim intelligit, spiritu vero loquitur mysteria, i. e. spiritu, quem donavit ei Deus, variis loquendi linguis in ædificationem Ecclesiæ loquitur abscondita, quæ non intelliguntur ab iis qui sunt ἰδιῶται, nec aliam linguam callent quàm maternam: ἀκούει frequenter in Veteri significat intelligit, ubi Hebræa vox est יָדַע; ut Gen. 42. 23. Deut. 28. 49. & alibi.
units.tr: C. 14, v. 2. "For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men but to God; for no one understands, but in the spirit he speaks mysteries" [Ὁ γὰρ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ οὐκ ἀνθρώποις λαλεῖ, ἀλλὰ τῷ Θεῷ· οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἀκούει, πνεῦμα δὲ λαλεῖ μυστήρια]. "He who speaks in a tongue," that is, in a foreign language, "does not speak to men but to God; for no one understands; but in the spirit he speaks mysteries," that is, in the spirit which God has given him, he speaks in various tongues, for the building up of the Church, hidden things which are not understood by those who are laymen [ἰδιῶται] and know no language but their mother tongue. In the Old Testament, "hears" [ἀκούει] often means "understands," where the Hebrew word is יָדַע, as in Gen. 42.23, Deut. 28.49, and elsewhere.

units.la: V. 13. Hic versus optimè distinguitur post προσευχέσθω. Λυέτω ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ προσευχέσθω, ἵνα διερμηνεύῃ. Quapropter qui lingua loquitur peregrina precetur, ut interpretetur. Ac- si diceret, si quis precetur lingua peregrina, precetur ita ut interpretur aliquis, quid precatus sit, quomodo enim aliter qui supplet locum idiota dicturus est Amen, si quid dictum sit, omnino non intelligar. Optime Valla, Non orat Deum ad hoc obtinendum ut interpretetur, sed si aliqua lingua preces ad Deum faciat, sic faciat ut ejus lingua interiorem sensum interpretetur, vel per se vel per alium: τὸ ἵνα videtur pari sensu accipi infrà 31. Δύνασθε γὰρ καθ' ἕνα πάντες προφητεύειν, ἵνα πάντες μανθάνωσι, &c. Potestis enim omnes alius post alium sive singulatim prophetare, ut omnes discant, i. e. ita ut omnes possint discere quod neutiquam fieri potuit, si multi loquerentur simul. ut etiam Joh. 10. 17. Quia ego pono animam meam, ἵνα πάλιν λάβω αὐτήν, ut iterum sumam eam, i. e. ut exponit Grotius, sed ita ut eam sim recepturus; vel ut Maldonatus, ita mori, ut paulo post ad vitam sit reditarus: τὸ ἵνα his locis non fi- nem indicat sed modum.
units.tr: V. 13. This verse is best punctuated after "let him pray." "Therefore let him who speaks in a tongue pray, that he may interpret" [Διὸ ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ προσευχέσθω, ἵνα διερμηνεύῃ]. "Therefore let him who speaks in a foreign tongue pray," that he may interpret. As if he said: if anyone prays in a foreign tongue, let him pray in such a way that someone interprets what he has prayed; "for how otherwise will the layman who fills the place say Amen," if something has been said, I shall not understand at all. Valla rightly renders: "He does not pray to God in order to obtain that he may interpret; but if he makes prayers to God in some language, let him do so in such a way that his tongue interprets the inner sense, either by himself or through another." The "that" [ἵνα] seems to be taken in the same sense below, at v. 31: "For you can all prophesy one by one, that all may learn" [Δύνασθε γὰρ καθ' ἕνα πάντες προφητεύειν, ἵνα πάντες μανθάνωσι], etc. That is, you can all prophesy, one after another or singly, so that all may learn, that is, so that all can learn; which could by no means have happened if many spoke at once. So also John 10.17: "Because I lay down my life, that [ἵνα] I may take it again," that is, as Grotius explains, "but in such a way that I am to receive it again"; or as Maldonatus has it, "to die in such a way that shortly afterwards I am to return to life." In these places, "that" [τὸ ἵνα] indicates not the end but the manner.

units.la: V.14. Ἐὰν γὰρ προσεύχωμαι γλώσσῃ τὸ πνεῦμα προσεύχεται, ὁ ὁ νοῦς μου ἄκαρπός ἐστι. Si enim precer lingua [peregrina] spiritus meus (quem dedit mihi Deus variis ut loquar linguis) precatur, sed mens mea est infructuosa, nemo enim intelligit. Mens mea, i. e. sensus meus. Quid igitur? προσεύξομαι τῷ πνεύματι, προσεύξομαι δὲ καὶ τῷ νοΐ. Precabor spiritu, (quem mihi dedit Deus) precabor etiam cum sensu, ita ut ab omnibus intelligar. Νοῦς, mens, sensus. Gloss. vet. τὶς ἔχει τινά; quis est horum verborum sensus? Aristoph. Aliqui τὸ πνεῦμα interpretantur vocem.
units.tr: V. 14. "For if I pray in a foreign tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful" [Ἐὰν γὰρ προσεύχωμαι γλώσσῃ, τὸ πνεῦμά μου προσεύχεται, ὁ δὲ νοῦς μου ἄκαρπός ἐστιν]. "My spirit" (which God gave me, so that I might speak in various tongues) prays, but "my mind," that is, my understanding, is unfruitful, for no one understands. What then? "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray also with the mind" [προσεύξομαι τῷ πνεύματι, προσεύξομαι δὲ καὶ τῷ νοΐ]. That is: I will pray with the spirit (which God has given me), and I will pray also with understanding, so that I may be understood by all. νοῦς means mind, understanding, sense. Old glossary: "τὶς ἔχει τινά"; what is the sense of these words? Aristophanes. Some interpret "spirit" [τὸ πνεῦμα] here as voice.

units.la: V. 25. Καὶ οὕτω τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς καρδίας αὐτοῦ φανερὰ γίνεται. subaudi αὐτῷ, post γίνεται. Et sic occulta cordis ejus manifesta ei fiunt. i. e. Ignorantia, incredulitas, & impietas cordis ejus quae tam diu latuit, nec si unquam antea innotuit, nunc fit ei manifesta, ita ut statim procidat in faciem, & adoret Deum. Eadem est elleiptica dicendi formula 16. 12. καὶ πάντως ἐν λῷ ξένια, nempe, αὐτός. Et prorsus non erat voluntas ei, ut nunc veniret.
units.tr: V. 25. "And so the secrets of his heart become manifest" [Καὶ οὕτω τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς καρδίας αὐτοῦ φανερὰ γίνεται]. Supply "to him" [αὐτῷ] after "become." And so the hidden things of his heart become manifest to him: the ignorance, unbelief and impiety of his heart, which has lain hidden so long, and which, if it was ever known before, now becomes plain to him, so that at once he "falls on his face and worships God." The same elliptical form of expression occurs at 16.12: "and altogether [it was not his will] to come" (supply "he"). Indeed it was altogether not his will that he should come at that time.

units.la: V. 27. Εἰ τε γλώσσῃ τις λαλεῖ, καὶ δύο ἢ τὸ πλεῖστον τρεῖς, καὶ ἀνὰ μέρος, καὶ εἷς διερμηνευέτω. Subaudi, ἐγώ, Si quis loquitur lingua [peregrina] duabus vel ad maximum tribus fiat, idque singulatim & unus interpretetur, &c. Plurimis linguis fieri potuit unum aliquem posse loqui, εὐταξίας δ' ἕνεκα, ordinis vero gratia duabus vel tribus ad plurimum permisit uti, iisque singulatim non confuse. Quod vero, καὶ δύο ἢ τὸ πλεῖστον τρεῖς, de personis aliqui intelligant, videtur mihi ab ipso sensu prorsus alienum. Quomodo enim loquatur quis per alium, nisi ipse, quid dicat, alii dicet, non intelligo. Atque hoc idem foret, nisi ipse sibi sit interpres. V. 30.
units.tr: V. 27. "If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be by two, or at most three, and in turn, and let one interpret" [Εἴ τε γλώσσῃ τις λαλεῖ, καὶ δύο ἢ τὸ πλεῖστον τρεῖς, καὶ ἀνὰ μέρος, καὶ εἷς διερμηνευέτω]. Supply "I" [ἐγώ]: if anyone speaks in a foreign tongue, let it be by two or at most three, each singly, and let one interpret, etc. With many tongues it could have been possible for anyone to speak, but for the sake of good order [εὐταξίας δ' ἕνεκα] he permitted the use of two or at most three, and these singly, not in confusion. But that some understand "two or at most three" of persons seems to me utterly alien to the sense. For how someone could speak through another, unless he himself tells another what he is saying, I do not understand. And it would be the same thing unless he were his own interpreter. See v. 30.

units.la: V. 29. 'Ἐὰν ἧ ἄλλῳ ἀποκαλυφθῇ, &c. Si vero quid alteri revelatum fuerit assidenti, prior silet, i. e. priusquam loquatur ille cui revelatum est, Potestis enim omnes singulatim, i.e. alius post alium prophetare, ita ut omnes discant, &c. χ᾿ πνεύματα προφητῶν προφήταις ὑποτάσσεται. Et Spiritus Prophetarum Prophetis sunt subjecti. Ita ut Propheta cui aliquid revelatum est, cum fit Dominus sui ipsius spiritus, ut pro suo arbitrio potest, ita omnino debet spiritum illum revelationis supprimere, usque dum alter finem loquendi fecerit, ut ordo servetur in Ecclesiis; ἐ γὰρ ἀκαταστασίας &c. Non enim est Deus confusionis Deus, sed pacis
units.tr: V. 29. "But if something is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first be silent" [Ἐὰν δὲ ἄλλῳ ἀποκαλυφθῇ, etc.]. That is, before the one to whom the revelation has been made speaks. "For you can all prophesy singly, one after another, so that all may learn," etc. "And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" [καὶ πνεύματα προφητῶν προφήταις ὑποτάσσεται]. So the prophet to whom something has been revealed, though he is master of his own spirit, to act as he pleases, must nonetheless altogether restrain that spirit of revelation until the other has finished speaking, so that order is kept in the churches; "for God is not a God of confusion but of peace" [οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἀκαταστασίας ὁ Θεὸς ἀλλὰ εἰρήνης].

units.la: C. 15. v. 29. 'Επεὶ τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, εἰ ὅλως νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται; Alioquin quid facient qui baptizantur pro mortuis, si omnino mortui non resurgunt? Cur immerguntur pro mortuis, i.e. tanquam mortui, συνταφέντες αὐτῷ ἐν τῷ βαπτίσματι, consepulti cum eo, nempe Christo, in baptismate, Rom. 6.4. & Col. 2.12. si non ut per emersionem ex aqua, quod est typus resurrectionis post sepulturam, certiores fiant, quod si etiam ipsi resurgant a morte in peccatis ad novitatem vitæ, resurgent etiam cum Christo post mortem in gloriam? quasi diceret, In vanum utitur Ecclesia, symbolo Baptismi, si non est resurrectio. Est enim Baptismus mortis & resurrectionis Christi, & etiam omnium fidelium typus, & sic apud antiquos universim accipitur, ut videre est in animad. 1 Pet. 3. 22. 23. Atque hanc doctrinam appellat Zonaras, τὸ καθ' ἡμᾶς μυστήριον τῆς δυνάμεως, vim mysterii religionis Christianæ; plane affirmans eos ματαιοπονεῖν, frustra laborare, sive operam perdere, qui baptizantur, si de resurrectione dubitent, per
units.tr: Chap. 15. v. 29. "Otherwise what will they do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all?" [Ἐπεὶ τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, εἰ ὅλως νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται;] Why are they immersed for the dead, that is, as if they were dead? Buried with him in baptism [συνταφέντες αὐτῷ ἐν τῷ βαπτίσματι], buried together with Christ, Rom. 6.4 and Col. 2.12, if not so that by emersion from the water, which is a type of resurrection after burial, they might be more certain that, if they rise from death in sin to newness of life, they will also rise with Christ after death into glory? It is as if he said: the Church uses the symbol of baptism in vain, if there is no resurrection. For baptism is a type of the death and resurrection of Christ, and also of all the faithful, and so it is generally understood by the ancients, as may be seen in animad. on 1 Pet. 3.22, 23. Zonaras calls this doctrine the power of the mystery [τὸ καθ' ἡμᾶς μυστήριον τῆς δυνάμεως] of the Christian religion, and plainly affirms that those who are baptized labour in vain, that is, waste their effort, if they doubt the resurrection, by

units.la: per baptismum nempe & emersionem in aquam baptiseris, & ex ea emersionem, mortem & resurrectionem denotantes, per ea vero quae dicunt de ea dubitantes, vel in ea fidem non habentes. Quod qui faciunt, certe faciunt frustra: ἐὰν δὲ νεκρῶν, intelligi ait Chrysostomus, σωμάτων, in majorem fidem addens, ἢ γὰρ ὅτι τὸ τῆς ἀναστάσεως σῶμα ἀνάστασιν πιστεύων, &c. Propter baptizaris mortuus corporis resurrectionem credens, nempe quod non manet mortuum. Et tu quidem per verba dicis sive profiteris mortuorum resurrectionem, sacerdos autem in quadam imagine quae credidisti & per verba es confessus, etiam per res ipsas ostendit; quando absque signo credis, tunc tibi etiam praebet signum. Adulti enim cum baptizarentur, ore prius confessi sunt se credere in resurrectionem mortuorum, & deinde in ea fide baptizati sunt. Sic etiam Tertullianus, Pro mortuis tingui est pro corporibus tingui, mortuum enim corpus ostendimus. Quid facient qui pro corporibus baptizantur, si corpora non resurgant? Atque huic sententiae accedit etiam Theodoretus, ὁ βαπτιζόμενος τῶν νεκρῶν οὐ συμπάσχεται &c. Qui baptizatur Lomino consepelitur, ut cum mortis fuerit particeps, sit etiam particeps resurrectionis; si autem corpus est mortuum, & non resurgit, cur tandem baptizatur? Atque in hac ego sententia plene acquiesco, quicquid praeter vel aliud proferunt doctissimi viri a scopo & mente Apostoli prorsus alienum & incertum judicans.
units.tr: by baptism, namely, by immersion in water and emersion from it, signifying death and resurrection, but by what they say while doubting it, or not having faith in it. Those who do this certainly do it in vain. Chrysostom says that the words, "if the dead [are not raised]" [ἐὰν δὲ νεκρῶν], are to be understood as "of bodies" [σωμάτων], adding greater force: "for the one who is baptized, believing in the resurrection of the body [ἢ γὰρ ὅτι τὸ τῆς ἀναστάσεως σῶμα ἀνάστασιν πιστεύων], is baptized on account of the dead, namely because the dead body does not remain dead." And you indeed say or profess in words the resurrection of the dead, but the priest shows it by a certain image, in deeds, what you have believed and confessed in words; when you believe without a sign, then he also gives you a sign. For adults, when they were baptized, first confessed with the mouth that they believed in the resurrection of the dead, and then were baptized in that faith. So also Tertullian: "To be dipped for the dead is to be dipped for bodies, for we show the body to be dead. What will those do who are baptized for bodies, if bodies do not rise?" Theodoret also agrees with this view: "He who is baptized is buried with the Lord, so that as he has shared in the death, he may also share in the resurrection; but if the body is dead and does not rise, why is he baptized at all?" I fully acquiesce in this view, judging whatever else or otherwise the most learned men put forward to be wholly foreign to the aim and mind of the Apostle and uncertain.

units.la: V. 3. Vulgo legitur, "Ἄφρων, οὐ ὁ Γνώθι: insipiens, tu quod feminas &c. Cur non potius distinguitur & legitur, "Ἄφρων οὐ, ὁ Γνῶθι &c. Insipiens tu, quod feminas &c ut sonat in Anglico, Thou fool, that which thou soweth &c. &c. Et sic cum magis Emphatico sensu vitatur non necessaria metathesis.
units.tr: V. 3. It is commonly read, "Fool, that which" [Ἄφρων, οὐ ὁ Γνῶθι]: "Foolish one, you: what you sow" [insipiens, tu quod feminas]. Why is it not rather punctuated and read, "Fool, you, that which" [Ἄφρων οὐ, ὁ Γνῶθι], "Foolish one, you, what you sow" and so on? As it sounds in English: "Thou fool, that which thou soweth." And so, with a more emphatic sense, the unnecessary metathesis is avoided.

units.la: C. 16. v. 3, "Οταν ἢ ἀποδεχθέναμαι, ὡς ἂν δο-κιμάσητε, διὰ ἐπιστολῶν τούτους πέμψω ἀπενεγ-κεῖν τὴν χάριν ὑμῶν εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ. Cùm au-tem adfuero, quoscunque probaveritis, per Epi-stolas mittam eos auferre beneficentiam vestram ad Ierusalem.
units.tr: Chap. 16. v. 3. "And when I shall have arrived, whomever you shall approve, I will send them with letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem" [Οταν ἢ ἀποδεχθέναμαι, ὡς ἂν δοκιμάσητε, διὰ ἐπιστολῶν τούτους πέμψω ἀπενεγκεῖν τὴν χάριν ὑμῶν εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ]. "But when I shall be present, whomever you approve, by letters I will send them to bring your bounty to Jerusalem."

units.la: In secundam Epistolam ad Corinthios.
units.tr: On the Second Epistle to the Corinthians.

units.la: COR. c. 1. v. 9. Ἀλλὰ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἑαυ-τοῖς τὸ ἀπόκεμα τοῦ Θανάτου ἐσχήκαμεν. Imò habuimus ipsi in nos condemnationem mortis: i. e. adjudicati fuimus morti, ut con-textus valde innuit: ἀπόκεμα, ἀποκείμενα. Hesych. & Phavor.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 1. 9. [Ἀλλὰ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς τὸ ἀπόκριμα τοῦ θανάτου ἐσχήκαμεν.] Indeed, we ourselves had the sentence of death within ourselves: that is, we were adjudged to death, as the context strongly suggests. [ἀπόκεμα, ἀποκείμενα.] Hesychius and Phavorinus.

units.la: C. 2. v. 12. Ἐλθὼν ἢ εἰς τὴν Τρωάδα, εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἡ θύρας μοι ἀνεωγμένης ἐν Κυρίῳ, ὡς ἔσχηκα &c. Quum venissem autem Troadem, & ostium mihi apertum esset per Domi-num ad Evangelium Christi, non habui requiem spiritui meo &c. eò quòd non invenerim Titum fratrem meum illic, qui si praesens levis set mihi onus, quod soli adeò presse impendebat, ut nullam relaxationem habuerim spiritui meo. Valde cru-ciatum animo fuisse affirmat Theodoretus, cùm vi-deret multos ad praedicationem accedere, non ba-beus bens socium ministerii. Trajectiones hujusmodi, ut saepius dixi, sunt frequentissimae.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 2. 12. [Ἐλθὼν δὲ εἰς τὴν Τρωάδα εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ θύρας μοι ἀνεῳγμένης ἐν Κυρίῳ, ὡς ἔσχηκα...] When I had come to Troas for the gospel of Christ, and a door was opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit, etc., because I did not find Titus my brother there. Had he been present, he would have been a light burden to me, a burden that pressed so heavily on me alone that I had no relief for my spirit. Theodoret affirms that Paul was greatly tormented in mind, seeing many come to the preaching while he had no fellow-worker in the ministry. Transpositions of this kind, as I have often said, are very frequent.

units.la: C. 4. v. 2. συνιζῶντες ἑαυτὸς. approbantes nosmetipsos In quo sensu vox eadem occurrit, 7.11. & alibi.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 4. 2. [συνιστῶντες ἑαυτούς] approving ourselves. The same word occurs in this sense at 7. 11 and elsewhere.

units.la: V. 4. Ἐν οἷς ὁ Θεὸς τῶν αἰῶνος τούτου ἐπύφλωσε τὰ νοήματα τῶν ἀπίστων εἰς τὸ μὴ αὐγάσαι αὐτοῖς τὸν φωτισμὸν τῆς εὐαγγελίου τῆς δόξης τοῦ Χριστοῦ. ut idoneus fiat sensus & constructio, τὸ ἐν vertendum reor, inter, & in hoc & in praecedente versu, sequentia vero per metathesin, ut fecerunt aliqui è Veteribus. Quod si opertum est Evangelium nostrum, ἐν ἀπολλυμένοις, inter eos qui percunt est opertum. Inter quos Deus excaecavit mentes infidelium hujus saeculi, nè luceat illis lux gloriosi Evangelii Christi, i. e. luceat ut videant & intelligant. Videtur Paulus respexisse ad Isaiae 6, 10. ubi dixit ei Dominus. Vade &c. Excaeca cor populi hujus, & aures ejus aggrava, & oculos ejus claude, ne forte videant oculis &c. & convertantur; ἰάσωμαι est proprie evum, & non mundus. Infidelium hujus saeculi intelligit praecipue Judaeos. Si quis in trajectione adhuc haereat, praeterquam quod é Veteribus senserunt idem, sciant velim innumeras esse ejusmodi in N.T. E. g. praeter quas jam alibi memoravimus. Job. 11. 4. ἀπῆλθεν εἰς Ἐφραΐμ, λεγομένην πόλιν, pro εἰς πόλιν λεγομένην Ἐφραΐμ, abiit in civitatem quae vocatur Ephraim. Act. 13.1. Ἦσαν δέ τινες ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ κατὰ τὴν οὖσαν ἐκκλησίαν προφῆται καὶ διδάσκαλοι, pro ἦσαν δέ τινες προφῆται καὶ διδάσκαλοι κατὰ τὴν οὖσαν ἐκκλησίαν ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ. Erant vero quidam Prophetae & Doctores in Ecclesia, quae fuit in Antiochia. & 25, 22. Ὁ δὲ ἀνέκαμψε, φησίν, ἀκούσομαί αὐτοῦ. pro Ὁ δὲ φησίν, ἀνέκαμψε αὐτός. Ille vero inquit, cras audies cum. elum. Vide etiam Animad. Act. 13. 27. 1 Pet. 3. 21, 22.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 4. 4. [Ἐν οἷς ὁ θεὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου ἐτύφλωσε τὰ νοήματα τῶν ἀπίστων εἰς τὸ μὴ αὐγάσαι αὐτοῖς τὸν φωτισμὸν τοῦ εὐαγγελίου τῆς δόξης τοῦ Χριστοῦ.] So that the sense and construction may be suitable, I think [ἐν] should be rendered "among", both in this verse and in the preceding one, while the following words should be taken by transposition, as some of the Ancients did. If our gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who perish. Among these the God of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ should shine on them; that is, it shines so that they may see and understand. Paul seems to have had in view Isaiah 6. 10, where the Lord said to him: "Go... make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest they see with their eyes... and be converted and I should heal them" [ἰάσωμαι]. The word [αἰῶνος] properly means "age", not "world". By "the unbelievers of this age" he chiefly means the Jews. If anyone is still troubled by the transposition, let him know that, besides the fact that some of the Ancients thought the same, there are countless such transpositions in the New Testament, e.g., besides those I have already mentioned elsewhere. John 11. 54: "he went away into a city called Ephraim", for "into the city called Ephraim". Acts 13. 1: [Ἦσαν δέ τινες ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ κατὰ τὴν οὖσαν ἐκκλησίαν προφῆται καὶ διδάσκαλοι], for "there were certain prophets and teachers in the church that was at Antioch". And Acts 25. 22: [Ὁ δὲ ἀνέκαμψε, φησίν, ἀκούσομαί αὐτοῦ], for "he said: tomorrow you shall hear him". See also my Animadversions on Acts 13. 27 and 1 Pet. 3. 21, 22.

units.la: V. 6. 'O εἰπὼν, qui jussit è tenebris lucem splendescere: εἰπον, ῥῆμα προστακτικόν. Vox mandatoria, ut vox אמר apud Hebraeos.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 4. 6. [Ὁ εἰπών], who commanded the light to shine out of darkness: [εἰπών] is an imperative verb, a word of command, like the word [אמר] among the Hebrews.

units.la: C. 5. v. 1. Ἐὰν ἡ ἐπίγειος ἡμῶν οἰκία τῆς σκηνῶς pro ἐὰν ἡ ἐπίγειος οἰκία τῆς (ζωῆς ἡμῶν καταλυθῇ. Si terrestris domus hujus nostri tabernaculi dissolvatur &c. τῆς positum est pro τότε. Vide similes metathesis: 2 Pet. 3. 2. Jud. 18. & alibi
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5. 1. [Ἐὰν ἡ ἐπίγειος ἡμῶν οἰκία τῆς σκηνῶς] for [ἐὰν ἡ ἐπίγειος οἰκία τῆς (ζωῆς ἡμῶν) καταλυθῇ]: If the earthly house of our tabernacle is dissolved, etc. [τῆς] stands for [τότε]. See similar transpositions at 2 Pet. 3. 2, Jude 18, and elsewhere.

units.la: V. 3. Versus iste, opinor, parenthesi includendus, (Εἴγε καὶ ἐνδυσάμενοι οὐ γυμνοὶ εὑρεθησόμεθα.) Et vero hoc loco videtur esse ῥῆμα ευκτικόν, & vim habet Optativi. Precationes enim ejusmodi apud Apostolum saepe interveniunt in medio sensu, et frequenter vacat. Adeo ut verborum sensus & ordo sit hujusmodi. In hoc enim domicilio ingemiscimus habitationem nostram, quae ex coelo est, superindui cupientes. (Utinam etiam induti non nudi reperiamur.) Nam qui sumus in hoc tabernaculo ingemiscimus gravati, non quod velimus e ui, sed superindui ut absorbeatur quod mortale est à vita. οὐ γὰρ ἀπεκδύσασθαι τὸ σῶμα, ἀλλ' ἐπενδύσασθαι τὴν ἀθανασίαν ὀφείλομεν, Non enim exuere corpus, sed superinducere immortalitatem cupimus. Theodoret. Continuare vitam lucrifacta morte per vicariam demutationem, ut Tertull. Precatur interim Apostolus, ut in ultimo die inveniantur coelestem habitationem superinduti, & non ea destituti. Timet, μή πως δοκῶ τις ἐξ ἀντῶν ὑστερηκέναι, ne quis eorum comperiatur se frustratus esse. Vide similes loquendi formas, Matth. 22. 11. & Apocal. 3. 18. 16. 15. Quoad usum τῆς Εἰ, in formula precationis sive Optativi, vide Animad. Luc. 12. 49.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5. 3. I think this verse should be enclosed in a parenthesis: [Εἴγε καὶ ἐνδυσάμενοι οὐ γυμνοὶ εὑρεθησόμεθα.] Here indeed [εἴγε] seems to be an optative verb and has the force of the optative. Prayers of this kind often occur in the Apostle's sentences, and are frequently superfluous. So the sense and order of the words are as follows: "For in this dwelling we groan, desiring to be clothed upon with our habitation which is from heaven" (I pray that we may be found clothed, not naked). "For we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened, not because we wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life." [οὐ γὰρ ἀπεκδύσασθαι τὸ σῶμα, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπενδύσασθαι τὴν ἀθανασίαν ὀφείλομεν]: we desire not to strip off the body, but to put on immortality. Theodoret. To continue life, death being gained through a substituted change, as Tertullian has it. Meanwhile the Apostle prays that on the last day they may be found clothed with the heavenly habitation and not stripped of it. He fears [μή πως δοκῶ τις ἐξ αὐτῶν ὑστερηκέναι], lest any of them be found to have been cheated. See similar forms of speech at Matt. 22. 11 and Rev. 3. 18; 16. 15. On the use of [εἰ] in the form of a prayer or optative, see my Animadversions on Luke 12. 49.
Chapter 6.

units.la: C. 6. v. 13. Τλὼ ἡ αὐτλὼ ἀντιμισθίαν (ὡς τέκνοις λέγω) πλατύνθητε καὶ ὑμεῖς. Subaudi xτ, secundum vero eandem compensationem (ut filiis loquor) dilatamini & vos. Quasi diceret, sicut cor meum dilatatum est erga vos, v. 11, sic etiam vicissim dilatamini & vos in visceribus vestris erga nos. Ubique locus est Accusativo, si intelligas xτ.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 6. 13. [Τὴν δὲ αὐτὴν ἀντιμισθίαν (ὡς τέκνοις λέγω) πλατύνθητε καὶ ὑμεῖς.] Supply a word such as [χάριν]: "Now in the same recompense (I speak as to children), you also be enlarged." As if he said: just as my heart has been enlarged toward you (v. 11), so in turn you also be enlarged in your bowels toward us. The accusative fits everywhere if you supply it.

units.la: C. 8. v. 1, Τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ &c. Ingentem beneficentiam, quae data est in Ecclesiis Macedoniae. Collectam significat, quae fiebat in Ecclesiis Macedoniae, quae abundavit etiam supra vires in copiosa benignitate in ministerium sanctorum Dei in Jerusalem, de qua Rom. 15. 26. χάρις, δώρεα, Hesych. χάριν Θεοῦ. Est Hebraismus, rectéque vertitur, ingentem beneficentiam, vel ingens donum quod datum est. Qualis est Jud. 13. 6. אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים, ἀνθρωπος Θεοῦ, vir Dei i.e. cujus species erat augustior quàm hominum communiter, ut Drusius, vel qui miram in modum erat faciei veneranda, ut Vatablus. Psal. 80.10. אֲרָזֵי אֵל, τὰς κέδρους τοῦ Θεοῦ, Cedros Dei, i.e. procerae Cedros & Psal. 36. 6. צִדְקָתְךָ כְּהַרְרֵי־אֵל, Justitia tua Domine, ὡς ὄρη Θεοῦ, sicut montes Dei, i.e. excelsi montes. Scriptura enim rem excellentem significaturā, subjungit ei unum ex Dei nominibus. Scbindi, ut videre est etiam in Hebraeo, Gen 30. 8. & 1 Sam 14. 15. Vide Bezam in verba illa, λύπη τοῦ Θεοῦ, 10. 4. atque hujus Epistolae 11. 2. ubi verba illa, ζηλῶ γὰρ ὑμᾶς Θεοῦ ζήλῳ. Schol. Græc. interpretatur, θεϊκῶς φιλῶ, Ardenter amo vos.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 8. 1. [Τὴν χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ, etc.] A great bounty, which was given in the churches of Macedonia. It signifies the collection which was made in the churches of Macedonia, which abounded even beyond their means in rich liberality, for the ministry to the saints of God in Jerusalem; see Rom. 15. 26. [χάρις] means gift, Hesychius. The phrase [χάριν Θεοῦ] is a Hebraism and is rightly rendered "a great bounty" or "a great gift which has been given". Such is Judg. 13. 6, [אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים, ἄνθρωπος Θεοῦ], "a man of God", that is, one whose appearance was more majestic than men generally, as Drusius says, or who had a face of wondrous venerable aspect, as Vatablus says. Psalm 80. 10, [אֲרָזֵי אֵל, τὰς κέδρους τοῦ Θεοῦ], "cedars of God", that is, tall cedars; and Psalm 36. 6, [צִדְקָתְךָ כְּהַרְרֵי־אֵל, ὡς ὄρη Θεοῦ], "your righteousness is like the mountains of God", that is, lofty mountains. For Scripture, wishing to signify an excellent thing, adds to it one of the names of God; this may be seen also in the Hebrew at Gen. 30. 8 and 1 Sam. 14. 15. See Beza on the words "sorrow of God", 10. 4, and of this Epistle at 11. 2, where the words [ζηλῶ γὰρ ὑμᾶς θεοῦ ζήλῳ] ("I am jealous over you with godly jealousy"). The Greek scholiast explains it as [θεϊκῶς φιλῶ], "I love you divinely", that is, I love you ardently.

units.la: V, 18, 19 Συνεπέμψαμεν δὲ μετ' αὐτοῦ τὸν ἀδελφὸν (οὗ ὁ ἔπαινος ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ διὰ πασῶν τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν, οὐ μόνον δὲ ἀλλὰ καὶ χειροτονηθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν συνέκδημος ἡμῶν) μὰν) αὐν ταύτῃ τῇ χάριτι τῇ διακονουμένῃ ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν τὸν Κυρίου δόξαν καὶ προθυμίαν ὑμῶν. Una vero misimus cum eo fratrem (cuius laus est in Evangelio, nec id solum, sed etiam qui constitutus est ab Ecclesiis socius peregrinationis nostrae; cum hoc ministerio sive dono, quod administratur a nobis ad ipsius Domini gloriam, & ad vestram animationem. Inprimis hoc loco visum est parenthesim latius extendere, magis enim consonum est dicere hunc fratrem missum à Paulo vel ab Ecclesiis una cum Tito, cum hoc ministerio sive dono, quàm ab Ecclesiis constitutum vel delectum socium peregrinationis cum eo ministerio vel dono dicere. Et deinde προθυμίαν ὑμῶν, recte opinor verti, ad animationem vestram. Est enim animare, προθυμίαν ἐμβάλλειν, nempe ut sitis in dando alacriores & promptiores, cum probos atque integros viros esse perspexeritis, qui pecunias vestras recipiunt & administrant, ut Chrysostomus.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 8. 18, 19. [Συνεπέμψαμεν δὲ μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ τὸν ἀδελφόν]: Together with him we sent the brother (whose praise is in the gospel through all the churches, and not only so, but who was also appointed by the churches as our companion on the journey), with this bounty, which is administered by us to the glory of the Lord himself and to your eagerness. In the first place, in this passage it seems better to extend the parenthesis more widely, for it is more fitting to say that this brother was sent by Paul or by the churches together with Titus, with this ministry or gift, than to say that he was appointed or chosen by the churches as a companion on the journey with that ministry or gift. Then, I think, [προθυμίαν ὑμῶν] is rightly rendered "to encourage you". For to encourage is [προθυμίαν ἐμβάλλειν], namely, that you may be more eager and ready in giving, once you have perceived that the men who receive and administer your money are upright and honest, as Chrysostom says.

units.la: V. 23. Εἴτε ὑπὲρ Τίτου &c. εἴτε ἀδελφοὶ ἡμῶν &c. post Titus repetendum ἀπὸ τῆς κοινῆς quod praecessit. v. 20. τὶς ἡμᾶς μωμήσεται, & ante ἀδελφοὶ ἡμῶν, subaudiendum ἐστιν. Sive quis nos carpat propter Titum, Socius est meus & apud vos adjutor, sive sunt fratres nostri, apostoli Ecclesiarum, gloria Christi. Commendat singulis separatim & conjunctim, primo fratrem cujus laus fuit in evangelio, v. 18. probabiliter Lucan, cum eo fratrem quem in multis probaverat diligentem, forte Barnabam, v. 22. tertio Titum quia erat socius &c. Et tum denique omnes tres conjunctim, quia erant fratres, apostoli ecclesiarum ad deportandum earum beneficentiam ad sanctos in Ierusalem, & gloria Christi. Atque hoc ab eo factum ut ab omni suspicione eos liberaret, ràret, ne quis illos vel ipsum carperet in plenitudine quæ administrata erat ab eis, providebant enim bona non solum coram Deo sed etiam coram hominibus. v. 20 & 21.
units.tr: Verse 23. "Whether concerning Titus [εἴτε ὑπὲρ Τίτου] &c., or our brothers [εἴτε ἀδελφοὶ ἡμῶν] &c." After "Titus" must be supplied what went before in verse 20, "from the common fund" [ἀπὸ τῆς κοινῆς], and before "our brothers" must be understood "is" [ἐστιν]. Whether someone finds fault with us on account of Titus, he is my partner and helper among you; or they are our brothers, apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ. He commends them separately and together: first, the brother whose praise is in the gospel (v. 18), probably Luke; with him, a brother whom he had proved diligent in many things, perhaps Barnabas (v. 22); third, Titus, because he was a partner &c. Finally, all three together, because they were brothers, apostles of the churches, for carrying their generosity to the saints in Jerusalem, and the glory of Christ. He did this so that he might free them from every suspicion, lest anyone blame them or himself in the abundance that was administered by them, for they provided good things not only in the sight of God but also in the sight of men. Verses 20 and 21.

units.la: C. 9. v. 5. Εὐλογίαν ὑμῶν, beneficentiam vel liberalem vestram collectionem, à λέγω colligo; εὐλογία, πλεονασμὸς ἀφδῶν ἐξ ἐκσότητος διὰ ᾱᾱ. Phav.
units.tr: Chapter 9, verse 5. "Your blessing [εὐλογίαν ὑμῶν]," that is, your bountiful or liberal collection, from λέγω, I gather. εὐλογία is a pleonasm [πλεονασμός] ... Phav.

units.la: V.8, 9, 10, &c. Δυνατὸς ἡ ὁ Θεὸς πᾶσαν χάριν περισσεῦσαι εἰς ὑμᾶς, ἵνα ἐν παντὶ πάντοτε πᾶσαν αὐτάρκειαν ἔχοντες περισσεύητε εἰς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθόν (καθὼς γέγραπται, ἐσκόρπισεν, ἔδωκε τοῖς πένησιν, ἡ δικαιοσύνη αὐτοῦ μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα· ὁ δὲ ἐπιχορηγῶν σπέρμα τῷ σπείροντι, καὶ ἄρτον εἰς βρῶσιν, χορηγήσει καὶ πληθυνεῖ τὸ σπέρμα ὑμῶν καὶ αὐξήσει τὰ γενήματα τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὑμῶν) ἐν παντὶ πλουτιζόμενοι εἰς πᾶσαν ἁπλότητα, ἥτις κατεργάζεται δι' ἡμῶν εὐχαριστίαν τῷ Θεῷ, ὅτι ἡ διακονία τῆς λειτουργίας ταύτης οὐ μόνον ἐστὶ προσαναπληροῦσα τὰ ὑστερήματα τῶν ἁγίων, ἀλλὰ καὶ περισσεύουσα διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστιῶν τῷ Θεῷ· διὰ τῆς δοκιμῆς τῆς διακονίας ταύτης δοξάζοντες τὸν Θεὸν ἐπὶ τῇ ὑποταγῇ κτλ. Qui verò potens est Deus omnem gratiam facere abundare in vobis, ut in omnibus semper omnem sufficientiam habeatis, abundantes in omne opus bonum, (sicut scriptum est, Dispersit, dedit pauperibus, misericordia ejus manet in æternum. At qui suppeditat semen seminanti, & panem ad escam, suppeditet & multiplicet sementem vestram, & augeat fructus misericordiæ vestræ) in omni divites facti ad omnem liberalitatem (quæ adoperatur gratiarum actionem per nos Deo, quoniam ministerium oblationis hujus non solum est supplens inopias sanctorum, sed etiam redundans per vel propter multas gratiarum actiones Deo) per probationem ministerii hujus hujus glorificantes Deum in subjectione &c. Non equidem video quid opus sit hoc loco vel Hebraismo vel Atticismo, ut salvetur sensus & constructio. Si enim bene animadvertantur binæ quæ in his verbis occurrunt parentheses, prout nunc distinctæ, adeo planus est sensus & syntaxis, ut liceat currenti legere & intelligere, participiis παντοχρατορὸς & δοξάζοντες regendis à verbo εὐχαριστοῦντες, v. 8. Satius etiam putavi in formula precationis vertere, quia solenne est Paulo, ut observant Patres, cum voto & prece concludere exhortationes. Multiplicet & augeat fructus misericordiæ vestræ, Est ingeminatio voti, nempe ne deficiant unquam, sed ut omni bono sufficienter abundantes, habeant semper quod dispergant in pauperes. Δικαιοσύνη enim proculdubio hoc loco significat misericordiam, ut sæpe alibi: & sic sensit Theophylactus. Vocem enim חסד LXX frequenter vertunt δικαιοσύνη, de quo vide animad. Matth. 1.
units.tr: Verses 8, 9, 10, &c. "But God is able to make all grace abound toward you [Δυνατὸς δὲ ὁ Θεὸς πᾶσαν χάριν περισσεῦσαι εἰς ὑμᾶς], that you, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work [ἵνα ἐν παντὶ πάντοτε πᾶσαν αὐτάρκειαν ἔχοντες περισσεύητε εἰς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθόν], (as it is written: He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever [καθὼς γέγραπται, ἐσκόρπισεν, ἔδωκε τοῖς πένησιν, ἡ δικαιοσύνη αὐτοῦ μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα]; and he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness [ὁ δὲ ἐπιχορηγῶν σπέρμα τῷ σπείροντι, καὶ ἄρτον εἰς βρῶσιν, χορηγήσει καὶ πληθυνεῖ τὸ σπέρμα ὑμῶν καὶ αὐξήσει τὰ γενήματα τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὑμῶν]), being enriched in everything for all liberality [ἐν παντὶ πλουτιζόμενοι εἰς πᾶσαν ἁπλότητα], which produces through us thanksgiving to God [ἥτις κατεργάζεται δι' ἡμῶν εὐχαριστίαν τῷ Θεῷ]; because the ministry of this service is not only supplying the wants of the saints, but also overflowing through many thanksgivings to God [ὅτι ἡ διακονία τῆς λειτουργίας ταύτης οὐ μόνον ἐστὶ προσαναπληροῦσα τὰ ὑστερήματα τῶν ἁγίων, ἀλλὰ καὶ περισσεύουσα διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστιῶν τῷ Θεῷ]; through the proof of this ministry glorifying God for your subjection [διὰ τῆς δοκιμῆς τῆς διακονίας ταύτης δοξάζοντες τὸν Θεὸν ἐπὶ τῇ ὑποταγῇ κτλ.]. But God, who is mighty, make all grace abound toward you, that you, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work (as it is written: He has dispersed abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever. Now he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, supply and multiply your seed, and increase the fruits of your righteousness), being made rich in everything to all liberality (which works thanksgiving to God through us, since the ministry of this offering is not only supplying the wants of the saints, but also overflowing through many thanksgivings to God), glorifying God through the proof of this ministry in subjection. &c. I certainly do not see what need there is in this place for either a Hebraism or an Atticism, so that the sense and construction may be saved. For if the two parentheses that occur in these words are rightly noted, as they are now distinguished, the sense and syntax are so plain that a reader running through may understand them, the participles [...] and δοξάζοντες being governed by the verb εὐχαριστοῦντες, verse 8. I have also thought it better to render it in the form of a prayer, because, as the Fathers observe, it is characteristic of Paul to conclude his exhortations with a wish and a prayer. May he multiply and increase the fruits of your mercy. This is a repetition of the wish, namely that they may never fail, but, abounding sufficiently in every good thing, they may always have something to scatter among the poor. For δικαιοσύνη in this place undoubtedly means mercy, as often elsewhere, and so Theophylact understood it. For the Seventy often render the word חסד by δικαιοσύνη, on which see my notes on Matthew 1.

units.la: C. 11. v. 4. Καλῶς ἠνείχεσθε: Dictum εἰρωνικῶς vel Ironice; ut est illud Mar. 7. 9. καλῶς ἀθετεῖτε, pulchrè sive belle rejicitis præceptum Dei, ut traditionem vestram observetis: & etiam hoc loco, Si quis enim veniens alium Jesum prædicet, quem nos non prædicavimus, &c. pulchrè sive belle toleraretis eum. Ἀνέχεσθε γὰρ &c. Toleratis enim si quis vos in servitutem redigat, v. 20. Levitatem eorum dum arguit, monstrat quomodo mentes eorum, quod modo dixerat, corrupta fuerint à simplicitate quæ est in Christo. Belle narras est Ironia Proverbialis de re dicta vehementer absurda. Eras.
units.tr: Chapter 11, verse 4. "For you suffer well [Καλῶς ἠνείχεσθε]": said ironically, or in irony, as in that saying of Mark 7:9, "you reject well [καλῶς ἀθετεῖτε] the commandment of God, that you may keep your tradition"; and in this place also: "For if one who comes preaches another Jesus, whom we have not preached," etc., you would bear with him well and nicely. "For you suffer [Ἀνέχεσθε γὰρ] &c." For you suffer it if anyone brings you into bondage, verse 20. While he rebukes their levity, he shows how their minds, as he had just said, were corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ. "Nicely you tell it" is a proverbial irony about a matter said to be extremely absurd. Erasmus.

units.la: C. 12. v. 21. Μὴ πάλιν ἐλθόντα με ταπεινώσῃ ὁ Θεός μου πρὸς ὑμᾶς. Ne rursus quando venero, Deus me vilem reddat apud vos. Alludens ad quod antea dixerat, 10 ɩ.ǒ xᾱ ᾱεξ̔ωπον μῆ πατπιρός, Qui coram vilis sum. Quasi diceret, Meuo ne quomodo me pro vili habuistis, cùm essem antea apud vos, sic etiam cùm rursus ad vos venero, Deus permittat me vilem haberi in oculis vestris, atque inde lugere cogar multos eorum qui peccaverunt, & non egerunt pænitentiam, nec, quia me despectui habent, curabunt agere. Ut πατπιρὸς est vilis, sic πατπεινόω est vilem reddo.
units.tr: Chapter 12, verse 21. "Lest again, when I come, my God humble me before you [Μὴ πάλιν ἐλθόντα με ταπεινώσῃ ὁ Θεός μου πρὸς ὑμᾶς]." Lest when I come again, God make me base in your sight. He alludes to what he had said before, who am base in presence [ὁ ἀπὼν ... ταπεινός? ], as if to say: just as you once regarded me as worthless when I was with you before, so, when I come to you again, may God allow me to be held in contempt in your eyes, and so I be forced to mourn many of those who have sinned and have not repented, nor will they, because they hold me in contempt, take care to repent. As πατπιρὸς is base, so ταπεινόω is I make base.

units.la: C. 13. v. 5. Ἑαυτὸς πειράζετε εἰ ἐστὲ ἐν τῇ πίστει, ἑαυτὸς δοκιμάζετε (ἢ οὐκ ἐπιγινώσκετε ἑαυτὸς ὅτι Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν ἐστιν;) εἰ μή τι ἀδόκιμοί ἐστε. Versus iste ut & proximè sequentes necessariò respiciunt & respondent verbis in initio tertii, sensu sequente in hunc modum. Ἐπεὶ δοκιμὴν ζητεῖτε τοῦ ἐν ἐμοὶ λαλοῦντος Χριστοῦ (ὃς εἰς ὑμᾶς οὐκ ἀσθενεῖ &c.) ἑαυτοὺς πειράζετε, εἰ ἐστὲ ἐν τῇ πίστει, ἑαυτοὺς δοκιμάζετε, εἰ μή τι ἀδόκιμοί ἐστε &c. Quandoquidem quaeritis probationem in me loquentis Christi (qui erga vos non infirmatur &c.) tentate vosmet ipsos num sitis in fide, vosmet ipsos probate, si vel utrum non sitis sine probatione in vobis loquentis Christi, quam in me quaerere non veremini. Spero autem vos cogniturus quod nos non sumus ἀδόκιμοι, i. e. ut respondeat tertio, sine probatione in me loquentis Christi. Precor autem Deum ne quid mali faciatis, non [precor] ut nos appareamus δόκιμοι, i. e. cum probatione in nobis loquentis Christi, sed ut vos faciatis quod bonum est, nos vero simus ἀδόκιμοι, sine probatione illa. Ἀδόκιμοι in hoc loco nil aliud significat quàm ἄρεu ὁ δόκιμος, ab ἀ privativa, & δόκιμοι, sine probatione vel in Apostolo vel in Corinthiis loquentis Christi. Verba praetermissa illaeso sensu parenthesi includuntur. Ut verò, si adhuc opus est, quid velim planius fiat, liceat sine tædio percurrere totum Apostoli de hac re sermonem brevi Paraphrasi. Audiverat Apostolus fuisse inter Corinthios qui ipsum non pro dignitate Apostoli æstimabant, sed habebant pro homine secundum carnem ambulante, 10. 2. qui inter se etiam dixerant, Epistolæ quidem ejus graves sunt & validæ, sed præsentia corporis infirma, & sermo contemptibilis, atque hinc sumpserunt sibi licentiam liberius peccandi, non credentes omnino venturum, ideoque inflati, 1 Cor. 4. 18. vel si veniret, non venturum cum virga & terrore; imò non veriti sunt ipsum Apostolatum in quæstionem vocare. Quærebant enim δοκιμὴν, probationem in eo loquentis Christi. Ut ergo horum audaciæ obvenirer, nec tamen cogeretur, quod nullo modo voluit, potestatem, quam dederat ei Deus ad ædificationem, & non ad destructionem, cum severitate exercere, placuit eos præmonere. Διὰ τοῦτο, propter hoc, ut est v. 10 hæc absens scribo vobis, & tertiâ hac vice, ut est in initio capitis, ad vos venio, nempe in hac Epistola, quoniam ex ore duorum vel trium testium stabilietur omne verbum, ut omnino absque dubio fiatis certiores me venturum, idque cum virga, sicut enim vobis antea dixerim cum essem vobiscum præsens, & uti absens vobis annuntiaverim in priore Epistola, sic etiam denuo vobis scribo, & iis qui peccaverunt, & reliquis omnibus fore ut si rursus venero non parcam. At verò quod audio, vos non creditis hanc mihi a Deo concreditam esse potestatem, sed pro contemptibili habetis, ideóque quæritis δοκιμὴν, probationem in me loquentis Christi, quem vos non invenietis infirmum si venero, sed potentem inter vos; nam etsi crucifixus fuit ex infirmitate, vivit tamen men ex potentia Dei; & etiam nos, quamvis infirmi sumus cum eo, vivemus cum eo ex potentia Dei adversum vos. Quoniam vero quaeritis probationem in nobis loquentis Christi, horror & admoneo vos, ut priusquam quaeratis eam in nobis, velitis vosmet ipsos experiri, num sitis in fide, δοκιμάζετε ἑαυτούς, εἰ μήν τι ἀδόκιμοί ἐστε, Probate vosmet ipsos, utrum non sitis sine probatione in vobis loquentis Christi, si forte possibile est, cum toties vobis praedicaverim, & scripserim, vos non scire vosmet ipsos, quod Jesus Christus sit in vobis. Spero autem vos olim cognituros, quod nos non sumus ἀδόκιμοι, i.e. sine probatione quam in me quaeritis, sed nollem ea uti, ideoque precor Deum, ne quid mali vos faciatis, ἵνα ἡμεῖς ἀδόκιμοι φανῶμεν, Non [precor] ut nos appareamus ἀδόκιμοι, cum probatione in nobis loquentis Christi, cum potestate Apostoli, sed ut vos quod bonum est faciatis, & ut nos simus tanquam ἀδόκιμοι, non habentes opus ut utamur potestate nostra cum severitate, quam dedit nobis Deus ad aedificationem, & non ad destructionem. Emendatio enim vestra est quam nos optamus, gaudentes cum vos sitis validi, nos vero infirmi, i.e. tanquam ἀδόκιμοι, non habentes occasionem potestatem vel authoritatem nostram demonstrandi. Quia non possumus aliquid contra veritatem, i.e. cum vos quod bonum est faciatis, sed pro veritate, quando vos contra ipsam non veremini peccare. Atque hic germanus mihi videtur sensus & scopus hujus loci, & vocis ἀδόκιμοι. Ludere videtur Apostolus in vocem δοκιμάζω, more scribendi apud ipsum familiari.
units.tr: Chapter 13, verse 5. "Test yourselves whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves [Ἑαυτὸς πειράζετε εἰ ἐστὲ ἐν τῇ πίστει, ἑαυτὸς δοκιμάζετε]; or do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? [ἢ οὐκ ἐπιγινώσκετε ἑαυτὸς ὅτι Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν ἐστιν;] unless perhaps you are reprobates [εἰ μή τι ἀδόκιμοί ἐστε]." This verse, like the ones immediately following, necessarily looks back to and answers the words at the beginning of the third chapter, the sense being as follows: Since you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me (who is not weak toward you, &c.), test yourselves whether you are in the faith, prove yourselves, unless you are reprobates &c. Since you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me (who is not weak toward you, &c.), test yourselves whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves, whether or not you are without proof of Christ speaking in you, which you do not hesitate to seek in me. I hope, however, that you will come to know that we are not ἀδόκιμοι, that is, as the third point answers, without proof of Christ speaking in me. But I pray God that you do no evil; not that we may appear δόκιμοι, that is, with proof of Christ speaking in us, but that you may do what is good, and we may be ἀδόκιμοι, without that proof. Ἀδόκιμοι in this place means nothing other than ἄρεu ὁ δόκιμος, from the privative ἀ and δόκιμος: without proof of Christ speaking either in the Apostle or among the Corinthians. Words omitted, with the sense left intact, are enclosed in parentheses. But so that my meaning may be made plainer, if it is still needed, let the reader run without weariness through the whole of the Apostle's discourse on this matter in a brief paraphrase. The Apostle had heard that there were among the Corinthians those who did not esteem him according to the dignity of an apostle, but regarded him as a man walking according to the flesh (2 Cor. 10:2), who also said among themselves: his letters are indeed weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible; and from this they took for themselves a licence to sin more freely, not believing that he would come at all, and therefore they were puffed up (1 Cor. 4:18), or if he came, that he would not come with a rod and in terror. Indeed they did not fear to call his very apostleship into question. For they sought a proof of Christ speaking in him. So, in order to meet the boldness of these men, yet without being compelled to do what he by no means wished, that is, to exercise with severity the power which God had given him for building up and not for tearing down, he resolved to forewarn them. On this account, that is, as in verse 10, I write these things while absent to you, and for the third time, as at the beginning of the chapter, I come to you, namely in this letter, since by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall be established; so that you may be made entirely certain without doubt that I am coming, and with a rod.
