For just as I told you before when I was present with you, and as I announced to you while absent in my former letter, so now I write to you again: to those who have sinned and to all the rest, that if I come again I will not spare. But what I hear is that you do not believe this power has been entrusted to me by God, but hold it in contempt, and therefore you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me, whom you will not find weak if I come, but mighty among you; for although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God; and we also, though we are weak with him, shall live with him by the power of God toward you. Since indeed you seek a proof of Christ speaking in us, I urge and admonish you that, before you seek it in us, you would wish to test yourselves, whether you are in the faith, [δοκιμάζετε ἑαυτούς, εἰ μήν τι ἀδόκιμοί ἐστε]; prove yourselves, whether you are not without proof of Christ speaking in you, if perhaps it is possible, since I have so often preached to you and written to you, that you do not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you. But I hope that you will one day know that we are not ἀδόκιμοι, that is, without the proof that you seek in me, but I would not wish to use it. Therefore I pray God that you do no evil, so that we may appear ἀδόκιμοι; not that we may appear ἀδόκιμοι, with proof of Christ speaking in us, with the power of an Apostle, but that you may do what is good, and that we may be as ἀδόκιμοι, having no need to use our power with severity, which God gave us for building up and not for tearing down. For your amendment is what we desire, rejoicing when you are strong, and we weak, that is, as ἀδόκιμοι, having no occasion to demonstrate our power or authority. For we can do nothing against the truth, that is, when you do what is good, but for the truth, when you do not hesitate to sin against it. This seems to me to be the genuine sense and aim of this place, and of the word ἀδόκιμοι. The Apostle seems to play on the word δοκιμάζω, in the manner of writing that is familiar to him.

units.la: In Epistolam ad Galatas.
units.tr: On the Epistle to the Galatians.

units.la: GAL. c. 2. v. 2, 3. &c. 'Ἀνέβλω ἡ καὶ ἀπο-καλυψιν, κ) ἀνεθέμην αὐτοῖς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, ὃ κηρύσσω ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι, καὶ ἰδίαν δὲ τοῖς δοκοῦσι, μήπως εἰς κενὸν τρέχω ἢ ἔδραμον. ἀλλ' οὐδὲ Τίτος ὁ σὺν ἐμοὶ Ἕλλην ὢν ἠναγκάσθη περιτμηθῆναι, διὰ δὲ τοὺς παρεισάκτους ψευδαδέλφους, οἵτινες παρεισῆλθον κατασκοπῆσαι τὴν ἐλευθερίαν ἡμῶν ἣν ἔχομεν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ἵνα ἡμᾶς καταδουλώσωνται· οἷς οὐδὲ πρὸς ὥραν εἴξαμεν τῇ ὑποταγῇ, ἵνα ἡ ἀλήθεια τοῦ εὐαγγελίου διαμείνῃ πρὸς ὑμᾶς. Ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν δοκούντων εἶναί τι, ὁποῖοί ποτε ἦσαν, οὐδέν μοι διαφέρει &c.
units.tr: Gal. 2:2, 3, etc.: "And I went up by revelation, and communicated to them the gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately to those who seemed to be something, lest I should run, or had run, in vain. But neither was Titus, who was with me, though a Greek, compelled to be circumcised; and that because of the false brethren brought in unawares, who came in privately to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage; to whom we did not yield by subjection, no, not for an hour, that the truth of the gospel might continue with you. But from those who seemed to be something, whatever they were, it makes no difference to me, etc." [Γάλ. 2:2–6: Ἀνέβην δὲ κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν, καὶ ἀνεθέμην αὐτοῖς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ὃ κηρύσσω ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, κατ' ἰδίαν δὲ τοῖς δοκοῦσιν, μήπως εἰς κενὸν τρέχω ἢ ἔδραμον. ἀλλ' οὐδὲ Τίτος ὁ σὺν ἐμοί, Ἕλλην ὤν, ἠναγκάσθη περιτμηθῆναι, διὰ δὲ τοὺς παρεισάκτους ψευδαδέλφους, οἵτινες παρεισῆλθον κατασκοπῆσαι τὴν ἐλευθερίαν ἡμῶν ἣν ἔχομεν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, ἵνα ἡμᾶς καταδουλώσωνται· οἷς οὐδὲ πρὸς ὥραν εἴξαμεν τῇ ὑποταγῇ, ἵνα ἡ ἀλήθεια τοῦ εὐαγγελίου διαμείνῃ πρὸς ὑμᾶς. Ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν δοκούντων εἶναί τι, ὁποῖοί ποτε ἦσαν, οὐδέν μοι διαφέρει, κτλ.]

units.la: Ascendi autem secundum revelationem, & contuli cum eis Evangelium quod prædico in gentibus, seorsim verò eminentioribus, sive iis qui videbantur esse aliquid, (ne forte in vanum currerem vel cucurrissem, sed neque Titus qui mecum erat, cùm esset Gentilis, coactus est circumcidi) propter verò irreptitios falsos fratres qui subintroibant, (i. e. solebant subintroire, est enim παρεισῆλθον tempus indefinitum) ut explorarent libertatem nostram quam habemus in Christo Iesu, ut nos in servitutem redigant. Quibus (i. e. eminentioribus, vel qui videbantur esse aliquid) ne ad horam quidem cessimus subjectione, ut veritas Evangelii apud vos permaneat. Quales verò aliquando illi fuerint, qui videbantur esse aliquid, nihil mea refert vel interest. Deus personam hominis non accipit, &c. Quod præcipuè hic animadverten-dum dum, non fuit propter irreptitios fratres, ut plerumque intelligitur, quod non coactus est Titus circumcidi, qui omnino non intererant, confulto enim proposuit Paulus Evangelium suum quod prædicaverat apud gentes primariis Apostolis κατ' ἰδίαν, privatim vel seorsim à cateris, nè subreperent falsi illi fratres ad explorandam libertatem. At vero propter veritatem Evangelii, ut illud nempe permaneret, nec videretur ipse in vanum cucurrisse, non coactus est Titus circumcidi. Recte Estius in persona Pauli, Quod si Apostoli, cum quibus Evangelium contuli, quod prædico in gentibus, sensissent observationem legis, cujus præcipua pars est circumcisio, necessariam esse Christianis, utiq; Titum quem mecum assumperam, jussissent circumcidi, atqui id factum non est. Neque τοῖς δοκοῦσι, v. 5. ut vulgo existimatur, est relativum τῶν, ψευδαδέλφοις, falsis fratribus qui omnino non intererant, v. 4. sed τοῖς δοκοῦσι, eminentioribus Apostolis, v. 2. quibus noluit pro momento cedere, ne vacillare videretur Evangelium quod prædicaverat apud gentes, Mosaicam nempe legem esse jam abolitam, ut postea se affirmat Petro ad faciem restitisse. Erant forte illi primarii Apostoli, qui columnæ esse videbantur. v. 9. nimium χαρίεν δοκοῦντες, & ad connivendum proni, ne fideles aliqui e Judæis (qui cum essent ζηλωταὶ τοῦ νόμου, Act. 21. 20. legem Mosis sibi mordicus retinendam putarunt) offenderentur, & à Christiana fide resilirent. Ob quam prudentiam non veritus est Paulus, ut observat Scholiastes Græcus, vocare illos δοκοῦντας, ἢ καταγνωσμένος, ἢ ὑποκειμένους, μὴ ὀρθῶς ἀπευθύνοντας, eminentiores, & reprehensibiles, & simulatores, non recte ambulantes. Κατ' ἀποκάλυψιν, secundum revelationem, nempe aliquam, quæ ei facta fuerat, sive fama, sive verbo, sive Epistolâ, cum diversam à ceteris Apostolis doctrinam divulgare, de quo Jacobus eum diserte monet Act. 21. 21. κατηχηθησαν περι σου[?], &c. Audiverunt de te quod Apostasiam à Mose[?] docens omnes Judæos inter gentes, dicens eos non debere circumcidere filios suos, nec in patriis ritibus ambulare. cujus manifestationis vel rumoris gratiâ forte dicit. Act. 20, 22. Ecce ego δεδεμένος[?] τῷ πνεύματι, &c. obstrictus animo proficiscor Hierosolymam, i. e. penitus statui quicquid de me fiat, proficisci ci Hierosolymam, ad satisfaciendum, ut sequitur, Evangelium gratiæ Dei. Utrum vero itinera fuerant οδσχεγρα; nolo fidenter statuere; certum vero est hoc loco eum ascendisse, ut testificaretur, & v indicaret Evangelium suum quod prædicaverat apud gentes. Ante ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρχῆς̃ Vetus ... subaudiendum ὅς, quale est Job.16. 17. ἐκ τοῦ ὢν ἐν τῇ μαθητῇ, pro ὅι ἐκ τῆς μαθητῆς, discerent discipuli, ut Vetus: & Luc. 21.16, ἀποθανοῦνται ἐξ ὑμῶν pro τὰς ἐξ ὑμῶν, morte afficient vos. Sic Matth.27.9. ἀπὸ 'υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, pro ὅι ἀπὸ 'υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ, filii Israel, ut exponunt Beza & Grotius. Phrasis est vulgaris, ut ὅι ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος, Platonici; ὅι ἀπὸ ταπεινῶν Plebeii; & ὅι ἐν πίστει, fideles. Gal. 3. 7. Δοκοῦσι, v. 2. recte exponitur, eminentioribus; πυγῶν ἀντὶ μηδὲν ὄντα, τὰ δὲ δοκοῦντα ἀπολλύμενα. Extollunt sursum humilia vel quæ nihil sunt, eminentiora vero subuiunt. Euripides de Diis. Δοκοῦντες, ἔνδοξοι. Phav.
units.tr: I went up according to revelation, and I laid before them the gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately before those who seemed to be something (lest by any chance I should run, or had run, in vain). But not even Titus, who was with me, though he was a Gentile, was compelled to be circumcised; and that because of the false brethren who had been smuggled in and who crept in to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might reduce us to slavery. To these men we did not yield in subjection, not even for an hour, so that the truth of the gospel might remain among you. As for those who seemed to be something, whatever they once were, it makes no difference to me. God does not accept the person of man, etc. What is chiefly to be noted here is that it was not on account of the false brethren, as is commonly understood, that Titus was not compelled to be circumcised, since they were not present at all. For Paul deliberately laid his gospel before the chief Apostles privately (κατ' ἰδίαν), that is, apart from the others, so that those false brethren should not creep in to spy out the liberty. But truly, for the sake of the truth of the gospel, that it might remain and that he himself might not seem to have run in vain, Titus was not compelled to be circumcised. Estius rightly puts this in the person of Paul: "If the Apostles, with whom I conferred the gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, had thought that the observance of the law, whose chief part is circumcision, was necessary for Christians, they would certainly have ordered Titus, whom I had taken with me, to be circumcised; but this has not been done." Nor is the phrase τοῖς δοκοῦσι in v. 5 (as is commonly thought) a relative of "the false brethren" (ψευδαδέλφοις, v. 4), who were not present at all; it refers to the eminent Apostles of v. 2, to whom Paul would not yield even for a moment, lest the gospel which he preached among the Gentiles should seem to waver, namely that the Mosaic law had already been abolished; as he afterwards says that he withstood Peter to his face. Perhaps those chief Apostles, who seemed to be pillars (v. 9), were rather too ready to conform, and inclined to connive, so that some believers from among the Jews (who, being zealots for the law, Acts 21:20, thought that the law of Moses was to be held fast) should not be offended and fall away from the Christian faith. For this prudence Paul did not hesitate, as the Greek Scholiast observes, to call them "those who seemed" (δοκοῦντας), or "those condemned" (καταγνωσμένος), or "those who dissemble" (ὑποκειμένους), "not walking uprightly" (μὴ ὀρθῶς ἀπευθύνοντας): eminent, and reprehensible, and hypocrites, not walking straight. Κατ' ἀποκάλυψιν, "according to revelation," namely some revelation made to him, whether by report, by word, or by letter, that he was spreading a doctrine different from that of the other Apostles; of which James expressly warns him, Acts 21:21: "They have heard concerning you" (κατηχήθησαν περὶ σοῦ), etc., "that you teach all the Jews among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their sons nor walk in the customs." Perhaps it is for the sake of this revelation or rumour that he says, Acts 20:22: "Behold, I go bound in the spirit" (δεδεμένος τῷ πνεύματι), etc., "bound in mind I go to Jerusalem," that is, I have fully resolved that whatever happens to me I will go to Jerusalem, to make satisfaction, as follows, "for the gospel of the grace of God." Whether these journeys were κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν I am not willing to assert confidently; but it is certain that in this place he went up to bear witness and to make known the gospel which he preached among the Gentiles. Before ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρχῆς, "Vetus..." one must understand ὅς, as in John 16:17, ἐκ τοῦ ὢν ἐν τῇ μαθητῇ, for οἱ ἐκ τῆς μαθητῆς ("the disciples," as Vetus renders it); and Luke 21:16, ἀποθανοῦνται ἐξ ὑμῶν, for τινὰς ἐξ ὑμῶν, "they will put some of you to death." So Matt. 27:9, ἀπὸ υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ, for οἱ ἀπὸ υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ, "the sons of Israel," as Beza and Grotius explain. It is a common idiom, like οἱ ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος, "the Platonists"; οἱ ἀπὸ ταπεινῶν, "the common people"; and οἱ ἐν πίστει, "the faithful." Gal. 3:7. The word δοκοῦσι in v. 2 is rightly explained as "eminent"; [πυγῶν] ... "they lift up the lowly, which are nothing, and bring down the things that seem to be eminent." Euripides, on the gods. δοκοῦντες, "the illustrious" [ἔνδοξοι]. Phavorinus.

units.la: C. 3. v. 20. ‘Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς εἷς ἐστιν. Optimus hujus loci Expositor est Interpres Æthiopicus; Deus tamen unus est duorum. Mediator unius non est, Deus vero unus est, i. e. duorum, necesse enim est ut sint personæ duæ inter quas sit mediator, ut fuit Moses inter Deum & populum Israelitticum. Ταῦτα ὁ νόμος &c. Haec sunt lex quam dedit Dominus inter se & filios Israel in monte Sina, ἐν χειρὶ, per manum Mosis. Levit. 26. 46. Atque haec interpretatio unicè quadrat cum scopo loci; quid verò ad rem ejus facit Dei unitas vel simplicitas?
units.tr: Gal. 3:20: "Now God is one" [Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς εἷς ἐστιν]. The best expositor of this passage is the Ethiopic interpreter: "God, however, is one of two." "A mediator is not of one, but God is one," that is, of two; for there must be two parties between whom the mediator stands, as Moses was between God and the people of Israel. "These are the statutes" [Ταῦτα ὁ νόμος], etc.: "These are the statutes, judgments, and laws which the Lord made between himself and the children of Israel in Mount Sinai by the hand" [ἐν χειρί] "of Moses," Lev. 26:46. This interpretation alone fits the purpose of the passage; but what bearing has the unity or simplicity of God upon its subject?

units.la: C. 4. v. 9, 10. Nunc autem cùm Deum cognoveritis, potiùs verò cogniti sitis à Deo. πῶς ἐπι-στρέφετε πάλιν εἰς τὰ ἀσθενῆ καὶ πτωχὰ στοιχεῖα, quomodo iterum revertimini ad impotentia & egena elementa, οἷς πάλιν ἀνωθεν δουλεύειν θέλετε; i. e. per trajectionem valde familiarem, vocem, cui τὸ οἷς est relativum, repetendo, ut necessario subauditur, οἷς ἀνωθεν στοιχείοις πάλιν δουλεύειν θέλετε; quibus superius vel à retro elementis rursus servire vultis? οἷς ἀνωθεν στοιχείοις, quibus superius elementis, ut οἱ ἀνωθεν, majores, qui superioribus temporibus fuerunt, & οἱ ἀνωθεν ἀρχοντες, retrò principes. Stepb. Occurrit parallelum Col. 2, 20, 21, 22. Si ergo mortui estis cum Christo, ἀπὸ τῶν στοιχείων τοῦ κόσμου, ab elementis mundi, τί ὡς ζῶντες ἐν κόσμῳ δογματίζεσθε; quid ut viventes in mundo dogmatizamini? i.e. traditionibus vel dogmatibus regimini? qualia sunt, Ne tetigeris, ne gustaveris, ne contrectaveris. Α᾽ ὅτι πάντα εἰς φθορὰν τῇ ἀποχρήσει, κατὰ τὰ ἐντάλματα & διδασκαλίας τῶν ἀνθρώπων, i.e. per Hyperbaton, Quae omnia, nempe elementa sive dogmata sunt secundum praecepta & doctrinas hominum ut intereant usu, vel quoad usum expiratura. Elementa vero ista sunt omnino eadem, ac τὰ ἀνωθεν στοιχεῖα, de quibus supra, quae erant tantùm μέχρι καιροῦ διορθώσεως ὑπηκοῦσα, usque ad tempus correctionis impositia: Heb. 9. 10. εἰς φθοράν, vertitur aptissimè, ut intereant, ant, pari modo quo verimus εἰς πίστιν, ut credatur, Rom. 1. 17. in quæ verba videre est quæ superius animadvertimus.
units.tr: Gal. 4:9, 10: "But now that you have known God, or rather are known by God, how do you turn again to the weak and beggarly elements" [πῶς ἐπιστρέφετε πάλιν εἰς τὰ ἀσθενῆ καὶ πτωχὰ στοιχεῖα], "to which you desire again to be in bondage from the beginning" [οἷς πάλιν ἄνωθεν δουλεύειν θέλετε]; that is, by a very common hyperbaton, the relative οἷς is resumed, and the phrase must be understood as: "To which elements from above you wish to be in bondage again?" "From above" like "those from above" (οἱ ἄνωθεν), the forefathers who lived in earlier times, and "the rulers from above" (οἱ ἄνωθεν ἄρχοντες), the earlier princes. Stephanus. There is a parallel at Col. 2:20–22: "If you died with Christ from the elements of the world" [ἀπὸ τῶν στοιχείων τοῦ κόσμου], "why, as though living in the world, are you subject to decrees" [τί ὡς ζῶντες ἐν κόσμῳ δογματίζεσθε]? That is, are you governed by traditions or dogmas? Such as: "Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle." "For all these things perish with the using" [ἃ ἐστιν πάντα εἰς φθορὰν τῇ ἀποχρήσει], "according to the commandments and doctrines of men." That is, by hyperbaton: "All these things, namely the elements or dogmas, are according to the precepts and doctrines of men, so that they perish with use, or are destined to expire in their use." These elements are altogether the same as "the elements from above" mentioned before, which were imposed only "until the time of reformation" (Heb. 9:10). The phrase εἰς φθοράν is most aptly rendered "so that they perish," in the same way as we render εἰς πίστιν as "so that it may be believed" (Rom. 1:17). On these words one may see what we noted above.

units.la: C. 6. v. 10. Ὡς καιρὸν ἔχομεν, dum habemus tempus. Ita vulgò, quasi poneretur ὡς pro ὡς. Quidni verò potius? Prout habemus opportunitatem, faciamus bonum omnibus. Benefaciendi nulla prætermittenda opportunitas.
units.tr: Gal. 6:10: "As we have opportunity" [Ὡς καιρὸν ἔχομεν], "while we have time." Thus it is commonly rendered, as if ὡς were put for ὡς, "as." Why not rather: "As we have opportunity, let us do good to all"? No opportunity of doing good is to be let slip.

units.la: In Epistolam ad Ephesios.
units.tr: On the Epistle to the Ephesians.

units.la: EPH. c. 2. v. 1. Καὶ ὑμᾶς ὄντας νεκροὺς &c. In regimine vocis ὑμᾶς, ni fallor (si fas sit dicere) diu cæcutierunt Interpretes, propter importunam capitum divisionem. Pleriqi in versione post ὑμᾶς, vos, addunt verbum, vivificavit, in supplementum sensus. Affirmat unus Accusativum ipsum ὑμᾶς regi à verbo συνεζωοποίησεν, v. 5. Est igitur, ait, hoc loco hyperbaton, & synchysis, & ἀποκοπὴ τῆς ἀναφορᾶς, quæ est species τῆς ἀναντιπόδοτος, cujus quidem anomaliæ causa est ἐπιμβολή, interjectio sententiæ prolixioris. Quorsum verò ille strepitus? Quid opus est tot figuris & ambagibus in re certe non ita obscura? Respice enim tantùm præcedentis capitis versum decimum nonum, & planissima sient omnia,
units.tr: Eph. 2. 1. And you, being dead [Καὶ ὑμᾶς ὄντας νεκροὺς] etc. In the construction of the word "you" (ὑμᾶς), unless I am mistaken (if I may say so), the interpreters have long been in the dark, owing to the troublesome division into chapters. Most of them, in translating, add the verb made alive after "you" to complete the sense. One alone maintains that the accusative ὑμᾶς itself is governed by the verb συνεζωοποίησεν of verse 5. So, he says, in this place there is a hyperbaton, a synchysis, and an apocope of the reference [ἀποκοπὴ τῆς ἀναφορᾶς], which is a kind of anantipodoton, and the cause of this irregularity is an epimbole, the interposition of a longer sentence. But why all that noise? Why need so many figures and circumlocutions in a matter that is certainly not so obscure? Look only at verse 19 of the preceding chapter, and everything will become perfectly plain,

units.la: sensus cohærentia & syntaxis sine vi vel figura: ἢ τί τὸ ὑπερέλλον μέγεθος ἀυ-τῆς εἰς ἡμᾶς τὴς πνεύοντας ἢ ὑμᾶς ὄντας ρηχεὺς &c. Et quæ sit superemineus magnitudo virtutis ejus in nos qui credimus, & vos qui eratis mortui in delictis & peccatis &c. Verbis intermedis κατ᾽ τὸν ἐνέργειαν τῆς κράτος &c. per operationem potentiæ virtutis ejus quam operatus est per Christum, & sic deinceps usque ad finem capitis primi parenthesi includendis. Objiciunt vero aliqui, prælonga est parenthesis. At vero obsecro, num parenthesis non erit æquè longa, si ὑμᾶς regatur à συνεζωοποίησε, v. 5. & constructio longè durior? Vide etiam Rom. 2. ubi v.13, 14. &c. 15. includuntur parenthesi non multò sanè hac breviori. Imò respice Rom. 1. ubi est parenthesis omninò æquè longa; incipit enim a versu primo, & definit in fine sexti, dum habeat interim duas alias in se inclusas. Præter loca etiam alia, in quibus occurrunt parenthesæ æquè ferè longæ, multò verò magis implicitæ. Eri autem interim quantas offuderit tenebras importuna capitum distinctio!
units.tr: the sense coherent and the syntax without force or figure: ἢ τί τὸ ὑπερέλλον μέγεθος ἀυ-τῆς εἰς ἡμᾶς τὴς πνεύοντας ἢ ὑμᾶς ὄντας ρηχεὺς etc. And what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, and you who were dead in trespasses and sins, etc. The intervening words, κατ᾽ τὸν ἐνέργειαν τῆς κράτος etc., according to the working of the strength of his power, etc., which he wrought in Christ, and so on to the end of the first chapter, are to be enclosed in a parenthesis. But some object that the parenthesis is excessively long. Yet I ask you: would the parenthesis not be just as long if ὑμᾶς were governed by συνεζωοποίησε in verse 5, and the construction much harsher? See also Rom. 2, where verses 13, 14, 15 are enclosed in a parenthesis not much shorter than this. Indeed, look at Rom. 1, where there is a parenthesis of exactly the same length: it begins at verse 1 and ends at the end of verse 6, while containing two others within it. Besides these, there are other passages in which parentheses of nearly the same length occur, and much more intricate ones. Meanwhile, consider how much darkness the troublesome division into chapters has spread!

units.la: V. 15. Τὸν ἐχθρὸν, ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν, ἐν δόγμασιν καταργήσας. Vertendum per hyperbaton, quale jam supra animadvertimus. Act. 13. 27. quasi legeretur, Τὸν ἐχθρὸν ἐν δόγμασιν τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ καταργήσας. Inimicitiam illam in ritibus legem mandatorum per carnem suam abolendo. Quale etiam est quod animadvertimus, Col. 2. 14. Expungens quod contra nos erat chirographum, τὸ καθ᾽ ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον, quod erat in ritibus nobis contrarium. Fuisse contra nos jam prius dixerat, posterius addit, in quo erat nobis contrarium, nempe in cæremoniis cæremoniis & ritibus. Idem enim sonant τῷ ἐχθεῳ ἐν δόγμασι, & τὸ ϗευαρτίον ἡμῶν ἐν δόγμασι, τῷ dicitur pro τῷ ταὐτῷ sive κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν.
units.tr: V. 15. Τὸν ἐχθρὸν, ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν, ἐν δόγμασιν καταργήσας. This must be rendered by a hyperbaton, of the kind we have already noted above, as Act. 13. 27, as if it read: Τὸν ἐχθρὸν ἐν δόγμασιν τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ καταργήσας, that is, having abolished in his flesh that enmity, the law of commandments in ordinances. Similar is what we note in Col. 2. 14: Expunging the handwriting that was against us, τὸ καθ᾽ ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον, which was contrary to us in its ritual observances. He had already said that it was "against us"; he afterwards adds "in which it was contrary to us," namely in ceremonies and rites. For τῷ ἐχθρῷ ἐν δόγμασι and τὸ ὑπεναντίον ἡμῶν ἐν δόγμασι mean the same thing, and "in ordinances" is put for "in the same," or κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν.

units.la: C 3. v. 10. "Ἵνα γνωρισθῇ νῦν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς καὶ ταῖς ἐξουσίαις ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις διὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἡ πολυποίκιλος σοφία τοῦ Θεοῦ. Ut nota nunc fiat principatibus & potestatibus multiformis sapientia Dei per Ecclesiam in cœlestibus. Nempe, rebus, quæ ad æternam vitam in cœlis transfigendam pertinent. Ut Joh. 3. 12. & Eph. 1. 3. Recte Chrysostomus, ἐπουράνια cælestia dicuntur, καὶ ἐν τῇ γῇ ὀφτέλλῃται, etiamsi in terra peragun-sur. Quod vero aliqui τὰς ἀέχὰς ϰ᾽ ἐξουσίας interpretentur Angelos, videtur mihi ab instituto prorsus alienum. Quid enim refert, si multa forte per prædicationem Evangelii innotuerunt Angelis Christianorum mysteria, quæ prius ignorabant? Data est hæc gratia Paulo, v. 8. hæc nota facere, at vero nemo opinor affirmaverit Paulum evangelizâsse. Angelis, sed principibus gentium, quales erant Herodes, Felix, Festus, & Agrippa, & magistratus qui erant Philippis, Thessalonicæ & Athenis. Annon erant hi omnes ἀέχὰς ϰ᾽ ἐξουσίας? De quibus loquitur Lucas, cùm ait, ὅταν ἠγεγερμένοι ὑμᾶς ἐπὶ τὰς συναγωγὰς ϰ᾽ τὰς ἀρχὰς ϰ᾽ ἐξουσίας; 12, 11. De quibus Paulus, cùm jubet Titum admonere ut subditi sint ταῖς ἀρχαῖς ϰ᾽ ἐξουσίαις, nisi de terrenis magistratibus? Aliis trajectio displicet. At pari ratione dicant Apostolum debuisse dicere, ἡ πολυποίκιλος σοφία τοῦ Θεοῦ διὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας, æque enim sunt transposita, ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις, & διὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας.
units.tr: C. 3. v. 10. "Ἵνα γνωρισθῇ νῦν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς καὶ ταῖς ἐξουσίαις ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις διὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἡ πολυποίκιλος σοφία τοῦ Θεοῦ. That now to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places might be made known the manifold wisdom of God through the Church. That is, by things which pertain to the transfer of eternal life into heaven, as in John 3. 12 and Eph. 1. 3. Chrysostom rightly says that the things are called heavenly, καὶ ἐν τῇ γῇ ὀφτέλλῃται, even though they are carried out on earth. But that some interpret τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ ἐξουσίας as angels seems to me wholly foreign to the purpose. For what does it matter whether, perhaps through the preaching of the Gospel, the mysteries of the Christians became known to angels, who previously did not know them? This grace was given to Paul, v. 8, to make these things known; but no one, I think, would assert that Paul preached to angels, but rather to rulers of the Gentiles, such as Herod, Felix, Festus and Agrippa, and the magistrates who were at Philippi, Thessalonica and Athens. Were not all these ἀρχαὶ καὶ ἐξουσίαι? Of these Luke speaks when he says: When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, Luke 12. 11. Of these Paul speaks when he bids Titus remind people to be subject to principalities and powers, does he not mean earthly magistrates? Others dislike the transposition. But by the same reasoning they might say that the Apostle ought to have written ἡ πολυποίκιλος σοφία τοῦ Θεοῦ διὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας, since ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις and διὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας are equally transposed.

units.la: C. 4. v. 1. Παρακαλῶ ἐν ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ ὁ δέσμιος ἐν Κυρίῳ ἀξίως περιπατῆσαι τῆς κλήσεως ῆς
units.tr: Eph. 4. 1. Παρακαλῶ ἐν ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ ὁ δέσμιος ἐν Κυρίῳ ἀξίως περιπατῆσαι τῆς κλήσεως [I beseech you, I the prisoner in the Lord, to walk worthily of the calling

units.la: ὡς ἐκλήθητε, μετὰ πάσης ταπεινοφροσύνης καὶ πραότητος, μετὰ μακροθυμίας ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων ἐν ἀγάπῃ &c Locus iste non caret vitio ut plerumque exponitur, non enim recte vertitur, ut ambuletis tolerantes, quia Participium ἀνεχόμενοι in Nominativo non potest convenire cum voce ὑμᾶς in Accusativo. Vertendum ergo in remedium cum puncto post ἐκλήθητε, ut supra. Obsecro itaque ego vos captivus in Domino ambulare digne vocatione qua vocati estis. Cum omni humilitate & mansuetudine, cum longanimitate tolerantes estote vel tolerate, alii alios in charitate. &c. ἀνεχόμενοι, ὀρθῶς vertitur, tolerantes estote vel tolerate, subaudiendo verbum substantivum, ἐστέ. Quale est, ἀνεχόμενοι τῇ πραότητι, estote contenti praesentibus, Heb. 13. 5. διδάσκοντες καὶ νουθετοῦντες ἑαυτούς &c. docete & commonete vosmetipsos psalmis &c. Col. 3. 16. Οἱ οἰκέται ὑποτασσόμενοι τοῖς δεσπόταις, Servi subditi estote Dominis. 1 Pet. 2.18. Οἱ καταεσθίοντες τὰς οἰκίας &c. qui devorant domos viduarum &c. Mar. 22. 40. ἐν ταύταις ταῖς ἐντολαῖς &c. Et elegit duodecim ex ipsis. Luc. 6. 13. καὶ εὑρόντες γὰρ τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον, invenimus enim hunc hominem &c. Act. 24. 5. In quibus singulis locis subauditur verbum substantivum ἐστὶ, εἰσὶν, ὦ vel ζῶν. Cujusmodi occurrunt in Homero, Sophocle, & Pindaro, ut monet Beza. Phrasis enim est vulgaris: ἐν αὐτοῖς ὢν διδάσκων αὐτοῖς, Et ipse innuebat illis. Luc. 1.22. τοῦτο γὰρ ἐστι λέγοντες, Hoc enim nostis, Eph. 5.5. Exhortatur primo ambulare digne vocatione qua vocati sunt. Deinde docet, quomodo id recte faciant, nempe si toleraverint se invicem in charitate, cum humilitate, mansuetudine, & longanimitate, studentes servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis. Ideoque dicit, tolerate, &c. Quid opus ergò est incogitantiam vel solœcismum impingere Apostolo, ut faciunt aliqui, constructionem tacitè perstringendo, quasi dixisset insolenter, ὀργίζεσθε pro ὀργίζεσθε.
units.tr: ἧς ὡς ἐκλήθητε, μετὰ πάσης ταπεινοφροσύνης καὶ πραότητος, μετὰ μακροθυμίας ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων ἐν ἀγάπῃ etc.] wherewith you were called, with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love, etc. This passage is not free from fault as it is commonly explained, for it is not rightly translated that you may walk, tolerating, because the participle ἀνεχόμενοι in the nominative cannot agree with the word ὑμᾶς in the accusative. It must therefore be rendered, with a full stop after ἐκλήθητε, as above: I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling wherewith you are called. With all humility and meekness, with longsuffering, tolerantes estote or tolerate, alii alios in charitate. etc. ἀνεχόμενοι is correctly translated be tolerant or tolerate, supplying the substantive verb ἐστέ. Similar is ἀνεχόμενοι τῇ πραότητι, be content with present things, Heb. 13. 5; διδάσκοντες καὶ νουθετοῦντες ἑαυτούς, teach and admonish yourselves with psalms, etc., Col. 3. 16; Οἱ οἰκέται ὑποτασσόμενοι τοῖς δεσπόταις, Servants, be subject to your masters, 1 Pet. 2. 18; Οἱ καταεσθίοντες τὰς οἰκίας, who devour widows' houses, etc.; Mark 22. 40, ἐν ταύταις ταῖς ἐντολαῖς, And he chose twelve of them, Luke 6. 13; καὶ εὑρόντες γὰρ τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον, for we have found this man, etc., Acts 24. 5. In each of these places the substantive verb ἐστί, εἰσί or ὢν is understood. Such constructions occur in Homer, Sophocles and Pindar, as Beza notes. For the phrase is common: ἐν αὐτοῖς ὢν διδάσκων αὐτοῖς, And he himself was making a sign to them, Luke 1. 22; τοῦτο γὰρ ἐστι λέγοντες, For this you know, Eph. 5. 5. He first exhorts them to walk worthily of the calling wherewith they were called. Then he teaches how they may do this rightly: namely, if they bear with one another in love, with humility, meekness and longsuffering, endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Therefore he says tolerate, etc. Why, then, should we charge the Apostle with carelessness or a solecism, as some do, tacitly censuring the construction as if he had written awkwardly, ὀργίζεσθε for ὀργίζεσθε?

units.la: V. 26. Ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε, Irascimini & nolite peccare. Non dubito quin mutuatus sit Apostolus hæc verba à Psalmista, ex psalmo 4. secundum LXX. Licet Beza, & Interpres Anglicus id in margine pro more suo non agnoscant. Ratio est, aliter interpretati sunt Hebræum, ut & alii, legentes in Psalmo, contremiscite, & nolite peccare. Verùm ego potiùs Musculo adstipulor, qui vulgarem lectionem retinuit, authoritate ductus Pauli, Irascimini & nolite peccare. Hebræum enim רגז, significat non solùm contremuit, sed & iratus est, commutus est animo vel præ metu vel præ irâ; facit enim & ira tremere. Nec verò habemus solùm authoritatem Pauli pro hac lectione, sed & expositionem etiam. Verba enim sequentia Pauli sunt mera expositio verborum sequentium in Psalmista; sensu enim sunt eadem. Ὁ ἥλιος μὴ ἐπιδυέτω, ait Apostolus, ὅτι τοῦ παροργισμοῦ ὑμῶν, μήτε διδόντε τύπον τῷ διαβόλῳ, Ne occidat Sol super iracundiam vestram, neque date locum diabolo. Psalmista verò λέγετε ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν, ὅτι ταῖς κλίναις ὑμῶν κατανύγητε, dicite in cordibus vestris, super cubilia vestra quieto sive sedato estote animo. Quasi dicerent, Irascimini, & nolite peccare, quod si forte accidat ut irascamini, neque ulla passio promptior, cavete ne peccetis irascendo ultra quàm par est, ne maneat iracundia vestra ad occasum Solis ut indormiatis ei, nec faciatis Diabolum istum iracundiæ nocturnum etiam hospitem, sinendo apud vos diutiùs commorari, sed omnino abigatur, priusquam eatis cubitum, ut super cubilia sedato sitis animo, ut possitis vobismet vobiscum colloqui, dicere orationem vestram in corde vestro, ut Chaldaus; plane innuentes quàm jucundum & necessarium sit meditationi piæ vacare, cùm primùm lecto decumbimus, cui nil magis inimicum quàm si exacerbatio aliqua iracundiæ maneat adhuc in animo: καταυόγητε, ἡσυχάσατε, καταύνυξις ἡσυχία. Hesych. Et sic in Psalmo, pro καταυύγητε, Aquila habet ἡσυχάσατε, quieti estote.
units.tr: V. 26. Ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε, Be angry and do not sin. I do not doubt that the Apostle borrowed these words from the Psalmist, from Psalm 4 according to the LXX, although Beza and the English translator, as is their custom, do not acknowledge this in the margin. The reason is that they have translated the Hebrew differently, as others also do, reading in the Psalm tremble, and do not sin. But I rather agree with Muscul[us], who kept the common reading, being led by the authority of Paul, Be angry and do not sin. For the Hebrew רגז signifies not only to tremble, but also to be angry, to be disturbed in mind, either from fear or from anger; for anger too makes one tremble. Nor do we have only the authority of Paul for this reading, but also his explanation. For the words that follow in Paul are a plain explanation of the words that follow in the Psalmist, since they mean the same. Let not the sun go down, says the Apostle, upon your wrath, nor give place to the devil, Ne occidat Sol super iracundiam vestram, neque date locum diabolo. But the Psalmist says: λέγετε ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν, ὅτι ταῖς κλίναις ὑμῶν κατανύγητε, say in your hearts, upon your beds, be still and be quiet in mind. As if they said: Be angry and do not sin; but if by chance it happens that you are angry, and no passion is more ready to rise, take care that you do not sin by being angry beyond what is right, lest your anger remain until sunset so that you fall asleep with it, and you do not make that demon of anger a night-guest, allowing him to linger with you for longer, but let him be altogether driven out before you go to bed, so that you may be quiet in mind upon your beds, and may be able to speak with yourselves, to say your prayer in your heart, as the Chaldee paraphrast has it, plainly indicating how pleasant and necessary it is to give oneself to pious meditation as soon as we lie down in bed, to which nothing is more hostile than if some irritation of anger still remains in the mind. καταυόγητε, ἡσυχάσατε, καταύνυξις ἡσυχία. Hesychius. And so in the Psalm, for καταυύγητε, Aquila has ἡσυχάσατε, be quiet.

units.la: C. 5. v. 8. Ἠτε γὰρ ποτε σκότος, νῦν δὲ φῶς ἐν Κυρίῳ, ὡς τέκνα φωτὸς περιπατεῖτε. Eratis enim olim tenebræ, nunc verò cum sitis lux in Domino, ut filii lucis ambulate subaudiendo, ὄντες, νῦν δὲ φῶς ὄντες ἐν Κυρίῳ. Appositivè dicitur.
units.tr: Chap. 5. v. 8. You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light. [Ἠτε γὰρ ποτε σκότος, νῦν δὲ φῶς ἐν Κυρίῳ, ὡς τέκνα φωτὸς περιπατεῖτε.] For you were once darkness, but now, since you are light in the Lord, walk as children of light, understanding being [ὄντες], "being light in the Lord." It is said in apposition.

units.la: V. 13. Τὰ δὲ πάντα, ἐλεγχόμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ φωτὸς, φανερούνται. i.e. per hyperbaton, Τὰ δὲ πάντα φανερούνται &c. Hæc verò omnia manifestantur cum à luce arguuntur. Quasi diceret, Hæc verò omnia τὰ κεκρυμμένα τῆς ἀισχύνης ut vocantur.
units.tr: V. 13. But all things, when reproved by the light, are made manifest. [Τὰ δὲ πάντα, ἐλεγχόμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ φωτὸς, φανερούνται.] That is, by hyperbaton: "But all things are made manifest," etc. Indeed all these things are manifested when they are reproved by the light. As if he said, these are all the hidden things of shame [τὰ κεκρυμμένα τῆς αἰσχύνης], as they are called.

units.la: 2 Cor. 4. 2. de quibus hic modo dictum est, & si ab illis quàm occultissimè perpetrentur, manifesta tamen fient cum ad lucem examinentur: Omnia enim lux manifestata facit, ut licitè etiam exponitur, per hyperbaton πᾶν γὰρ τὸ φῶς ἐστι φανερούμενον. Transponitur enim suo loco tantum vox unica φανερούμενον, quod etiam activè accipitur, quo nil vulgarius. Tà dicitur pro ταῦτα, ut sensus & ordo verborum postulat. ἔλεγξις, φανέρωσις τῶν κεκρυμμένων. Phav.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 4. 2. Of the things just mentioned here, even if they are committed as secretly as possible, they will nevertheless be made manifest when they are examined in the light: for everything made manifest is light, as it is also rightly explained by hyperbaton: [πᾶν γὰρ τὸ φῶς ἐστι φανερούμενον]. For only the single word φανερούμενον is transposed from its place, and it is also taken actively, which is nothing unusual. Τά is said for ταῦτα, as the sense and order of the words require. [ἔλεγξις, φανέρωσις τῶν κεκρυμμένων.] Phav.

units.la: V. 14. Διὸ λέγει, ἔγειρε &c. Quæritur verò, quis dicit, expergiscere &c? Ego nullus dubito, quin respexit Paulus vocem Πνεύμα-τος. 7 @. v. 9. Quapropter dicit spiritus. Expergiscere &c. Nec sunt ejusmodi transitiones apud Apostolum infrequentes, praeterquam etiam quod forte proximè respondeat; Non enim versus iste suo loco apponitur, sed à textu reliquo parenthesi distinguitur eò quòd interrumpat sensum & syntaxim. Utitur etiam eâdem dicendi formula. 1. Tim. 1. Τὸ δὲ Πνεῦμα ῥητῶς λέγει. Spiritus autem expressè dicit. Et quid ni per Paulum utrumque dicat spiritus. Nusquam verò legas, dicit lux, nec vox scriptura usquam intelligitur, nisi ubi praecessit in terminis, ut Jac. 4. 5. & 6.
units.tr: V. 14. Wherefore he says, Awake, etc. But the question is, who says, Awake, etc.? I have no doubt that Paul had in mind the phrase [Πνεύματ-ος]. Heb. 3. v. 7. Wherefore the Spirit says: Awake, etc. Such transitions are not infrequent in the Apostle, and besides, perhaps it corresponds closely; for this verse is not placed in its proper position, but is set off by a parenthesis from the rest of the text, because it interrupts the sense and syntax. He also uses the same form of speech in 1 Tim. 1. [Τὸ δὲ Πνεῦμα ῥητῶς λέγει.] But the Spirit expressly says. And why should Paul not say that the Spirit says both things? But you will never read light says, nor is the word Scripture ever understood unless it has gone before in the terms, as in Jas. 4. 5. and 6.

units.la: C. 6. v. 20. Ὑπὲρ οὗ πρεσβεύω ἐν ἁλύσει, pro quo legatione fungor in vinculis. Quid ni potius Pro quo senesco in vinculis. Sic Paulus seipsum nominat, Philem. 9. Παῦλος πρεσβύτης ἢ Χριστοῦ, Paulus senex & vinctus. Epistola utraque scripta fuit à Roma cùm ibi vinctus erat Paulus, ubi non parvo quidem tempore, scilicet biennio etsi in libera custodia, detentus erat, ut non sit mirum dicere, senesco in vinculis, cùm in iis tam diu foret.
units.tr: Chap. 6. v. 20. [Ὑπὲρ οὗ πρεσβεύω ἐν ἁλύσει.] For which I am an ambassador in chains. Why not rather: For which I grow old in chains? So Paul names himself in Philem. 9: [Παῦλος πρεσβύτης ἢ Χριστοῦ] Paul the aged and also a prisoner. Both epistles were written from Rome, when Paul was a prisoner there. There he was detained for no short time, namely two years, though in free custody, so it is no wonder that he says I grow old in chains, since he was in them for so long.

units.la: In Epistolam ad Philippenses.
units.tr: In the Epistle to the Philippians.

units.la: PHILIP. c. 2. v. 16. Λόγον ζωῆς ἐπέχοντες, Verbum vitae firmiter tenentes, ut gloriari possim in die Christi. En mercedem Pauli, eorum nempe perseverantiam.
units.tr: PHIL. ch. 2. v. 16. Holding fast the word of life, so that I may glory in the day of Christ. [Λόγον ζωῆς ἐπέχοντες.] Behold Paul's reward, namely their perseverance.

units.la: Vide 1 Cor. 3. 14, 15. & 2 Joh. 8. ἐπίχοντες, ἐργάτας. Hesych.
units.tr: See 1 Cor. 3. 14, 15, and 2 John 8. [ἐπίχοντες, ἐργάτας.] Hesych.

units.la: C. 3. v. 5. Περιτομὴ ὀκτάμερος &c. Frustrà est repetere varias de horum verborum lectione & syntaxi opiniones, quæ non mediocriter vexárunt ingenia Interpretum, ut nodum tandem in scirpo reperirent, cùm fine ulla variatione lectionis vel figurâ syntaxis sit planissimè obvia, subaudiendo tantum ἡ vel ἦν, quod toties occurrit unaquâque ferè paginâ, Περιτομὴ ἐκ ὀκταημέρας, ἐκ γένους Ισραὴλ &c. Si quis alius videtur habere fiduciam in carne, ego magis. Circumcisio erat octiduana, i. e. octavo die, ut pateat, ut ait Chrysostomus, non fuisse proselytum, Ex gente sui Israelis, ut pateat neque à parentibus quidem natum proselytis &c.
units.tr: Chap. 3. v. 5. [Περιτομὴ ὀκτάμερος.] Circumcised the eighth day, etc. It is pointless to repeat the various opinions about the reading and syntax of these words, which have greatly exercised the minds of interpreters, so that they finally found a knot in a bulrush. Without any variation of reading or figure of syntax, the meaning is quite plain, supplying only ἡ or ἦν, which occurs almost on every page: [Περιτομὴ ἐξ ὀκταημέρας, ἐκ γένους Ισραὴλ] etc. If anyone else seems to have confidence in the flesh, I more so. Circumcision was on the eighth day, that is, on the eighth day, so that it is plain, as Chrysostom says, that he was not a proselyte; of the nation of Israel, so that it is plain that he was not even born of proselyte parents, etc.

units.la: V. 15. 16. "Οσοι οὖν τέλειοι, τοῦτο φρονῶμεν, καὶ εἰ τι ἑτέρως φρονεῖτε, καὶ τοῦτο ὁ Θεὸς ὑμῖν ἀποκαλύψει· πλὴν εἰς ὃ ἐφθάσαμεν, τῷ αὐτῷ στοιχεῖν κανόνι, τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν. Quotquot ergo perfecti sumus, hoc sentiamus, & si quid aliter sentitis, & hoc quoque revelet vobis Deus (præter ad quod pervasimus) eadem incedere regula, idem sentire. Futurum frequenter usurpatur pro Imperativo. Quod verò adeò multi vertunt, Eâdem incedamus regulâ, idem sentiamus, est neque sensui nec syntaxi consonum, sed ab omni more loquendi alienum.
units.tr: V. 15, 16. [Ὅσοι οὖν τέλειοι, τοῦτο φρονῶμεν, καὶ εἰ τι ἑτέρως φρονεῖτε, καὶ τοῦτο ὁ Θεὸς ὑμῖν ἀποκαλύψει· πλὴν εἰς ὃ ἐφθάσαμεν, τῷ αὐτῷ στοιχεῖν κανόνι, τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν.] As many of us then as are perfect, let us think this; and if you think otherwise in anything, God will reveal this to you also; only, let us walk by the same rule to which we have attained, and think the same thing. The future is frequently used for the imperative. But the rendering that so many give, "Let us walk by the same rule, let us think the same thing," agrees neither with the sense nor with the syntax, and is alien to every manner of speaking.

units.la: In Epistolam ad Colos- senses.
units.tr: In the Epistle to the Colossians

units.la: COLOSS. c 1. v. 2. Τοῖς ἐν Κολοσσαῖς ἁγίοις καὶ πιστοῖς &c. ἅγιοι & πιστοὶ sunt viri sibi is Ecclesia in Colossis.
units.tr: COLOSS. 1. v. 2. To the saints and faithful brethren in Colossae [Τοῖς ἐν Κολοσσαῖς ἁγίοις καὶ πιστοῖς] etc. "Saints" and "faithful" are the men of the church in Colossae.

units.la: V. 27. Οἷς ἠθέλησεν ὁ Θεὸς γνωρίσαι τίς ὁ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης τοῦ μυστηρίου τούτου ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, ὅς ἐστι Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς δόξης &c. Ut constructio fiat, ὅς absque dubio est relativum voci πλούτου. Quibus voluit Deus notum facere quae sit opulentia gloriae huius mysterii inter gentes, quae est Christus inter vos, spes gloriae.
units.tr: V. 27. To whom God willed to make known what is the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory [Οἷς ἠθέλησεν ὁ Θεὸς γνωρίσαι τίς ὁ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης τοῦ μυστηρίου τούτου ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, ὅς ἐστι Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς δόξης] etc. For the construction to work, ὅς is undoubtedly relative to the word "riches": to whom God wished to make known what is the abundance of the glory of this mystery among the nations, which is Christ among you, the hope of glory.

units.la: C. 2. v. 14. Ἐξαλείψας τὸ καθ' ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον, τοῖς δόγμασιν ὁ ἦν ὑπεναντίον ἡμῖν. Expungens quod adversum nos erat Chirographum, quod erat in traditionibus nobis contrarium.
units.tr: C. 2. v. 14. Blotting out the handwriting that was against us, which was contrary to us in its decrees [Ἐξαλείψας τὸ καθ' ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον, τοῖς δόγμασιν ὁ ἦν ὑπεναντίον ἡμῖν]. Blotting out the bond that stood against us, which was opposed to us in its traditions.

units.la: V. 18. Μηδεὶς ὑμᾶς καταβραβευέτω θέλων ἐν ταπεινοφροσύνῃ καὶ θρησκείᾳ τῶν ἀγγέλων, ἃ μὴ ἑώρακεν ἐμβατεύων. Nemo vos subdola argumentatione fallat, qui delectatur in humilitate & cultu Angelorum, ingrediens in ea quae non vidit, temere inflatus à sensu carnis suae. καταβραβευέτω, ἐμβατεύων. Phavor. θέλω, ἐνδοχῶ: ibidem. ut Mar. 12. 38. & Psal. 147. 10, ἐμβατεύων Hieronymus & Erasmus vertunt fastuose incedens in ea quae non vidit, i.e. audens differere vel affirmare de iis quae non vidit, vel intelligit, temere inflatus à suâ ipsius carnali phantasiâ.
units.tr: V. 18. Let no one condemn you, desiring to do so in humility and the worship of angels, things which he has not seen, entering into them [Μηδεὶς ὑμᾶς καταβραβευέτω θέλων ἐν ταπεινοφροσύνῃ καὶ θρησκείᾳ τῶν ἀγγέλων, ἃ μὴ ἑώρακεν ἐμβατεύων]. Let no one deceive you with a crafty argument, he who delights in humility and the worship of angels, entering into things he has not seen, rashly puffed up by the sense of his flesh. [On] καταβραβευέτω and ἐμβατεύων, see Phavorinus. [On] θέλω, see ἐνδοχῶ in the same place, as in Mark 12:38 and Psalm 147:10. Jerome and Erasmus translate ἐμβατεύων as "walking haughtily into things he has not seen", that is, presuming to discourse on or affirm things he has not seen or understood, rashly puffed up by his own carnal fancy.

units.la: V. 22. "Ἅτινά ἐστι λόγον μὲν ἔχοντα σοφίας ἐν ἐθελοθρησκίᾳ [?] καὶ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ, καὶ ἀφειδίᾳ σώματος, οὐκ ἐν τιμῇ τινι πρὸς πλησμονὴν τῆς σαρκός. Post ὥν vel τινὶς subaudi ὄντα. Quae rationem quidem habent sapientiae in voluntario cultu & humilitate, & neglectu corporis, quod non est in pretio aliquo ut saturetur caro, i. e. ad saturitatem carnis.
units.tr: V. 22. Which indeed have a show of wisdom in self-chosen worship [?], humility, and severity to the body, but not in any honour that serves to satisfy the flesh [Ἅτινά ἐστι λόγον μὲν ἔχοντα σοφίας ἐν ἐθελοθρησκίᾳ [?] καὶ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ, καὶ ἀφειδίᾳ σώματος, οὐκ ἐν τιμῇ τινι πρὸς πλησμονὴν τῆς σαρκός]. After ὥν or τινὶς understand ὄντα. Which indeed have a reputation for wisdom in voluntary worship and humility and neglect of the body, which is of no value for satisfying the flesh, that is, for the gratification of the flesh.

units.la: C. 3, v. 7, "Ὅτε ἐζῆτε ἐν αὐτοῖς, cùm viveretis inter illos, i. e. ἐν τοῖς υἱοῖς τῆς ἀπειθείας, inter filios inobedientiae, v. 6.
units.tr: C. 3, v. 7. When you lived among them [Ὅτε ἐζῆτε ἐν αὐτοῖς], that is, among the sons of disobedience [ἐν τοῖς υἱοῖς τῆς ἀπειθείας], v. 6.

units.la: C. 4, v. 16. Καὶ τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας. Nil opus est cum Grotio variare lectionem, expungendo ἐν, contra omnium codicum fidem, cùm sit ἐκ dictum cum Vetere. Et eam quae est Laodicensium vos legatis. Non quae à Laodicensibus ad illos missa fuerat, sed quae ab Apostolo ad Laodicenses scripta. Quae cur vel quomodo perierit, ut & altera ad Corinthios, & altera ad Ephesios, soli notum est Deo. Vulgò usurpatur in hoc sensu τὸ ἐν ᾧ ut τίνες τῇ ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇς, Quidam Synagogae, οἱ ἐκ πίστεως, fideles, οἱ ἐν Στοᾶς, Stoici, ἄνεμοι ἐν νυκτὶ χαλεποί, Venti nocturni graecos.
units.tr: C. 4, v. 16. And the one from Laodicea [Καὶ τὴν ἐκ Λαοδικείας]. There is no need, with Grotius, to vary the reading by deleting ἐν, against the testimony of all the manuscripts, since the old reading is ἐκ. Read also the letter which is the Laodiceans'. This is not the letter that was sent to them from the Laodiceans, but the one written by the Apostle to the Laodiceans. Why or how it perished, as with the other letter to the Corinthians and the one to the Ephesians, is known to God alone. In this sense the phrase τὸ ἐν ᾧ is commonly used, as in τινὲς τῆς ἐν τῇ συναγωγῇς [certain of the synagogue], οἱ ἐκ πίστεως [those of faith, the faithful], οἱ ἐν Στοᾶς [those of the Stoa, the Stoics], ἄνεμοι ἐν νυκτὶ χαλεποί [winds, grievous in the night].

units.la: In Epistolam primam ad Thessalonicenses.
units.tr: On the First Epistle to the Thessalonians.

units.la: THES. c. 2. v. 16. Ἔφθασε δὲ ἐπ' αὐτὺς ἡ ὀργὴ εἰς τέλος. Pervenit verò in eos vindicta in fine. De Iudaeis loquitur. Occiderunt Iesum & suos Prophetas, & nos persecuti sunt, nec Deum curant, & contrarii sunt omnibus, prohibentes nos etiam praedicare vobis ut salvemini, sed pervenit in eos vindicta in fine, sive ira Dei. ut Vetus. Adfuit tempus excidii Hierosolymae, & recens in eos supervenerat διαζωμέ.
units.tr: Thess. ch. 2, v. 16: But wrath came upon them at last [Ἔφθασε δὲ ἐπ' αὐτοὺς ἡ ὀργὴ εἰς τέλος]. The Latin is: But vengeance came upon them to the end. He speaks of the Jews. They killed Jesus and their own prophets, and have persecuted us; they do not please God, and they are opposed to all men, forbidding us even to preach to you that you may be saved; but wrath has come upon them at the end, or the anger of God, as the Old translator has it. The time of the destruction of Jerusalem had come, and the wrath had recently overtaken them [διαζωμέ].

units.la: In secundam Epistolam ad Thessalonicenses.
units.tr: On the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians.

units.la: THES. c. 2. v. 1. Ἐρωτῶμεν δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοί &c. Rogamus verò vos fratres de adventu Domini &c. i e. ut rectissimè Zegerus, quoad adventum Domini, sic movemini &c. ὑπὲρ super, de, apud Grammaticos. ut ὑπὲρ ὡς ἐν οἰκείῳ τόπῳ διαλέξομαι. de vel super per quae suo loco dicam Dion. Halic, & Multa super Priamo rogitans, super Hectore multa. Virg. Atque hic sensus unice quadrat cum scopo Loci. ὡσαύτως τὰ αὐτὰ. Pharo.
units.tr: THESS. ch. 2 v. 1. "We ask you, brothers," etc. [Ἐρωτῶμεν δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοί]. "We beseech you, brothers, concerning the coming of the Lord," etc. That is, as Zegerus rightly puts it, "with regard to the coming of the Lord, be moved in this way," etc. "ὑπέρ" [huper] means "over, concerning," among the grammarians, as in "ὑπὲρ ὡς ἐν οἰκείῳ τόπῳ διαλέξομαι" [huper hōs en oikeiō topō dialexomai], "I shall speak of it in its proper place," Dionysius of Halicarnassus. "De" or "super," which I shall explain in their proper places. Virgil: "asking much about Priam, much about Hector." And this sense alone fits the purpose of the passage. "ὡσαύτως τὰ αὐτὰ" [hōsautōs ta auta], "likewise the same things." Pharo.

units.la: V. 3. Μή τις ὑμᾶς ἐξαπατήσῃ κατὰ μηδένα τρόπον, ὅτι, ἐὰν μὴ ἔλθῃ ἡ ἀποστασία πρῶτον. Post ὅτι, subaudi ἐνέστηκεν, quae vox ἀπὸ τῆς κοινῆς repetenda. Ne cito mente commoveamini, neque turbemini, neque per spiritum, neque per sermonem, neque per Epistolam, tanquam per nos, ὡς ὅτι ἐνέστηκεν ἡμέρα τοῦ Χριστοῦ, tanquam quod instet dies Christi; μήτις ὑμᾶς ἐξαπατήσῃ κατὰ μηδένα τρόπον, ὅτι. Ne quis seducat vos ullo modo quod instet, si non venerit prius apostasia &c. Interpretes excudunt sensum, non sunt vero de Syntaxi soliciti. Quid enim velit, ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ, ut universim distinguitur, fateor equidem me non intelligere.
units.tr: V. 3. "Let no one deceive you in any way, for unless the falling away comes first..." [Μή τις ὑμᾶς ἐξαπατήσῃ κατὰ μηδένα τρόπον, ὅτι, ἐὰν μὴ ἔλθῃ ἡ ἀποστασία πρῶτον]. After "ὅτι" [hoti] one must supply "ἐνέστηκεν" [enestēken, "is at hand"], a word which is to be carried over from the common clause [ἀπὸ τῆς κοινῆς]. "That you be not quickly shaken in mind, nor troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter, as if from us, as though the day of Christ were at hand"; [μήτις ὑμᾶς ἐξαπατήσῃ κατὰ μηδένα τρόπον, ὅτι]. "Let no one deceive you in any way, that it is at hand, unless the apostasy come first," etc. The translators hammer out the sense, but they are not really concerned with the syntax. For what "ὅτι ἐὰν μή" [hoti ean mē] means, as it is generally construed, I frankly confess I do not understand.

units.la: V. 6, 7. Καὶ νῦν τὸ κατέχον οἴδατε, εἰς τὸ ἀποκαλυφθῆναι αὐτὸν ἐν ἑαυτῷ καιρῷ. Τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας, μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται. Verbum substantivum in utroque loco subaudiendum, nempe post τὸ κατέχον, εἶναι, & post ὁ κατέχων, ἔστι, Hebraeorum more, cujus exempla reperire licet & in novo & in vetere unaquaque fere pagina, ne dicam linea. Ec nunc esse quod obstat, scitis, ut reveletur ille in suo tempore. Mysterium enim iniquitatis jam jam operatur, tantum est qui ad praesens obstat, usque dum e medio fiat. Non sciverunt quid vel quis obstaret, ignotum enim erat, neque certum est in hunc usque diem, sed a Paulo, ut videtur, edocti fuerant, aliquid esse quod obstaret, usque dum e medio tolleretur. Dixerunt e Veteribus. Romanum fuisse statum, quod quod obstabat, usque dum è medio tolleretur, sed scienter nemo. Vide 1 Joh. 2. 18, 4. 3.
units.tr: V. 6, 7. "And now you know what restrains, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only he who now restrains will do so until he is taken out of the way" [Καὶ νῦν τὸ κατέχον οἴδατε, εἰς τὸ ἀποκαλυφθῆναι αὐτὸν ἐν ἑαυτῷ καιρῷ. Τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας, μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται]. The substantive verb is to be supplied in both places: after "τὸ κατέχον" [to katechon] the word "εἶναι" [einai, "to be"], and after "ὁ κατέχων" [ho katechōn] the word "ἔστι" [esti, "is"], after the manner of the Hebrews, of which examples may be found in the New and Old Testaments on almost every page, not to say every line. "And now you know what is the obstacle, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; there is only one who at present hinders, until he is taken out of the way." They did not know what or who was hindering; for it was unknown, and it is not certain even to this day. But they had been taught by Paul, it seems, that there was something which hindered until it was taken out of the way. Some of the Ancients have said that it was the Roman state which hindered until it was taken out of the way, but no one has said so with certainty. See 1 John 2. 18, 4. 3.

units.la: In Epistolam primam ad Timotheum.
units.tr: On the First Epistle to Timothy.

units.la: TIM. c. 1. v. 3. Καθὼς προσεμάλσω σε, προσεμεῖναι ἐν Ἐφέσῳ, πορευόμενος εἰς Μακεδονίαν, ἵνα παραγγείλῃς &c. Quod si circumflectitur vox προσεμεῖναι, subauditur Imperativus, θέλε vel μένωνοv. De quo vide Animad. ad Acts. 1. 4. Si vero acuitur tertiâ à fine, προσέμεινον, ut forte debuit, non sunt enim accentus ex Authore, tum demùm est Imperativus Aoristus vocis mediæ, qui frequenter usurpatur in Veteri, adeò ut nihil opus sit supplemento, Grammaticè enim & rectè dicitur utrovis modo, Quemadmodum admonui te, mane, vel manere memento in Ephesō proficiscens in Macedoniam, ut denunties, &c.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 1. 3. "As I besought thee [Καθὼς παρεκάλεσά σε] to remain at Ephesus when I went into Macedonia, that thou mightest charge [...] &c." If the word προσεμεῖναι is given a circumflex, an imperative is understood, either θέλε or μένων. On this see my notes on Acts 1. 4. But if it is given an acute on the third syllable from the end, προσέμεινον, as perhaps it should be (the accents are not the author's own), then it is the aorist imperative of the middle voice, which is often used in the Old Testament, so that no supplement is needed. For it is grammatical and correct to say it either way: "As I admonished you, remain at Ephesus, or remember to remain there when you set out for Macedonia, that you may announce..." &c.

units.la: C. 2. v. 6, 7. Ὁ δὸς ἑαυτὸν ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων, τὸ μαρτύριον καιροῖς ἰδίοις εἰς ὃ ἐτέθην ἐγὼ κήρυξ καὶ Ἀπόστολος &c. Ut sensus fiat manifestior & constructio, quam vulgò solet, repetenda sunt verba proximè praecedentia, Εἷς γὰρ Θεὸς &c. Unus enim est Deus, unus etiam mediator Dei & hominum, homo Christus Iesus, ὁ δοὺς quì dedit se redemptionis pretium pro omnibus. τὸ μαρτύριον, ipsum Evangelium, cujus ego proprio tempore constitutus sum prædicator, & Apostolus &c. Tὸ sumitur appositive, sive ut aiunt πιχνικῶς. Quasi diceret, summam Evangelii, cujus ipse constitutus est prædicator & Apostolus proprio tempore, esse in notione vel scientiâ unius Dei, & unius Mediatoris Christi Jesu, qui se dedit redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, μαρτύριον, usurpatur pro Evangelio. 1Cor. 1. 6. 2. 1. 2Tim. 1. 8. &10. Quoad trajectionem nil vulgarius. Applicatur eodem modo, καιρὸς ἰδίοις, Tit. 1. 3.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 2. 6, 7. "Who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time, whereunto I am ordained a preacher and an apostle [ὁ δοὺς ἑαυτὸν ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων, τὸ μαρτύριον καιροῖς ἰδίοις, εἰς ὃ ἐτέθην ἐγὼ κήρυξ καὶ Ἀπόστολος] &c." To make the sense plainer and the construction clearer than is usual, the words immediately preceding must be repeated: "For there is one God [Εἷς γὰρ Θεὸς] &c.: one God, and also one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as the price of redemption for all [ὁ δοὺς]. The testimony [τὸ μαρτύριον], that is, the Gospel itself, of which I was appointed preacher and apostle in due time &c." The article is used appositively, or, as they say, epexegetically. It is as if he said: the sum of the Gospel, of which he himself was appointed preacher and apostle in due time, lies in the knowledge of the one God and of the one Mediator Christ Jesus, who gave himself as the price of redemption for all. μαρτύριον is used for the Gospel (1 Cor. 1. 6; 2. 1; 2 Tim. 1. 8 and 10). As for the transposition, nothing is more common. It is applied in the same way to καιρὸς ἰδίοις, Tit. 1. 3.

units.la: V. 10. Ἀλλ' ὃ πρέπει γυναιξὶν ἐπαγγελλομέναις θεοσέβειαν διὰ ἔργων ἀγαθῶν. Melius cum Stephano omittitur parenthesis. Ante ὃ, subaudi χρὴ. Sed quemadmodum decet mulieres quæ pietatem spondent per bona opera. Est enim inconcinnum etiam & insolens dicere, κοσμεῖν ἑαυτὰς διὰ ἔργων ἀγαθῶν, quod potius debuit exprimi cum præpositione, ἐν, ut in præcedentibus μὴ ἐν πλέγμασιν &c. ἀλλ' ἐν ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς, sic vidua eligatur ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς μαρτυρουμένη, quæ testimonium habuit in bonis operibus. 1Tim. 5. 10.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 5. 10. "But which becometh women professing godliness through good works [Ἀλλ' ὃ πρέπει γυναιξὶν ἐπαγγελλομέναις θεοσέβειαν διὰ ἔργων ἀγαθῶν]." Better, with Stephanus, the parenthesis is omitted. Before ὃ supply χρὴ, so that it reads: "as it becomes women who profess piety, to do so through good works." For it is awkward and unusual to say κοσμεῖν ἑαυτὰς διὰ ἔργων ἀγαθῶν; it ought rather to have been expressed with the preposition ἐν, as in the preceding μὴ ἐν πλέγμασιν &c. ἀλλ' ἐν ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς. So too a widow is chosen ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς μαρτυρουμένη, "who has testimony for good works" (1 Tim. 5. 10).

units.la: V. 15. Σωθήσεται δὲ διὰ τῆς τεκνογονίας, Salvabitur verò per generationem filii, i.e. per semen mulieris, quod conteret caput serpentis, per quod & Adam & Eva, & eorum posteri salvabuntur, si manserint in fide. Atque ita sensisse aliquos ante ipsius tempora refert Theophylactus, Τεκνογονία, ἐνόπλως, τῷ δὲ Θεοδώρῳ, de generatione intellexerunt Deipara.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 2. 15. "Notwithstanding she shall be saved in childbearing [Σωθήσεται δὲ διὰ τῆς τεκνογονίας]." That is, she shall be saved through the begetting of a son, that is, through the seed of the woman, which shall bruise the serpent's head, through whom both Adam and Eve and their posterity shall be saved, if they remain in the faith. Theophylact reports that some before his time understood it in this way, and Theodore understood the "generation" to refer to the Mother of God [Deipara].

units.la: V. 15 & 16. &C. 4. v. 1. Hitts ἐκκλησία Θεοῦ ζῶντος, στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας, &c. Quæ est ecclesia viventis Dei, columna & firmamentum veritatis, &c. Quid opus est confugere ad interpretationes violentas? Qualis est corum eorum qui hæc verba, σιλε̃ ν̈ ἐλεγίαμα τ̃ ἐλλʒείας, laborant adeò connectere cum sequentibus, quasi scribendum foret vel eo ordine saltem intelligendum, σιλε̃ ν̈ ἐλεγίαμα τ̃ ἀληθείας ν̈ ὁμολογουμένως μέγα τ̃ ἐυσεβείας μυστήριον ὅς, τὸ Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ &c. Columna & firmamentum veritatis & citrà controversiam magnum pietatis est mysterium, nempè Deus manifestatus est in carne. Quæ metathesis est adeò meis auribus dura, ut nullo modo possim eam cum silentio præterire, præsertim cùm nec omninò sit necessaria. Verè enim & οὕτως Ecclesia Dei est columna & firmamentum veritatis, In Ecclesia enim Dei recta fides in Deum colitur, quæ, certè est columna & firmamentum veritatis. Quod si quæ dicitur ecclesia non recta fide Deum amplectitur manifestatum in carne, non est amplius ecclesia Dei. Domus cœlorum Dei, si fiduciam & gloriam spei [nominè in Christo] teneamus firmam usque ad finem Heb. 3. 6. Si verò non teneant confessionem spei sine declinatione, sed prolapsi fuerint ἐγκαταλείποντες τὴν ἐπισυναγωγὴν, deferentes congregationem, 10. 25. non sunt amplius ecclesia vel domus Dei, sed apostatæ. Ecclesia enim & veritas sunt ita inter se relatæ & mutuò complicatæ, ut altera sine altera esse nequeat, ut altera, altera necessariò supponatur. Ubi enim veritas ibi est ecclesia, & ubi est ecclesia ibi veritas. Adeò ut rectè cum Chrysostomo dicatur etiam veritas columna & firmamentum ecclesiæ, vel ecclesia potest dici columna & firmamentum veritatis μετωνυμικῶς idque variis modis, Vel possessore posito pro re possessa, quale est illud apud Virgilium: Iam proximus ardet Ucalegon, cum non ille sed domus ejus flagraret. Est enim nim ecclesia possessor & custos rectæ in Deum fidei, quæ est columnia veritatis. Vel continente posito pro re contenta, quale est apud Lucam, 22. 20. Hoc poculum est Novum Testamentum, cum non poculum, sed vinum in poculo effect Testamentum. In ecclesia enim conservatur recta in Deum fides, quæ est veritas. Vel adjuncto posito pro subjecto, Ecclesia ponitur pro petra super quam ædificata est ecclesia, quæ petra certe fuit columna & firmamentum veritatis, & mysterium illud magnum quod nec caro nec sanguis revelavit, scilicet, Σὺ εἶ ὁ Χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος. Tu es ipse Christus filius viventis Dei Matth. 16. 16. Adeo ut sensu divisio sequatur opportune Καὶ ὁμολογουμένως μέγα ἐστὶ τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον, Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί, ἐδικαιώθη ἐν Πνεύματι, &c. Et citra controversiam magnum est pietatis mysterium, Deus manifestatus est in carne, justificatus est per spiritum, &c. Non enim oratio est biulca vel suspensa, ut interpretes illi volunt, sed per se perfecta admodum & emphatica, his verbis non solum fidem sed & admirationem postulantibus, est enim τὸ, ὦ, hoc loco admirationis nota. Ineffabile enim & mirandum est mysterium, Deus manifestatus est in carne. Quod verbum Caro factum sit, quod homo Christus sit filius viventis Dei, est citra controversiam religionis nostræ mysterium ingens, quod nec caro nec sanguis unquam revelavit. Quæ sequuntur, ἐδικαιώθη ἐν Πνεύματι, &c. non sunt mysteria, sed testimonia rem vere prout dicitur ita se habere, nempe, Deum manifestatum esse in carne, ideoque Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί, referrtur ἀπὸ τῆς κοινῆς ad ea singula. Justificatus est per spiritum Deus manifestatus esse in carne, cum sedit super cum spiritus in specie columbæ & audita est vox à cælo, Hic est filius meus &c. Matth. 3. 16. & 17. ut etiam alibi per miracula quæ edidit per virtutem spiritus. Sic etiam visus est ab Angelis, eius in carne, Matth. 4. 11. Luc. 2. 13, 14. & Act. 1. 9, 10, & 11. Atque ita prædicatus est in gentibus, creditus in mundo, & assumptus est in gloria. Mirum vero, stupendum sane, contra tot & tantos testes futuros fuisse aliquos, qui oculos occluderent vel averterent; Licet enim Deum manifestatum esse in carne, testetur Spiritus, testantur Angeli, testetur prædicatio Evangelii cui fides est exhibita per totum mundum, & conspicua ejus in cœlum assumptio, immediatè sequitur. c. 4. v. 1. connexione admodum apposita etsi dividantur capita. Τὸ Πνεῦμα &c. Spiritus tamen expressè dicit quod in posteris temporibus, ἀποστήσονταί τινες ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως, defscisent aliqui ab hac [ipsa] fide attendentes spiritibus erroris &c. ὑ positio pro πνεύματος. ut vult etiam Medus noster. Quod ipsum prædixit Petrus, 2. ep. 2. 1. & inter vos erunt falsi doctores qui introducent hæreses perditionis & qui etiam eos Dominum negaverunt i. e. Deum qui manifestatus est in carne. ἐδικαιώθη, justificatus est, sensu quo vulgo loquimur Anglicè, a will is such a thing to be so or so, vel ut explanatur apud legis peritos nostros. Justificationis an upholding, or shewing a good reason in court, why he did such a thing he was called to answer. Brooke, titulo Replevim. Quale est illud Matth. 11. 19 καὶ ἐδικαιώθη ἡ σοφία &c. & justificata est hæc sapientia à filiis ejus, i.e. ab iis declarata fuisse ipsorum sensu ipsa vera, à quo sensu nec omnino differt τὸ ἀποδεδειγμένον, Act. 2. 22. ut ibidem supra animadvertimus. madvertimus. In summa, τὸ δίκαιον, est justis argumentis & testimoniis comprobare. Τὸ ἐν cum Dativo passim ponitur pro διὰ cum Genitivo, ut, εἰ δὲ ἐγὼ ἐν πνεύματι Θεοῦ ἐκβάλλω τὰ δαιμόνια &c. Et si ego per spiritum Dei ejicio daemonia, &c. Matth. 12. 28 & ἐν ἀνδρὶ ᾧ ὥρισε, per hominem quem statuit. Act. 17. 31. & gentes alibi in N.T.
units.tr: 1 Tim. 3. 15, 16; 4. 1. "Which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth [Ἥτις ἐστὶν ἐκκλησία Θεοῦ ζῶντος, στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας] &c." Why must one take refuge in forced interpretations? Those who labour to connect these words, στῦλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας, with what follows, as though it should be written, or at least understood in this order, "the pillar and ground of the truth, and confessedly great is the mystery of godliness, which [Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί]," that is, "the pillar and ground of the truth, and without controversy the great mystery of godliness, namely, God was manifest in the flesh," are making a transposition which is so harsh to my ears that I cannot pass it over in silence, especially since it is not necessary at all. For truly and thus the Church of God is the pillar and ground of the truth. For in the Church of God the right faith in God is maintained, and this is surely the pillar and ground of the truth. But if any congregation does not embrace God, manifested in the flesh, with the right faith, it is no longer the Church of God. "Whose house we are, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end" (Heb. 3. 6). But if they do not hold fast the profession of hope without wavering, but fall away, "forsaking the assembling of themselves together" (Heb. 10. 25), they are no longer the Church or house of God, but apostates. For the Church and the truth are so related to each other and so mutually interwoven that the one cannot exist without the other, so that each necessarily presupposes the other. For where the truth is, there is the Church, and where the Church is, there is the truth. So that it is rightly said with Chrysostom that the truth is also the pillar and ground of the Church, or the Church may be called the pillar and ground of the truth metonymically, and this in various ways. Either the possessor is put for the thing possessed, as in Virgil: "Now Ucalegon is already burning," when it was not he but his house that was on fire. For the Church is the possessor and guardian of the right faith in God, which is the pillar of the truth. Or the container is put for the thing contained, as in Luke 22. 20: "This cup is the New Testament," where it is not the cup but the wine in the cup that is the testament. For in the Church the right faith in God, which is the truth, is preserved. Or the adjunct is put for the subject: the Church is put for the rock upon which the Church is built, and this rock was certainly the pillar and ground of the truth, and that great mystery which flesh and blood did not reveal, namely, "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matt. 16. 16). So the division that follows fits the sense well: "And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, &c." For the sentence is not broken off or suspended, as those interpreters want, but is complete in itself and very emphatic, demanding by these words not only faith but also admiration, for τὸ ὦ here is a mark of admiration. For the mystery is ineffable and marvellous: God was manifest in the flesh. That the Word was made flesh, that the man Christ is the Son of the living God, is beyond controversy a great mystery of our religion, which flesh and blood never revealed. What follows, "justified in the Spirit, &c.," is not further mysteries but testimonies that the thing is really as it is said to be, namely, that God was manifested in the flesh. Therefore "God was manifest in the flesh" refers by the common [construction] to each of the following clauses. He was justified in the Spirit, God manifested in the flesh, when the Spirit rested upon him in the form of a dove and a voice was heard from heaven, "This is my beloved Son" (Matt. 3. 16, 17), and also elsewhere through the miracles which he performed by the power of the Spirit. So also he was seen by angels in the flesh (Matt. 4. 11; Luke 2. 13, 14; Acts 1. 9, 10, 11). And so he was preached among the nations, believed in the world, and taken up in glory. It is indeed marvellous and truly astonishing that there should be any who would close or turn away their eyes against so many and so great witnesses. For although the Spirit testifies that God was manifest in the flesh, the angels testify it, the preaching of the Gospel, to which faith has been given throughout the whole world, testifies it, and his visible assumption into heaven immediately follows, in a connection very apt even though the chapters are divided. (1 Tim. 4. 1.) "Now the Spirit [Τὸ Πνεῦμα] &c." The Spirit, however, expressly says that in later times "some shall depart from the faith" [ἀποστήσονταί τινες ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως], that is, shall fall away from this very faith, "giving heed to seducing spirits" &c., the ὑ being put for πνεύματος, as our Mede also holds. Peter predicted the same thing: "And there shall be false teachers among you, who shall privily bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord" (2 Pet. 2. 1), that is, God who was manifest in the flesh. "Justified" [ἐδικαιώθη] is used in the sense in which we speak in English: "a will is such a thing to be so or so," or as it is explained among our lawyers: "Justification, an upholding, or shewing a good reason in court, why he did such a thing he was called to answer." Brooke, under the title Replevin. Such is that passage in Matt. 11. 19: "And wisdom was justified [καὶ ἐδικαιώθη ἡ σοφία] of her children," that is, the true sense of wisdom was declared by them; from this sense the expression τὸ ἀποδεδειγμένον, Acts 2. 22, does not differ at all, as we noted above in that place. In short, τὸ δίκαιον means to prove by just arguments and testimonies. The ἐν with the dative is often put for διὰ with the genitive, as "If I by the Spirit of God cast out devils" (Matt. 12. 28), and "by the man whom he hath ordained" [ἐν ἀνδρὶ ᾧ ὥρισε] (Acts 17. 31), and elsewhere in the New Testament.

units.la: V. 1. Προσέχοντες πνεύμασι πλάνοις καὶ διδασκαλίαις δαιμονίων, ἐν ὑποκρίσει ψευδολόγων &c. Attendentes spiritibus erroris, & doctrinis daemoniorum, per hypocrisin hominum falsiloquorum, ut animadvertit Castalio, addens ultra, hominum addidi, ne falsiloquorum, & sequentia referrentur ad Daemonia. Quod certè, ut observavit Medus noster, foret prodigiosum dicere, Daemonia nempe loqui mendacia in hypocrisi, & habere conscientias cauteriatas, &c. qui etiam διδασκαλίας δαιμονίων, vult intelligi, doctrinis de Daemoniis, i.e. de Canonizatis sanctis, & imaginibus vel Idolis. Daemonia enim legitimè exponi Idola, authoritatem habemus, Psal. 96. 5. כִּי כָל אֱלֹהֵי הָעַמִּים אֱלִילִים, ὅτι οἱ Θεοὶ πάντες τῶν ἐθνῶν δαιμόνια, Quoniam omnes Dii gentium idola sunt, ut Paraphr. Chal. Ver. Lat. & Interpres Anglicus; ut etiam verunt ipsissima verba LXX, 1 Paral. 16. 26. ὅτι πάντες οἱ Θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν εἴδωλα. Sic Clemens Alexandrinus, in admonitione ad gentes, εἴδωλα γὰρ εἰκῇ τοῖς αὐτοῖς δαίμοσιν ὑμῶν αὐτοὶ κεκλήκατε, Similiter eos vos ipsi idola & daemones vocatis. Et sic etiam 1 Cor. 10 20. quae gentes dicuntur immolare daemoniis, 8 4. & 7. vocantur εἰδωλόθυτα, quae idolis immolantur.
units.tr: V. 1. "Attending to erring spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars" [Προσέχοντες πνεύμασι πλάνοις καὶ διδασκαλίαις δαιμονίων, ἐν ὑποκρίσει ψευδολόγων &c.]. Castalio renders this "by the hypocrisy of men who speak falsely", and he adds "of men" so that "of liars" and what follows are not referred to the demons. Our Medus observed that it would surely be monstrous to say that demons tell lies in hypocrisy and have seared consciences. Medus also wants "doctrines of demons" understood as doctrines about demons, that is, about canonized saints and images or idols. We have authority for properly explaining "demons" as idols. Psalm 96:5 reads, in Hebrew, "for all the gods of the peoples are idols" [כִּי כָל אֱלֹהֵי הָעַמִּים אֱלִילִים], and in the Septuagint, "for all the gods of the nations are demons" [ὅτι οἱ Θεοὶ πάντες τῶν ἐθνῶν δαιμόνια]. The Chaldee paraphrase, the Latin version and the English interpreter all render it "all the gods of the nations are idols". So too the very words of the Seventy at 1 Chron. 16:26: "all the gods of the nations are idols" [ὅτι πάντες οἱ Θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν εἴδωλα]. Clement of Alexandria likewise, in his Exhortation to the Greeks: "For you yourselves have called idols by the same name as your demons" [εἴδωλα γὰρ εἰκῇ τοῖς αὐτοῖς δαίμοσιν ὑμῶν αὐτοὶ κεκλήκατε], that is, you call them idols and demons alike. So also at 1 Cor. 10:20, the things which the Gentiles are said to sacrifice to demons, and at 8:4 and 7, are called "things sacrificed to idols" [εἰδωλόθυτα].

units.la: V. 3. Κολλούμενοι χαμὴν, ἀπέχεσθαι βδελυ-γμα-τος. τῶν &c. Miror interpretes plerumque animum non advertere ad ea quæ Scholiastes Græcus in hæc verba observaverit. Nempe in iis esse nullum κοίλμα κολλυγαφικόν, ut quidam volunt, nec ullum περίεργον Αποσολικόν, ut alii, sed proprie et ὀρθῶς esse dictum secundum genuinum Atticismum, ut ὀπώλυε μὴ κλίπτειν, prohibuit furari, ὀπώλυεν ἀπέχεσθαι ἀφροσυνῶν, vetuit abstinere nefandorum. Quomodo etiam hoc loco repetendo vocem κωλυόντων, ἀπὸ τῆς χοινῆς, recte dicitur, κωλυόντων γαμεῖν, κωλυόντων ἀπέχεσθαι βρωμάτων, prohibentium conjugium, prohibentium cibos, &c. Verbis enim, quæ sunt per se negantia, Attici negationem addunt. Vide simile 1 Joh. 2. 22.
units.tr: V. 3. "Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats" [Κολλούμενοι χαμὴν, ἀπέχεσθαι βδελυγματος τῶν &c.]. I am surprised that most interpreters do not give heed to what the Greek Scholiast observed on these words. Namely, that there is in them no kollygraphic hollow [κοίλμα κολλυγαφικόν], as some hold, nor any apostolic superfluity [περίεργον Αποστολικόν], as others hold. It is said properly and correctly, according to genuine Attic usage, as in "he forbade [ὀπώλυε] to steal" and "he forbade [ὀπώλυεν] to abstain from wicked things". So here too, by repeating the word "forbidding" [κωλυόντων] from the common construction, it is rightly said "forbidding to marry" [κωλυόντων γαμεῖν] and "forbidding to abstain from meats" [κωλυόντων ἀπέχεσθαι βρωμάτων]. For the Attic writers add a negation to verbs that are already negative. See a similar case at 1 John 2:22.

units.la: V. 14. Μὴ ἀμέλει τῆς ἐν σοὶ χαρίσματος, ὃ ἐδόθη σοι διὰ προφητείας, μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου. i. e. trajectione frequentissima, & τῶν positio pro πάντων, & vertendo διὰ προφητείας in plurali, Noli negligere gratiam quæ in te est, quæ data est tibi propter prophetias presbyterii, per impositionem harum manuum. Atque ita locus iste congruit cum 2 Tim. 1. 6. ubi dicitur, τῶν χειρῶν μου manuum mearum. Propter Prophetias, i. e. propter προηγούμενας præcedentes de te prophetias presbyterii, quales jam antea memoravit. 1. 18. Propter hanc enim causam, eò quòd prophetæ & doctores ecclesiæ [qui collective fecerunt presbyterium] constanter de Timothei fide & bona conscientia prædixerunt sive propheràrunt, quas eum ibi retinere jubet Paulus, videtur forte solus ei imposuisse manus & ordinasse episcopum, ut etiam solus in Creta reliquit Titum, ὅπλ(χοντων πεσίτου ... μὴ πόσως cum prius fecisset episcopum ut Schol. Grac. Vel τῇ προηγουμένῃ potest convenire cum γαεἰζματτ© & denotare officium, ut Calvinus & alii. Noli negligere gratiam presbyterii, quae in te est, quae data est tibi propter prophetias [nempe de te praecedentes ut supra] cum impositione harum manuum. Διὰ cum Accusativo proprie propter. Ideo dicit prophetias, quia iussu & instinctu praedixerunt Spiritus. Nec est vulgarius aliquid quam ? pro τούτων. Sciat vero Lector me non haec apponere eo quod aliorum interpretationes improbem, sed quia nostra non videtur omnino contemnenda.
units.tr: V. 14. "Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecies, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery" [Μὴ ἀμέλει τῆς ἐν σοὶ χαρίσματος, ὃ ἐδόθη σοι διὰ προφητείας, μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου]. That is, with a very frequent transposition, and with "of the" [τῶν] standing for "of all" [πάντων], and rendering "through prophecies" [διὰ προφητείας] in the plural: "Do not neglect the grace of the presbytery that is in you, which was given to you on account of the prophecies, with the imposition of these hands." In this way the passage agrees with 2 Tim. 1:6, where it says "of my hands" [τῶν χειρῶν μου]. "On account of the prophecies" means on account of the prophecies made beforehand about you by the presbytery, such as he has already mentioned at 1:18. For on this account, because the prophets and teachers of the Church [who collectively formed the presbytery] constantly foretold, or prophesied, concerning Timothy's faith and good conscience, which Paul bids him keep, it seems perhaps that he alone laid hands on him and ordained him bishop, just as he alone left Titus in Crete, when he had first made him bishop, as the Greek Scholiast says. Or the Greek phrase may agree with the [garbled in the scan] and denote the office, as Calvin and others hold. "Do not neglect the grace of the presbytery which is in you, which was given to you on account of the prophecies [namely those made about you beforehand, as above], with the imposition of these hands." "Through" [Διὰ] with the accusative properly means "on account of". He says "prophecies" because they foretold by the command and inspiration of the Spirit. Nor is anything more commonplace than reading "?" for "of these". Let the reader know that I do not set these things forth because I disapprove of the interpretations of others, but because ours does not seem altogether to be despised.

units.la: C. 5. v. 4. Εἰ δέ τις χήρα τέκνα ἢ ἔκγονα ἔχει, μανθανέτωσαν πρῶτον τὸν ἴδιον οἶκον εὐσεβεῖν, καὶ ἀμοιβὰς ἀποδιδόναι τοῖς γονεῦσιν. Quod si qua vidua liberos habet vel nepotes, discant in primis propriam domum officiose colere, et vicem rependere parentibus. Τὸ εὐσεβεῖν quandoque significat pietatis officio fungi erga parentes; est enim & in parentes pietas, hinc apud Virgilium, Sum pius Aeneas, propter pietatem erga parentem Anchisem, eo quod portarit eum humeris iam valde senem in cumbustione Troiae. Sic Cic. 3. Offic. Ipsi patriae conducit pios habere cives in parentes, Et Quintilianus, Praestanda pietas parentibus. Et Solinus, Ciconiis etiam pietas eximia inest, enim quantum temporis suis foetibus educandis elargiuntur, tantum et ipse a pullis suis invicem aluntur. Hinc ἀντιπελαργεῖν, apud Suidam, est Ciconiarum more vicem rependere vel gratiam referre; οἱ γὰρ πελαργοὶ τὸν πεπρηγότας Ciconiae enim parentes senio confectos in alis gestant. Scopus loci est, quod si aliquando sit vidua senex, quae prae senio non possit seipsam alere, liberos eius vel nepotes debere eius in primis curam gerere. C. 6. v. 5. Νομιζόντων ποείσθαι εἶναι τὴν εὐσέβειαν, Existimantium pietatem esse quæstum sive mercaturam: ut Interpres Arabicus. De iis loquitur qui religionem profitentur ut ditescant: ποείσθαι, modus victum quærendi, vel quæstum faciendi. Ipsa actio comparandi & acquirendi. Steph. φησὶ γὰρ δύο μόνοις χρὴ ζῆν τοῖς ποείσθαι γεωργία καὶ φειδώ: Dicunt enim duobus tantum modis faciendi quæstum, agricultura & parsimonia. Plut.
units.tr: C. 5. v. 4.
