"But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to show piety to their own household and to repay their parents in return" [Εἰ δέ τις χήρα τέκνα ἢ ἔκγονα ἔχει, μανθανέτωσαν πρῶτον τὸν ἴδιον οἶκον εὐσεβεῖν, καὶ ἀμοιβὰς ἀποδιδόναι τοῖς γονεῦσιν]. If any widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to be dutiful toward their own household and to repay their parents. The verb "to show piety" [εὐσεβεῖν] sometimes means to perform the duty of piety toward parents, for there is also piety toward parents. Hence in Virgil, I am pious Aeneas, from his piety toward his father Anchises, whom he carried on his shoulders, already very old, when Troy was burning. So Cicero, in On Duties book 3: It is useful to the fatherland itself to have citizens who are pious toward their parents. And Quintilian: Piety is to be shown to parents. And Solinus: Storks also have outstanding piety, for as much time as they spend in rearing their young, so much they themselves are fed in turn by their chicks. Hence antipelargein [ἀντιπελαργεῖν] in Suidas means, in the manner of storks, to repay in turn or to return thanks; for storks carry their aged parents, worn out with years, on their wings. The point of the passage is this: if a widow is elderly and, because of her age, cannot support herself, her children or grandchildren ought above all to take care of her. C. 6. v. 5. "Supposing that piety is a means of gain" [Νομιζόντων ποείσθαι εἶναι τὴν εὐσέβειαν], that is, supposing piety to be a source of profit or trade, as the Arabic interpreter has it. He speaks of those who profess religion in order to grow rich. [ποείσθαι] denotes a way of seeking a living, or of making a profit, that is, the very act of acquiring and gaining. Stephanus says: "For they say there are only two ways of making a living, agriculture and thrift" [φησὶ γὰρ δύο μόνοις χρὴ ζῆν τοῖς ποείσθαι γεωργία καὶ φειδώ]. Plutarch.

units.la: In Epistolam Secundam ad Timotheum.
units.tr: On the Second Epistle to Timothy.

units.la: 1 TIM. c 1. v. 3. Χάριν ἔχω τῷ Θεῷ &c. ὡς ἀδιάλειπτον ἔχω τὴν περὶ σὲ μνείαν; Gratias ago Deo &c. hac eo quam continuam de te memoriam in precibus meis noctu & die.
units.tr: 1 TIM. c 1. v. 3. "I thank God, etc." Greek: "as I constantly have remembrance of you." Latin: "I thank God, etc., that is, how continual a memory of you I keep in my prayers night and day." [Greek: Χάριν ἔχω τῷ Θεῷ, ὡς ἀδιάλειπτον ἔχω τὴν περὶ σὲ μνείαν]

units.la: C. 2. v. 2. Καὶ ἃ ἤκουσας παρ' ἐμοῦ, διὰ πολλῶν μαρτυρῶν ταῦτα παράθου πιστοῖς ἀνθρώποις &c. Et quæ audivisti à me, tu ea multis testans commenda fidelibus hominibus, &c. Vel Καὶ ἃ ἤκουσας παρ' ἐμοῦ διὰ πολλῶν, μαρτυρῶν ταῦτα παράθου &c. Et quæ audivisti à me multis, tu ea testans commenda, vel testare & commenda fidelibus hominibus, &c. Διὰ πολλῶν, ut dià ἀλλήλων, 1 Pet. 5. 12. & διὰ ἐγχείρων, Heb. 13. 22. Neque vero sunt commutata aut accentus ab Authore adeo adeò ut veniam mihi fore sperem, si præter sententiam veterum distinctionem mutem & accentum, præsertim si eo facto faciliorem & gratiorem reddam sensum. Ægre enim διὰ πολλῶν μαχριμέων cum Grammatica, & recto exponuntur sensu. Quid enim sibi velit, quæ audivisti à me per multos testes, non bene convenit inter Interpretes.
units.tr: C. 2. v. 2. "And the things you have heard from me, commit these through many witnesses to faithful men, etc." Or, reading the Greek as "And the things you heard from me through many, bearing witness, commit these, etc.": "And what you heard from me among many, bear witness and commit these to faithful men, etc." The phrase "through many" [dia pollōn] is used as "through one another" (1 Pet. 5:12) and "through letters" (Heb. 13:22). I do not hold that the author's words or accents have been altered, yet I hope to be pardoned if, against the opinion of the ancients, I change the punctuation and accent, especially since by doing so I make the sense easier and more agreeable. For "through many witnesses" [dia pollōn martyrōn] is hardly explained with grammatical and proper sense. Indeed, what is meant by "what you heard from me through many witnesses" is not well agreed upon among the interpreters. [Greek: Καὶ ἃ ἤκουσας παρ' ἐμοῦ, διὰ πολλῶν μαρτυρῶν ταῦτα παράθου πιστοῖς ἀνθρώποις]

units.la: C. 2. v. 25. Μήποτε δῷ αὐτοῖς ὁ Θεὸς μετάνοιαν &c. Cum lenitate eos corripientem qui resistunt, forte dabit eis Deus pœnitentiam &c. ἴσως, φησίν, ἔσται τις διόρθωσις. Forte, inquit, erit aliqua emendatio, fortasse dederit Dominus pœnitentiam. Theophylact. LXX vocem אולי forte, sæpius vertunt μήποτε, ut Gen. 24. 5. & 39. 43. 12. 59. 15. & alibi.
units.tr: C. 2. v. 25. "Lest God perhaps give them repentance, etc." Greek: "correcting with gentleness those who resist, God perhaps will give them repentance, etc." [Greek: Μήποτε δῷ αὐτοῖς ὁ Θεὸς μετάνοιαν]. "Perhaps," he says, "there will be some correction; perhaps the Lord will give repentance." So Theophylact. The Seventy often render the Hebrew word for "perhaps" [ulai, אולי] by μήποτε, as in Gen. 24:5, 39:43, 12:59, 15:... and elsewhere.

units.la: In Epistolam ad Titum.
units.tr: On the Epistle to Titus.

units.la: TIT. 1. 1. Παῦλος δοῦλος Θεοῦ, ἀπόστολος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ κατὰ πίστιν ἐκλεκτῶν Θεοῦ, καὶ ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας τῆς κατ' εὐσέβειαν ἐπ' ἐλπίδι ζωῆς αἰωνίου, 2. (Ἣν ἐπηγγείλατο ὁ ἀψευδὴς Θεὸς πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων, ἐφανέρωσε δὲ καιροῖς ἰδίοις) 3. τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ ἐν κηρύγματι ὃ ἐπιστεύθην ἐγώ, &c. Paulus servus Dei, Apostolus autem Jesu Christi secundum fidem electorum Dei, & scientiam veritatis quæ est secundum pietatem in spe vitæ æternæ, 2. (Quam promisit qui non mentitur Deus ante tempora sæcularia, manifestavit autem in temporibus suis.) 3. Ipsum verbum ejus in prædicatione quæ mihi concredita est per præceptum Dei salvatoris nostri. Τὸν λόγον αὐτῆς, ipsum verbum ejus, videtur appositivum τῆς, χρ[?] πίστιν ἐκλεκτῶν Θεῦ, &c. secundum fidem electorum Dei, &c. v.1. Quasi innueret summam verbi Dei, i. e. Evangelii, ut vocatur Col.1. 25. esse vel comprehendi in fide electorum dei, & scientia veritatis quae est secundum pietatem in spe vitae aeternae. Cujus non omnino absimilis est sensus & constructio, ut supra animadvertimus, 1. Tim. 2.6.7. Εἷς γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς, εἷς καὶ μεσίτης Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων, ἄνθρωπος Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς, ὁ δοὺς ἑαυτὸν ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων, τὸ μαρτύριον, &c. ubi τὸ μαρτύριον est certè appositivum. Unus enim est Deus, unus etiam mediator Dei et hominum, homo Christus Iesus, qui dedit se redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, ipsum Evangelium, vel testimonium, cujus ego proprio tempore constitutus sum praedicator et Apostolus. Quid enim est fides electorum Dei, &c. nisi fides & scientia unum esse Deum, et unum Mediatorem Iesum Christum, qui dedit se redemptionis pretium pro omnibus? An non hoc est verbum Dei per praedicationem quae concredita est Paulo per praeceptum Dei Salvatoris nostri? Act. 20. 24. Gal. 1. 1.
units.tr: Tit. 1:1. "Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness, in hope of eternal life, (2) which God, who cannot lie, promised before the ages began, but in due time manifested (3) his word in the preaching entrusted to me, etc." Here "his word" [ton logon autou] seems to be in apposition with "according to the faith of God's elect," as though the sum of God's word, that is, the Gospel (as it is called in Col. 1:25), were comprehended in the faith of God's elect and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness, in hope of eternal life. Its sense and construction are not entirely unlike what we noted above at 1 Tim. 2:5-7: "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself a ransom for all, the testimony" [to martyrion], where "the testimony" is certainly in apposition: one God, and one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as the price of redemption for all, namely the Gospel or testimony, of which I am appointed preacher and apostle in its proper time. For what is the faith of God's elect, etc., but the faith and knowledge that there is one God and one Mediator, Jesus Christ, who gave himself as the price of redemption for all? Is this not the word of God, through the preaching entrusted to Paul by the command of God our Saviour? See Acts 20:24; Gal. 1:1.

units.la: C. 3. v. 7. Κληρονόμοι γενώμεθα (κατ' ἐλπίδα) ζωῆς αἰωνίου, Heredes simus (secundum spem) aeternae vitae.
units.tr: C. 3. v. 7. "That we might become heirs (according to hope) of eternal life."

units.la: In Epistolam ad Hebræos.
units.tr: In the Epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: "Os ὢν ἀπαύγασμα, Qui cùm sit radius gloria [ejus] ut interpret Syrus. Est enim certè ἀπαύγασμα a iquid amplius hoc loco quàm simplex ἀυγάζμαι ἀπαύγασμα, ἀυγάζμα ἀπὸ τ δόξης Splendor emicans e gloria Lei, ἐκλαμψις, ut Phavor. relucentia, seu refulgentia, aliquid quod ex alio resplendet, ut Erasm. & Vatab. φῶς ἐκ φωτὸς, ut Schol Græc. ἀ πίρροια τ τῦ παντοκράτορος δόξης. Emanatio gloriæ omnipotentis. Sap. Solom. 7. 25.
units.tr: "Who, being the brightness [ἀπαύγασμα] of glory," as the Syriac interpreter renders it: "who, being the radiance of his glory." Here ἀπαύγασμα certainly means something more than the simple ἀυγάζομαι. It is a splendour shining forth from the glory of God [ἀυγάζμα ἀπὸ τῆς δόξης], a flashing forth [ἔκλαμψις], as Pharaoh's... Here the sense is a reflection or refulgence, something that shines out from another, as Erasmus and Vatablus take it. It is "light from light" [φῶς ἐκ φωτός], as the Greek scholia put it, and "an effluence of the glory of the Almighty" [ἀπόῤῥοια τῆς τοῦ παντοκράτορος δόξης], an emanation of omnipotent glory. Compare Wisdom of Solomon 7:25.

units.la: V. 4. Τοσούτῳ κρείττων γινόμενος τῶν ἀγγέλων, Tanto superior factus Angelis. Τὸ ἐλαττον ὑπὸ τὸ κρεῖττον εὐλογεῖται, Minus seu inferius à superiore benedicitur. 7. 7: & apud Philemonem Ἀγαθὴ γυναικὸς ὅτι ὢ Νικοστράτη Μὴ κρείττον εἶναι τ' ἀνδρὸς ἀλλ' ὑπήκοον. Bonam uxorem decet, Nicostrate, nun esse superiorem viro sed obedientem.
units.tr: Heb. 1:4. "Having become so much superior to the angels" [Τοσούτῳ κρείττων γινόμενος τῶν ἀγγέλων]. "The lesser is blessed by the greater" [Τὸ ἔλαττον ὑπὸ τοῦ κρείττονος εὐλογεῖται]. Compare Philemon: "It is good for a wife, Nicostrate, not to be superior to her husband but to be obedient" [Ἀγαθὴ γυνὴ ὅτι ὢ Νικοστράτη, Μὴ κρείττον εἶναι τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἀλλ' ὑπήκοον]: a good wife ought, Nicostrate, not to be superior to her husband but obedient.

units.la: V. 7. 'O ποιῶν τὸς Ἀγγέλους αὐτῦ, πνεύματα καὶ τὰς λειτουργὸς αὐτῦ, πυρὸς φλόγα, Qui facit Angelos suos, spiritus, & ministros suos, flammam ignis. v. 14. vocat conjunctim λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα, quos hic divisim nominat πνεύματα, καὶ τὰς λειτουργὸς αὐτῦ. Πυρὸς φλόγα, flammam ignis ut or appositive dici. Omnino ac si diceret, 'O ποιῶν τὸς Ἀγγέλους αὐτῦ, πυρὸς φλόγα, Qui facit Angelos suos flammam ignis. Sic fere dicitur Exod. 3. 2. ὤφθη δὲ αὐτῷ Ἄγγελος Κυρίου ἐν φλογὶ πυρὸς, Et apparuit ei Angelus Domini. mini in flamma ignis, i. e. in specie flammæ ignis. Varias enim frequens est Angelos Dei induere formas, dum funguntur ejụ ministerio.
units.tr: Heb. 1:7. "Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire" [Ὁ ποιῶν τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πυρὸς φλόγα]. In verse 14 he calls them together "ministering spirits" [λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα], whereas here he names them separately, "spirits" and "his ministers". "A flame of fire" [πυρὸς φλόγα] is to be taken as an appositive, as if he had said: "who makes his angels a flame of fire." This is much like Exodus 3:2: "And the Angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire," that is, in the form of a flame of fire. For it is frequent for the angels of God to put on various forms while they discharge their ministry.

units.la: C. 2. v. 5. 'Οὐ γὰρ 'Αγγέλοις ὑπέταξε τὴν οἰκουμένην τὴν μέλλουσαν, περὶ ἡς λαλοῦμεν, Non enim Angelis subjecit mundum hunc futurum de quo loquimur. Futurus mundus, de quo nunc loquitur, est ætas mundi in qua incœpit salutis ipsius, de qua v. 3. per Christum & Apostolos dispensatio, quæ quidem ministrationi Angelorum non subjecta fuit, ut erat lex prioribus sæculis, quæ ordinata est per Angelos. Act. 7. 53 & Gal 3. 19. Antequam enim veniret fides, sub lege custodiebamur conclusi in eam quæ revelanda erat fidem. Gal. 3. 23. Atque hujus fidei ministratio non subjecta fuit Angelis, sed regno Christi, quod per Evangelii prædicationem ἐν ὑσ᾽ὲσις καιροῖς, in posterioribus temporibus ministratum est, cum signis & miraculis, καὶ ποικίλαις δυνάμεσι, & multis virtutibus, quas etiam vocat, 6. 5. Δυνάμεις μέλλοντος αἰῶνος, Virtutes futuri sæculi. Quod quidem non potest esse aliud quàm ἡ οἰκουμένη μέλλουσα. hic futurus mundus sæculum salutis, mundus Evangelii.
units.tr: Heb. 2:5. "For he did not subject to the angels the world to come, of which we speak" [Οὐ γὰρ ἀγγέλοις ὑπέταξε τὴν οἰκουμένην τὴν μέλλουσαν, περὶ ἧς λαλοῦμεν]. The future world of which he now speaks is the age of the world in which the salvation itself began, of which in verse 3 he speaks as the dispensation through Christ and the Apostles. This dispensation was indeed not subject to the ministry of angels, as the law was in earlier ages, which was ordained through angels (Acts 7:53; Gal. 3:19). For before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up to the faith which was to be revealed (Gal. 3:23). The ministry of this faith was not subject to the angels but to the kingdom of Christ, which was administered through the preaching of the Gospel in these last times [ἐπ' ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν / ἐν ὑστέροις καιροῖς], with signs and wonders [καὶ ποικίλαις δυνάμεσι], and various powers, which he also calls the powers of the age to come (Heb. 6:5) [Δυνάμεις μέλλοντος αἰῶνος]. This can surely be nothing other than the future world here: the age of salvation, the world of the Gospel.

units.la: C. 6. v. 4. &c. 'Αδύνατον γὰρ τοὺς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας &c. καὶ παραπεσόντας πάλιν ἀνακαινίζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν, ἀνασταυροῦντας ἑαυτοῖς τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ παραδειγματίζοντας. Impossibile est enim eos qui semel sunt illuminati & gustarunt donum cœleste, & participes facti sunt spiritus sancti, & gustarunt bonum verbum Dei, & virtutes futuri sæculi, & prolapsi fuerint rursum sibi metipsis crucifigentes filium Dei, & ad ignominiam exponentes denuo renovare ad pœnitentiam
units.tr: Heb. 6:4 etc. "For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened and have tasted the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to renew them again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to shame" [Ἀδύνατον γὰρ τοὺς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας ... καὶ παραπεσόντας πάλιν ἀνακαινίζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν, ἀνασταυροῦντας ἑαυτοῖς τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ παραδειγματίζοντας].

units.la: [The bottom line of the page: marginal text cut off at the foot.] am. Est etiam necessario in hoc loco metathesis, Nam certè τὸ πάλιν ἀναχαινίζειν εἰς με- τάνοιαν non suo loco apponitur, vel enim sequi debuit ἀναςαυροῦντας ἑαυτοῖς ἀ̓ψὸν τὸ Θεοῦ ᾧ παραδειγματίζοντας, vel praecedere post ἀδύ- νατον ςὸ v. 4.
units.tr: [The bottom line of the page: marginal text cut off at the foot.] ...am. There is also necessarily a metathesis (transposition) in this place. For the words "to renew again to repentance" [τὸ πάλιν ἀνακαινίζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν] are not placed in their proper position. Either the clause should have followed "crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to shame," or it should have come before "impossible" in verse 4.

units.la: C. 7. v. 1. Οὑτος γὰρ ὁ Μελχισεδὲκ &c. Ut recta fiat interpretatio, recurrendum ad versum decimum nonum praecedentis capitis. Καὶ ὑσος- χομένῳ εἰς τὸ ἐσώτερον τῆς καταπετάσματος, ὅπου πρόδρομος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν εἰσῆλθεν Ἰησοῦς κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδὲκ ἀρχιερεὺς γενόμενος εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. Οὗτος γὰρ ὁ Μελχισεδὲκ βασιλεὺς Σαλήμ, ἱερεὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου, ὁ συναντήσας Ἀβραὰμ ὑποστρέφοντι ἀπὸ τῆς κοπῆς τῶν βασιλέων, καὶ εὐλογήσας αὐτόν. ᾧ καὶ δεκάτην ἀπὸ πάντων ἐμέρισεν Ἀβραάμ, πρῶτον μὲν ἑρμηνευόμενος βασιλεὺς δικαιοσύνης, ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ βασιλεὺς Σαλήμ, ὅ ἐστι, βασιλεὺς εἰρήνης, ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, μήτε ἀρχὴν ἡμερῶν μήτε ζωῆς τέλος ἔχων, ἀφωμοιωμένος δὲ τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ, μένει ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸ διηνεκές. Εἰς ὑσ- cedentem in interiora velaminis, ubi praecursor pro nobis introiit Jesus secundum similitudinem Melchisedec Pontifex factus in aeternum. Hic enim [Jesus] (ipse Melchisedec rex Salem, sacerdos Dei altissimi, qui occurrit Abrahae revertenti à caede regum, & benedixit ei, cui & decimas ex omnibus divisit Abraham, qui quidem primùm est interpretatione Rex justitiae, deinde autem & rex Salem, quod est rex pacis, sine patre sine matre, sine genealogia, neque initium dierum, neque finem vitae habens, sed assimilatus filio Dei, ) manet sacerdos in aeternum. Vox Jesus, à communi repetenda. Hic enim Jesus, qui introiit in interiora velaminis, pontifex factus in aeternum secundum similitudinem. litudinem Melchisedec, ipse, verus existens Melchisedecus, praefiguratus vero in Melchisedeco, qui obviavit Abrahamo, &c. erat enim ille nisi figura Christi. Hic Jesus, aio, manet sacerdos in aeternum. Dicitur Melchisedec assimilatus filio Dei, eo quod vocatur sacerdos Dei altissimi, Rex justitiae & pacis, neque dierum initium, neque finem vitae habens, &c. quae attributa sunt soli congrua filio Dei; licet tamen quodammodo Melchisedeco communicabilia, quia nec pater, nec mater, nec aetas ejus memoratur in Scriptura. Atque haec lectio, distinctio, & interpretatio, quae sunt in se admodum legitimae, vitant duas egregias ἀμφιβολίας, alteram in natura, mortalem vivere in perpetuum; alteram in fide, duos esse sacerdotes qui remanent in aeternum. Adeo ut nihil restet, his expeditis, quod impediat difficillimae quaestionis solutionem, nisi verba quae sequuntur. v. 8. Καὶ ὧδε μὲν δεκάτας ἀποδιδόντες ἄνθρωποι λαμβάνουσιν, ἐκεῖ δὲ μαρτυρούμενος ὅτι ζῇ. Quae verba si pari modo recte exponantur (ut heri poterat licite) omnia salva sunt, nec est quod quis ultra de mente hujus loci dubiter. Atqui ut id fiat, post subaudiendum ἐκεῖ, & non λαμβάνει: ἐκεῖ δὲ μαρτυρούμενος ὅτι ζῇ. Atque hic quidem decimas accipiunt morientes homines, ibi vero est de quo testatum est quod vivit. Ut semel dicam, ὧδε, hic, i. e. in hoc mundo homines qui moriuntur sunt sacerdotes, illi enim soli accipiebant decimas; ἐκεῖ δέ, ibi vero, i. e. ἐν τῷ ἐσωτέρῳ τῆς καταπετάσματος, &c. in interiore velaminis ubi praecursor pro nobis introiit Jesus, nempe in summo coelo est ille de quo testatum est, quod factus sit sacerdos in aeternum secundum similitudinem Melchisedec, qui semper vivit Jesus Christus. Atque hoc totidem fere verbis ipsissimo sensu repetit Apostolus, v. 23.24 & 25. quasi de industria ut mentem hujus loci explicet. Καὶ οἱ μὲν πλείονές εἰσι γεγονότες ἱερεῖς &c. Et illi quidem, qui sunt ὧδε, hic, in hoc mundo, plures sunt facti sacerdotes, idcirco quod morte prohiberentur permanere; hic vero [nempe Jesus] eò quòd maneat in aeternum, sempiternum habet sacerdotium, unde & salvare in perpetuum potest accedentes per semetipsum ad Deum, πάντοτε ζῶν, semper vivens ad interpellandum pro eis. Ita ut qui accipiunt decimas & moriuntur, v. 8. non possint esse alii quàm plures sacerdotes qui morte prohibebantur permanere, v. 23. Neque ille de quo testatum est quod vivit, v. 8. potest esse alius quàm ipse Jesus, qui v. 24. dicitur manere in æternum, & v. 25. semper vivens. De mente igitur huius loci non est opinor quod quis ultra dubitet, nisi sponte occludat oculos. Et quidem Heinsius positivè affirmavit, necessariò ipsissimos eosdemque esse utrisque locis nominatos, in majorem fidem Ambrosii testimonium addens. Quis est qui vivit? Ille etiam qui secundum ordinem Melchisedec factus est sacerdos in aeternum. Multa plura possunt addi, sed hæc reor sufficere ad demonstrandum, verba illa, manet sacerdos in æternum, v. 3. & de quo testatum est quod vivit, v. 8. unicè intelligi de ipso Jesu, nullo verò modo de Melchisedeco. Adeò ut evanescat prorsus opinio Cunæi, qui Christum voluit ipsum eundemque fuisse Melchisedecum, qui obviavit Abrahamo, Gen. 14. species humana, sacerdotis, regisque habitu indutus. De qua opinione non amplius addam, quàm quod pronunciavit Beza. Eos nempè esse aperte fanaticos qui eam tuebantur; & argumentum Epiphanii, Οὐ γὰρ τις ἑαυτῷ ὅμοιος γίνεταί ποτε, Non enim sibi similis quisquam unquam
units.tr: Heb. 7:1. "For this Melchizedek etc." [Οὗτος γὰρ ὁ Μελχισεδὲκ]. To make the interpretation correct, we must return to verse 19 of the preceding chapter: "...and which enters into that within the veil, where the forerunner Jesus has entered for us, having become high priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek" [Εἰς τὸ ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος, ὅπου πρόδρομος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν εἰσῆλθεν Ἰησοῦς κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδὲκ ἀρχιερεὺς γενόμενος εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα]. "For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, to whom also Abraham divided a tenth of all, first being interpreted king of righteousness, and then also king of Salem, that is, king of peace, without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, remains a priest for ever" [Οὗτος γὰρ ὁ Μελχισεδὲκ βασιλεὺς Σαλήμ, ἱερεὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου, ὁ συναντήσας Ἀβραὰμ ὑποστρέφοντι ἀπὸ τῆς κοπῆς τῶν βασιλέων, καὶ εὐλογήσας αὐτόν, ᾧ καὶ δεκάτην ἀπὸ πάντων ἐμέρισεν Ἀβραάμ, πρῶτον μὲν ἑρμηνευόμενος βασιλεὺς δικαιοσύνης, ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ βασιλεὺς Σαλήμ, ὅ ἐστι, βασιλεὺς εἰρήνης, ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, μήτε ἀρχὴν ἡμερῶν μήτε ζωῆς τέλος ἔχων, ἀφωμοιωμένος δὲ τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ, μένει ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸ διηνεκές]. The word "Jesus" is to be repeated from the common text: "For this Jesus, who entered within the veil, became high priest for ever according to the similitude of Melchizedek," who is himself the true Melchizedek, though prefigured in the Melchizedek who met Abraham, and so on, for that man was nothing but a figure of Christ. This Jesus, I say, remains a priest for ever. Melchizedek is said to be made like the Son of God because he is called priest of the most high God, king of righteousness and peace, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, and so on, which attributes belong only to the Son of God; yet they can in some measure be communicated to Melchizedek, since neither father, mother nor age of his is recorded in Scripture. This reading, distinction and interpretation, which are in themselves quite legitimate, avoid two notable ambiguities: one in nature, that a mortal should live for ever; the other in faith, that there should be two priests who remain for ever. So that, once these are cleared away, nothing remains to hinder the solution of this most difficult question except the words that follow, verse 8: "And here indeed dying men receive tithes, but there it is witnessed of him that he lives" [Καὶ ὧδε μὲν δεκάτας ἀποδιδόντες ἄνθρωποι λαμβάνουσιν, ἐκεῖ δὲ μαρτυρούμενος ὅτι ζῇ]. If these words are rightly expounded in the same way (as yesterday I could lawfully do), all is safe, and there is nothing further to doubt about the meaning of this place. But so that this may be done, after supplying ἐκεῖ, and not λαμβάνει, we read: "and there it is witnessed that he lives." So here indeed dying men receive tithes, but there is one of whom it is witnessed that he lives. To put it briefly: ὧδε, "here," that is, in this world, men who die are priests, for only they received tithes; ἐκεῖ δέ, "but there," that is, in the inner part of the veil, and so on, where the forerunner Jesus has entered for us, namely in the highest heaven, is he of whom it is witnessed that he has been made a priest for ever according to the likeness of Melchizedek, who lives for ever, Jesus Christ. The Apostle repeats this in almost the same words and with exactly the same sense in verses 23, 24 and 25, as if on purpose to explain the meaning of this place: "And indeed those were made priests in greater number" [Καὶ οἱ μὲν πλείονές εἰσι γεγονότες ἱερεῖς] and so on. Those indeed who are ὧδε, here, in this world, were made priests in greater number, because death prevented them from remaining; but he [namely Jesus], because he remains for ever, has an everlasting priesthood, whence he is also able to save for ever those who come to God through him, always living [πάντοτε ζῶν], to make intercession for them always. Thus those who receive tithes and die (verse 8) cannot be other than the many priests who were prevented by death from remaining (verse 23). Nor can he of whom it is witnessed that he lives (verse 8) be anyone other than Jesus himself, who in verse 24 is said to remain for ever, and in verse 25 always living. Therefore, I think, there is no reason to doubt the meaning of this place further, unless one wilfully shuts one's eyes. Indeed, Heinsius affirmed positively that of necessity the very same person is named in both places, adding the testimony of Ambrose in greater confidence: "Who is it that lives? He also who was made a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek." Many more things could be added, but these I think suffice to show that the words "remains a priest for ever" (verse 3) and "of whom it is witnessed that he lives" (verse 8) are understood solely of Jesus himself, and in no way of Melchizedek. So the opinion of Cunaeus vanishes altogether, who wished Christ to be the very same person as the Melchizedek who met Abraham (Gen. 14), clothed in human form, with the habit of priest and king. On this opinion I will add no more than what Beza pronounced: that those who defended it are plainly fanatics. And Epiphanius's argument: "For no one is ever like himself" [Οὐ γάρ τις ἑαυτῷ ὅμοιος γίνεταί ποτε], for no one is ever, or can be called, like himself.

units.tr: The text is cut off at the bottom of the page. will ever be or can be called, as the Interpreter has it. Apostle himself explains κατὰ τάξιν [according to the order] as κατὰ τὴν ὁμοιότητα [according to the likeness], after the likeness of Melchizedek, v. 15, and the interpreters generally explain it in this way.

units.la: V. 4. ὧ χ͞ρ Ἀεκάτλω Ἀβραὰμ ἔδωκεν ἐν τ ἀκεῳδινίων ὁ πατριάρχης. Insigne est & hic Hyperbaton pro ὧ χ͞ρ Ἀεκάτλω ὁ πατριάρχης Ἀβραάμ &c.
units.tr: v. 4. ᾧ καὶ δεκάτην Ἀβραὰμ ἔδωκεν ἐκ τῶν ἀκροθινίων ὁ πατριάρχης [to whom also Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils]. Here too is a notable hyperbaton, for ᾧ καὶ δεκάτην ὁ πατριάρχης Ἀβραὰμ, etc.

units.la: C. 9, v. 1. Τὸ, τε ἅγιον κοσμικόν, Sanctuarium mundanum, i. e. Sanctuarium factum opificio humano, ἀντίτυπον τῆς ἀληθινῆς, antitypum veri Sanctuarii in quod ingressus est Christus, nempe εἰς αὐτὸν τ ἐρανὸν, in ipsum caelum. v. 24. vocatur etiam v. 11 χειροποίητον, τυτέστι, ταύτης τ κτίσεως, manufactum, i. e. hujus mundi, Distinguit inter sanctuarium coeleste, quod fixit Deus, & non homo, 8. 2. cujus minister est Christus, & inter sanctuarium mundanum, quod fabricavit Solomon ope humanâ, cujus ministri sunt sacerdotes Aaronici. Neque vero atrium Gentium, quod aliqui hoc loco volunt esse τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν usquam vocatur ἅγιον. Imo ipsi, quibus patebat atrium gentium, ἐντὸς τῆς ἁγίας παρεῖναι, &c transfire in locum sanctum, scripto literis Graecis & Latinis prohibebantur. Josephus de bell. Jud. lib. 6. c. 6.
units.tr: C. 9, v. 1. τὸ τε ἅγιον κοσμικόν [the worldly sanctuary], a worldly sanctuary, that is, a sanctuary made by human workmanship, ἀντίτυπον τῆς ἀληθινῆς [a copy of the true one], a copy of the true sanctuary into which Christ entered, namely εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν οὐρανόν [into heaven itself], into heaven itself. At v. 24 it is also called, at v. 11, χειροποίητον [made by hand], that is, τῆς ταύτης κτίσεως [of this creation], made by hand, that is, of this world. He distinguishes between the heavenly sanctuary, which God fixed and not man (8.2), whose minister is Christ, and the worldly sanctuary, which Solomon built with human means, and whose ministers are the Aaronic priests. Nor is the court of the Gentiles, which some wish to be τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικόν in this place, anywhere called ἅγιον [holy]. Indeed, those to whom the court of the Gentiles was open were forbidden, by an inscription in Greek and Latin letters, to go within the holy place, to pass into the holy place. Josephus, Bell. Jud. bk. 6, ch. 6.

units.la: V. 15. Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο διαθήκης καινῆς μεσίτης ἐστὶν, ὅπως θανάτου γενομένου εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῶν ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεων, τὸ ἐπαγγελίαν λάβωσιν οἱ κεκλημένοι τῆς αἰωνίου κληρονομίας. Et propter hoc novi testamenti mediator est, ut, morte facta [nempe sua] in redemptionem sub priore testamento transgressionum, promissionem accipiant qui vocati sunt aeternae haereditatis
units.tr: v. 15. Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο διαθήκης καινῆς μεσίτης ἐστίν, ὅπως θανάτου γενομένου εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῶν ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεων, τὸ ἐπαγγελίαν λάβωσιν οἱ κεκλημένοι τῆς αἰωνίου κληρονομίας. And for this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that, a death having taken place [namely his own] for the redemption of the transgressions under the first covenant, those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.

units.la: i. e. accipiant omnes qui vocati sunt vel sub priore vel sub novo testamento. Vel aliter, ut, morte facta vitulorum nempe & hircorum ad expiandum peccata sacerdotis & populi sub testamento priore, Lev. 16. qui vocati sunt sub testamento novo per prædicationem Evangelii, accipiant promissionem æternæ hæreditatis; Per prædicationem aio Evangelii, est enim τὸ κηρυγμα in spirituali sensu sive spiritualiter intellectum verbum pure Evangelicum. Potrò per prædicationem Evangelii didicimus, quòd Christus ingressus est in sancta, i. e. in summum cœlum per proprium sanguinem, suâ morte pro nobis æternam redemptionem adeptus, v. 12. Atque hinc idoneo sensu sequitur v. 16. & 22. Nam ubi testamentum est, mortem necesse est intercedere testatoris, & absque sanguinis effusione non fit remissio. Mors enim & effusio sanguinis hircorum & vitulorum sub lege typus erat mortis Christi sub Evangelio, adeò ut salvarentur patres per fidem in venturo Christo dum typicè peragebant ejus mortis symbola per effusionem sanguinis hircorum & vitulorum pro expiatione peccatorum, ut salvantur nunc fideles per fidem suam in Christo jam exhibito. Vel adhuc aliter, locus enim est non adeò facilis; Ut, morte existente in priore Testamento ad redemptionem transgressionum, promissionem accipiant qui vocati sunt æternæ hæreditatis, morte e isticnte, i.e. ἀπολυτρώσεως, quod Anglicè diceremus, ut Rom. 4. 19. There being a deadness in the first Testament as to the redemption of transgressions. Quasi diceret, Idcirco mediator est novi Testamenti, ut, cum prius sit quasi emortuum sine viribus ad liberandum servientes a peccatis, promissionem nunc accipiant. ant æterne hereditatis, qui voca- carionem Evangelii, quæ hdem p Christi, propterea quod Lex num hostiis accedentes perfectos possunt hostiæ peccata auferre. c. Propterea quod emortuum & prius testamentum ad peccata r Iesus Christus mediator novi. vacasset culpâ, non quæreretur Heb. 8. 7.
units.tr: That is, all who are called, whether under the former or the new covenant, may receive. Or otherwise: that, a death having occurred of calves and goats, namely to atone for the sins of the priest and the people under the former covenant (Lev. 16), those who are called under the new covenant through the preaching of the Gospel may receive the promise of eternal inheritance. I say through the preaching of the Gospel, for τὸ κηρυγμα [the proclamation] is, in a spiritual sense, the word taken purely in its Gospel sense. For through the preaching of the Gospel we have learned that Christ entered into the holy places, that is, into the highest heaven, through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption by his death for us (v. 12). And from this, in a fitting sense, there follows v. 16 and v. 22: For where there is a testament, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator, and without shedding of blood there is no remission. For the death and shedding of the blood of goats and calves under the law was a type of the death of Christ under the Gospel, so that the fathers were saved through faith in the coming Christ, while they symbolically performed the signs of his death by shedding the blood of goats and calves for the expiation of sins, just as the faithful are now saved through their faith in Christ already revealed. Or else, in yet another way, for the passage is not so easy: so that, death being in the former Testament for the redemption of transgressions, they who are called may receive the promise of eternal inheritance, death being present, that is, of ἀπολυτρώσεως [redemption], which we would say in English, as in Rom. 4:19: There being a deadness in the first Testament as to the redemption of transgressions. As if he were saying: Therefore he is mediator of the new Testament, so that, since the former was as it were dead and without strength to free those in bondage to sins, they may now receive the promise of eternal inheritance, they who are called… (the rest of this sentence is illegible in the scan, and the text is broken off here: the Gospel, which is the sacrifice of Christ, because the law could not by its sacrifices make the worshippers perfect and take away sins; and because the first covenant, being dead and fallen through fault, would not have been sought: Heb. 8:7).

units.la: C. 10. v. 26. ʿΕκουσίως γὰρ ἁμαρτανόντων ἡμῶν. Voluntariè enim peccantibus nobis notitiam veritatis non amplius relinquitur sacrificium pro peccatis hostia. Sic 2 Macc. 14. [?]
units.tr: ch. 10, v. 26. Ἑκουσίως γὰρ ἁμαρτανόντων ἡμῶν [For if we sin wilfully]. For if we sin wilfully, after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains. So 2 Macc. 14 [?].

units.la: λυμαίνεσθαι, Voluntariè coinquinat locis Vetus, i. e. volente animo, prudenter, & scienter, ut dicimus ip, in quo sensu se dicit Cicero pro cupiditate, sed ne ipse quidem pro tem tanquam ad interitum ruit.
units.tr: λυμαίνεσθαι [to defile]: wilfully defiles, in the passages of the Old (Testament), that is, with a willing mind, deliberately and knowingly, as we say of purpose. In this sense Cicero says of himself that he is driven by desire, but not even he rushes to ruin as though to destruction.

units.la: Qui vero voluntariè post acceptam veritatis peccant, sunt Apostatæ, resiliunt à Christo, ut bellum indi quantum in se est rursum crucifigunt & ad ignominiam exponunt, c. 6. volenter renunciârint, quid aliud stare nisi horrendum judicium, sum non sit in mundo pro peccatis
units.tr: But those who sin wilfully after receiving the truth are apostates; they fall away from Christ, and as far as in them lies they crucify him again and expose him to shame (ch. 6). Having wilfully renounced [the truth], what else remains but a dreadful judgment, since there is no longer a sacrifice for sins in the world?

units.la: C. 11. v. 4. Καὶ ἀὐτῆς ἀποθανόντος ἔτι λαλεῖται. Subaudiendum sive, Elle mâ, i. e. ἀποθανὼν ἔστι. Et pro dicitur esse mortuus, nempè propter rem enim suum occidisse Cain pro quam testimonium obtinuit quod huc in hunc usque diem dicimus.
units.tr: ch. 11, v. 4. Καὶ αὐτῆς ἀποθανόντος ἔτι λαλεῖται [And through it, though dead, he still speaks]. Understand or, ἀποθανὼν ἐστί [he is dead]. And he is said to be dead, namely because Cain slew him, and on account of this he obtained the testimony which we speak of to this day.
