units.la: V. II.

V. 11. Εἰς καταβολὴν (σπέρματος) Virtutem accepit in fundationem seminis, quod futurum erat, ut sequitur, tanquam sydera cœli in multitudine, &c. In quo benedicenda erant omnes familiae terrae. Καταβολὴ dicitur, cùm res aliqua sumit exordium. Hieron ut καταβολὴ κόσμου, Fundatio mundi. Matth. 13. 35. Luc. 11. 50. Heb. 4. 3. Apocal. 13 8. 17, 8. Quâ verò Philosophiâ, Logicâ, Grammaticâ, vel quo Lexico poterit verti, virtutem in conceptionem feminis accepit, vel ad ejaculatum semen concipiendum, magis literatis inquirendum egomet relinquo.
units.tr: v. 11. Εἰς καταβολὴν (σπέρματος) [for the conception (of seed)]: she received strength for the laying down of seed, which was to come, as follows, like the stars of heaven in multitude, etc., in whom all the families of the earth were to be blessed. Καταβολὴ is used when a thing takes its beginning, as in καταβολὴ κόσμου [foundation of the world] (Matt. 13:35; Luke 11:50; Heb. 4:3; Rev. 13:8, 17:8). But by what philosophy, logic or grammar, or by what lexicon, it can be rendered she received strength for the conception of seed, or for conceiving the emitted seed, I leave for the more learned to inquire.

units.la: V. 37. Ἐπειράσθησαν, Tentati sunt: ut Job. Schol. Græc. ut Abraham & Isaac. Theodoret. Sed plerique recentes, ut & aliqui inter Veteres, alterius sunt sententiæ, ideoque dicunt irrepsisse hoc verbum imperitia Amanuensis, vel non recte scribi vel per περίεργα καλλιγραφικὸν vel ἀπυσολικόν. Eò enim quòd tautologia foret dicere ἐπειράσθησαν, tentati sunt, cùm modò dictum fit περιῆλθον, quod unum idemque sonat, & quia sunt ab utraque manu verba denotantia aliquod genus mortis, probabile existimant, vel hoc verbum non debere omninò legi, ut à Syro, Æthiopico, Chrysostomo, & aliis omittitur; vel si legatur, debere intelligi in aliquâ notione, cujus nulla antea facta est mentio, & quæ genus aliquod mortis denotat. Atque inde moti legerunt aliqui, ἐπυρώθησαν, alii ἐπυρώθησαν, cremati sunt. At verò si quis est conjecturæ locus, crediderim ego potius debuisse scribi, ἐπιξήθησαν, propter magis gratam paranomasiam, quæ familiaris erat Paulo; ἐλιθάσθησαν, ἐπειράσθησαν, ἐπρίσθησαν, lapidati sunt, serrâ dissecti sunt, transfossi vel transfixi sunt, Mortis genere adeò noto, ut non sit credibile Apostolum hoc loco illud posse praeterire, ubi singulatim enumerat tot mortis genera, quae Christiani iis temporibus, & Prophetae olim perpessi sunt propter fidem; Inter quae Nicephorus & Eusebius ex Dionysii scriptis de Martyribus Alexandrinis enumerant etiam transverberationem viscerum per sudes, quod apud Phavorinum ἀναςκολοπίζειν dicitur. Τὸ γὰρ παλαιὸν τὰς κακουργοῦντας ἀναςκολοπίζον (ὀξύνοντες ξύλον διὰ τῆς ῥάχεως τῆς νώτου) καθάπερ τὰς ὀπτωμένας ἰχθύας ὅπι ὀξελισκων. Olim enim malefactores transfigebant (figentes palum per spinam dorsi) quemadmodum pisces assatos in verubus.
units.tr: v. 37. ἐπειράσθησαν [they were tempted]: as in Job. Greek scholia, and as with Abraham and Isaac, Theodoret. But most recent writers, and some of the ancients too, take a different view, and therefore say this word crept in through the ignorance of a copyist, or is wrongly written, or is a superfluous calligraphic flourish. For since it would be tautological to say ἐπειράσθησαν, they were tempted, when περιῆλθον [they went about] has just been said, which means much the same, and since the other words in the sequence denote some kind of death, they think it probable either that this word should not be read at all, as it is omitted by the Syriac, the Ethiopic, Chrysostom and others; or, if it is read, it must be understood in some sense not previously mentioned, denoting a kind of death. Moved by this, some have read ἐπυρώθησαν [they were burned], others [read another word]. But if there is any room for conjecture, I would rather believe it ought to have been written ἐπιξήθησαν, for the sake of the more pleasing paronomasia which was familiar to Paul: ἐλιθάσθησαν, ἐπειράσθησαν, ἐπρίσθησαν [they were stoned, they were tempted, they were sawn asunder], stoned, sawn asunder, pierced through, a kind of death so well known that it is not credible the Apostle would pass it over here, where he individually enumerates so many kinds of death which Christians in those times, and the prophets of old, suffered for the faith. Among these Nicephorus and Eusebius, from Dionysius's writings on the Alexandrian martyrs, also list transfixion of the bowels by stakes, which in Phavorinus is called ἀναςκολοπίζειν [to impale]. For of old they impaled malefactors (driving a stake through the spine of the back), just as fish are skewered on spits for roasting. [Τὸ γὰρ παλαιὸν τοὺς κακουργοῦντας ἀνασκολοπίζον (ὀξύνοντες ξύλον διὰ τῆς ῥάχεως τῆς νώτου) καθάπερ τοὺς ὀπτωμένους ἰχθύας ἐπὶ ὀβελισκῶν.]

units.la: C. 12. v. 24. Καὶ αἵματι ῥαντισμοῦ κρεῖττον λαλοῦντι παρὰ τὸν Ἄβελ. Et ad sanguinem aspersionis quae meliora loquitur quam Abelis aspersio: sive ut quidam codices legunt, παρὰ τὸ, quam sanguis Abelis, sive ut Interlinearis in Bibliis nostris Polyglottis, Et sanguine aspersionis meliora loquentem quam Abel. Legas vero quocunque modo velis, sensus eodem recidit, & plane est hujusmodi. Sacrificium sive oblationem Christi in cruce meliora loqui ad placandam iram Dei, quam sacrificium vel oblatio Abelis, i.e. quam locutus est sanguis, quem obtulit Abel Deo in sacrificium, quod scilicet erat typus, isque omnium quos novimus primus magni illius sacrificii, quod in plenitudine temporis obtulit in cruce per effusionem sanguinis sui Christus propter peccata mundi; & propter hoc ipsum quod Abel primus omnium viventium obtulit oblationem Domino de primogenitis gregis sui, per quam testificatus est fidem in venturo Christo, & sese oblaturo pro peccatis mundi, omnino videtur Deus respexisse ad Abelem & oblationem ejus. Fide enim dicitur tur Abel obtulisse Deo melius sacrificium quàm Cain, & per hanc sive propter hanc fidem testimonium consecutus est quod esset justus. Adeò ut nihil aliud denoter hoc loco τὸ Ἁβέλ, quàm ritus & oblationes veteris Testamenti, unico exemplo eóque nobilissimo posito pro omnibus. Dicere vero, quòd sanguis Christi meliora loquitur quàm sanguis Abelis, qui clamat ad cœlum pro vindicta contra Cain, ut mitius dicam, non convenit cum scopo loci, cùm Apostolus ferè totus in hoc laborat, ut palam faciat quàm invalidæ cæremoniæ veteris legis erant ad acquirendam vitam æternam, & quantum fœdus Evangelii præstiterit fœderi veteris Testamenti, ut liquidò manifestum est per totam sermonis seriem, c. 9. & 10. Sed ut rem ipsam salvâ reverentiâ dicam, expositio illa est plane ἀντιστροφή, contraria ipsi Logicæ. Comparata enim esse oportet secundum magis & minus ejusdem speciei & naturæ, ita, ut in comparatione melioritatis alterum dici possit aliquo modo & gradu bonum ad id, ad quod alterum melius dicitur; τὸ κρεῖττον κατὰ πινὸς δεῖ κρεῖττον. Quod melius est, melius est aliquo quod bonum est, Chrysost. At verò sanguis Abelis proprius non fuit omnino bonus, ad id, ad quod valebat sanguis Christi.
units.tr: Chapter 12, verse 24: "And to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than Abel" [Καὶ αἵματι ῥαντισμοῦ κρεῖττον λαλοῦντι παρὰ τὸν Ἄβελ]. Or, as some manuscripts read, "than that of Abel" [παρὰ τὸ]; or, as the Interlinear in our Polyglot Bibles has it, "And to the blood of sprinkling speaking better things than Abel." Whichever way one reads it, the sense comes to the same thing, and it is plainly this: the sacrifice or offering of Christ on the cross speaks better, in appeasing the anger of God, than the sacrifice or offering of Abel, that is, than the blood which Abel offered to God in sacrifice, which was of course a type, and the first of all those we know of that great sacrifice which Christ offered in the fullness of time on the cross, by the shedding of his blood, for the sins of the world. And because Abel was the first of all living men to offer to the Lord a sacrifice of the firstlings of his flock, by which he bore witness to his faith in the Christ who was to come and offer himself for the sins of the world, God clearly looked with favour on Abel and his offering. For it is said that by faith Abel offered to God a better sacrifice than Cain, and through this faith, or because of it, he obtained the testimony that he was righteous. So that the phrase "the blood of Abel" in this place denotes nothing else than the rites and offerings of the Old Testament, set forth through one example, and that a most noble one, for all. To say, however, that the blood of Christ speaks better things than the blood of Abel, which cries out to heaven for vengeance against Cain, does not (to put it mildly) fit the purpose of the passage, since the Apostle labours almost entirely to make plain how powerless the ceremonies of the old law were for obtaining eternal life, and how much the covenant of the Gospel excelled the covenant of the Old Testament, as is clear throughout the whole course of his discourse, in chapters 9 and 10. But, to speak the matter itself with due respect, that interpretation is simply an inversion (ἀντιστροφή), contrary to logic itself. For things compared must be of the same kind and nature, differing in degree, so that in a comparison of superiority one of them can be said in some way and degree to be good with respect to that in which the other is said to be better. "What is better is better than something which is good" (Chrysostom). But the blood of Abel, taken by itself, was not in any way good for that purpose for which the blood of Christ was effective.

units.la: C. 13. v. 4. Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσι καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος. Verba sunt mandatoria, ut præcedentia & subsequentia, subaudiendo ἔστω. Memores esto Ante mortem, &c. Conjugium sit supra omnia pretiosum vel honorabile, & torus impollutus. Sint mores alieni ab avaritia, contenti esse præsentibus.
units.tr: Chapter 13, verse 4: "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled" [Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσι καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος]. These are words of command, like those before and after them, with ἔστω ("let it be") understood: "Remember ... etc.; let marriage be held in honour above all things, and the marriage bed undefiled. Let your manners be free from covetousness, and be content with what you have."

units.la: V. 12. Ἀπέχεσθε τῆς λόγης τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, Rogo autem vos fratres ut sufferatis hoc verbum exhortationis, τὸ pro τέτε.
units.tr: Verse 22: "I beseech you, brethren, bear with this word of exhortation" [ἀνέχεσθε τοῦ λόγου τῆς παρακλήσεως]. Here the article τὸ is used for τέτε ("this").

units.la: In Jacobum.
units.tr: In Jacobum.

units.la: JAC. c. 2. v. 1. Nolite habere in acceptione personarum, τὴν πίστιν τῆς Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τῆς δόξης: nobilis trajectio, pro τὴν πίστιν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν τῆς δόξης. Fidem Iesu Christi Domini nostri gloria. Qualis etiam occurrit. 3.1. Μὴ πολλοὶ διδάσκαλοι γίνεσθε, pro μὴ πολλοὶ γίνεσθε διδάσκαλοι. Nolite multi [veltrum] fieri doctores, scientes quod gravius accipiemus judicium. Et etiam 3. τῶν ἵππων τὰς χαλινοὺς εἰς τὰ στόματα βάλλομεν, pro τὰς χαλινοὺς εἰς τὰ στόματα τῶν ἵππων βάλλομεν. Frena immittimus in ora equorum, ne quis dubitet eam etiam esse de industria affectatam elegantiæ gratiâ.
units.tr: JAC. 2:1. "Do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons" [τὴν πίστιν τῆς Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τῆς δόξης]. This is a striking transposition, for τὴν πίστιν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν τῆς δόξης. The Latin is "Fidem Iesu Christi Domini nostri gloria." A similar case occurs in 3:1: "Be not many teachers" [μὴ πολλοὶ διδάσκαλοι γίνεσθε], for μὴ πολλοὶ γίνεσθε διδάσκαλοι. The Latin is "Nolite multi [vestrum] fieri doctores, knowing that we shall receive the heavier judgment." Also in 3:3: "We put bits into the mouths of horses" [τῶν ἵππων τὰς χαλινοὺς εἰς τὰ στόματα βάλλομεν], for τὰς χαλινοὺς εἰς τὰ στόματα τῶν ἵππων βάλλομεν. The Latin is "Frena immittimus in ora equorum," so that no one may doubt that this too was deliberately arranged for the sake of elegance.

units.la: C. 4. v. 5, 6. Ἢ δοκεῖτε ὅτι κενῶς ἡ γραφὴ λέγει, πρὸς φθόνον ἐπιποθεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα, ὁ κατῴκησεν ἐν ἡμῖν; Μείζονα δὲ δίδωσι χάριν, διὸ λέγει, ὁ Θεὸς ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται &c. Vel putatis frustra Scripturam dicere, spiritus, qui habitat in nobis, concupiscit sive appetentiâ quâdam fertur ad invidiam? Majorem verò dat gratiam, in eo quod dicit, Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Ubi reperiatur scriptum in terminis, (Spiritus qui habitat in nobis concupiscit ad invidiam) non liquet, periit ergò ut & alia Scripturæ multa. Sensum verò petendum arbitror ex iis quæ præcedunt. Dicitur enim v. 2. ἀπεῖνα ἐπιθυμεῖτε καὶ οὐκ ἔχετε, φονεύετε καὶ ζηλοῦτε, καὶ οὐ δύνασθε ἐπιτυχεῖν, μάχεσθε καὶ πολεμεῖτε, λεμξετε, &c. Concupiscitis & non habetis, invi-detis & æmulamini & non potestis adipisci, pugnatis & belligeratis, sed non habetis propterea quod non petitis. Fate orin omnibus quos vidi codicibus legi φονεύετε κ) ζηλᾶτε, occiditis & æmulamini, sed multo magis conveniunt sensu φθονεῖτε κ) ζηλᾶτε, (ut debere legi opinatur Beza) quia sunt Synonyma, ut sunt μαχεσθε κ) πολεμεῖτε: quid etiam æmulentur si occiderint: Quod si omnino legatur vox φονεύετε, sequeretur aptius post μάχεσθε κ) πολεμεῖτε, pugnatis & belligeratis & occiditis, importune enim certe connectitur cum ζηλᾶτε. Sententia Apostoli ex ordine verborum videtur esse, ut ostendat quomodo ex concupiscentia ista, quæ habitat in nobis, oriantur bella. Primo inquit concupiscitis, deinde quia non habetis quod concupiscitis, invidetis proximo qui potitur eo quod concupiscitis, & ultimo quia non potestis aliter adipisci, ad pugnam itur & ad bellum, ut illud vi extorqueatis. Atque hinc docemur, quomodo spiritus qui habitat in nobis concupiscit ad invidiam. Propter concupiscentiam alicujus rei quam non habemus, spiritus noster fertur ad invidiam proximi, ex qua bellum oritur & contentio. Concupiscentia mater invidiæ, invidia belli. Sequitur, majorem vero dat gratiam, in eo quod dicit, i. e. Scriptura utroque loco, non est enim aliud antecedens. Quasi diceret Apostolus, Scriptura quidem dicit naturaliter nos esse ad invidiam, & consequenter ad omne malum pronos, sed magis alibi est propitia, ubi dicit, Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Iob. 22. 29. Prov. 3. 34. Eo ipso monens, quod si velimus spiritum illum, quo ita proni ferimur ad invidiam, compescere, & subjicere nos Deo & kamiliari coram eo, ut sequitur 7. & 10. cum velle suo tempore nos extollere.
units.tr: C. 4:5, 6. "Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain, that the Spirit who dwells in us lusts toward envy? But he gives a greater grace, wherefore he says, God resists the proud, &c." [Ἢ δοκεῖτε ὅτι κενῶς ἡ γραφὴ λέγει, πρὸς φθόνον ἐπιποθεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα, ὁ κατῴκησεν ἐν ἡμῖν; Μείζονα δὲ δίδωσι χάριν, διὸ λέγει, ὁ Θεὸς ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται]. Or do you think the Scripture speaks in vain, that the Spirit who dwells in us longs for envy, or is carried by a certain desire toward jealousy? But he gives the greater grace, in that he says, "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." Where it is written word for word, "The Spirit that dwells in us lusts toward envy," is not clear to me; so perhaps it has been lost, as many other passages of Scripture have been. I think the sense must rather be sought from what goes before. For in verse 2 it is said: "You lust and do not have; you kill and covet, and cannot obtain; you fight and make war" [ἐπιθυμεῖτε καὶ οὐκ ἔχετε, φονεύετε καὶ ζηλοῦτε, καὶ οὐ δύνασθε ἐπιτυχεῖν, μάχεσθε καὶ πολεμεῖτε]. You lust and do not have, you envy and emulate and cannot attain, you fight and make war, but you do not have because you do not ask. I admit that in all the manuscripts I have seen the reading is φονεύετε καὶ ζηλᾶτε, "you kill and emulate." But the words fit much better with φθονεῖτε καὶ ζηλᾶτε, "you envy and emulate" (as Beza thinks it ought to be read), since these are synonyms, as μάχεσθε and πολεμεῖτε are. Besides, why should they emulate if they have killed? But if φονεύετε is retained, it would follow more fittingly after μάχεσθε and πολεμεῖτε: "you fight and make war and kill," for it is certainly an awkward connection with ζηλᾶτε. The Apostle's meaning, from the order of the words, seems to be this: to show how wars arise from that lust which dwells in us. First, he says, you lust; then, because you do not have what you lust after, you envy your neighbour who possesses what you desire; and lastly, because you cannot otherwise obtain it, you go to battle and to war, so that you may wrest it by force. And thus we are taught how "the spirit who dwells in us lusts toward envy": on account of desire for something we do not have, our spirit is carried toward envy of our neighbour, from which arise strife and contention. Desire is the mother of envy, envy of war. There follows, "but he gives a greater grace, in that he says," that is, Scripture in either place, for there is no other antecedent. As if the Apostle said: Scripture indeed says that we are naturally inclined to envy, and consequently prone to every evil; but elsewhere it is more favourable, where it says, "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble" (Job 22:29; Prov. 3:34). By this very thing it warns us that, if we wish to restrain that spirit by which we are so readily carried toward envy, we must submit ourselves to God and be familiar with him, as follows in verses 7 and 10, when he wishes to exalt us in his own time.

units.la: C. 5. v. 9. Μὴ στενάζετε κατ' ἀλλήλων. Nolite ingemiscere in alterutrum, vel lugere vosmet ipsos invicem. Verbis praeuntibus patientes esse jubet, & stabilire corda, quoniam adfuit adventus Domini. Hic rursus suadet non despondere animum, & se lugere invicem, ne propter impatientiam condemnentur, nam ecce Judex, qui fuit eos vindicaturus, erat pro foribus, ante januam astitit, &c. Καταστενάζω, cum gemitu deploro. Basil. Μὴ στενάζετε κατ' ἀλλήλων, idem est ac si dixisset, μὴ καταστενάζετε ἀλλήλων, ne ingemiscatis alius super alium, Sed prius mollius sonat, eo quod hiatum tollat; κατὰ cum Genitivo, super.
units.tr: C. 5:9. "Do not groan against one another" [Μὴ στενάζετε κατ' ἀλλήλων]. Or, "do not lament yourselves one against another." In the words before, he bids them be patient and "establish their hearts," since the coming of the Lord is at hand. Here again he urges them not to despair, nor to lament one another, lest they be condemned for impatience; for behold, the Judge who was to avenge them is at the door, has stood before the gate, and so on. Καταστενάζω means to lament with a groan. Basil. "Μὴ στενάζετε κατ' ἀλλήλων" is the same as if he had said, "μὴ καταστενάζετε ἀλλήλων," "do not groan one over another." But the first form sounds softer, because it avoids the hiatus; κατά with the genitive means "over" or "against."

units.la: V. 16. πολὺ ἰσχύει δέησις δικαίου ἐνεργουμένη. Multum valet potens oratio justi. The powerfull prayer of a righteous man availeth much, ἐνεργὴς, δυνατὸς, ἰσχυρὸς, potens, validus vel fortis. Hesych. i. e. ut Erasmus, deprecatio ex animo profusa, intenta & instans ut assequatur quod petit. Qualis fuit Annae cum profudit animam coram Deo 1 Sam. 1. 15. vel Jacobi cum luctabatur cum Angelo. Gen. 32. 24. & 28. vel Mosis cum adeo instaret, ut diceret ei Dominus, dimitte me &c. Exod. 32. 10. 11. Atque haec versio mihi videtur aptior, quam est, efficax, effectuall. Efficax enim proprie est quod certo efficit, & non quod aptum est efficere. At non dicitur πάνυ ἰσχύει, omninò valet, sed πολὺ multùm valet potens oratio justi. Ut habet versio Aethiopica pro more suo paraphrastice. Multum juvat: oratio justi, potens est & assistit. ἐνεργουμένη est potenter operans, sed non semper effectivè. Et sic opinor aptius vertitur. Gal. 2. 8. ʽO γὰρ ἐνεργήσας Πέτρῳ &c. Quì enim potenter operatus est Petro ad apostolatum circumcisionis, ἐνήργησε καὶ ἐμοὶ εἰς τὰ ἔθνη, potenter etiam operatus est mihi ad gentes. ℣ 8. He that wrought powerfully in Peter toward the Apostleship of the circumcision, wrought also powerfully in me toward the gentiles.
units.tr: V. 16. πολὺ ἰσχύει δέησις δικαίου ἐνεργουμένη [much avails the prayer of a righteous man when it is energized]. The prayer of a righteous man, being powerful, avails much. The powerfull prayer of a righteous man availeth much. ἐνεργὴς [energēs], δυνατὸς [dynatos], ἰσχυρὸς [ischyros]: powerful, mighty, strong, or fit. Hesychius: that is, as Erasmus renders it, a prayer poured out from the heart, intent and insistent, so as to obtain what it asks. Such was Hannah's, when she poured out her soul before God (1 Sam. 1. 15), or Jacob's, when he wrestled with the Angel (Gen. 32. 24, and 28), or Moses', when he so pressed that the Lord said to him, "Let me alone," etc. (Exod. 32. 10, 11). This rendering seems to me more suitable than "efficacious" or "effectual". For "efficacious" properly means that which certainly produces an effect, not that which is apt to produce it. Yet the text does not say πάνυ ἰσχύει [panu ischyei], "altogether avails", but πολὺ, "much avails". The Ethiopic version, after its own manner, paraphrases: It greatly helps: the prayer of the righteous is powerful and stands by. ἐνεργουμένη means "working powerfully", but not always "effectively", and so I think it is translated more aptly thus. Gal. 2. 8: ʽO γὰρ ἐνεργήσας Πέτρῳ [ho gar energēsas Petrō] etc., "For he who worked powerfully in Peter" for the apostleship of the circumcision, ἐνήργησε καὶ ἐμοὶ εἰς τὰ ἔθνη [enērgēse kai emoi eis ta ethnē], "worked powerfully in me also toward the Gentiles." ℣ 8. He that wrought powerfully in Peter toward the Apostleship of the circumcision, wrought also powerfully in me toward the gentiles.

units.la: In Epistolam primam Petri.
units.tr: On the First Epistle of Peter.

units.la: I. PET. 1. v. 1.2. Hi duo versus poterunt distingui aliter quàm vulgò solent, & verba forte exponi magis accommodè per Hyperbaton, construendo τὸ κατὰ πρόγνωσιν Θεοῦ πατρὸς, cum Πέτρος ἀπόστολος Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ, & non cum ἐκλεκτοῖς &c. 1. Πέτρος ἀπόστολος Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἐκλεκτοῖς παρεπιδήμοις διασπορᾶς Πόντου, Γαλατίας, Καππαδοκίας, Ἀσίας, καὶ Βιθυνίας, κατὰ πρόγνωσιν Θεοῦ πατρὸς, 2. ἐν ἁγιασμῷ Πνεύματος εἰς ὑπακοὴν καὶ ῥαντισμὸν αἵματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη πληθυνθείη. Petrus Apostolus Jesu Christi secundum [vel] per præscientiam Dei Patris Electis peregrinis dispersionis, Ponti, Galatiæ, Cappadociæ & Bithyniæ, 2. Gratia vobis & pax multiplicetur in sanctificatione Spiritus ad [vel] per obedientiam & asperfionem sanguinis Iesu Christi. Quali non omnino absimili pro loquendi formulâ salutatione utitur 2 Ep. c. 1. v. 2. χάρις ὑμῖν &c. Gratia vobis & pax multiplicetur in scientia Dei & Iesu Christi Domini nostri. Trajectiones ejusmodi non sunt apud Petrum, nec alibi in N. T. inusitatæ, ut jam sæpius dictum est. Ἀπόστολος χαὶ πρόγνωσιν Θεοῦ, idem omnino sonat quod fere dicitur in omnibus Pauli Epistolis, Παῦλος Ἀπόστολος διὰ θελήματος Θεοῦ, Paulus Apostolus per voluntatem Dei; & 1 Tim. 1.1. κατ᾽ ἐπιταγὴν Θεοῦ, per ordinationem Dei, ἐκλεκτοῖς idem est ac si dixisset, ἁγίοις sanctis vel πιστοῖς fidelibus. Eph. 1.1. & alibi. Sed hæc ἀπειλὴ πάσως dicta sunto, ὡς ἵνα ζῴχον δεί-καλω, non ut vinculum imponam, liberum est cuique prout vult sentire.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 1:1-2. These two verses could be divided differently from the usual way, and the words may perhaps be explained more suitably by hyperbaton, by construing according to the foreknowledge of God the Father [τὸ κατὰ πρόγνωσιν Θεοῦ πατρὸς] with "Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ" [Πέτρος ἀπόστολος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ], and not with "to the elect" [ἐκλεκτοῖς] etc. "1. Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the elect strangers of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, 2. through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: grace to you and peace be multiplied." Peter, apostle of Jesus Christ, according to [or through] the foreknowledge of God the Father, to the elect strangers of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia and Bithynia; 2. grace and peace be multiplied to you in the sanctification of the Spirit, through obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ. Peter uses a salutation of much the same kind in 2 Pet. 1:2: "Grace to you [χάρις ὑμῖν] and peace be multiplied in the knowledge of God and of Jesus Christ our Lord." Transpositions of this sort are not unusual in Peter, or anywhere else in the New Testament, as has already been said many times. Paulus Apostolus per voluntatem Dei ["Paul, an apostle by the will of God"], which is found in almost all of Paul's Epistles, means essentially the same as "apostle according to the foreknowledge of God" [Ἀπόστολος κατὰ πρόγνωσιν Θεοῦ]. Compare 1 Tim. 1:1, per ordinationem Dei ["by the ordinance of God"] [κατ᾽ ἐπιταγὴν Θεοῦ]. "The elect" [ἐκλεκτοῖς] is the same as if he had said "the saints" [ἁγίοις] or "the faithful" [πιστοῖς]; compare Eph. 1:1 and elsewhere. But these things are not to be taken as a threat of any kind, as if I were putting a fetter on anyone; each man is free to think as he pleases.

units.la: C. 2. v. 7. Ὑμῖν οὖν ἡ τιμὴ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν, ἀπει-θοῦσι δέ, λίθον ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδο-μοῦντες, οὗτος ἐγενήθη εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας, καὶ λίθος προσκόμματος καὶ πέτρα σκανδάλου. Aut verba illa [λίθον ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες οὗτος ἐγενήθη εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας] non debuerunt omnino legi, ut omissa sunt à Syros aut periocha ista est exponenda per metathesim, ut distincta supra; neque sunt ejusmodi metatheses in N. T. omnino infrequentes, ut videre est in animad. Act. 13. 27. & alibi. πρῶ, ἀπειθοῦσι δέ, sequente recto sensu post γωνίας, Quasi legeretur, ὑμῖν οὖν ἡ τιμὴ τοῖς πιστεύουσι λίθον ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες οὗτος ἐγενήθη εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας, ἀπειθοῦσι δὲ λίθος προσκόμματος καὶ πέτρα σκανδάλου. i.e. Construendo ἡ τιμὴ appositive. Vobis igitur honor credentibus lapis ille quem reprobave-runt runt ædificantes factus est in caput anguli, non credentibus autem & lapis offensionis & petra scandali. In quo fere ordine & sensu exponit etiam per metathesim Scholiastes Græcus. ἔςαι ἓν τὸ ὅλον ἔτως· Ἰδοὺ τίθημι ἐν Σιὼν λίθον ἀκρογωνιαῖον &c. ἔντιμον ὑμῖν τοῖς πιστεύουσιν, ἀπειθοῦσι δὲ λίθον προσκόμματος, ὃν λίθον μὴ ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες, ἔτω δὲ ἐγενήθη εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας, συνάπτων μὲν τοὺς πιστεύοντας εἰς αὐτὸν, λίθω δὲ προσκόμματος καὶ πέτρα σκανδάλου τοῖς ἀπειθοῦσι τῷ λόγῳ &c. Est igitur totius summa hujusmodi. Ecce pono in Sion lapidem summum angularem &c. pretiosum vobis qui creditis, at vero non credentibus lapidem offensionis, quem lapidem reprobaverunt quidem ædificantes, sed factus est ille in caput anguli, connectens sibi eos qui credunt, lapis vero offensionis iis, qui impingunt non credentes verbo evangelii in id ad quod erant positi. Aut potuit ista τῶ, ἀπειθοῦσι δὲ transpositio aliquo fato accidere, forte erat apposita in margine & incuria apographi non suo loco inserta. Nullo enim opinor sensu potest dici vel intelligi, Christum fuisse factum non credentibus caput anguli: Licet tamen ita exponant aliqui, nempe, Christum vel invitis ac rejicientibus cum Judæis factum esse templi spiritualis caput. Sed expositio ista est coacta, nec quadrat cum scopo loci, qui prorsus est hujusmodi. Vobis igitur quod honor est credentibus lapis ille, quem reprobaverunt ædificantes in nullo habentes pretio, factus est lapis summus angularis, in quem vos estis omnes ædificati Eph. 2. 22. dum interim lapis idem fit factus non credentibus lapis offensionis & petra scandali, in quem impingentes confundentur. λίθον ὃν, per trajectionem dicitur, pro ὃν λίθον, quale est illud apud Virgilium, Urlem quam statuo vestra est. forte per Antiptosin.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 2:7. "To you therefore who believe is the honour; but to those who are disobedient, the stone which the builders rejected, the same is made the head of the corner, and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence" [λίθον ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες οὗτος ἐγενήθη εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας, καὶ λίθος προσκόμματος καὶ πέτρα σκανδάλου]. Either those words [λίθον ὃν ἀπεδοκίμασαν οἱ οἰκοδομοῦντες οὗτος ἐγενήθη εἰς κεφαλὴν γωνίας] ought not to be read at all, as the Syriac has omitted them, or this clause must be explained by a transposition, as I have set out above. Such transpositions are by no means rare in the New Testament, as can be seen in animad. Act. 13:27 and elsewhere. The sense runs straight on after "corner" if we read "but to those who are disobedient" [ἀπειθοῦσι δέ] as following; as if it read: "To you therefore who believe is the honour, the stone which the builders rejected, this one was made the head of the corner; but to the disobedient, a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence." Here ἡ τιμὴ is construed in apposition. To you therefore who believe is the honour: that stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner; but to those who do not believe it is a stone of offence and a rock of scandal. The Greek scholiast also explains it by transposition, and nearly in this order and sense: "The whole thing comes to this: Behold, I lay in Zion a chief corner stone [etc.]; precious to you who believe, but to the disobedient a stone of stumbling, which stone the builders did not reject, but so it was made the head of the corner, joining those who believe in it, but to those who are disobedient to the word a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence [etc.]." The sum of the whole is therefore this: Behold, I lay in Zion the chief corner stone [etc.], precious to you who believe, but to those who do not believe a stone of offence, which the builders indeed rejected, but that stone has become the head of the corner, joining to itself those who believe, while to those who do not believe the gospel it is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence, against which they strike, in the very purpose for which they were appointed. Or perhaps this transposition of τῶ, ἀπειθοῦσι δέ happened by some accident: it may have been written in the margin and, through the carelessness of a copyist, inserted out of place. For I think no sense can be given or understood by which Christ is said to have been made the head of the corner for those who do not believe. Some do explain it so, namely that Christ became the head of the spiritual temple even against the will of those who reject him, along with the Jews. But that explanation is forced and does not fit the purpose of the passage, which is entirely this: "To you therefore who believe, that stone which the builders rejected, holding it of no value, is an honour, since it has become the chief corner stone, in which you all are built (Eph. 2:22); while at the same time that same stone becomes to those who do not believe a stone of offence and a rock of scandal, against which those who stumble will be confounded." The phrase "λίθον ὃν" is put by a transposition for "ὃν λίθον," like that line in Virgil, "Urbem quam statuo, vestra est" ["the city which I am founding is yours"]; perhaps it is an antiptosis.

units.la: V. 12. Ἐν τῇ καλῇ ἀναστροφῇ ἔχοντες ἐπιπηδεύοντες, Ut in eo quod loquuntur contra vos uti malefi.os, spectantes vestra bona opera, glorificent Deum in die visitationis. Subaudiendo τὰ & repetendo ὑμῶν à communi, i. e. τὰ ἐν τῇ καλῇ ἐργῶν ὑμῶν. Dictio est elleiptica, qualis est Luc. 21. 16. ἐξ ὑμῶν pro τὸς ἐξ ὑμῶν. Et trucidabunt vos, & Psal. 78. 31. ἀπέκτειναν ἐν τῇς πόσιν αὐτῶν pro τὰς ἐν τῇς πόσιν αὐτῶν. Et occidit pingues eorum & 1 Joh. 4. 5. ἐκ τῆς κόσμου λαλοῦσι, mundana loquuntur, ut reddit Beza, subin elligendo etiam τὰ ἐν τῇ κόσμῳ. Eadem est fere phrasis. 1 Pet. 5. 9. τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν παθημάτων, easdem afflictiones.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 2:12. "Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation." Supply "the" [τὰ] and repeat "your" [ὑμῶν] from what is common, that is, "the good works of you" [τὰ ἐν τῇ καλῇ ἐργῶν ὑμῶν]. The expression is elliptical, of the same kind as Luke 21:16, "some of you" [ἐξ ὑμῶν] for "those of you" [τοὺς ἐξ ὑμῶν], as in "they shall put you to death" [θανατώσουσιν ὑμᾶς]. Compare Ps. 78:31, "he slew the fat ones" [ἀπέκτειναν ἐν τῇς πόσιν αὐτῶν] for "those in their drink" [τὰς ἐν τῇς πόσιν αὐτῶν], and 1 John 4:5, "they are of the world" [ἐκ τῆς κόσμου λαλοῦσι], that is, "they speak worldly things," as Beza renders it, sometimes supplying also "the things that are in the world" [τὰ ἐν τῇ κόσμῳ]. The phrase is nearly the same at 1 Pet. 5:9, "the same afflictions of the sufferings" [τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν παθημάτων], that is, the same afflictions.

units.la: Cap. V. 20. 21. Εἰς ὀλίγαι (τυτέστιν ὀκτὼ) ψυχαὶ διεσώθησαν. Ὃ καὶ ὑμᾶς ἀντίτυπον νῦν σώζει βάπτισμα, οὐ σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου, ἀλλὰ συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς Θεὸν διὰ ἀναστάσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. In diebus Noæ cùm fabricaretur arca, in qua pauca (id est octo) animæ servatæ sunt; per aquam etiam quod est antitypum nos nunc servat baptisma, non depositio sordium carnis, sed bonæ conscientiæ stipulatio in Deum per resurrectionem Jesu Christi. Atque hac trajectione, distinctione, & versione, subaudiendo ὅς (quod est adeo familiare) vitatur insolentia vocis δια, ut plerumque exponitur, articulus ὁ appositè respondet voci Βάπτισμα, (neque verò potest alterius vocis esse relativum, βάπτισμα enim non est antitypum ὕδατος, sed ᾧ ὃ, quæ vox est fœminini generis,) & verus etiam scopus mentis Apostolica fit multo multò planior. Neque est haec trajectio omnino dura, imò tantum abest ab insolentia vel duritie, ut potius videatur grata. Trajectione enim simili sæpius usum esse Demosthenem affirmat Stephanus ad venustatem sermoni conciliandam, quales etiam asse: âsse & alios Græcos & Latinos, atq; ipsos etiam Apostolos est abundè notum. Est enim alia in hoc ipso loco translocatio non invenusta, nè dicam affectata; ὁ σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου, pro ὁ ῥύπος σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις: & alia, 2 Ep. 1. 19. ὃ καλὸς ποιεῖτε ἀγαθοποιοῦντες, pro ὧ ἀγαθοποιοῦντες καλὸς ποιεῖτε. Vide etiam Animad. Ad 13. 17. 2 Cor. 4.4 Jac. 2. 1 & 3. 3. In summâ sensus est: Baptisma quod nunc nos servat per aquam, i. e. per ministerium aquæ, & est antitypum arcæ Noæ, non significat depositionem sordium carnis ΕΠΕΡΩΤΗΜΑ per aquam, sed bonæ conscientiæ stipulationem in Deum, dum immerginitur in aquam, (quod est verus usus aquæ in baptismate) ut resuscitemur fidem in resurrectione Jesu Christi. Adeo ut manifesta sit antithesis inter ἀπόθεσις & ἐπερώτημα, & in eâ non ingrata elegantia. Ac si diceret, Arca Noæ [non Diluvium] erat Baptismi typus, & Baptismus erat Arcæ antitypum, sed non in eo quòd Baptismo fit ablutio sordium carnis per aquam, in quo non omnino respondet arcæ, sed quia fit bonæ conscientiæ in Deum stipulatio per resurrectionem Jesu Christi, in cujus resurrectionis fide nos nunc servamur, ut servati sunt illi in arca Noæ. Resurrectionis enim & arca Noæ, & Baptismus erant utrique typus & figura. Ita ut proprius finis baptismi non debeat intelligi quasi signum foret abluionis peccatorum (etsi ita sæpius in novo fœdere, & à Patribus accipiatur μετανοίας) sed signum resurrectionis, per fidem in resurrectionę restione Jesu Christi. Cujus baptisma maximè viva & Emphatica est figura, sicut erat & arca Noe, ex quâ Noab rediit tanquam è sepulchro ad vitam novam, ideoque non inepte a Philone dictus πελαγοφυλακίας ἡμέρων, & zuvier Cete, ex quo post triduanam sepulturam resurrexit Jonah; & nubes, & mare rubrum, in quibus populus Israelisticus dicitur fuisse baptizatus, i. e. non ablutus sed sepultus. Omnia enim erant typi ejusdem rei cum baptismo, non ablutionis peccatorum, i, e. depositionis sordium carnis, sed mortis & resurrectionis Christi simul & nostrum. Atque huic veritati suffragantur Apostoli, Patres, Scholastici, & Interpretes fere omnes. Res est quidem ita manifesta, ut testimoniis non indigeat, quoniam vero sunt non pauci, qui non ita vulgò docent, non supervacuum erit, ne gratis loqui videar, aliquâ et innumeris proferre testimonia. Et primo initium sumamus a Sancto Paulo. Ἠ ἀγνοεῖτε ὅτι ὅσοι ἐβαπτίσθημεν εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν, εἰς τὸν θάνατον αὐτοῦ ἐβαπτίσθημεν; &c. An ignoratis quod quicunque baptizati sumus in Christum Jesum, in ejus mortem baptizati sumus? consepulti enim sumus cum illo per baptismum in mortem, ut quomodo Christus surrexit a mortuis per gloriam Patris, ita & nos in novitate vitæ ambulemus &c. Rom. 6. 3. 4. & Coloss. 2. 12. ut etiam 1 Cor. 15. 29. Ἐπεὶ τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, &c. Alioquin quid facient qui baptizantur pro mortuis, si omnino mortui non resurgunt? ad si dicerer, si non est resurrectio, ad quid baptizamur? in vanum utitur Ecclesia symbolo Baptismi, si mortui non resurgant. Occurrunt similia passim testimonia apud Patres, e. g. ut credentes in ejus mortem dià τῆς βαπτίσματος, per baptismum fiunt participes ejus resurrectionis. Ignat. Ep. ad Trall. Βάπτισμα εἰς τὸ θάνατον τοῦ Κυρίου δίδομενον. Baptisma datum in mortem Domini. Ep. ad Philadel. nomine Ignatii. Τῆς πάθους καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως αὐτοῦ ἐν τῷ βαπτισματι τελοῦμεν τὰ σύμβολα. Passionis & resurrectionis ejus in Baptismo peragimus symbola. Just. Mart. Unum novimus salutiferum baptisma, quandoquidem una est pro mundo mors, & una ex mortuis resurrectio, ὧν τύπος ἐστὶ τὸ βάπτισμα, quorum typus est baptismus. Basil. Mag. Audi clamantem Paulum, Mare transsierunt, & omnes baptizati sunt in nube & in mari, βάπτισμα χαλεῖ τὴν θάλασσαν ὁδὸν, θανάτῳ δὲ τῶν φυγὴ πληρωμένη διὰ ὕδατος. Baptisma vocat viam maris, fuga enim erat mortis impletae per aquam. Basil. Seleuc. Τὸ γὰρ Καταδύεσθαι καταδύσεως ὅτι σύμβολον τῆς ἐκείνου ἀνόδου. Baptizari enim & demergi, deinde sursum remeare & emergere, est symbolum sive signum descensus ad inferos sive Hadem, & ex eo ascensus sive reditus. Chrysost. Baptismus resurrectionis pignus & imago. Ambros. Baptismus arrhabo resurrectionis. Lactan. Mersio mortis & sepulturae formam gerit. Bern. Innumera possem accumulare testimonia, sed haec opinor abunde sufficient ad probandum, Baptismum esse proprie typum mortis & resurrectionis Jesu Christi, (ex quo agnoscimus mysterium religionis nostrae, nempe, humanitatem & deitatem ejus Rom. 1. 4.) ac etiam omnium fidelium, qui in ejus fidem baptizati sunt, à morte in peccato ad novitatem vitae, quod si fecerint in hoc mundo, habent spem firmissimam se post mortem cum Christo in futuro resurrecturos ad gloriam. Unicum liceat ultra judicium apponere viri ingenii & literati, cujus in hac re testimonium nec suspicari possumus nec subterfugere. Verba ejus sunt ejusmodi. Porro quamvis immersionis cæremonia & olim fuit communior,ut patet ex communi Patrum sermone, quoties de Baptismo loquuntur, & expressius repræsentet mortem, sepulturam, ac resurrectionem Domini simul et nostram, quæ fit mystice in Baptismo, quam immersionis significationem diligenter urgent Patres, &c. unde & laudabiliorem esse immergendi ritum S. Thomas affirmat,multæ tamen rationes extiterunt ob quas mutari interdum immersionem convenichat in cæremoniam vicinam, &c. Hinc igitur perfusionis cæremonia tanquam inter aspersionem & immersionem media multum obtinuit; quem morem refert Bonaventura jam tum suo tempore servatum fuisse in Ecclesiis Gallicanis & nonnullis aliis, licèt fateatur immersionis ritum & communiorem esse & aptiorem, & securiorem, quemadmodum S. Thomas docet. Veruntamen ubicunque perfu sionis vel aspersionis ritus jam obtinet, privatâ authoritate mutari non debet: imò quoniam nunc passim obtinet per Ecclesiam, in re tam necessaria ad salutem non debet ullo modo revocari in dubium. Hactenus Estius. In cujus verbis manifestam habemus & ingenuam confessionem, Immersionem fuisse cæremoniam veterem, quam constanter urgebant Patres, utpote expressius repræsentantem mortem,' sepulturam, & resurrectionem Christi simul & nostram ; eandem tenuisse Scholasticos, pro ritu maximè laudabili, apto & securo; cæremoniam verò perfusionis accidenter irrepsisse in Ecclesiam, quibus de causis silet. Quoniam verò illa à longo tempore jam obtinuit, non æquum esse vel expediens vocari nunc in dubium num valeat. Atque in hac sententiâ lubens ego acquiesco, modò baptismatis ministri veram illam & genuinam ejus institutionis rationem doceant, & non allegoricam illam, ut mos est, ablutionis solum; quam etiam non negarim & pie & utiliter quandoque usurpari, fecerunt enim id Apostoli & Patres. Et si haec ita sint, quae tam visibilis, obsecro, est affinitas sepulturae cum ablutione, ut baptismus Christianus putetur originem trahere a Judaicis lotionibus; & baptismis? Quod si verum esset baptismum nostrum lotionem vel ablutionem significare, vel si verum esset Judaeos ab initio vel suos vel Proselytos admisisse in Ecclesiam suam per baptismi collationem, quod a doctissimis viris a diebus nuperis promulgatum est, argumentum foret fatear probabile institutionem baptismi nostri peti a baptismis Judaeorum; sed cum de priore, ut supra ostendimus, contrarium, & de altero nihil certi constet, multo aptius & etiam fortius esse equidem credo vetus Circumcisionis argumentum pro baptismo Infantium, quam hoc novum & incertum. Baptismum enim nostrum vere esse typum sepulturae & resurrectionis, non vero lavationis jam satis dictum est; quoad vero argumentum eorum, quo peti volunt baptismum nostrum a Judaicis lotionibus, ut de eo nihil certi constat, ita etiam adeo procul est ab eo omnis sacrae Scripturae authoritas, ut vix ejus in veteri vestigia reperire queam. Originem volunt petere a voce בָּאַח lavit vel purgavit, Exod. 19. 10. At Magistri, ni fallor, habent pro Baptismo vocem טְבִילָה, quae significat immersionem, satis ei indicantes se debere notionem istius vocis Graecis vel potius Christianus. Quid enim affine est inter lotionem & immersionem? Legimus enim quosdam arena etiam baptizatos. Adeo vero ipsa res incerta est, ut neque de Rab-binis
units.tr: Chapter 5, verses 20–21: "Few, that is eight, souls were saved." "This also now saves you, baptism, which is the antitype: not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ." [Εἰς ὀλίγαι (τυτέστιν ὀκτὼ) ψυχαὶ διεσώθησαν. Ὃ καὶ ὑμᾶς ἀντίτυπον νῦν σώζει βάπτισμα, οὐ σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου, ἀλλὰ συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς Θεὸν διὰ ἀναστάσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.] In the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few (that is, eight) souls were saved; through water, which is the antitype, baptism now saves us, not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the pledge of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. By this transposition, this distinction and this rendering, with ὅς understood (which is so very common), the awkwardness of the word διά is avoided, as it is usually explained; the article ὁ corresponds neatly to the word Βάπτισμα (and it cannot be the relative of another word, since βάπτισμα is not the antitype of water, but of ᾧ, which is feminine), and the true aim of the apostolic mind becomes much plainer. Nor is this transposition at all harsh; in fact it is so far from awkward or harsh that it rather seems pleasing. For Stephanus affirms that Demosthenes often used such a transposition to lend charm to his speech, and it is well known that other Greeks and Latins, and even the Apostles themselves, did the same. In this very passage there is another transposition, not unpleasing, not to say affected: ὁ σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου for ὁ ῥύπος σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις; and another at 2 Pet. 1.19: ὃ καλὸς ποιεῖτε ἀγαθοποιοῦντες for ὧ ἀγαθοποιοῦντες καλὸς ποιεῖτε. See also Animad. Ad 13.17; 2 Cor. 4.4; Jas. 2.1 and 3.3. In sum, the sense is: the baptism which now saves us through water, that is, through the ministry of water, and which is the antitype of Noah's ark, does not signify the putting away of the filth of the flesh by water, but the pledge of a good conscience toward God, while we are immersed in the water (which is the true use of water in baptism), so that we are raised up in faith in the resurrection of Jesus Christ. Thus the antithesis between ἀπόθεσις and ἐπερώτημα is clear, and it has a not unpleasing elegance. It is as if he said: Noah's ark [not the Flood] was a type of Baptism, and Baptism was the antitype of the ark; not in that Baptism effects the washing away of the filth of the flesh by water (in which respect it does not wholly correspond to the ark), but because it is a pledge of a good conscience toward God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, by faith in whose resurrection we are now saved, as those in Noah's ark were saved. For both the resurrection, and Noah's ark, and Baptism, were each a type and figure of the other. So the proper purpose of baptism should not be understood as though it were a sign of the washing away of sins (although it is so often taken that way in the New Covenant, and by the Fathers, of repentance), but as a sign of the resurrection, through faith in the resurrection of Jesus Christ. Its figure is most lively and emphatic, as was Noah's ark, out of which Noah came as from a tomb into a new life; and so Philo rightly called it "the guardian of the sea-going" [πελαγοφυλακίας ἡμέρων]; and the whale [κῆτος], from which Jonah rose after three days in the grave; and the cloud and the Red Sea, in which the Israelite people are said to have been baptized, that is, not washed but buried. For all these were types of the same thing as baptism, not of the washing away of sins, that is, the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but of the death and resurrection of Christ, and of ours along with it. The Apostles, the Fathers, the Schoolmen and almost all the interpreters support this truth. The matter is indeed so clear that it needs no testimonies; but since there are not a few who do not teach it in this way commonly, it will not be superfluous, lest I seem to speak without grounds, to bring forward some testimonies, indeed innumerable ones. And first let us begin with St. Paul: "Or do you not know that as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? etc." [Ἢ ἀγνοεῖτε ὅτι ὅσοι ἐβαπτίσθημεν εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν, εἰς τὸν θάνατον αὐτοῦ ἐβαπτίσθημεν; &c.] "Do you not know that as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also should walk in newness of life, etc." (Rom. 6.3–4; also Col. 2.12). Likewise 1 Cor. 15.29: "Otherwise what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all?" [Ἐπεὶ τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, &c.] "Otherwise what will they do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? If there is no resurrection, why are we baptized? In vain does the Church use the symbol of baptism, if the dead do not rise." Similar testimonies occur everywhere among the Fathers: for example, that believers who, through baptism, believe in his death, through baptism become partakers of his resurrection. Ignatius, Epistle to the Trallians: "Baptism given unto the death of the Lord" [Βάπτισμα εἰς τὸ θάνατον τοῦ Κυρίου δίδομενον]. Epistle to the Philadelphians, under Ignatius's name: "In baptism we complete the symbols of his passion and resurrection" [Τῆς πάθους καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως αὐτοῦ ἐν τῷ βαπτισματι τελοῦμεν τὰ σύμβολα]. Justin Martyr: "We know one saving baptism, since there is one death for the world and one resurrection from the dead, of which baptism is the type" [ὧν τύπος ἐστὶ τὸ βάπτισμα]. Basil the Great: "Hear Paul crying out, 'They passed through the sea, and all were baptized in the cloud and in the sea'; he calls the sea a baptism, a way, for the flight from death was accomplished through water" [βάπτισμα χαλεῖ τὴν θάλασσαν ὁδὸν, θανάτῳ δὲ τῶν φυγὴ πληρωμένη διὰ ὕδατος]. Basil of Seleucia: "For to be plunged down and to be sunk under is a symbol of his descent, and to rise up again and emerge is a symbol of his ascent" [Τὸ γὰρ Καταδύεσθαι καταδύσεως ὅτι σύμβολον τῆς ἐκείνου ἀνόδου]: "to be baptized and sunk, and then to come back up and emerge, is a symbol or sign of descent to the underworld or Hades, and of ascent or return from it." Chrysostom: "Baptism is the pledge and image of the resurrection." Ambrose: "Baptism is the earnest of the resurrection." Lactantius: "Immersion takes the form of death and burial." Bernard: "I could heap up countless testimonies, but I think these are abundantly enough to prove that Baptism is properly a type of the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ (from which we recognise the mystery of our religion, namely his humanity and deity, Rom. 1.4), and also of all the faithful who have been baptized into his faith, from death in sin to newness of life; and if they do this in this world, they have the most firm hope that after death they will rise with Christ to glory in the future." Let me add one more witness, a man of talent and learning, whose testimony in this matter we can neither suspect nor evade. His words are as follows: Moreover, although the ceremony of immersion was once more common, as is clear from the common speech of the Fathers whenever they speak of Baptism, and it more expressly represents the death, burial and resurrection of the Lord together with our own, which is mystically effected in Baptism, a meaning of immersion which the Fathers diligently urge, etc.; whence St. Thomas also affirms that the rite of immersion is more laudable; yet many reasons arose on account of which it was sometimes fitting that immersion be changed to a nearby ceremony, etc. Hence the ceremony of pouring, as something midway between sprinkling and immersion, gained much currency; Bonaventure reports that this custom was already observed in his time in the Gallican Churches and some others, although he admits that the rite of immersion is both more common and more suitable and safer, as St. Thomas teaches. However, wherever the rite of pouring or sprinkling already prevails, it must not be changed on private authority; indeed, since it now prevails everywhere through the Church, in a matter so necessary to salvation it ought in no way to be called into doubt. So far Estius. From his words we have a clear and frank confession: that immersion was the ancient ceremony, which the Fathers constantly urged, as more expressly representing the death, burial and resurrection of Christ together with our own; that the Schoolmen kept it as the most laudable, suitable and safe rite; but that the ceremony of pouring crept into the Church by accident, for reasons on which he is silent. Yet since it has now prevailed for a long time, it is neither fair nor expedient to call into doubt whether it is valid. I gladly acquiesce in this view, provided only that the ministers of baptism teach its true and genuine reason of institution, and not that allegorical notion, as is customary, of washing alone; which I would not deny may sometimes be piously and usefully employed, for the Apostles and Fathers did so. And if these things are so, what, I ask you, is the visible affinity of burial with washing, that Christian baptism is thought to derive its origin from the Jewish washings and baptisms? But if it were true that our baptism signifies a washing or ablution, or if it were true that the Jews from the beginning admitted either their own people or proselytes into their Church by the conferring of baptism, as has been put forward in recent days by very learned men, the argument would be, I admit, a probable one, that the institution of our baptism is to be sought from the baptisms of the Jews. But since, as we have shown above, the opposite is true of the former, and nothing certain is established about the latter, I truly believe that the old argument from circumcision for the baptism of infants is much more apt and also stronger than this new and uncertain one. For it has already been sufficiently said that our baptism is truly a type of burial and resurrection, and not of washing. As for their argument, by which they wish to derive our baptism from the Jewish washings, since nothing certain is established about it, so also the authority of Holy Scripture is so far from it that I can scarcely find any trace of it in the Old Testament. They want to derive the origin from the word בָּאַח, he washed or he cleansed, Exod. 19.10. But the Masters, unless I am mistaken, have for Baptism the word טְבִילָה, which means immersion, thus sufficiently indicating that they had to take the meaning of this word from the Greeks or rather from the Christians. For what has washing in common with immersion? For we read that some were even baptized in sand. The matter is indeed so uncertain that it cannot even be asserted about the Rabbis that there were no disagreements among them over this question.

units.la: {Hebrew} Vide Maimonidem, Hilchoth Mikvaoth. binis affirmari posset, non fuisse inter ipsos qui de hac re dissentirent: in ipso enim textu, quem laudant doctissimi viri, Rabbi Eliezer expresse contradicit Rabbi Josua, qui primus quod novi hoc Baptismi genus inter Judaeos asseruit; Rabbi enim Eliezer, (ut ex Talmudo affirmatur) qui Josuae fuit coaetaneus, si non aetate prior, aperte dicit, Proselytum circumcisum & non baptizatum verum esse Proselytum, nam sic legimus de Patribus, Abraham, Isaaco, & Jacobo, qui circumcisi erant & non baptizati. Affirmat vero e contrario Rabbi Josua, eum, qui baptizatus est, & non circumcisus, esse Proselytum; uri vero potius assentiar? Eliezero, qui affirmat quod Scriptura docet, an Josuae qui affirmat quod Scriptura nusquam habet? Magistri vero (quid mirum?) stabant pro Rabbi Josua, faciebat enim in rem suam, in honorem scilicet religionis Judaicae, Christianos mutuo petere ab ipsis suas caeremonias. At cum videam summi judicii viros in his temporibus e Rabbinis fundamenta petere veritatis, non possum non tantiper haesitare; Unde enim nobis missus est Talmudus (verba sunt Buxtorfii in suâ Synagogâ Judaicâ) ut eis nos tantum fidei adhibere debeamus, ut ex eo legem Mosaicam intelligi vel posse vel debere credamus? Multo minus Evangelium, cui ex professo erant inimici. Vocatur enim Talmudus errorum Labyrinthus, & fabularum Judaicarum fundamentum: perfectus est, & pro Authentica habitus quingentis post Christum annis; non est ergo aequum ejus testimonio acquiescere. Et quod me magis movet, ipse Josephus, ut taceam universos Patres ante Talmudi tempora, qui etiam Judaeus, & Rabbi Eliezero coaevus, qui etiam de industriâ scripsit de ritibus, moribus, & gestis Judaeorum, totus in hac
units.tr: See Maimonides, Hilchoth Mikvaoth. It could be affirmed among the Rabbis that there was no disagreement among them on this matter. In the very text that the most learned men cite, Rabbi Eliezer expressly contradicts Rabbi Joshua, who first asserted this new kind of baptism among the Jews. For Rabbi Eliezer (as the Talmud affirms), who was a contemporary of Joshua, if not his senior in age, plainly says that a proselyte who is circumcised and not baptized is a true proselyte. For so we read of the Fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who were circumcised and not baptized. Rabbi Joshua, on the other hand, maintains the contrary, that a man who is baptized and not circumcised is a proselyte. Which should I rather agree with: Eliezer, who affirms what Scripture teaches, or Joshua, who affirms what Scripture nowhere contains? The Magistri (why should this surprise us?) sided with Rabbi Joshua, for it served their purpose, namely, to the honour of the Jewish religion, that Christians should borrow their ceremonies from them. But since I see men of the highest judgement in these times seeking the foundations of truth from the Rabbis, I cannot but hesitate a little. For whence has the Talmud been sent to us (these are the words of Buxtorf in his Jewish Synagogue), that we should give it such credence, that we may believe the Mosaic law can or must be understood from it? Much less the Gospel, to which they were avowed enemies. For the Talmud is called a labyrinth of errors and the foundation of Jewish fables. It was completed, and held as authoritative, five hundred years after Christ; it is therefore not fair to rest on its testimony. And what moves me more is that Josephus himself, not to mention all the Fathers before the time of the Talmud, who was also a Jew and a contemporary of Rabbi Eliezer, and who wrote deliberately about the rites, customs, and deeds of the Jews, is entirely silent on this matter.

units.la: Note: the lines in the facing left-hand strip are not transcribed. bac ie silet, adeò ut mihi fit argumentum demonstrationi proximum, nempe duos tantæ eminentiæ viros, utròsque Judæos, & ccævos, alterum disertè negare, alterum in suâ historiâ de hac baptismo nullam omninò mentionem facere. Præterea si baptismus hodierno sensu fuisset in usu apud Judæos temporibus priscis, cur dicerunt Baptistæ Pharisæi, Quid ergo baptizas, si tu non es Christus, neque Elias, neque Propheta iste? Joh. 1. 25. An non plane innuunt nullum fuisse antea baptismi usum, & receptam fuisse opinionem inter ipsos nullum debere esse usquedum veniret Christus vel Elias vel Propheta iste? Quomodo igitur tanta sit affinitas inter baptismum nostrum & baptismos Judæorum, ut alter alteri ullo jure vel prætextu putetur succedere, est fateor ultra fidem meam. Arrianum vero aiunt vocare Judæum Ἐσβαμμένον, verùm ego cum ejus Commentatore Lntio, ipsum confuse loqui, & velle potiùs Christianum Judæum, ut etiam alibi vocat Christianos Galilæos; ut Lubinus etiam in illud Juvenalis:
units.tr: Note: the lines in the facing left-hand strip are not transcribed. In this matter he is silent, so that I have an argument next to a demonstration: two men of such great eminence, both Jews and contemporaries, one of whom expressly denies it, while the other makes no mention of this baptism at all in his history. Moreover, if baptism in its present sense had been in use among the Jews in earlier times, why would the Pharisees who were sent say, Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor that Prophet? John 1. 25. Do they not plainly imply that there was no earlier use of baptism, and that the common opinion among them was that there should be none until Christ, or Elijah, or that Prophet came? How there can be such an affinity between our baptism and the baptisms of the Jews that one is thought, by any right or pretext, to succeed the other, I confess is beyond my belief. They say that Arrian called the Jew [Ἐσβαμμένον], but I, with his commentator Lintio, think he is speaking confusedly and means rather a Christian Jew, as he elsewhere calls Christians Galileans; so too Lubinus on that line of Juvenal:

units.la: Nunc sacri fontis nemus & delubra locantur Judæis. &c.
units.tr: Now the grove and the shrines of the holy spring are let out to the Jews, etc.

units.la: Judæis vult intelligi Christianis, qui edicto Domitiani urbe pulsi, sylvas illas inhabitare cogebantur, quæ sacræ erant superstitioni Gentilium. Ut vero imponam finem, aio cum Alexandro de Halys, Tinctio est formalis causa baptismi. Quoad vocem ἐπερώτημα, adeò frequenter pro stipulatione accipitur, ut de eâ non sit opus quicquam addere. Diutius forte nimis hæsi in his verbis, ut ostenderem germanum esse Baptismi finem, ut monstret mortem & resurrectionem Christi simul & nostram, nostrámque in eâ fidem, non verò esse proprie abluitionis signum à peccato, quod
units.tr: Lubinus wishes "Jews" to be understood as Christians, who, expelled from the city by the edict of Domitian, were compelled to inhabit those woods which were sacred to the superstition of the Gentiles. To bring this to an end, I say with Alexander of Hales that immersion is the formal cause of baptism. As for the word [ἐπερώτημα], it is so often taken to mean a pledge that there is no need to add anything about it. I have perhaps lingered too long over these words, in order to show that the true end of baptism is to show the death and resurrection of Christ together with our own, and our faith in them, and that it is not properly a sign of washing away sin, which

units.la: Apostolus videtur his verbis quasi de industriâ di-ferte negare.
units.tr: the Apostle seems in these words to deny quite deliberately.

units.la: C. 4. v. 6 Εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ νεκροῖς εὐηγγελίσθη, ἵνα κριθῶσι μὲν κατὰ ἀνθρώπους σαρκὶ, ζῶσι δὲ κατὰ Θεὸν πνεύματι. Subaudiendum οἱ, ante ἀνθρώπους, & ante Θεὸν, Elleipsi admodum familiari, de qua vide Animad. 1 Cor. 2.2. Ad hoc enim & mortuis praedicatum est five Evangelizatum, ut damnarentur qui erant secundum homines in carne, vivant autem qui erant secundum Deum in Spiritu, i e. ut damnarentur qui incedebant vel vivebant ἐν ἀνθρώπων ἐπιθυμίαις &c. in cupiditatibus hominum; salvenciur vero qui vivebant ἐν θελήματι Θεοῦ, in voluntate Dei, ut est v. 2. Phrasis est omnino eadem apud Paulum, Rom. 8. 5. Οἱ γὰρ κατὰ σάρκα ὄντες τὰ τῆς σαρκὸς φρονοῦσιν, οἱ δὲ κατὰ πνεῦμα τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος. Qui enim sunt secundum carnem quae carnis sunt sapiunt, qui vero sunt secundum Spiritum, ea quae sunt Spiritus.
units.tr: Chap. 4 v. 6: [Εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ νεκροῖς εὐηγγελίσθη, ἵνα κριθῶσι μὲν κατὰ ἀνθρώπους σαρκὶ, ζῶσι δὲ κατὰ Θεὸν πνεύματι.] The article οἱ [οἱ] is to be understood before ἀνθρώπους and before Θεὸν, a very familiar ellipsis, on which see my notes on 1 Cor. 2.2. For to this end was the gospel preached also to the dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit, that is, that those who walked or lived in the lusts of men [ἐν ἀνθρώπων ἐπιθυμίαις] etc. might be condemned; but those who lived in the will of God [ἐν θελήματι Θεοῦ] might be saved, as in verse 2. The phrase is entirely the same in Paul, Rom. 8. 5: [Οἱ γὰρ κατὰ σάρκα ὄντες τὰ τῆς σαρκὸς φρονοῦσιν, οἱ δὲ κατὰ πνεῦμα τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος.] For those who are according to the flesh mind the things of the flesh, but those who are according to the Spirit the things of the Spirit.

units.la: In Epistolam secundam Petri.
units.tr: On the Second Epistle of Peter.

units.la: PET. c. I. v. 5. Καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο δὲ Σπουδὴν πᾶσαν παρεισενέγκαντες ἐπιχορηγήσατε ἐν τῇ πίστει ὑμῶν τὴν ἀρετήν, ἐν δὲ τῇ ἀρετῇ τὴν γνῶσιν &c. Ante vocem Σπουδὴν subaudi χρῆ sive ἐν frequenter pro οὖν cum. Et hoc ipsum cum omni diligentiâ introducentes, jungite invicem cum fide virtutem, cum virtute scientiam, cum scientia temperantiam, cum temperantia autem patientiam, cum patientia pietatem, cum pietate vero fraternum amorem. Introducentes, i e. conantes introducere, hoc ipsum cum omni diligentiâ promoventes. Respexisse videtur Apostolus ad antiquum morem ducendi choros; vox enim ἐπιχορηγεῖν proprie significat chorum ducere. In choris vero συνεπλέκοντο ἀλλήλοις, complicabantur invicem.
units.tr: PET. c. I. v. 5. Καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο δὲ σπουδὴν πᾶσαν παρεισενέγκαντες ἐπιχορηγήσατε ἐν τῇ πίστει ὑμῶν τὴν ἀρετήν, ἐν δὲ τῇ ἀρετῇ τὴν γνῶσιν &c. [And for this very reason, bringing in all diligence, supply in your faith virtue, and in virtue knowledge, etc.] Before the word spoudēn one must understand [χρῆ] or [ἐν], which is often used for οὖν, or "therefore." And for this very reason, bringing in all diligence, join together with one another: to faith virtue, to virtue knowledge, to knowledge temperance, to temperance patience, to patience godliness, to godliness brotherly love. Bringing in, that is, trying to bring in, promoting this very thing with all diligence. The Apostle seems to have had in mind the ancient custom of leading dances, for the verb epichorēgein properly means to lead a chorus. In choruses, [συνεπλέκοντο ἀλλήλοις], they were linked together with one another.

units.la: Ὀρχοῦντ' ἀλλήλων ὃπι καρπῷ χείρας ἔχον-τες.
units.tr: Ὀρχοῦντ' ἀλλήλων ὃπι καρπῷ χείρας ἔχοντες. [Dancing, each holding the other's hands at the wrist.]

units.la: Saltabant tenentes manus invicem per volam. Hom. Saltabant invicem juncti complicatis manibus, alii aliis famulantes vel ministrantes, & se invicem sustinentes. Unde vox ista, ἐπιχορηγεῖν, omnes has videtur obtinuisse significationes. En vero hic bellum Gratiarum chorum, ubi chorum ducit fides, eique invicem complicatae famulantur reliquae Gratiae sese mutuo sustinentes. Graphicum in choris saltandi morem videre est apud les tableaux de Philostrate in figura.
units.tr: They danced holding hands with one another by the palm. Hom. They danced linked with one another, hands interlaced, some serving or ministering to others, and supporting one another. Hence this word epichorēgein seems to have taken on all these meanings. Here indeed we have the dance of the Graces, where Faith leads the chorus, and the remaining Graces, joined hand in hand, serve her and mutually sustain one another. A picture of the custom of dancing in choruses can be seen in the Pictures of Philostratus.

units.la: V.'20. "Οτι πᾶσα προφητεία γραφῆς ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως οὐ γίνεται. Quòd omnis Prophetia Scripturæ propriâ interpretatione non fit, ut Interlinearis & Vetus, γίνεται, ἀπολελύεται, εἰς τὰ λοιπὰ ἐπιγέγραπται. Phav. Adeo ut sensus meâ sententiâ sit hujusmodi. Omnis Prophetia non perficitur secundum literalem (literalis enim est ordinariè propria) interpretationem Scripturæ. Vel reddi poterit, omnis prophetia Scripturæ propriâ interpretatione vel solutione non fit. Prophetiæ enim plerumque habent sensum typicum, mysticum, & analogicum. Atque hic sensus admodum quadrat cum contextu, ᾧ ἐν ἡμῖν &c. Et habemus firmiorem propheticum sermonem, cui bene facitis attendentes quasi lucerna lucenti in caliginoso loco, donec dies illucescat, & Lucifer oriatur in cordibus vestris. Quidnam verò est hæc lucerna lucens in caliginoso loco, nisi Prophetiæ de Christo, in propriâ interpretatione Scripturæ, i.e. ordinariâ, obscuræ & caligine obvolutæ, usque dum typum & mysterium lux evolvat Evangelii in cordibus; ideóque hoc præcipuè monet dignoscere & cavere, nè hærerent nimium in nudâ literâ, sed animum potius adverterent ad mentem Prophetiæ, ad mysterium quod velatum erat in litera, ᾧ ἐν ἡμῖν &c. Non enim voluntate hominis allata est olim prophetia, i.e. non pro suo libitu prophetárunt homines, sed locuti sunt sancti Dei homines prout agebantur spiritu; sensu aliquando typico, aliquando mystico, in ænigmate, ut videntes γίνεσθε, non viderent ἀπαγγέλλουσιν, nisi in quorum cordibus illuxit dies Evangelii.
units.tr: v. 20. "Ὅτι πᾶσα προφητεία γραφῆς ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως οὐ γίνεται. Because every prophecy of Scripture does not come about by private interpretation." The Interlinear and the Old read γίνεται, ἀπολελύεται, εἰς τὰ λοιπὰ ἐπιγέγραπται. Phav. So that, in my judgment, the sense is of this kind: no prophecy is fulfilled according to the literal interpretation of Scripture (for the literal is ordinarily the proper one). Or it may be rendered: no prophecy of Scripture comes about by its own interpretation or solution. For prophecies for the most part have a typical, mystical and analogical sense. And this sense fits very well with the context, [ᾧ ἐν ἡμῖν &c.]. "And we have the more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts." What, then, is this lamp shining in a dark place, if not the prophecies about Christ, which in the proper, that is the ordinary, interpretation of Scripture are obscure and wrapped in darkness, until the light of the Gospel unfolds the type and the mystery in the hearts? Therefore he especially urges us to discern and beware, lest they cling too much to the bare letter, but rather turn their minds to the sense of the prophecy, to the mystery which was veiled in the letter, [ᾧ ἐν ἡμῖν &c.]. For prophecy was not brought of old by the will of man; that is, men did not prophesy at their own pleasure, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Spirit; sometimes with a typical sense, sometimes with a mystical one, in an enigma, so that, seeing, they might not see [γίνεσθε], [ἀπαγγέλλουσιν], unless in whose hearts the day of the Gospel has dawned.

units.la: C.3.v.2. Καὶ ἡ τῶν Αποστόλων ἡμῶν ἐντολὴ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡ σωτηρία. Est & hic trajectio notabilis, recta enim constructione dicitur, ἡ ἀπὸ ἐντολῆς τῶν Ἀποστόλων τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος, ut est infra, v. 8. Ut memores sitis verborum quae praedicta sunt à sanctis prophetis, & praeceptí Apostolorum Domini & servatoris nostri. Quae fere ipsissima habet Judas, v. 17, μνήσθητε τῶν ῥημάτων τῶν προειρημένων ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.
units.tr: C.3.v.2. Καὶ ἡ τῶν Ἀποστόλων ἡμῶν ἐντολὴ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡ σωτηρία. There is also a notable transposition here, for in the proper construction it is said: ἡ ἀπὸ ἐντολῆς τῶν Ἀποστόλων τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν καὶ σωτῆρος, as below at v. 8: "That you may be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and of the precept of the Apostles of the Lord and Saviour." Jude has nearly the very same words at v. 17: μνήσθητε τῶν ῥημάτων τῶν προειρημένων ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, "Remember the words which were spoken before by the Apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ."

units.la: V. 6. Δι᾽ ὧν ὁ τότε κόσμος ὕδατι καταχλυσθεὶς ἀπώλετο. Δι᾽ ὧν, idem significat quod ἐν᾽ ᾧ, propterea, idcirco, quamobrem. Propter quae qui tunc erat mundus aquâ inundatus periit. Sensus est, Mundum illum, qui olim fuerat, diluvio periisse propter ea ipsa, propter quae qui nunc est mundus igni repositus, & reservatus est in diem judicii. Nempe quia erant in illis diebus, ut erunt in novissimis, irrisores, juxta proprias concupiscentias ambulantes, & dicentes, ubi est pollicitatio adventus ejus? qui volenter ignorantes, noluerunt credere praedicationi Noë, quapropter in eos supervenit Diluvium, ut fur etiam in nocte. Vide Luc. 17. 26.
units.tr: v. 6. Δι᾽ ὧν ὁ τότε κόσμος ὕδατι καταχλυσθεὶς ἀπώλετο. "By which the world of that time, overflowed with water, perished." Δι᾽ ὧν means the same as ἐν᾽ ᾧ: on account of which, for this reason, wherefore. The sense is that the world which once was perished by the flood for the very reasons for which the present world is kept in store by fire and reserved until the day of judgment. Namely, because in those days, as will be in the last days, there were scoffers, walking according to their own lusts, and saying, "Where is the promise of his coming?" who wilfully ignored, and were unwilling to believe Noah's preaching; wherefore the Flood came upon them, like a thief even in the night. See Luke 17. 26.

units.la: In Epistolam 1. Johannis.
units.tr: In Epistolam 1. Johannis.

units.la: 1 JOH c. 1, v. 2. Καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη &c. Et haec vita manifestata est & vidimus & testamur & annuntiamus vobis τὴν ζωὴν τὴν αἰώνιον hanc vitam aeternam, quae erat apud Patrem, & nobis manifestata est. ἡ pro αὕτη & τὴν pro τάυτην.
units.tr: 1 John ch. 1, v. 2. "And the life was manifested" [Καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη] etc. "And this life was manifested, and we have seen, and we testify and proclaim to you the eternal life [τὴν ζωὴν τὴν αἰώνιον], this life eternal, which was with the Father and was manifested to us." Here ἡ stands for αὕτη [αὕτη] and τὴν for ταύτην [ταύτην].

units.la: C. 2. v. 22. Τίς ἐστιν ὁ ψεύστης εἰ μὴ ὁ ἀρνούμενος ῾ὁμολογῶν ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐκ θεοῦ ἐστιν ὁ Χριστός. Verbis, quae sunt per se negantia, Attici negationem addunt. Quis est mendax nisi qui negat quòd Iesus est Christus? Importunum vero hoc loco videtur addere, quae restituit Beza & Interpres Anglicus ex manuscripto codice Syro & Latino, viz. Qui confitetur filium & patrem habet. Quae verba sunt omnino superflua, nec ulli serviunt usui, imò potius destruunt sensum. Verba enim, omnis qui negat filium, nec patrem habet, adducuntur in probationem propositionis praecedentis, nimirum, quòd ille est Antichristus, qui negat patrem & filium. Quali si objiceret quisquam, Ego non sum Antichristus, quia ego non nego patrem & filium, agnosco enim patrem, respondeatur illico, At vero tu es Antichristus, qui ita dicis & negas filium. Qui enim negat filium, non habet patrem. Quisquis enim diligit genitorem, diligit etiam eum qui ex eo genitus est. 1. Joh. 5. 1. & qui non honorat filium, non honorat patrem qui misit filium. Joh. 5.23.
units.tr: Ch. 2, v. 22. "Who is the liar but the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ?" [Τίς ἐστιν ὁ ψεύστης εἰ μὴ ὁ ἀρνούμενος ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν ὁ Χριστός]. The Attics add a negation to words that are negative in themselves. "Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ?" It seems out of place here to add what Beza and the English translator restored from the Syriac and Latin manuscript, namely, "Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also." These words are wholly superfluous, serve no purpose, and rather destroy the sense. For the words whoever denies the Son does not have the Father are adduced in proof of the preceding proposition, namely, that he is the Antichrist who denies the Father and the Son. If someone were to object, "I am not the Antichrist, because I do not deny the Father and the Son; I acknowledge the Father," the answer would come at once: "But you are the Antichrist, since you speak thus and deny the Son. For he who denies the Son does not have the Father. Whoever loves the begetter also loves the one begotten of him" (1 John 5:1), "and he who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent the Son" (John 5:23).

units.la: In Iudam.
units.tr: On Jude.

units.la: IUD. v.18. Κατὰ τὰς ἑαυτῶν ἐπιθυμίας πορευόμενοι τῆς ἀσεβείας. Est etiam in hoc loco Hyperbaton non vulgare, nec enim parum vexavit interpretes pro τὰς ἐπιθυμίας πορευόμενοι τῆς ἑαυτῶν ἀσεβείας unica voce tantum ἑαυτῶν transposita. Et secundum cupiditates incedentes suarum impietatum, vel secundum impias suas cupiditates incedentes. Adeò ut fatendum sit in singulis Apostolis reperiri Hyperbata, ne quis ultra in iis haereat.
units.tr: Jude v. 18: "Walking according to their own ungodly desires" [Κατὰ τὰς ἑαυτῶν ἐπιθυμίας πορευόμενοι τῆς ἀσεβείας]. There is also an unusual hyperbaton in this passage, and it has troubled the interpreters not a little, since the ordinary order would be [τὰς ἐπιθυμίας πορευόμενοι τῆς ἑαυτῶν ἀσεβείας], with only the single word ἑαυτῶν transposed. So the sense is either "walking according to the desires of their impieties" or "walking according to their impious desires." It must therefore be admitted that hyperbata are found in each of the Apostles, lest anyone stick at them any further.

units.la: In Apocalypsin.
units.tr: On the Apocalypse.

units.la: APOC. c. 1, v. 5, 6. Τῷ ἀγαπῶντι ἡμᾶς καὶ λύσαντι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ αἵματι αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐποίησεν ἡμᾶς βασιλείς καὶ ἱερεῖς τῷ Θεῷ καὶ πατρὶ αὐτοῦ, αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα &c. Et qui dilexit nos, & lavit nos à peccatis nostris sanguine suo, qui fecit nos reges & sacerdotes Deo & Patri ejus, ipsi gloria & imperium in saecula saeculorum. Amen. Secundum vulgarem syntaxin oportuit scribi, καὶ ποιήσαντι, sed locutus est Apostolus eadem phrasi quâ usus est in Evangelio, 15 6. ἐξελήλυθα ἐξω ὡς τὸ κλῆμα καὶ ἐξηράνθη, Projicitur foras ut palmes qui exaruit, de qua vide animad. suo loco.
units.tr: Rev. 1:5, 6. "To him who loves us and has washed us from our sins in his blood, and has made us kings and priests to God and his Father; to him be the glory" [Τῷ ἀγαπῶντι ἡμᾶς καὶ λύσαντι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ αἵματι αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐποίησεν ἡμᾶς βασιλείς καὶ ἱερεῖς τῷ Θεῷ καὶ πατρὶ αὐτοῦ, αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα]. The Latin reads: "To him who loved us and washed us from our sins by his blood, who made us kings and priests to God and his Father, to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen." By ordinary syntax it should have been written καὶ ποιήσαντι, but the Apostle speaks in the same phrasing he used in the Gospel, John 15:6: "I am cast out as a branch that has withered" [ἐξελήλυθα ἐξω ὡς τὸ κλῆμα καὶ ἐξηράνθη], "is cast out as a branch that has withered." On this see my notes in their place.

units.la: C. 2. v. 22. Ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ βάλλω αὐτὴν εἰς κλίνην καὶ τοὺς μοιχεύοντας μετ' αὐτῆς εἰς θλῖψιν μεγάλην. Ecce ego mittam eam, & eos qui machantur cum ea in lecto in afflictionem magnam. Trajectio ista est adeò abunde frequens in N. T. ut in eâ quenquam haerere, non possum mirari sanè, prae ceteris cùm vulgaris versio sit ita insignificans. Codex Alexandrinus legit φυλάξω pro πλύνω, sed quia solus, non ei acquiescendum reor; neque verò est ista lectio ita commoda, ut in ea admodum delectetur.
units.tr: Rev. 2:22. "Behold, I cast her into a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great tribulation" [Ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ βάλλω αὐτὴν εἰς κλίνην καὶ τοὺς μοιχεύοντας μετ' αὐτῆς εἰς θλῖψιν μεγάλην]. The Latin reads: "Behold, I will send her into a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great affliction." This transposition is so abundantly frequent in the New Testament that I cannot be surprised if anyone sticks at it, especially since the common version is so meaningless. The Codex Alexandrinus reads φυλάξω for πλύνω, but since it stands alone I think one should not agree with it; nor indeed is that reading so convenient that one should take great delight in it.

units.la: C. 13. v. 8. Ὧν οὐ γέγραπται τὰ ὀνόματα ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ ἀρνίου τοῦ ἐσφαγμένου ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου. Quòd si haec verba intelligantur de agno occiso ab origine mundi, quod adeò multi putant, intelligenda reor de Christo exhibito in typo Agni, qui ab origine mundi pro sacrificio occisus ab Abele. Sed fortè melius dicendum cum Scholiaste Graeco, ᾿Εν ϲφαβατῳ ἀνυσ-τὸν, ὧν γέγεαπται, ἀπὸ καταβολῆς γέγεαπται. Quasi legendum foret, Quorum nomina ab origine mundi non erant scripta in libro agni occisi. Ut fuerunt, qui non adorabant Draconem, quales etiam fuerant πάντες οἱ ἁλι ευσεβεῖαν μαρτυρούμενοι ἐν τῇ παλαιᾷ, Omnes qui fuerant martyres in Veteri. Quomodo etiam Lucas ait in Evangelio, Gaudete quòd nomina vestra scripta sunt in cœlis. Atque hanc trajectionem confirmat etiam 17. 8. Et mirabantur inhabitantes terram, ὧν ἐ γέγραπται τὰ ὀνόματα ἐπὶ τὸ βιβλίον τῆς ζωῆς ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, Quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitæ ab origine mundi: ubi nulla mentio agni occisi, Quod planè innuit, τὸ ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου debere construi cum ὧν ἐ γέγεαπται, & non cum τῷ ἀρνίῳ ἐσφαγμένῳ.
units.tr: Rev. 13:8. "Whose names have not been written in the book of life of the Lamb that was slain from the foundation of the world" [Ὧν οὐ γέγραπται τὰ ὀνόματα ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ ἀρνίου τοῦ ἐσφαγμένου ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου]. If these words are understood of the Lamb slain from the origin of the world, as very many think, I judge they should be understood of Christ exhibited in the type of the Lamb, who was slain as a sacrifice by Abel from the origin of the world. But perhaps it is better to say, with the Greek Scholiast, that the text reads ὧν γέγραπται, and that ἀπὸ καταβολῆς belongs with γέγραπται [ὧν γέγραπται ... ἀπὸ καταβολῆς γέγραπται]. It is as if one ought to read: "Those whose names were not written from the origin of the world in the book of the slain Lamb." As they were who did not worship the Dragon; such were also all who were attested for piety under the Old (Covenant), all who were martyrs under the Old. So too Luke says in the Gospel: "Rejoice because your names are written in heaven." This transposition is also confirmed by Rev. 17:8: "And those who dwell on the earth marvelled, whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world," where there is no mention of the slain Lamb. This plainly suggests that ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου ought to be construed with ὧν οὐ γέγραπται, and not with τῷ ἀρνίῳ ἐσφαγμένῳ.
